en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory. [One should honor] Vyāsa, the grandson of Vasiṣṭha and great-grandson of Śakti, who is free from all taint.
I bow to the son of Parāśara, the father of Śuka, the treasure-house of austerity.
Salutations to Vyāsa, who is a form of Viṣṇu; salutations to Viṣṇu in the form of Vyāsa. Salutations again and again to the son of Vasiṣṭha, the treasure-house of Brahman.
Janamejaya said:
How did those heroes— the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Somakas—
as well as the highly fortunate kings assembled from various lands, fight?
How did they fight in battle against Bhīṣma, the scorcher of enemies?
Or how did all the Kauravas, with Bhīmasena as their commander-in-chief, take up their positions for combat? Tell me that, O high-minded one.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O lord of the earth, hear how the heroes— the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Somakas— fought on Kurukṣetra, the field of austerity.
Having descended upon Kurukṣetra, the Pāṇḍavas, together with the Somakas,
advanced against the Kauravas, desiring victory and endowed with great strength. All of them were perfected in the study of the Vedas and delighted in battle.
Hoping for victory in battle or facing death in the fray,
they stood in the eastern part of the field, facing westward in combat;
and having advanced against the invincible army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, they took their positions.
Facing the east, they settled with their troops on the western side;
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, had thousands of camps constructed according to rule outside of Samantapañcaka.
The entire earth was as if empty, with only children and the elderly remaining; it was devoid of horses and men, and bereft of chariots and elephants,
for as far as the sun shines over the circle of Jambūdvīpa.
O best of kings, in that very time the army returned;
all those castes gathered in one place and traversed a circle many yojanas in extent,
crossing over countries, rivers, mountains, and forests.
O bull among men, King Yudhiṣṭhira assigned to all of them— the best of men— the finest food and provisions for their mounts. Furthermore,
Yudhiṣṭhira established various distinct designations for each of them.
"He who speaks thus must be known as a Pāṇḍava. Then, as the time for battle approached, the Kuru prince arranged the identifying marks, names, and ornaments of all of them.
Seeing the top of the Pārthas’ banner, the high-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
together with all the lords of the earth, drew up his battle array against the Pāṇḍavas,
while a white parasol was being held over his head.
Seeing Duryodhana in the midst of a thousand *nāgas*, surrounded by his brothers, all the Pāṇḍava soldiers were filled with joy;
their faces then beamed with delight.
They entered the field of battle;
all of them blew their great conchs and struck thousands of kettledrums.
Then, beholding their own army thus exultant, the Pāṇḍavas—

The valiant Vāsudeva and his followers became joyful in heart. Then, gladdening the warriors, those two tigers among men, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya, standing upon their chariot, blew their divine conchs.
Hearing the roar of both the Pāñcajanya and the Devadatta,
the warriors along with their mounts discharged excrement and urine,
just as other animals do upon hearing the sound of a roaring lion.
In that very manner, the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons was then struck with terror;
a cloud of dust arose from the earth, so that nothing could be discerned,
and the sun vanished, shrouded by the dust raised by the host.
And there Parjanya rained down a shower of flesh and blood, drenching all the armies; it was like a marvel. Then a wind arose from below, dragging along pebbles.
Striking down those divisions and dispersing that dust,
O King, both armies then stood on Kurukṣetra, highly delighted for battle, resembling two agitated oceans.
The encounter between those two armies was extraordinary,
like the meeting of two oceans when the end of a cosmic age has arrived;
the entire earth became empty, with only children and the elderly remaining.
When that host had been assembled by the Kauravas,
they then established an agreement for battle so that there might be mutual goodwill;
meanwhile, from all sides, the mountain-like [army] roared like a mountain.
Then those Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and Somakas made a covenant and established the rules of conduct for battles, O bull of the Bharatas:
"When our battle has ceased, there shall be mutual affection between us."

One should act as before and as appropriate, and there should be no further deception; when a battle of words has commenced, one should not counter-attack with words alone. One who has withdrawn from the midst of the army must never, under any circumstances, be slain.
O Bhārata, a chariot-warrior should fight with a chariot-warrior, one mounted on an elephant with one on an elephant, a horseman with a horseman, and a foot-soldier with a foot-soldier;
according to suitability, according to prowess, according to energy, and according to age.

One should strike only after having addressed the opponent; one must not strike one who is trusting or distracted. Furthermore, one who is engaged with another, one who is heedless, one who has turned away, one whose weapons are exhausted, and one who is without armor should never be killed under any circumstances.

"One must not strike under any circumstances those who are charioteers, those who are draft animals, those who carry weapons, or those who sound drums and conchs. Having thus established this agreement, the Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and Somakas [proceeded]."
They were filled with supreme wonder as they looked at one another;
and having settled there, those high-souled bulls among men,
together with their soldiers, became joyful in appearance and well-disposed in mind.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
having observed both the morning and evening twilights,
the venerable seer Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī and the best among all knowers of the Vedas, [spoke].
"In the terrible battle that is to come, the grandfather of the Bharatas—
the blessed one who perceives all things directly and knows the past, present, and future—
spoke this secret to King Vaicitravīrya."
Then, as he was grieving, distressed, and brooding over the misfortune of his sons,
Vyāsa said:
"O King, the time has come for your sons and the other rulers of the earth."
They will slay one another upon encountering each other in battle. When they have been overtaken by time and are perishing, O Bhārata,
recognize the turn of time and do not set your mind on grief.
"O lord of the people, if you wish to see him in battle, I shall grant you sight; behold this combat!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O best of Brahman-sages, I do not wish to witness the slaughter of my kinsmen;
rather, by your power, I would hear this battle in its entirety.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When he did not wish to see the battle but desired to hear about it,
the Lord of Boons, the Giver, granted a boon to Sañjaya.
Vyāsa said:
"O King, this Saṃjaya shall speak of this battle to you;
everything in the conflict will not be hidden from him.
O King, this Saṃjaya is endowed with divine vision."
He will describe the battle to you and he shall become all-knowing;
whether public or secret, by night or by day—
even that which is merely conceived in the mind— all this Saṃjaya shall know.
"Neither weapons shall pierce him, nor shall fatigue overcome him;
this son of Gavalgaṇa shall be released alive from this battle.
And I [shall preserve] the fame of these Kurus, O bull of the Bharatas."
"I shall proclaim this to all the Pāṇḍavas; do not grieve.
This was ordained long ago, and you ought not to mourn over it. It is impossible to restrain destiny; where there is dharma, there is victory."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed great-grandfather of the Kurus addressed the mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra once again.
"O great king, in this battle there will be a great destruction,
since I perceive these omens today as portents of fear.
Hawks, vultures, crows, and herons are gathered together with their troops."
They flock together in the forest regions and hold assemblies;
the twice-born birds, filled with joy, behold a most fierce battle and will devour the flesh of elephants and horses.
Screaming "khaṭākhaṭa" with a terrifying sound that portends fear,
the kahu-birds fly through the center toward the southern direction.
O Bhārata, I constantly behold both the morning and evening twilights in this manner.
O Bhārata,
when the sky is filled with dust, all ill omens appear; at both sunrise and sunset, the sun is surrounded by headless trunks (kabandhas).
White at their edges and red, with black necks and streaks of lightning,
three-colored portents like iron bars obstruct the sun at the junction of day and night; the sun, moon, and stars blaze, making no distinction between day and night.
For a day and night I have seen this, which will lead to his destruction; on the full moon of Kārttika, the moon became invisible, devoid of luster,
and took on the color of fire within the expanse of the sky.
Slain, the heroic kings and princes, those brave men with arms like iron clubs, will sleep covering the earth; they will lie there like the two—
both the boar and the wildcat— in the sky.
I constantly observe a fierce clamor arising from those fighting at night;
even the images of the deities tremble and laugh,
vomit blood from their mouths, perspire, and fall down.
O lord of the people, unstruck drums resound; and great chariot-warriors among the Kṣatriyas set forth even without being yoked.
Likewise, cuckoos, woodpeckers, blue jays, hawks, and parrots [are heard].
Cranes and peacocks utter harsh cries;
and those clad in armor, bearing weapons and ornaments, mounted upon the backs of horses,
are seen by the hundreds at the break of dawn like swarms of locusts.
Both twilights shone forth accompanied by the burning of the quarters;
there was a rain of blood and a rain of bones, O Bhārata.
And that which is renowned in the three worlds, O King, and esteemed by the virtuous—
"Even by Arundhatī, this Vasiṣṭha has been cast behind her. O King, this Śanaiścara stands afflicting Rohiṇī;
the mark of the Moon has turned away, and there will be great danger."
And even though there are no clouds, a most terrible thundering is heard incessantly,
and drops of tears fall from the weeping mounts.
Vyāsa said:
Asses are born from cows, and sons take pleasure with their own mothers; trees in the forest display flowers and fruit out of season,
and the princesses, though pregnant, give birth to terrifying monsters.
Carnivorous birds, jackals, and other beasts;
animals with three horns, four eyes, five feet, two urethras,
two heads, and two tails— such were the inauspicious creatures with fangs.
There were born those with gaping mouths, uttering inauspicious cries;
three-footed peacocks, four-tusked Tārkṣyas, and horned creatures;
likewise, other such things and women were seen by the teachers of the Veda.
O lord of the earth, in your city, vultures are giving birth to peacocks;
mares are bearing calves, and dogs are giving birth to jackals.
Furthermore, female ospreys, mynas, and parrots are all uttering inauspicious cries.
Some women give birth to four or five daughters;
as soon as they are born, they dance, sing, and laugh.
In the house of a thief, there are common children who suckle at the breast.

Driven by Time, some dance and sing aloud, foreboding great terror; others, urged on by Fate, draw images of themselves bearing weapons; and children run toward one another, clutching sticks in their hands.
Having besieged the cities, they stand there desiring to fight.
Lotuses, blue lotuses, and water-lilies grow upon the trees;
fierce winds blow from all directions, and the dust does not settle.
The earth trembles constantly, and Rāhu has swallowed the sun;
likewise, the white planet stands having transgressed Citrā. Indeed, it forebodes the total destruction of the Kurus.
The most terrible comet, a great planet, stands having assailed the constellation Puṣya;
it will bring about a horrific and inauspicious calamity for the two armies.
Furthermore, Mars is retrograde in Maghā, and Jupiter is in Śravaṇā.
Having ascended the constellation Bhāgya, it is afflicted by the son of the Sun;
O Lord of the People, Śukra, having mounted the Pūrva-proṣṭhapadas and having circled around the Uttara-proṣṭhapadas, gazes back at them together.
The dark planet, blazing with smoke and fire,
stands having seized the radiant constellation Jyeṣṭhā belonging to Indra;
the Pole Star (Dhruva) blazes fiercely and revolves in a sinister, counter-clockwise direction.
Thus Rohiṇī is afflicted, as are both the Moon and the Sun; moreover,
a harsh planet, possessing the brilliance of fire, stands between Citrā and Svātī,
having performed a retrograde and then a direct motion in Śravaṇā.
The red-bodied planet Mars stood encompassing the mass of the moon;
the earth was covered with all kinds of crops and garlanded with fruit,
while the barley had five ears and the rice had a hundred.

The cows, who are the foremost in all the world and upon whom this entire universe depends, now that they have been milked by their calves, are shedding blood instead. And from their coverings, flaming swords issued forth intensely.
The weapons clearly perceive that battle is at hand;
for the luster of the weapons and the water is like the color of fire.
There will be a great destruction of armor and banners.
O King, descendant of Bharata, during this slaughter of the Kurus by the Pāṇḍavas, the earth has become a whirlpool of blood, crowded with banners as its rafts;
and beasts and birds, with mouths aflame in every direction, utter cries of alarm.
Displaying a dire portent, they announce a great danger:
a bird that moves through the air at night, with one wing, eye, and foot,
speaks fiercely in agitation, vomiting blood repeatedly.
The two planets, with their copper-red crests, stood as if blazing,
completely obscuring the radiance of the noble Seven Sages;
both planets remained thus for a full year, glowing intensely.
Bṛhaspati and Śanaiścara were situated near Viśākhā;
a fierce planet blazed in the first lunar mansion, Kṛttikā, standing like a comet, seizing forms with its radiance.
O Lord of the People, when Mercury repeatedly passes through all three of these former constellations, it causes great distress and produces immense,
heart-rending fear.
I have known the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the sixteenth day as it was before;
but I do not know this new-moon day as the thirteenth,
when both the moon and the sun are eclipsed within a single month.
These two planets, appearing out of season, will destroy all living beings. All the quarters are enveloped in dust from showers of fine particles on every side,
and fierce portentous clouds rain blood at night.

Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at midnight, there was once again a fierce and most terrible rain of flesh; there the rākṣasas were not satiated. Rivers and streams flowed upstream, their waters consisting of blood.
The wells are foaming like bellowing bulls;
meteors fall with thunderous crashes, mingled with dry lightning bolts.
And this very night, as it turns to dawn, the rising sun is struck.
With four great blazing meteors approaching the sun from every direction,
the great seers there spoke:
"The earth shall drink the blood of thousands of kings."
From Mount Kailāsa, Mandara, and likewise from the Himavat mountain,
thousands of peaks fell with a great roar;
and during the earthquake, the great elements [shook] the four oceans individually.
They surged against the shore, agitating it again and again;
fierce winds, dragging along gravel, blew uprooting the trees.
Broken by the mighty gales and struck down by thunderbolts, they lay scattered.
The sacred trees in the villages and cities are falling;
and the fire, offered by the twice-born, blazes with yellow, red, and blue hues—
its flames turned to the left, smelling of corpses, filled with smoke, and making a harsh sound.
O Lord of the Earth, touches, smells, and tastes have indeed become perverted;
the banners of the kings smoke as they tremble again and again,
while the kettledrums and war-drums likewise emit showers of glowing embers.
Indeed, fierce vultures are swooping down upon the tops of the palace towers and at the city gates, circling toward the left;
and the birds are crying out repeatedly with harsh, discordant notes.
They hide themselves upon the tips of the banners for the destruction of the lords of the earth;
brooding and tossing their manes, trembling with agitation,
thousands of horses and elephants weep in distress.
In houses, fields, threshing floors, and the like, there are anthills and honeycombs; likewise, elephant stables, horse stables, and chariot sheds are inhabited by pigeons.

These and many other portents of terrible appearance are all indeed harbingers of destruction for the worlds of the protectors of the earth; such an ill omen as this portends the ruin of the rulers of the earth.

Terrestrial, celestial, and atmospheric— thus it arises incessantly in three ways. Having heard this, O Bhārata, you should determine what is appropriate for this occasion, so that this world may not go to total destruction.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of his father, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke this:
"I believe this was ordained long ago; it will come to pass, there is no doubt."
If Kṣatriyas are slain in battle according to the duty of a warrior,
they will reach the world of heroes and obtain nothing but happiness— renown in this world and great, long-lasting bliss in the world beyond.
"Those tigers among men shall attain [the highest state] after casting off their lives in the great battle.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O best of kings, having been thus addressed, the sage, that lord of poets, spoke the truth."
With his son Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he entered into supreme meditation.
Then once again, the great ascetic, who spoke of the timing of events, uttered these words:
"O lord of kings, there is no doubt that Time destroys the universe."
He creates the worlds again; nothing here is eternal.
Teach the path of righteousness to your kinsmen, the Kurus, and likewise to your relatives and friends, for you are indeed capable of restraining them.
"They say the slaughter of one's own kin is a trivial thing; do not do what is unpleasant to me.
O Lord of Men, this Time has been born to you in the form of a son.
Killing is not honored in the Veda; this is by no means beneficial."
He alone would be a slayer who would destroy his own body, which is the dharma of his lineage. You will go astray in time, even though the path is possible,
for the destruction of this family as well as of the rulers of the earth.

"Abandon this misfortune in the form of a kingdom, which brings nothing but unhappiness. Your wisdom has been eclipsed by another; show the path of righteousness to your sons. O invincible one, what use have you for a kingdom, by which you have incurred such sin?"
Protecting your honor, righteousness, and fame, you shall attain heaven. Let the Pāṇḍavas obtain the kingdom, and let the Kauravas find peace.
Moreover, I shall restrain both Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīma in battle.
When the lord of brahmins had spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā,
who was skilled in speech, rebuked his words and replied once more through the path of discourse.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"As you know, so do I know;
existence and non-existence are known by me as they truly are.
For in matters concerning one's own self, O dear one, the world is utterly deluded."
And know me also as being of the very nature of the world; I propitiate you, who possess incomparable power—
you are our refuge and our wise guide.
"O Great Seer, they are not under my control;
you ought not to bring defilement upon me here. For you are Dharma, purity, glory, fame, fortitude, and memory."
"You are the grandfather, honored by both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
Perform that which is right; for there is no one more worthy of honor than you.
Vyāsa said:
"O King, son of Vicitravīrya, whatever dwells in your mind, speak it as you desire; I shall sever your doubt.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear in truth all those signs that appear for those who are about to be victorious in battle. Vyāsa said:
The fire blazes with a serene luster, its rays directed upward; its smokeless flames curl to the right,
and the holy fragrances of the oblations waft abroad.
They say this is the sign of one who is destined for victory:
where conchs and drums, deep-toned and loud-sounding, resound.
The sun and the moon shine with pure rays;
they say this is a sign of future victory. Desirable words [are heard], and crows follow behind.
O King, those who are behind urge on those who have already set out or are about to go,
while those who are in front restrain them.
Where there are auspiciously-voiced birds— royal swans,
parrots, cranes, and woodpeckers— and where they move clockwise in battle;
The Brahmins declare certain victory there by means of ornaments, armor, and banners,
as well as by the cheerful countenances and golden complexions of the men.
Radiant and difficult to gaze upon,
those whose armies possess such [qualities] conquer their enemies;
O Bhārata, where the speech and the spirit of the warriors are thus joyful.
Their garlands do not wither, and they overcome their enemies in battle.
For one who has entered [the fray], the wind blows favorably; for one wishing to enter, it blows from the south. From behind, it accomplishes his purpose; from the front, it wards him off.
When sounds, forms, tastes, touches, and scents are auspiciously manifested,
and when the warriors are always joyful, victory is certain for them;
likewise, the winds, clouds, and birds blow and fly in their favor.
The clouds follow them, as do rainbows;
O lord of the people, these are the signs of those who are victorious,
while the opposite occurs for those about to die, O ruler of men.
Whether the army be small or large, it is certain that the joy of the host of warriors is said to be the sole sign of victory. A single man, once broken, causes even a very great army to break.
When he has broken through, even the most heroic warriors break along with him;
a great army, once shattered, is most difficult to restrain,
like a mighty torrent of water or like a terrified herd of deer.
A great army cannot be rallied in the midst of a battle;
once broken, even the most heroic warriors break along with them.
Seeing those who are terrified and routed, fear increases all the more.
O King, suddenly shattered and thrown into confusion by the enemies,
that great army could not be steadied even by heroes;
yet the lord of the earth had assembled that vast fourfold host.
Even one equal to Indra in battle cannot restore what has been shattered;
therefore, a wise man, ever-exerting himself, should strive by means of strategic methods.
They say that victory through strategy is the best, while victory through sowing dissension is middling.
O Lord of the People, this victory which is achieved through battle is the lowest;
it is a great evil, a confluence of calamities, and is therefore called "mutilated.
Even when great armies gaze upon one another, they are terrified even by the gods.
They cannot be rallied at all, being broken and overwhelmed by fear;
though they know one another, they are now jubilant, scattered, and resolute—
even fifty such heroes can crush a vast army.
Or else, five, six, or seven may advance victoriously without turning back;
for even Vainateya Garuḍa does not praise a great multitude,
O Bhārata, no matter how vast their gathering of beautiful wings may be.

Victory does not come through mere numerical superiority in an army, O Bhārata; for victory is indeed uncertain, and destiny is the ultimate factor here. Even those who are victorious in battle suffer losses as well.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vyāsa departed;
and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard that, fell into deep reflection.
Having meditated for a moment and sighing repeatedly,
O bull of the Bharata race, he whose soul was disciplined questioned Saṃjaya:
"O Saṃjaya, these kings are heroes who delight in battle."
For the sake of the earth, kings who have utterly abandoned their lives strike one another with various weapons;
yet they do not desist from slaying, as they increase the population of Yama’s abode.
Desiring earthly sovereignty, they cannot tolerate one another.
I consider the earth to possess many virtues; tell me about that, Sañjaya.
There are many thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions [of them].
And ten million heroes of the world have assembled in Kurujāṅgala.
O Sañjaya, I wish to hear in truth the dimensions of the countries and the cities from which these men have come together.
"Endowed with the lamp of divine intellect and the eye of knowledge through the grace of that brahmin-sage Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor," Saṃjaya said.
O one of great wisdom, according to my own understanding I shall describe to you the qualities of earthly beings;
look with the eye of the scriptures, for salutations to you, O bull among the Bharatas!
Here, living beings are of two kinds: those that move and those that are stationary.
For mobile beings, there are three kinds of birth: from eggs, from sweat, and from the womb.
O King, among all mobile beings, those born from the womb are indeed the most excellent;
and among those born from the womb, humans and domestic animals are the preeminent.
Bearing various forms, their divisions number fourteen:
seven are forest-dwellers and seven are village-dwellers;
these are the lions, tigers, boars, buffaloes, and elephants.
O King, bears and monkeys are known as the seven wild animals;
cows, goats, humans, rams, horses, mules, and donkeys—
these are declared by the wise to be the seven domestic animals.

"O King, these indeed are the fourteen domestic and wild animals declared in the Vedas, O protector of the earth, upon which sacrifices are established. Among the domestic animals, man is the foremost; among those dwelling in the forest, the lion."
All living beings indeed subsist upon one another.
Those that sprout from the earth are called stationary; they consist of five types:
trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and species of grasses with fibrous bark.
Twenty-nine of these [syllables] are in the five great elements;
thus twenty-four are declared as the *gāyatrī* esteemed by the world. He who knows this meritorious *gāyatrī*, endowed with all virtues, [attains the highest goal].
In truth, O best of the Bharatas, he does not perish from the worlds.
For everything is born from the earth, and everything perishes in the earth. The earth is the foundation of all beings; the earth alone is the ultimate refuge.
"Whosoever possesses the earth possesses the entire world, both the stationary and the moving;
yet, greedy for it, kings slaughter one another.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:

O Sañjaya, you who know all measurements, tell me the names of the rivers and mountains, as well as those of the provinces and whatever other things are situated upon the earth, and the dimensions of the entire world in every respect.
"O Saṃjaya, describe in full the forests as well.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Great King, in brief, there are these five great elements."
The wise say that all things existing in the world are equal;
yet earth, water, air, fire, and space—
each possesses an increasing number of qualities, among which earth is preeminent.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these are declared by the seers who know the truth to be the qualities of earth.
Sound, touch, form, and taste are also proclaimed [as the qualities of water].
O King, there are four qualities in water, but among them, smell is not found.
Sound, touch, and form are the three qualities of fire.
Sound and touch belong to wind, while in space, there is sound alone.
O King, these five qualities exist within the five great elements throughout all worlds, upon which the worlds are established;
they do not overcome one another when there is indeed a state of equilibrium.
But when they enter into a state of mutual imbalance,
then embodied beings emerge from their bodies, and not otherwise;
and by not resorting to such a state, they do not go to destruction, and not otherwise.
They perish in succession and are born in succession;
all these immeasurable things constitute their sovereign form. For everywhere are seen the elements composed of the five gross substances.
Humans explain the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for those [objects] through reasoning (*tarka*).
Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be established by means of reasoning.
That which is beyond the primary elements (*prakṛti*) is the characteristic of the inconceivable.
O descendant of Kuru, O great king, I shall now describe to you the island of Sudarśana;
that island is circular and shaped like a wheel,
covered with river waters and mountains resembling clouds.

It was surrounded on all sides by oceans of salt water, and likewise by cities of various forms and delightful provinces; it was endowed with trees laden with flowers and fruit, and possessed abundant wealth and grain.
Just as a man might see his own face in a mirror,
so too is the continent Sudarśana seen within the lunar disc. Therein,
the Pippala tree occupies two parts, and the great hare occupies two parts.
Enriched on all sides by the inclusion of all medicinal herbs, water is to be understood as distinct from those; this is the summary being stated.
Furthermore, that which is other than this is now described; listen to it in brief.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, you have described the island in brief; now speak of it in detail, O wise one, according to the proper method."
"You are a knower of the reality of all things...
as far as this expanse of earth is visible upon the moon, tell me its measure; after that, you shall speak of the *pippala* tree."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the king, Saṃjaya spoke these words:
"O great king, stretching out toward the east are these six mountains of jewels."
Having reached the ocean, she stood there, and then descended;
indeed, she plunged into both oceans, the eastern and the western.
[There are] Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha, the best of mountains.
The mountain named Śṛṅgavān is blue and composed of lapis lazuli, white with the luster of silver, and entwined with all kinds of minerals;
these, O King, are the mountains frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
The distance between them is thousands of yojanas.
Therein, O Bhārata, are the meritorious regions known as the *varṣas*;
in them dwell beings of various kinds in every way.

Gandharvas and others dwell there, served by throngs of Apsarases. Beyond this Bhārata-varṣa lies Haimavata-varṣa; beyond that is the region of Kiṃpuruṣa, situated further beyond the Himavat mountains.
Beyond Hemakūṭa, they declare the region of Harivarṣa. To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha, O Great King, lies the mountain named Mālyavat, extending toward the east.
Beyond Mālyavat lies the mountain Gandhamādana;
by that same sequence, there is the mountain Gandhamādana. Between those two is the circular, golden mountain Meru.
Resplendent with the luster of the young sun, like a fire without smoke,
it is said, O lord of the earth, to extend sixteen thousand *yojanas* below and eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above.
It stands encompassing the worlds above, within, and across.
O Lord, these four continents are situated at its sides:
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, Jambūdvīpa, and Bhārata.
And Ketumāla is the fourth, situated to the west of Meru;
and the Northern Kurus are the refuge for those who have performed meritorious deeds,
where it is said the bird Sumukha, the son of Suparṇa, dwells.
Seeing those golden crows, he reflected:
"Since Meru makes no distinction between superior, middling, and inferior birds, therefore I shall abandon it."
The Sun, the lord of luminaries, constantly circumambulates it, as do the Moon with the constellations and Vāyu, keeping him to their right.
O great king, that mountain is endowed with divine flowers and fruits.
It is covered on all sides by beautiful palaces made of Jāmbūnada gold.
There, O King, hosts of gods, Gandharvas, Asuras, and Rākṣasas,
accompanied by throngs of Apsarases, sport perpetually upon that mountain.
There, Brahmā, Rudra, and Śakra, the lord of the gods,
having assembled, worship with various sacrifices accompanied by manifold sacrificial fees;
as do Tumburu, Nārada, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Huhū.
O Lord, having approached you, the best of the immortals praise you with hymns; the high-souled Seven Seers and Kaśyapa, the lord of progeny,
go there at every auspicious festival— may prosperity be yours.
O lord of the earth, Uśanas Kāvya [dwells] upon his very summit along with the Daityas;
for these jewels belong to him, and these mountains of jewels are his. Therefore, the blessed Kubera enjoys a fourth share of them.
Then he bestows a sixteenth part of his wealth upon human beings.
To his north is a divine and auspicious grove of *karṇikāra* trees, beautiful with flowers of every season and rising from a network of rocks.

There, Paśupati himself, the Lord who brings beings into existence, dwells together with Umā, surrounded by divine spirits. Wearing a garland made of *karṇikāra* flowers that hangs down to his feet, the Blessed One rejoices there.
Illuminated by three eyes, as if by three risen suns,
Maheśvara is beheld by those perfected ones of fierce austerity who are firm in their vows and speakers of truth; indeed, he cannot be seen by those of evil conduct.

O lord of men, from the peak of that mountain flows the auspicious Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī, a stream of milk as wide as thirty outstretched arms, possessing a terrifying roar, holy and frequented by those who are most meritorious.
She fell with inexhaustible force into the auspicious lake of the Moon;
for by her, that meritorious lake was produced, resembling the ocean.
In ancient times, she, who was difficult even for mountains to sustain, was held up by him.
For a hundred thousand years, Maheśvara indeed bore [the mountain] upon his head.
O lord of the earth, on the western side of Meru lies Ketumāla;
and right there is the very great Jambū-ṣaṇḍa, which is like the Nandana grove.
O Bhārata, the lifespan there is ten thousand years;
the men are golden-hued, and the women are like apsarases. They are free from disease, devoid of sorrow, and their minds are perpetually joyful.
There, human beings are born with the radiance of refined gold.
To the east of it stands the famous mountain Gandhamādana;
upon the peaks of Gandhamādana, Kubera dwells together with the *rākṣasas*.
Surrounded by throngs of apsarases, the lord of the Guhyakas rejoices on the slopes of Gandhamādana. Beyond these are the Aparagaṇḍikas;
there, the maximum lifespan is eleven thousand years.
There, O King, the men are dark-complexioned, endowed with splendor and great strength;
and all the women have the luster of lotus petals and are exceedingly beautiful to behold.
Beyond Nīla is Śveta, and beyond Śveta is Hiraṇyaka.
O lord of men, the region beyond the White Mountain is Hiraṇmaya; beyond that, O King, from the Śṛṅgavat mountain, is the Kuru-varṣa;
and beyond Śṛṅgavat is the region named Airāvata.
O Great King, when [the sun] is situated in the bow [constellation], there are two regions, one to the south and one to the north;
Ilāvṛta is in the middle, and there are indeed five regions.
Each successive region beyond these excels the preceding one in its qualities.
O Bhārata, during those years, all living beings were endowed with longevity, health, righteousness, pleasure, and wealth. Thus,
O Great King, is this earth covered with mountains.
The very great Hemakūṭa is the mountain named Kailāsa,
where King Vaiśravaṇa rejoices together with the Guhyakas;
there the god Mahādeva dwells eternally along with Umā.
On a beautiful and variegated rocky surface, worshipped by hosts of celestial sages,
there exists to the north of Kailāsa, toward Mount Maināka,
a vast, divine mountain made of jewels with golden peaks.
Beside it is a great, divine, and auspicious lake with golden sands,
beautiful and named Bindusaras, where King Bhagīratha dwelt for many years after beholding the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Bhagīratha.
There the sacrificial posts were made of jewels and the altars were made of gold;
having performed sacrifices there, the highly illustrious thousand-eyed Indra attained perfection.
It was there that the eternal Lord of Beings created all the worlds.
The one of fierce splendor is worshipped there by assembled beings;
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Manu, and Sthāṇu as the fifth [are present].
There, the goddess who flows through the three paths was first established.
Descending from the world of Brahmā, she divides into seven streams:
the Vasvokasārā, the Nalinī, the Pāvanā, the Sarasvatī,
the Jambūnadī, the Sītā, and the Gaṅgā as the seventh, along with the Sindhu.
Inconceivable and divine is this ordinance of the Lord, His very resolve: that there, at the conclusion of a thousand yugas, they perform a sacrificial session (*sattra*),
and there the river Sarasvatī becomes both visible and invisible in various places.
These seven divine Gaṅgās are renowned throughout the three worlds. Indeed, the Rākṣasas dwell on Himavat, while the Guhyakas reside on Hemakūṭa.
The Sarpas and Nāgas are on Niṣadha, and those whose wealth is asceticism (tapodhana) are on Gokarṇa.
The White Mountain is said to be the abode of the gods and asuras;
on Mount Niṣadha dwell the Gandharvas, O King, and on the Blue Mountain dwell the Brahman-sages. But Śṛṅgavān, O great king, is the resort of the ancestors.
Thus, O Great King, these seven regions are situated in their respective parts,
containing beings both mobile and immobile;
their manifold prosperity, both divine and human, is visible.
It is impossible to enumerate them in full, yet they must be believed by one who desires spiritual welfare.
O King, as for this divine form in the shape of a hare that you ask me about,
it is the reflection of the entire form of Jambūdvīpa upon the lunar disc.

That island of Sudarśana appears like the hare-mark on the moon; on its two sides, the southern and the northern, are two regions (*varṣa*). The other five regions are likewise conceived as being situated within the throat.
The two ears are Nāgadvīpa and Kaśyapadvīpa;
O King, the illustrious Tāmravarṇa and the Malaya mountain are the head. This second part of the island is seen to be shaped like a hare.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, O one of great intelligence, describe to me in full the northern and eastern sides of Meru, as well as the Mālyavat mountain."
Saṃjaya said:
"To the south of Nīla and likewise on the northern side of Meru,
O King, lie the sacred Northern Kurus, inhabited by the Siddhas."
There, the trees bear honey-sweet fruit and are perpetually endowed with flowers and fruit;
their flowers are fragrant and their fruits are succulent.
O lord of men, some of those trees there yield every desired fruit.
O lord of men, there are other trees there called Kṣīrin,
which constantly exude milk that possesses the six flavors and is like nectar;
they also produce garments and ornaments from their fruits.
The entire ground is made of jewels, with fine golden sand; it appears there as a delightful region resembling precious gems, like diamond and lapis lazuli,
and possessing a luster equal to ruby.
O lord of men, everywhere there are beautiful lotus ponds, free from mud, pleasant to the touch, delightful, and refreshing;
all the humans born there have descended from the world of the gods.
Endowed with equal beauty and virtue, couples are born alike in both even and uneven regions; and the women are like celestial nymphs (apsarases).
They drink the milk of those milky trees, which is like nectar.
O Lord, as each pair is born, they grow up equally,
endowed with identical forms and qualities, dressed alike,
and each devoted to the other like a pair of cakravāka birds.
Death occurs at the same time for those two pairs of mates;
free from disease, devoid of sorrow, and always joyful in mind,
they live for ten thousand and one thousand years.
O Great King, those birds named Bhāruṇḍas— sharp-beaked and possessed of great strength— live together and do not kill one another;
they carry away the dead and cast them into mountain caves.
O King, the Northern Kurus have been described to you in brief.
Now, I shall describe the eastern side of Meru exactly as it is. The region named Bhadrāśva lies indeed to the east of Gandhamādana.
O lord of the people, his former consecration took place in Bhadrāśva,
where there is the Bhadrasāla forest and the great tree Kālāmra.
O great king, that auspicious Kālāmra tree is always laden with flowers and fruit.
And the island rises one *yojana* in height, frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*.
There, those men are white, endowed with splendor, and possessed of great strength;
the women have the hue of white water-lilies (*kumuda*), beautiful and lovely to behold.
They possess the radiance of the moon, the complexion of the moon, and faces resembling the full moon; their limbs are as cool as the moon, and they are experts in dance and song.
O bull of the Bharata lineage, the lifespan there is ten thousand years.
Drinking the juice of the black mango (*kālāmra*), they remain eternally youthful. To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha stands the great,
eternal Jambū tree named Sudarśana.
Yielding all desired fruits, meritorious, and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
that eternal land is known by his name as Jambūdvīpa;
it measures one thousand and one hundred yojanas, O bull of the Bharatas.
O Lord of Men, the height of that king of trees touched the heavens,
measuring one thousand and fifteen hundred *aratnis*; as for the circumference of that tree, it was filled with fruits dripping with juice.
Falling upon the vast earth, O King, they produce a great sound and release a sap resembling silver. From that *jambu* tree, O lord of men, the juice of the fruit becomes a river.
Having circumambulated Mount Meru, they proceed to the Northern Kurus;
O lord of men, the people there always drink that juice with joy. When that fruit-juice has been drunk, old age does not afflict them.
There, a gold known as Jāmbūnada, which serves as an ornament for the gods, is produced; it is brilliant and resembles the indragopaka insect.
Furthermore, the human beings born there possess the complexion of the rising sun.

Likewise, O bull of the Bharatas, on the peak of Mālyavat the fire that carries the oblations blazes there, known by the name Saṃvartaka, the fire of time. Similarly, on the eastern peak of Mālyavat is the Pūrvāntagaṇḍikā.
The Mālyavat mountain stands fifty thousand yojanas [in extent].
There, human beings are born resembling great silver;
they have all descended from the world of Brahmā, and all are exponents of the Veda.

Performing ascetic penance, they indeed become those whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas); for the sake of protecting all beings, they enter the sun. There are sixty thousand and sixty hundred of them.
Surrounding the sun, they proceed ahead of Aruṇa;
for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years,
scorched by the heat of the sun, they enter the lunar orb.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, tell me truly the names of the regions and the mountains, as well as those who dwell upon the mountains."
Saṃjaya said:
To the south of Śveta and to the north of Nīla is the region named Ramaṇaka;
there the human beings are born.
All the men born there are endowed with pure lineage, very handsome to behold, and devoted primarily to pleasure;
they live for ten thousand years and fifteen hundred years.
O Great King, they live there with minds always joyful.
To the south of Śṛṅgin and to the north of Śveta is the region named Hairaṇvata,
where the river Hairaṇvatī flows.
And where, O Great King, this king of birds, the best of winged creatures,
dwells— there, O Great King, are the Yakṣas, followers of that lord, wealthy, handsome to behold, possessed of great strength, and always joyful in mind, O King.
O Great King, that yakṣa as well, who belongs to the lineage of the Yakṣa King Gautama, O Lord of Men,
lives for a lifespan of eleven thousand years and fifteen hundred years.
O lord of men, the Śṛṅgavat mountain indeed has three peaks:
one there is made of jewels, another is wonderful and made of gold,
and the third consists of all kinds of gems and is adorned with palaces.

There, the goddess Śāṇḍilī, who is self-luminous, dwells eternally. To the north of Mount Śṛṅgavat, at the edge of the ocean, O lord of men, lies the region named Airāvata, which is beyond that mountain.
There the sun does not scorch, nor do those men grow old;
and the moon, together with the stars, is shrouded as if it were a mere light.
They possess the luster of lotuses, the color of lotuses, and eyes like lotus petals.
And there, O King, human beings are born with the fragrance of lotus petals;
they are motionless, fragrant, abstaining from food, and have conquered their senses;
all of them have descended from the world of the gods and are free from passion.
O lord of men, O best of the Bharatas, those men live for a lifespan of thirteen thousand years. Likewise,
the Lord [resides] to the north of the Ocean of Milk.
Hari, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, dwells in a chariot made of gold;
that vehicle has eight wheels, is yoked by the elements, and is as swift as thought. It is fire-colored, possesses great speed, and is adorned with refined gold.
O bull of the Bharatas, he is the lord and the all-pervading master of all beings;
he is both the contraction and the expansion, the doer and the one who causes others to act.
O King, he is earth, water, space, wind, and fire.
That sacrifice is the mouth of all beings, and the consumer of oblations (Agni) stands within it,
pervading the world of the moving and the unmoving across thousands of locations.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Sañjaya, the high-minded King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O lord of men, fell into deep reflection concerning his sons. Having pondered this, O great king, he spoke these words once again.
O son of a Sūta, there is no doubt that Time contracts the universe and creates it all once again; nothing here is eternal. Nara and Nārāyaṇa alone are omniscient and the sustainers of all beings.
"The gods call him Vaikuṇṭha, and the Vedas call the Lord Viṣṇu.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"This is the land of Bhārata, wherein this army has fainted."

"Tell me the truth of this matter, for you are skilled, O Saṃjaya: that my son Duryodhana is excessively greedy for it, and where the sons of Pāṇḍu are likewise eager, and where my own mind is attached."
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, listen to my words: the Pāṇḍavas were not greedy for that [wealth];
it was Duryodhana and Śakuni, the son of Subala, who were greedy for it."
Furthermore, there are other Kṣatriyas, lords of various provinces,
who are greedy for the land of Bhārata and cannot tolerate one another. Here, O Bhārata, I shall describe to you that region of Bhārata.
It is dear to the god Indra, to Manu the son of Vivasvat,
to Pṛthu the son of Vena, O King, as well as to the high-souled Ikṣvāku,
to Yayāti, Ambarīṣa, Māndhātṛ, and Nahuṣa.
Likewise, O invincible one, [the glory] of Mucukunda, of Śibi the son of Uśīnara, of Ṛṣabha, of Aila, of King Nṛga, of Kuśika, and of the high-souled Gādhi.
O invincible one, O great king, O Bharata, this Bhārata is dear to all— both to Somaka and Dilīpa, as well as to other powerful Kṣatriyas, O Indra among kings.
O subduer of enemies, I shall describe those regions to you exactly as I have heard them;
listen, O King, as I speak what you ask of me.
[There are] Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and also Ṛkṣavat.

The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra— these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas). O King, by their thousands, there are other mountains in their vicinity that are renowned, substantial, vast, and possessed of variegated peaks.
Others there, O Kauravya, are unrefined, short-lived, and subsisting on meager means; they include both Āryas and Mlecchas, O Lord,
and men mixed with them drink from many rivers— the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, and the Sarasvatī.
The Godāvarī, the Narmadā, and the great river Bāhudā;
the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, and the great river Yamunā; the Dṛṣadvatī, the Vipāśā, the Vipāpā, and the Sthūlavālukā.
The river Vetravatī and the flowing Kṛṣṇaveṇā,
the Irāvatī, the Vitastā, and the Payoṣṇī as well as the Devikā;
the Vedasmṛti, the Vetasinī, the Tridivā, and the Iṣkumālinī.
The Karīṣiṇī, the Citravahā, and the river Citrasenā;
the Gomatī, the Dhūtapāpā, and the great river Vandana; the Kauśikī, the Tridivā, the Kṛtyā, the Vicitrā, and the Lohatāriṇī.
O lord of men, [he saw] the Rathasthā, the Śatakumbhā, and the Sarayū; likewise the Carmaṇvatī, the Vetravatī, the Hastisomā, and the Diśā;
as well as the Śatāvarī, the Payoṣṇī, and the supreme Bhaimarathī.
O lord of men, [he saw] the Kāverī, the Cūlikā, the Vāpī, and also the Śatabalā; the Nicīrā, the Mahitā, and the Suprayogā;
the pure Kuṇḍalā, the Sindhu, the Vājinī, and the Puramālinī.
[He saw] the Pūrvābhirāmā, the Vīrā, the Bhīmā, and likewise the Oghavatī;
the Palāśinī, the Pāpaharā, the Mahendrā, and the Pippalāvatī; the Pāriṣeṇā, the Asiknī, the Saralā, and the Bhāramardinī.
O Kaurava, [he went to] Puruhī, Pravarā, Menā, Moghā, and likewise Ghṛtavatī; to Dhūmatī and Atikṛṣṇā, Sūcī and Chāvī,
Sadānīrā, the unassailable [river], and the great river Kuśadhārā.
Śaśikāntā, Śivā, and likewise Vīravatī; Vāstu, Suvāstu, Gaurī, Kampanā, and Hiraṇvatī;
Hiraṇvatī, Citravatī, and the river Citrasenā.
The Rathacitrā, Jyotirathā, Viśvāmitrā, Kapiñjalā, Upendrā, Bahulā, Kucarā, Ambuvāhinī,
Vainandī, Piñjalā, Veṇṇā, and the great river Tuṅgaveṇā.
The Vidiśā, the Kṛṣṇaveṇṇā, the Tāmrā, and the Kapilā;
the Śalū, the Suvāmā, the Vedāśvā, and the great river Harisrāvā; as well as the Śīghrā, the Picchilā, and the river Bhāradvājī.
The Kauśikī river, the Śoṇā, the Bāhudā, and the Candanā; the Durgā, the Antaḥśilā, the Brahmamedhyā, and the Bṛhadvatī;
the Carakṣā, the Mahirohī, and likewise the Jambūnadī.
O lord of men, [he saw] the Sunasā, the Tamasā, the Dāsī, the Trasā, and another, the Varāṇasī;
also the Loloddhṛtakarā and the Mahānadī, whose hopes are fulfilled;
as well as the Mānavī and the Vṛṣabhā—these great rivers.
Always free from affliction, flowing slowly and gently,
pure as Brahman, and possessing great waters—
these and many other [rivers] in various ways.
O Bhārata, [he saw] Brahmāṇī, Mahāgaurī, and Durgā as well; Citropalā, Citrabarhā, Mañju, and Makaravāhinī;
and the Mandākinī, the Vaitaraṇī, and the great river Kokā.
O Bhārata, [he visited] the Śuktimatī, the Araṇyā, the Puṣpaveṇī, and the Utpalāvatī;
likewise the Lohityā, the Karatoyā, and the Vṛṣabhaṅginī;
as well as the Kumārī, the Ṛṣikulyā, and the Brahmakulyā.
O noble one, there are the most meritorious Sarasvatīs and all the Gaṅgās; O Bhārata, lord of men, there are also the Mahānads: Brahmāṇī, Mahāgaurī, Suvāśī, Mānavī, and Vṛṣabhā.
All of them are mothers of the universe and all possess great strength;
likewise, there are rivers that remain unmanifest by the hundreds and thousands.
Thus, O King, these rivers have been described according to my recollection.
Henceforth, learn from me as I speak of the various regions:
here are the Kurus, the Pañcālas, the Śālvas, the Mādreyas, and the Jāṅgalas;
likewise the Videhas, the Māgadhas, the Siṃhas, and the Mahadāyatas.
The Śūrasenas, the Kaliṅgas, the Bodhas, and likewise the Maukas;
the Matsyas, the Sukuṭyas, the Saubalyas, the Kuntalas, the Kāśis, and the Kośalas; the Cedis, the Vatsas, the Karūṣas, the Bhojas, and the Sindhu-Pulindakas.
Uttamaujas, the Daśārṇas, and the Mekalas together with the Utkalas;
the Pañcālas, the Kauśijas, the Ekapṛṣṭhas, and the Yugandharas; the Saudhas, the Madras, the Bhujiṅgas, the Kāśis, and the Aparakāśis.

The Jaṭharas, the Kukkuśas, and the Sudāśārṇas, O Bhārata; the Kuntis, the Avantis, and likewise the Aparakuntis; the Govindas, the Mandakas, the Ṣaṇḍas, and the inhabitants of Vidarbha and the coastal marshlands.
The Aśmakas, the Pāṃsurāṣṭras, the Goparāṣṭras, the Panītakas,
the Ādirāṣṭras, the Sukuṭṭas, and the entire Balirāṣṭra; the Vānarāsyas, the Pravāhas, the Vakras, the Vakrabhayas, and the Śakas.
The Videhas, the Māgadhas, the Suhmas, and likewise the Vijayas;
the Aṅgas, the Vaṅgas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Yakṛllomas;
the Mallas, the Sudeṣṇas, the Prāhūtas, as well as the Māhiṣakas and the Ārṣikas.
The Vāhīkas, the Vāṭadhānas, the Ābhīras, the Kālatoyakas,
the Aparandhras, the Śūdras, the Pahlavas, the Carmakhaṇḍikas,
the Aṭavī-Śabaras, and the Marubhaumas, O noble one.
The Upāvṛścas and Anupāvṛścas, the Surāṣṭras and likewise the Kekayas;
the Kuṭṭas, Aparāntas, Dvaidheyas, Kākṣas, and Sāmudraniṣkuṭas; the Kaṭyas, Pātavaibodhas, Yākās, and Sāmudraniṣkadās.
O King, there were many Andhras, as well as those from Antargiri; likewise the Bahirgiris, Aṅgas, Maladas, Māgadhas, and Mānavarjakas—
both those from Antargiri and those from Bahirgiri.
O lord of men, the Mahyuttaras, the Prāvṛṣeyas, and the Bhārgavas;
the Puṇḍras, the Bhārgas, the Kirātas, the Sudoṣṇas, and likewise the Pramudas;
the Śakas, the Niṣādas, the Niṣadhas, as well as the Ānartas and the Nairṛtas.
The Dugūlas, the Pratimatsyas, the skilled Kunaṭas,
the Tīragrāhas, the Taratoyas, the hosts of Rājikas and Rasyakas,
the Tilakas, the Pārasīkas, the Madhumantas, and the Prakutsakas.
The people of Kaśmīra, Sindhu, Sauvīra, Gāndhāra, and Daśaka;
the Abhīsāras, Kulūtas, Śaivalas, and Bāhlikas;
as well as the Darvīkas along with the Kacas, the Darvas, Vātajas, Amarathas, and Uragas.
O Kauravya, there were also the Bahuvādya, Sudāmana, Sumallika, Vadhra, Karīṣaka, Kulindopatyaka,
Vanāyu, Daśāpārśva, Romāṇa, and Kuśabindu.
The Kacchas, the Gopālakacchas, the Lāṅgalas, the Paravallakas,
the Kirātas, the Barbaras, the Siddhas, the Videhas, the Tāmraliṅgakas,
the Oṣṭras, the Puṇḍras, along with the Sairandhras and the mountaineers (Pārvatīyas), O noble one.
Furthermore, O bull of the Bharatas, there are other southern regions:
the Dravidas, the Keralas, the easterners, the Bhūṣikas, and the Vanavāsins; as well as the Unnattyakas, the Māhiṣakas, the Vikalpas, and the Mūṣakas.
The Karṇikas, Kuntikas, Saudbhidas, Nalakālakas,
Kaukuṭṭakas, as well as the Colas, Koṅkaṇas, Mālavāṇakas, Samaṅgas, Kopanas, Kukuras, Aṅgadas, and Māriṣas.
The Dhvajins, the Utsavasamketas, the Trigartas with their entire armies,
the Tryangas, the Kekarakas, the Proṣṭhas, the Parasaṃcarakas, as well as the Vindhyapulakas, the Pulindas, along with the Kalkalais; [all these were summoned].
The Mālakas and Mallakas, as well as the Aparavartakas;
the Kulindas and Kulakas, as well as the Karaṇṭhas and Kurakas; the Mūṣakas and Stanabālas, and the Satiyas and Pattipañjakas.
The Ādidāyas, the Sirālās, the Stūbakas, and likewise the Stanapas;
the Hṛṣīvidarbhās, the Kāntīkas, the Taṅgaṇas, and the Parataṅgaṇas;
and other Mleccha peoples to the north, O best of the Bharatas.
The Yavanas along with the Kambojas, the fierce tribes of Mlecchas,
the Sakṣaddruhas, the Kuntalas, the Hūṇas together with the Pāratakas, as well as the Maradhas, the Cīnas, and likewise the Daśamālikas.
The settlements of the Kṣatriyas, the families of Vaiśyas and Śūdras,
the Śūdras, Ābhīras, Daradas, and Kāśmīras together with their cattle; the Khaśikas, Tukhāras, Pallavas, and those dwelling in mountain caves.

The Ātreyas together with the Bharadvājas, as well as the Stanayoṣikas, the Aupakas, the Kaliṅgas, and the various tribes of the Kirātas; the Kāraskaras, the Vaṃśas, the Āndhras, and likewise the Dramiḍas.
The Colas, as well as the Pandyas, the Ceras, and the excellent Simhalas; the Tamaras, the Hamsamargas, and likewise the Karabhanjakas—
these and other regions, both eastern and northern.
O Lord, I have merely mentioned these regions in brief; yet,
when properly cultivated, the earth yields the great fruit of the three goals of life (trivarga) according to one's merit and strength, like a wish-fulfilling cow.
Kings who are heroic and skilled in the matters of dharma and artha covet that earth;
eager for its essence, those swift ones abandon their lives in battle.
Indeed, the earth is the ultimate refuge for the bodies of both gods and men.
O best of the Bharatas, kings who desire to enjoy the earth snatch it from one another like dogs fighting over meat;
yet, no one here finds satisfaction in their desires.
Therefore, O King, the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas strive for the possession of the earth through conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and even force;
for father, mother, son, the sky, and heaven, O bull among men, [are all dependent upon it].
The earth becomes for all beings a ground that perceives correctly and without flaw.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Of this land of Bhārata as well as of Haimavata..."

O Sūta, O Saṃjaya, tell me in detail the duration of their lifespan and their auspicious and inauspicious fruits— both those yet to come, those already passed, and those of the present— as well as concerning Harivarṣa.
Saṃjaya said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, O enhancer of the Kurus, there are four ages in the land of Bhārata:
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Puṣya."
First, O Lord, was the age named Kṛta, followed by the Tretāyuga;
then, in brief, came Dvāpara, and after that the Puṣya (Kali) age begins. And the four thousand years, O best of the Kurus, [constitute the duration of the first age].
O best of kings, the lifespan in the Kṛta Yuga is reckoned as such;
likewise, O lord of men, it is three thousand years in the Tretā Yuga,
and two thousand in the Dvāpara Yuga, while at present it stands at one hundred.
O bull of the Bharatas, there is indeed no stability of the means of valid cognition during this Puṣya age;
here, those still in the womb die, and likewise those already born die. [Yet] there are those of great strength and great being, endowed with the qualities of progeny.
O King, in the Kṛta age, sages rich in asceticism were born by the hundreds and thousands;
they were high-spirited, great-souled, righteous, and speakers of truth.
O King, those born in the Kṛta Yuga were wealthy, handsome,
long-lived, great heroes, and the best of archers in battle; these most excellent Kṣatriya warriors were born worthy of the highest honors in combat.

In the Tretā age, heroic Kṣatriyas are born as universal monarchs (cakravartins). O Great King, when the Dvāpara age prevails, people of all castes are born with great energy and great prowess, seeking to slay one another.

O King, O Bhārata, men born under Puṣya are endowed with little vigor; they are prone to anger, greedy, and indeed untruthful. Furthermore, envy, pride, wrath, deceit, and malice likewise arise within them.

O Bhārata, in the Puṣya age, mortals are characterized by passion and greed; O King, lord of men, in this Dvāpara age, things proceed in a state of contraction. Beyond that is Harivarṣa, which is superior in quality to Haimavata.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, you have described the region of Jambūkhaṇḍa here exactly as it is;
now tell me truly its extent and its dimensions."
O Saṃjaya, you who possess unerring vision, tell me accurately the measurement of the ocean, as well as Śākadvīpa and Kuśadvīpa,
and indeed the truth concerning Śālmala and Krauñcadvīpa.
"Tell me everything, O son of Gavalgaṇa, regarding Rāhu, Soma, and the Sun.
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, there are very many islands by which this world is pervaded."
But I shall describe the seven [suns], as well as the moon, the sun, and the planets. O Lord of the People, the diameter of Jambūdvīpa is eighteen thousand and six hundred full *yojanas*.
The width of the salt ocean is recorded as being double that;
it is filled with various inhabited regions and adorned with jewels and corals,
and is further beautified by mountains variegated with many kinds of minerals.
The circular ocean, crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
is thus described. O King, descendant of Kuru, listen as I duly describe Śākadvīpa to you according to the truth.
O lord of men, O great king, that ocean is twice the size of Jambūdvīpa in its breadth according to its divisions;
and Śālmala, Kuśa, and Krauñca are each twice as large as the one preceding it.
O best of the Bharatas, the Ocean of Milk, which is surrounded by the oceans of wine, clarified butter, and milk respectively,
is situated there; in that place are holy regions where no person ever dies.
How indeed could there be famine [there], for they are endowed with patience and splendor?
O bull of the Bharatas, this summary of Śākadvīpa has been told to you exactly as it is, O great king; what else do you wish to hear?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, O highly blessed one, you have duly described here the summary of Śākadvīpa; now tell me its details in truth."
Saṃjaya said:
"In that same way, O King, there are seven mountains here adorned with jewels, as well as mines of gems and rivers; hear their names from me."
O lord of men, everything there is exceedingly virtuous and meritorious;
joined by celestial sages and gandharvas, it is called the supreme Mount Meru.
O great king, extending toward the east is the mountain named Malaya.
From where the clouds arise and originate in every direction,
beyond that, O Kauravya, lies the great mountain Jaladhāra,
where Vāsava constantly takes up the supreme water.
O Lord of Men, from that place the rain originates during the rainy season;
there stands the lofty Mount Raivataka, eternally established,
where the constellation Revatī resides in the sky according to the ordinance ordained by the Grandfather.
To the north, O Indra among kings, is the great mountain named Śyāma;
it possesses the luster of a fresh cloud, is lofty, glorious, and of radiant form,
from which the people have acquired their dark complexion, O lord of the realm.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, a very great doubt has arisen in me today regarding what you have spoken.
O son of a Sūta, how did the subjects here come to attain this dark complexion?"
Saṃjaya said:
"O highly wise descendant of Kuru, O King, in all the islands indeed there are two complexions, fair and dark; between these two, there is an intermediate complexion."
O Bhārata, I shall tell you why it is called Śyāma; the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa resides here, and because of his dark luster, it has attained the state of being "Śyāma.
Beyond that, O Indra among the Kauravas, is the highly prosperous mountain Durgaśaila.

Kesarī is endowed with kesara (filaments); from it the wind blows forth. O Kauravya, the wise have declared that the extent of those regions is double [the previous] for each successive division, and they are called varṣas (regions).
Mahāmeru, Mahākāśa, Jalada, Kumudottara,
and beyond Jaladhāra, O King, is the one known as Sukumāra. Furthermore,
the son of Raivata was Kaumāra, and the son of Śyāma was Maṇīcaka.
Beyond Kesara is Modākī, and beyond that, O Kauravya, is the Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa). Surrounded by Jambūdvīpa— both in length and breadth— in its center stands a famous great tree.
O Great King, in the center of that island is a place named Śāka;
there are holy regions there, and Śaṅkara is worshipped there.
There, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and deities go.

O King, descendant of Bharata, the subjects were righteous, and the four castes were exceedingly devoted to their own duties; no thief was seen there. O great king, they were long-lived and free from old age and death.
There, the subjects flourish like rivers flowing to the ocean during the rainy season;
there are rivers of holy water, and the Gaṅgā flows there in many courses—
namely the Sukumārī, the Kumārī, the Sītā, and the Kāverakā.

O Kauravya, there is the Mahānadī, as well as the river Maṇijalā; O best of the Bharatas, there is also the Ikṣuvardhanikā. From these, O upholder of the Kuru lineage, flow rivers of meritorious waters.
When Vāsava pours down hundreds of thousands of streams,
it is impossible to enumerate their names or even their measure; for those excellent rivers are indeed meritorious.
There, four meritorious provinces, esteemed by the world, are found:
Maga, Maśaka, Mānasa, and Mandaga.
O King, the Magas are preponderantly Brahmins and are devoted to their own duties.
In the Maśakas, however, O Great King, there are righteous Kṣatriyas who grant all desires;
in the Mānasas, there are Vaiśyas who live by their occupations,
endowed with all objects of desire, heroic, and resolute in matters of dharma and artha.
But during the period of slow-moving [Saturn], O Indra among kings, men are always devoted to righteousness;
there is no king there, no punishment, and no punishers,
for they protect one another’s dharma through their own inherent dharma alone.
"Only this much can be spoken regarding that island;
only this much is to be heard concerning the mighty Śākadvīpa.
Sanjaya said:

But regarding the northern Kaurava islands, O Great King, listen as I relate to you the story exactly as it has been heard by me. There is another ocean of milk-water, and then one with sugarcane-juice for its water.
Here is the ocean of clarified butter, and another with water of curd-cream;
likewise there is the sea of wine and another sea of warm milk.
Furthermore, there are the oceans of sugarcane juice, wine, ghee, and milk.
There is another ocean of curd-cream, and then the great ocean of pure water;
O lord of men, all the continents are each double the size of the preceding one,
and they are surrounded on all sides by mountains, O Great King.
On the middle island, O King, there is a great mountain of realgar called Gaura;
to its west is a black mountain resembling Nārāyaṇa,
where Keśava himself guards divine jewels.
Sitting near Prajāpati, he bestowed happiness upon all creatures.
In Kuśadvīpa, a clump of *kuśa* grass stands in the center of the region; indeed, it is worshipped there, as is the *plakṣa* tree in its own land.
O King, just as the Śalmali tree, which gives its name to the continent, is worshipped in the Śālmala-dvīpa,
so too in Krauñca-dvīpa is the Mahākrauñca mountain, a source of heaps of jewels.
O Great King, he is constantly worshipped by the four castes.
O King, there is the mountain Gomanta, which is very great and possesses all minerals;
there the glorious, lotus-eyed one dwells eternally.

Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is eternally praised by those seeking liberation. O king of kings, in Kuśadvīpa there is a mountain composed of coral named Sudhāmā; it is difficult to assail, and a second mountain there is made of gold.
O Kauravya, the third mountain is named Dyutimān, and Kumuda is the fourth; the fourth is named Puṣpavān, while the fifth is Kuśeśaya;
the sixth is named Harigiri—these six are the most excellent of mountains.
The diameter of each of these is double [the preceding] in its respective division. The first rain-cloud is Audbhida; the second is Veṇumaṇḍala;
the third is indeed Rathākāra; and the fourth is known as Pālana.
The fifth region is Dhṛtimat, the sixth is Prabhākara, and the seventh is Kāpila; these are the seven clusters of regions. O Lord of the World, in these dwell the gods, Gandharvas, and living beings.
They dwell there and take delight; no person dies among them. O King, there are no bandits there, nor even tribes of Mlecchas;
O Ruler of the Earth, all the people are predominantly fair-skinned and delicate.
O lord of men, I shall describe the remaining continents as I have heard them; O great king, listen with an undistracted mind. O great king, in Krauñcadvīpa there is a great mountain named Krauñca.
Beyond Krauñca is Vāmanaka; beyond Vāmanaka is Andhakāraka.
Beyond Andhakāraka, O King, is Maināka, the best of mountains. Beyond Maināka, O King, is Govinda, the supreme mountain.
But beyond Govinda, O King, is the mountain named Nibida;
its width, O increaser of the lineage, is twice that of those [preceding].
I shall describe the regions there; listen as I speak of them.
The region of Krauñca is Kuśala, and that of Vāmana is Manonuga.
Beyond Manonuga, O scion of the Kuru lineage, is the region of Uṣṇa;
beyond Uṣṇa is Prāvaraka, and beyond Prāvaraka is Andhakāraka.
The region of the Munis is remembered as being beyond the region of Andhakāraka; and beyond the region of the Munis, O lord of men, is proclaimed the region Dundubhisvana,
which is crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas and inhabited mostly by fair-complexioned people.
O Great King, these regions are frequented by gods and gandharvas.
In Puṣkara is a mountain named Puṣkara, filled with jewels and gems;
there the Lord Prajāpati himself dwells eternally.
All the gods, together with the great seers, constantly attend upon him,
O lord of men, honoring him with words that are pleasing to the mind. Furthermore,
various kinds of jewels flow forth from Jambūdvīpa.
O descendant of Kuru, among all those islands, for the people,
the Brahmins, through their celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint,
[attain] health and lifespan that are each double [the preceding] in turn.
O King, descendant of Bharata, among these islands there is but one single country where a singular dharma is observed; there,
Prajāpati himself, wielding the rod of punishment, acts as the sovereign.
O great king, he remains constantly protecting these continents. He is the king, O King; he is Śiva; he is the father and the grandfather.
O best of men, he protects all subjects, both the ignorant and the wise.
And there, O Kauravya, food appeared of its own accord before the subjects;
O Great King, they always ate it there as if it were already prepared.
Beyond that, the world-structure known as Samā is seen.
O Great King, the square [region] consists of thirty-three [squares], while the circle consists of thirty-four.
Therein, O Kauravya, stand four elephants honored by the world— the elephants of the quarters, O best of the Bharatas, such as Vāmana, Airāvata, and the others.
Likewise, O King, there was Supratīka, with temples and mouth flowing with rut;
I am not able here to calculate his size,
for he is indeed constantly immeasurable— horizontally, upwards, and downwards as well.
There, O Great King, winds blow from all directions; those elephants, however, restrain them without obstruction with their trunks,
which resemble lotuses, are massive, and possess great luster.

They constantly release winds again, both slowly and swiftly; O Great King, when the winds are released here by the breathing elephants of the quarters, living beings then come forth and indeed remain.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, you have indeed described the details at great length;
the configuration of the continents has been shown. Speak now what follows, O Sañjaya."
Saṃjaya said:
"O great king, the islands have been described; now hear from me the truth concerning the planets, O best of the Kauravas, as far as their power extends."
"O Great King, it is heard that the planet Svarbhānu is perfectly circular;
its diameter is twelve thousand *yojanas*, O sinless one, and its circumference is thirty-six thousand *yojanas* in breadth."
The wise ancient authorities say that it measures sixty hundred [yojanas];
O King, best of the Kurus, it is recorded that the moon is eleven thousand [yojanas] in diameter,
while its orb is thirty-three [thousand].
The diameter of the great-souled Śītaraśmi is fifty-nine thousand yojanas, O descendant of Kuru;
the sun, however, is eight thousand and two more. From that, O King, its circle is thirty thousand yojanas in circumference.
"O King, O sinless one, it is heard that this most noble Pataṅga, Vibhāvasu, is fifty-eight [yojanas] in breadth; such is the measurement of the Sun specified here,
O Bhārata."
O Great King, Rāhu covers these two, the moon and the sun, at the proper time due to his great size; this has been stated as a brief summary.
Thus, O Great King, have I answered you who asked with the eye of the scriptures.
Everything has been told according to reality; therefore, attain tranquility.
This world, along with its means of liberation, has been described by me exactly as it was perceived. Therefore, O Kauravya, take heart regarding your son Duryodhana.
O best of the Bharatas, having heard this delightful Bhūmiparvan,
a noble king becomes illustrious, achieves his goals, and is honored by the virtuous;
his lifespan, strength, valor, and splendor increase.
O protector of the earth, those who listen to this [section] on the holy days while restrained by their vows—
his ancestors and likewise his grandfathers are gratified.
This, however, is the land of Bhārata-varṣa where we ourselves reside.
"Previously, merit was set in motion; you have heard all of that.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"At the word of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he indeed went to Kurukṣetra."
O King, having been granted a boon by Vyāsa, Saṃjaya hastened and,
having seen [the battle], returned from the field in a mere moment. Then the wise Saṃjaya, son of Gavalgaṇa, arrived from the battle.
The seer of all things, who knows the past, the present, and the future,
approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra in his grief and, meditating,
suddenly announced that Bhīṣma— the peerless among the Bharatas— had been slain.
"I am Sañjaya, O Great King; salutations to you, O bull of the Bharatas!
Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu and the grandfather of the Bharatas, has been slain—he who was the preeminent peak of all warriors and the abode of all archers."
Today that grandfather of the Kurus lies upon a bed of arrows, O King,
he whose prowess your son relied upon when he held the gambling match;
that Bhīṣma now lies slain in battle by Śikhaṇḍin.
That great car-warrior, born of the Vasus, who with a single chariot alone conquered all the assembled rulers of the earth in a great battle at the city of Kāśī,
and who, having fought Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, in combat—
He who was not slain by the son of Jamadagni has today been slain by Śikhaṇḍin—
he who was like Mahendra in heroism, like the Himavat in steadfastness,
like the ocean in depth, and equal to the earth in forbearance.
With arrows for his fangs, a bow for his mouth, and a sword for his tongue— difficult to approach,
a lion among men— your father has today been struck down by the Pāñcālya.
Seeing him rising in battle, the great army of the Pāṇḍavas [was filled with fear].
Trembling and agitated with fear like a herd of cattle upon seeing a lion,
he protected that army for ten nights; then, having performed a most difficult feat, that slayer of enemy hosts set out as the sun goes to its setting.
He who was like Śakra, unshakable as he rained down arrows by the thousands,
and who in ten days slew a hundred million warriors in battle—
he now lies groaning upon the earth like a tree uprooted by the wind.
"O King, through your evil counsel, that which was unworthy has occurred, O Bhārata.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How was Bhīṣma, the bull among the Kurus, slain by Śikhaṇḍin?"
"How did my father, who was like Vāsava himself, fall from his chariot?
And how, O Saṃjaya, were my sons left deprived of Bhīṣma—
that powerful one, equal to a god, who had observed the vow of celibacy for the sake of his preceptor?"
When that great being, the mighty archer of great strength, that great chariot-warrior and tiger among men had been slain, what was in the mind at that time?
For supreme anguish has entered me, since you tell me he is killed.
Who followed that bull among the Kurus, the unshakable hero, that foremost of men, as he marched forth? Who were his precursors?
Who remained behind, who turned back, and who followed after him, O Sañjaya?

Who were the heroes who followed from behind with sudden force that tiger among chariot-warriors, the infallible bull among Kṣatriyas, as he plunged into the enemy host— that slayer of foes who dispels the darkness of the hostile army like the sun?
Resembling the thousand-rayed sun and instilling fear in his enemies,
he performed a most difficult feat in battle by the command of the Kaurava;
those who sought to surround him found themselves being swallowed up by his ranks.
How did the Pāṇḍavas resist in battle that son of Śantanu— the skillful and invincible one, who was advancing directly toward them— while he,
the energetic warrior with arrows for teeth, was cutting through the ranks?

How did the son of Kuntī strike down in battle that unconquered one— who had a terrible face wide-gaping like a bow, whose tongue was a sword, who was difficult to approach, who surpassed all other tigers among men, and who was modest?
Seeing him in battle, with his formidable bow and fierce arrows, stationed upon his excellent chariot, plucking off the heads of his enemies with sharp shafts—
that great army of the Pāṇḍavas rose up [in terror] at the sight of him.
Like the irresistible fire of cosmic destruction, he constantly surrounded me;
having drawn my army away for ten nights, that slayer of hosts,
having performed a most difficult feat, has set like the sun.
He who, like Śakra, released an inexhaustible rain of arrows and slew a hundred million warriors in battle within ten days—
now he lies groaning upon the earth like a tree uprooted by the wind.
"O Bhārata, because of my evil counsel,
how was it that the army of the Pāṇḍavas, upon seeing the son of Śaṃtanu,
Bhīṣma of terrible prowess, was unable to strike him there, though he did not deserve such treatment?"
How did the sons of Pāṇḍu engage in battle with Bhīṣma? And why, O Sañjaya, did Bhīṣma not achieve victory while Droṇa was still alive and Kṛpa, the son of Bharadvāja, was present there?
How did Bhīṣma, the best among strikers, meet his end? And how was Bhīṣma— who was difficult even for the gods to withstand— slain in battle by that Atiratha, Śikhaṇḍin of the Pañcālas?
He who always vied in battle with the mighty son of Jamadagni—
unconquered by the son of Jamadagni and equal to Śakra in prowess—
that Bhīṣma, who was worthy of the strength of a great chariot-warrior, has been slain in combat.
O Sañjaya, tell me of that hero by whom we find no refuge.
Which of my great archers did not abandon the immovable one? And which heroes, commanded by Duryodhana, surrounded him?
When all the Pāṇḍavas, led by Śikhaṇḍin, advanced against Bhīṣma,
did the Kurus, O Sañjaya, not abandon that infallible one out of fear?
He whose thunder was the twang of his bowstring and who was great with the rain of his arrows— did they forsake him?
With a great roar like the twang of a bow, rising like a massive cloud,
that hero rained down [arrows] upon the sons of Kuntī, along with the Pañcālas and Sṛñjayas—
slaying the enemy charioteers as the wielder of the thunderbolt slays the Dānavas.
A terrible ocean of missiles and weapons, difficult to approach, with arrows for its crocodiles; possessing waves of bows, inexhaustible, without an island, and without a raft in battle;
with maces and swords for its whirlpools, horses for its crocodiles, and teeming with elephants.
Thick with infantry-fish, resounding with the blasts of conchs and drums,
he was swiftly submerging numerous horses, elephants, foot-soldiers, and chariots in battle—
him who carried away the heroes of the enemy.

O Sañjaya, what heroes surrounded that scorcher of foes as he was burning with wrath and energy, like the shore surrounding the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters? Tell me, O Sañjaya, what deed Bhīṣma, the slayer of enemies, performed in battle.
For the sake of Duryodhana’s welfare, who were then in his vanguard?
