Who protected the right wheel of Bhīṣma, who possesses immeasurable splendor? And which heroes of firm vows followed behind to harass the enemies?
Who were those who stood in front, protecting Bhīṣma in his vicinity?
Which heroes protected the left wheel of that hero as he fought?
And who, stationed on the left wheel, O Saṃjaya, struck down the Sṛñjayas?
O Sañjaya, who protected that unassailable vanguard when it was assembled in the ranks?
Who followed at its flanks as it proceeded along that difficult path?
And who, O Sañjaya, fought against the enemy heroes in that great encounter?
How was it that those heroes, while being protected by him, and he himself being guarded by them,
did not swiftly conquer the armies of the invincible in battle—
armies that were like those of the Supreme Lord of All Worlds, the Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin?
O Sañjaya, how were the Pāṇḍavas even able to strike him—
him who was the island upon which the Kurus relied while fighting their enemies?
You tell me, O Sañjaya, that Bhīṣma, that tiger among men, has been submerged.

How was he slain by his enemies— he whose valor my son Bṛhadbala relied upon when he no longer took the Pāṇḍavas into account? He who, fierce in battle, had formerly been sought for assistance by the gods led by Indra.
My father, who observed great vows, was longed for by those slaying the Dānavas;
when that one of great heroism was born— a bringer of welfare to the world— he abandoned sorrow, suffering, and dejection, for he possessed the auspicious marks of a son.

How can you tell me that he is slain— he who was devoted to wisdom, a knower of that [truth], delighting in the true Dharma, and pure; who knew the essence of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and was endowed with the discipline of all weapons, self-controlled, tranquil, and high-minded?

Having heard that the son of Śantanu has been slain, I consider the rest of the army as already destroyed. It is my conviction that unrighteousness has become stronger than righteousness, since the Pāṇḍavas desire the kingdom after having killed their aged elder.
In former times, Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who was unsurpassed in his knowledge of all weapons,
was defeated in battle by Bhīṣma while striving for the sake of Ambā.
Yet he was one whose deeds were equal to Indra’s and who was the preeminent leader among all archers.

"You tell me that Bhīṣma has been slain; what indeed could be more painful than this? By him, the multitudes of Kṣatriyas were repeatedly defeated in battle, as was Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who is the slayer of enemy heroes."
"He who was not slain— that one of great intelligence— is today slain by Śikhaṇḍin.
Therefore, Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Drupada, must surely be superior in splendor, heroism, and strength to that Bhārgava of great prowess, who is intoxicated with battle."
Who were the heroes that followed that bull of the Bharatas— the slayer of enemies in battle, skilled and accomplished, learned in all scriptures, a hero proficient in supreme weapons—
into the assembly of his foes?
Tell me how that battle between Bhīṣma and the Pāṇḍavas occurred.
O Sañjaya, my son’s army is like a woman whose hero has been slain;
that force of mine is like a bewildered herd of cows without a cowherd.
O Sañjaya, when he whose prowess in the great battle was supreme for all the world has been struck down, how was your mind then? And what capacity do we still have even for life today?
Having caused the death of their father, who was possessed of great heroism and righteous toward the world—
just as those seeking the far shore see a boat sinking in bottomless water—
I believe the sons grieve intensely out of sorrow now that Bhīṣma has been slain.
"Surely my heart is made of the essence of stone and is exceedingly firm,
since it does not shatter upon hearing that Bhīṣma, that tiger among men, has been slain—
he in whom, O bull of the Bharatas, were weapons, wisdom, and statesmanship."
O invincible one, how was he slain in battle— he who was immeasurable?
No one is ever liberated from death by means of weapons, nor by heroism, nor by austerity, nor by intelligence, nor by fortitude, nor even by renunciation.
"Time is surely of great power and difficult for all the world to overcome,
O Sañjaya, since you report that Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, has been slain—
[he who was] consumed by grief for his sons and contemplating no small sorrow."
"I had previously hoped for protection from Bhīṣma, the joy of Śaṃtanu.
When Duryodhana beheld that son of Śaṃtanu fallen upon the earth like the sun, O Sañjaya, what did he do then?"

"O Sañjaya, as I reflect with my intellect upon my own people and those of the enemy, I do not see even a remnant remaining among the kings in the opposing ranks. Terrible indeed is this duty of the warrior class as it has been fully revealed by the seers."
Wherein the Pāṇḍavas desire the kingdom after having slain the son of Śāntanu,
or where we ourselves desire the kingdom after having caused our grandfather to be killed— standing firm in the duty of the Kṣatriya, the sons of Pṛthā, my dear children, have committed no offense.
"O Sañjaya, this is what a noble man must do in times of dire distress:
he must exert his prowess to the utmost of his power, and that quality is firmly established in him—
he who slays the enemy ranks, being modest and unconquered."
O dear Sañjaya, how did the sons of Pāṇḍu strike down the son of Śāntanu?
How were the armies arrayed, and how did the battle proceed with those great-souled ones?
And how was my father Bhīṣma slain by the enemies?
When Bhīṣma had been slain, what did Duryodhana, Karṇa, Śakuni the son of Subala, and the gambler Duḥśāsana say,
as they beheld that field strewn with the bodies of men, elephants, and horses?

The foolish gamblers entered that terrifying assembly hall, which was like a battlefield difficult to approach due to its arrows, spears, maces, swords, and *tomaras* as its dice. In that perilous game of dice where lives were staked, which bulls among men played?
Who were victorious there and who were defeated? Who had their aims frustrated and were struck down by Bhīṣma, the son of Śāṃtanu? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya;
for I find no peace here now that Devavrata has been slain in battle.

Hearing that my father, whose deeds were terrible, has perished, grief has entered me. O Saṃjaya, you are fanning into flame the great anguish rooted in my heart caused by my son, like pouring clarified butter upon a fire.
"O Sañjaya, you tell me that Bhīṣma— that tiger among men, who had lifted a great burden renowned throughout all the worlds—
is now submerged; seeing Bhīṣma slain, I believe my sons are grieving."
"I shall hear of those sufferings caused by Duryodhana; therefore,
O Sañjaya, tell me everything that occurred there in the battle of the lords of the earth, which arose from the lack of wisdom of that fool."
Tell me, Saṃjaya,
whether it was poorly executed or well-executed; tell me in its entirety what was done there in battle by Bhīṣma, who was endowed with splendor and skilled in weapons, as he desired victory.
How that battle between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas occurred—
in what sequence, at what time, and in what manner— and whatever transpired,
and at what time, and how it all came to pass.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Great King, this follow-up question is worthy of you, as is your manner;
yet, you ought not to attribute this fault to Duryodhana."
If a man should incur misfortune through his own misconduct,
he ought not to suspect another of that sin.
O Great King, he who would practice every form of reprehensible conduct among men [is himself to blame].
Deserving of death by all the world for practicing such censurable deeds, he was humiliated by the Pāṇḍavas— who, though wise in deceit, acted out of regard for you—
and along with his ministers, he endured this in the forest for a very long time.

"O protector of the earth, hear that which was seen by me directly with my own eyes and through the power of yoga— concerning the horses, the elephants, and the heroes of immeasurable prowess— and do not set your mind on grief."
"O lord of men, this was surely ordained of old; it must happen thus.
Having paid homage to your father, the wise son of Parāśara, it is by his grace that I have obtained this supreme, divine knowledge."
O King, there is vision beyond the reach of the senses, as well as hearing from afar;
there is knowledge of the minds of others, and of the past and the future;
there is knowledge of the arising of those who have emerged [from meditation], and constant movement through the sky.
Due to the boon granted by the Great-Souled One, he was unassailable by weapons in battles. Listen to me in detail about this wonderful and most marvelous account—
how the great war of the Bharatas took place, causing the hair to stand on end.
When those divisions had been arrayed according to rule,
O great king, Duryodhana then spoke to Duḥśāsana:
"Duḥśāsana, let the chariots for the protection of Bhīṣma be yoked quickly."
"Quickly urge forward all the divisions!
This meeting of the Pāṇḍavas with their armies and the Kurus, which I have contemplated for many years, has now arrived."
"I consider nothing more important than the protection of Bhīṣma in battle;
for if he is protected, he will slay the Pārthas, the Somakas, and the Sṛñjayas.
And that pure-souled one has declared: 'I shall not kill Śikhaṇḍin.'"
"It is heard that she was formerly a woman; therefore, she must be avoided by me in battle.
For this reason, it is my opinion that Bhīṣma must be protected with special care. Let all my men stand ready, intent upon the slaying of Śikhaṇḍin."
Likewise, let those from the east and the west, and those from the south and the northern regions— all skilled in every weapon and missile— protect the Grandfather;
for if he were left unprotected, even a wolf might slay a lion of great strength.
"Let us not allow the lion to be slain by Śikhaṇḍin, as if by a jackal.
Yudhāmanyu shall protect the left wheel and Uttamaujas the right;
these two are the protectors of Phalguna, and Phalguna himself is the protector of Śikhaṇḍin."
"O Duḥśāsana, act in such a way that he, while being protected by Pārtha and avoided by Bhīṣma, shall not slay the son of Gaṅgā. Then,
when the night had turned to dawn, a great clamor arose.
While the kings were crying out, "Yoke!
Yoke!", O Bhārata, amidst the sounds of conchs and drums, the roars of lions,
the neighing of horses, and the clatter of chariot wheels, [the battle began].
With the trumpeting of the great elephants and the roaring of the warriors,
a tumultuous din arose on all sides from their lion-roars, the slapping of arms, and their shouts;
O Great King, everything was prepared in its entirety.
At sunrise, O king of kings, there was a great army of both the Kuru and Pāṇḍava hosts—
your sons' and likewise those of the Pāṇḍavas—
possessing invincible weapons, as well as arms and armor.
Then, O Bhārata, when it became light, the vast armies of your men and those of the enemy were seen, equipped with weapons;
there were elephants and chariots adorned with gold.
Shining brightly, they appeared like clouds accompanied by lightning;
the armored warriors were seen stationed within their own ranks,
and the arrays of chariots appeared in great numbers like cities.
There your father shone exceedingly like the full moon;
the warriors stood within their own ranks, equipped with bows, spears, swords, maces, javelins, and lances— shining weapons in hand.
O lord of the people, elephants, chariots, infantry,
and horses stood in hundreds and thousands, arranged like a snare;
and banners of various forms were seen raised aloft.
Thousands of radiant banners belonging to both their own side and that of the enemy—
golden, with parts variegated by jewels, blazing like fires,
and emitting flames— shone forth by the thousands upon the kings.
Resplendent like the banners of Mahendra upon the dwellings of Mahendra,
those heroes, clad in armor and eager for battle, were seen there—
variegated with uplifted weapons, wearing leather finger-guards, and carrying quivers.
Those lords of men with eyes like bulls shone at the head of the army:
Śakuni the son of Subala, Śalya, Jayadratha the king of the Sindhus, Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja.
The highly heroic Bhagadatta, Bṛhadratha of Kosala,
Śrutāyudha of Kaliṅga, King Jayatsena,
Bṛhadbala of Kosala, and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvatas.
These ten tigers among men, heroes with arms like iron clubs, are the lords of *akṣauhiṇīs*; they are performers of sacrifices who have bestowed abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
These and many others follow the will of Duryodhana.
Kings and princes, wise in policy and possessed of great strength,
were seen standing in their respective divisions, fully armored.
All of them wore black antelope skins, carried banners, and were adorned with garlands of *muñja* grass.

Ten fully equipped *vāhinīs* stood ready, having been mobilized for the sake of Duryodhana and consecrated for the world of Brahmā; the eleventh was the great army of the Kauravas belonging to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
At the head of all the armies, where the son of Śantanu was the leader— O Great King, we beheld the infallible Bhīṣma, with his white turban, white horses, and white armor, like the risen moon.

The Kurus and Pāṇḍavas beheld Bhīṣma, who stood upon his chariot bearing a banner of red palm trees, shining like the sun amidst white clouds. Seeing Bhīṣma at the head of the army, the Pāṇḍavas trembled.
And the Sṛñjayas, those great archers led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
like small animals upon seeing a yawning great lion,
were all struck with repeated terror at the sight of him who was headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
O Bhārata, these eleven illustrious divisions belong to you,
while the Pāṇḍavas likewise have seven, protected by great men.
Both armies are like oceans with their maddened crocodiles and whirlpools, teeming with massive sea-monsters.
At the end of an eon, two [armies] encountered like two oceans;
O King, such a gathering of assembled forces has never been seen or heard of by us before.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Having seen both armies there, the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas,
tell me now of the omens, for you are skilled, O Sañjaya."
Saṃjaya said:
Just as the blessed Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana had declared,
so indeed did all the rulers of the earth assemble together.
On that day, the Moon entered the constellation Maghā,
and the seven great planets, blazing brightly, converged in the sky. At sunrise, the Sun appeared as if split in two.
The sun rose in the sky with a blazing crest of light,
while jackals and crows shrieked in the glowing quarter of the horizon— those flesh-eaters and blood-drinkers, seeking to devour the corpses.

Day after day, the aged grandfather of the Kurus and the son of Bharadvāja, those two subduers of enemies, rising at dawn and remaining self-restrained, would say: "May victory belong to the sons of Pāṇḍu."
They fought for your sake, just as that agreement had been made.
Your father Devavrata, who was knowledgeable in all the distinctions of dharma,
having assembled the lords of the earth, spoke these words:
"O Kṣatriyas, here is the great door to heaven opened for you;
go through it to the same world as Śakra and Brahmā.
This is your eternal path, traveled by those of old and even older."
Honor yourselves by remaining undistracted in battle;
for Nabhaga, Yayati, Mandhatri, Nahusha, Nriga, Arjuna, Sagara, Vainya, and other such preeminent Kshatriyas [attained their status through such resolve].

Having attained perfection, they have gone to the supreme state by means of such deeds as these. For a Kṣatriya, death from disease at home is unrighteous; that he meets his end in battle is his eternal duty.
O bull of the Bharata race, having been thus addressed by Bhīṣma,
the rulers of the earth set out with their own armies, beautifying them with their excellent chariots.
But that Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, departed together with his ministers and kinsmen.
O bull of the Bharatas, Bhīṣma had laid down his weapons in battle;
then your sons and the kings on your side, deprived of Karṇa,
marched forth, making the ten directions resound with lion-like roars.
Those armies shone with white umbrellas, banners, standards, elephants, and horses,
as well as with chariots and foot soldiers;
they resounded with the sounds of kettledrums and small drums, and the clamor of war-drums.
The earth was agitated by the rattling of chariot rims;
and the great car-warriors, resplendent with golden armlets, bracelets, and bows,
appeared like moving mountains.
With his great palm-tree banner marked with five stars, Bhīṣma,
the commander of the Kuru army, stood there, resembling the stainless sun. As for those great archers, the kings on your side, O bull of the Bharatas—
And your sons, O Indra among kings, with their riders, chariots, and elephants,
proceeded according to the instructions of the son of Śantanu,
O King. But Govāsana Śaibya, accompanied by all the kings, [followed].
He proceeded on a royal elephant worthy of a king and adorned with banners;
Padmavarṇa, however, stood at the very front of all the divisions. Aśvatthāman, whose banner bore the emblem of a lion’s tail, advanced with vigilance.
Śrutāyus, Citrasena, Purumitra, Vivimśati,
Śalya, Bhūriśravas, and the great car-warrior Vikarṇa—
these seven mighty archers, led by the son of Droṇa, [stood ready].
In beautiful, radiant chariots, they were the precursors of Bhīṣma.
And upon their excellent chariots,
towering standards made of gold, shining brilliantly, were seen adorning them.
The standard of Droṇa, the foremost of preceptors, together with his bow, was a sacrificial altar made of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with a water-pot;
it led an army of many hundreds of thousands.
Duryodhana’s great standard bore the emblem of a jeweled elephant;
at its front stood the chariot-warriors Paurava, Kāliṅga, Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja, Kṣemadhanvan, and Sumitra.
The King of Magadha advanced, as if drawing the very front of the army with his highly precious chariot and his bull-standard,
protected by the Lord of Aṅga and the high-souled Kṛpa.
The army of the easterners resembled a mass of autumnal clouds.
Standing at the head of the host with his preeminent silver standard bearing the emblem of a boar, the highly illustrious Jayadratha shone resplendently.
Under his command were a hundred thousand chariots,
eight thousand elephants, and sixty thousand cavalrymen;
O King, that vanguard of the army was protected by the Lord of Sindhu.
That great army, consisting of chariots, elephants, and horses without interval, shone brilliantly; with sixty thousand chariots and ten thousand elephants,
the lord of all the Kaliṅgas marched forth together with Ketumān.
His great elephants, resembling mountains, shone forth,
adorned with mechanical engines, *tomara* spears, quivers, and banners;
and the Lord of Kaliṅga was resplendent with his preeminent standard-tree.
O King, Ketumān also, mounted upon an elephant adorned with a white umbrella, a golden neck-ornament, and yak-tail fans, and equipped with a variegated supreme goad,
appeared in battle like the sun situated amidst the clouds.

Blazing with splendor and mounted upon an excellent elephant, King Bhagadatta advanced like the wielder of the thunderbolt himself. Those two, who were equal to Bhagadatta, remained stationed upon the shoulders of their elephants.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, devoted to Ketumān,
[advanced]. That fierce array, possessing a multitude of chariots, with elephants as its supreme head and horses as its wings,
fell upon the enemy from all sides like a winged bird.
O King, it was ordained by Droṇa, by the king Śāntanava, as well as by the son of the preceptor, by Bāhlika, and by Kṛpa. Saṃjaya said:
Then, O Great King, after a moment, a tumultuous sound that made the heart tremble was heard from the warriors eager for battle,
amidst the blare of conchs and drums and the trumpeting of elephants.
With the roar of chariot rims, the earth seemed to split asunder;
with the neighing of horses and the shouting of warriors there,
the sky and all directions were then filled with sound in an instant.
O invincible one, at the mutual encounter of your sons and those of the Pāṇḍavas,
the armies trembled;
there, elephants and chariots were adorned with gold.
O lord of men, the banners of your warriors, appearing in many forms, shone brilliantly like clouds accompanied by lightning;
adorned with golden armlets, they gleamed like blazing fires.

O Bhārata, the bright banners of both one's own side and those of the enemy appeared like the standards of Mahendra in the abodes of Mahendra; the heroes were clad in golden armor that possessed a radiance equal to fire and the sun.
O King, the foremost warriors of the Kurus appeared like blazing planets, fully armored and equipped with various weapons and bows; they stood with their diverse arms raised,
wearing leather finger-guards and carrying banners.
Those great archers with eyes like bulls shone as they stood at the head of the army.
But the protectors of Bhīṣma’s rear, O lord of men, were your sons:
Duḥśāsana, Durviṣaha, Durmukha, and likewise Duḥsaha.
Viviṃśati, Citrasena, and the great car-warrior Vikarṇa; Satyavrata, Purumitra, Jaya, Bhūriśravas, and Śala—
these twenty thousand chariot-warriors were their followers.
The Abhiṣāhas, Śūrasenas, Śibis, and Vasātis; the Śālvas, Matsyas, Ambaṣṭhas, Trigartas, and Kekayas;
as well as the Sauvīras, Kitavas, the Easterners, the Westerners, the Northerners, and the Mālavas.
All these twelve peoples were heroes ready to lay down their lives;
with a great multitude of chariots, they protected the Grandfather. There was also a division of ten thousand swift elephants.
The King of Magadha followed that chariot division toward the monarch; and within the midst of the army, there were sixty million chariot-guards and foot-guards for the elephants.
And foot soldiers went ahead, bows, shields, and swords in their hands—
many hundreds of thousands who fought with claws and spears;
O Bhārata, there were eleven akṣauhiṇīs belonging to your son.
They appeared, O great king, like the Gaṅgā within the Yamunā.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Having seen those eleven akṣauhiṇīs arrayed in battle formation, Yudhiṣṭhira—"
How did the Pāṇḍava,
who knew the human, divine, Gāndharva, and Asura arrays, form a counter-array with such a small army? How did that son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava, counter-array against Bhīṣma?
Saṃjaya said:
Having seen the armies of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up in battle array,
the righteous-souled Dharmarāja addressed Dhananjaya.
"O dear one, they declare from the words of the great seer Bṛhaspati:

'One should make a small number of troops fight in close formation, but one may extend a large number at will. When a small force is engaged with many, the army should be in the shape of a needle-point.'"
"And our army is likewise smaller, especially compared to the enemy.
Having understood these words of the great seer, O Pāṇḍava,
Phalguna, having heard that speech of Dharmarāja, replied.
"O King, I shall now form for you this most invincible array,
named Acala and called Vajra, which was devised by Vajrapāṇi himself. Like a wind that has been stirred up, it is unbearable for enemies in battle."
That Bhīma, the best among strikers, will indeed fight at our front;
let Dhṛṣṭadyumna go ahead, terrifying the enemy armies,
that best of men crushing the splendors of the hostile forces.
"Skilled in the means of warfare, he shall go at our head as our leader;
he is a worthy commander of the army, like the son of Agni for the gods.
Upon seeing him, all the kings, led by Duryodhana..."
They will turn back in confusion, like small animals before a lion;
we shall all take refuge in him, who is like a rampart providing fearlessness from every side—
a terrible man, the best among strikers, like the wielder of the thunderbolt among the immortals.
For there is no man in this world who could withstand Vṛkodara, that bull among men of most fierce deeds, when he is enraged.
Bhīmasena wields a firm mace made of the essence of thunderbolts.
Moving with great speed, he could even dry up the ocean.
O Lord of Men, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the heroic Kekaya—
these stand here with their ministers as your spectators.
O King, pointing out that mighty Bhīmasena at that time,
Bībhatsu said, "These are the heirs of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O noble one, as Pārtha was speaking thus, all the troops [listened].
Then, in that battle, they honored him with favorable words.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya acted accordingly;
having quickly arrayed those forces, Phalguna then set forth.
Seeing the Kurus advancing, the great army of the Pāṇḍavas appeared like the full Ganges— calm yet surging forward;
Bhīmasena was at their head, along with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata.
Then Nakula, Sahadeva, and the heroic Dhṛṣṭaketu, having mobilized their forces, followed behind; and the king himself, surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī,
protected them from the rear along with his brothers and sons.
The two sons of Mādrī, endowed with great splendor, were the protectors of Bhīma’s wheels;
the energetic sons of Draupadī, together with the son of Subhadrā, were the protectors of his rear;
and the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna of the Pañcālas was their guardian.
Accompanied by the Prabhadrakas, those foremost chariot-warriors and heroes of the army,
Śikhaṇḍin then followed behind, protected by Arjuna;
O bull of the Bharatas, he advanced with diligence for the destruction of Bhīṣma.
Yuyudhāna, the great car-warrior, was the rear-guard for Arjuna;
the two Pāñcāla princes, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, were the protectors of his wheels. King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, was at the center of the army.
With large, rutting elephants that moved like mountains,
and with an *akṣauhiṇī* of troops, the high-minded and valiant Yajñasena, the King of Pañcāla,
followed behind Virāṭa for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
O King, upon their chariots were great banners possessing the luster of the sun and moon, adorned with the finest gold and bearing various emblems. Then,
having moved forward from behind, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna followed.
Together with his brothers and sons, he protected Yudhiṣṭhira;
and having overwhelmed the various banners on the chariots of both your men and the enemy,
the great ape remained alone upon Arjuna’s banner.
From the tip of the banner, the terrifying roar of that monkey was heard again and again;
making the ten directions resound with its fearsome cry,
the lord of monkeys struck terror into them upon seeing him.
With the twitching, raising, and tossing of his tail, the monkey again displayed himself in the sky with a great roar in response to the echo. Meanwhile,
the foot soldiers went ahead, swords, spears, and double-edged blades in their hands.
There were many hundreds of thousands of Bhīmasena’s protectors,
and ten thousand elephants with temples and mouths flowing with rut,
heroic as they were, shining like mountains with nets of gold.
Adorned with bells, golden girths, and banners,
like clouds raining down, moist with ichor and fragrant as lotuses,
they followed behind the king like moving mountains.
Drawing his terrible mace, which resembled an iron club, the high-minded and invincible Bhīmasena dragged along that great army;
he was as difficult to behold as the sun scorching with its garland of rays.
The warriors were unable to look at him from any side when he was near;
this array, named Vajra, is impenetrable and faces in all directions. It is terrible, with bows for its lightning and banners, and is protected by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Having arrayed themselves against your army, the Pāṇḍavas stand there—
invincible in the world of men, protected by the Pāṇḍavas—
as the armies remain at twilight awaiting the rising of the sun.
A wind carrying spray blew forth, accompanied by thunder even though the sky was cloudless; fierce winds blew from all directions, dragging pebbles along the ground,
and the rising dust shrouded the world in darkness.
O bull of the Bharatas, a great meteor fell facing the east;
having struck the rising sun, it shattered with a tremendous roar.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, as the armies were being arrayed...
The sun rose devoid of luster, and the earth shook with a roar;
at that time, O best of the Bharatas, the mountains crumbled,
and many thunderclaps occurred in all directions, O King.
A thick dust arose so that nothing could be discerned,
amidst the sounds of banners being suddenly shaken by the wind— banners bound with networks of small bells and adorned with golden garlands.
With their great banners and with splendor equal to the sun,
everything became filled with a rattling sound like that of groves of palm trees;
thus did those tigers among men, the Pāṇḍavas, rejoice in battle.
Having arrayed themselves in counter-formation against the army of your son,
O bull of the Bharatas,
the very marrow of the warriors seemed to fail them upon seeing Bhīmasena standing before them with mace in hand.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, at sunrise, who indeed were those eager for battle who appeared as if rejoicing?"
Whether it be my own men led by Bhīṣma in the encounter,
or the Pāṇḍavas led by Bhīma at that time—
for which side were the moon, the sun, and the wind inferior?
Whose army do the beasts of prey howl at?
Whose young men have such bright complexions?
Tell me all this exactly as it is, according to the truth.
Saṃjaya said:
O lord of men, both armies approached as if equal in strength; both were drawn up in battle array and appeared joyful.
Both armies were wonderful, appearing like rows of forests; likewise, both were filled with elephants, chariots, and horses.
Both armies were vast and terrible in appearance.
In that same way, O Bhārata, both are difficult to withstand;
likewise, both were created for the conquest of heaven,
and thus both are protected by virtuous and noble men.
The Kurus, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, stood facing west,
while the Pārthas stood facing east, eager for battle; the army of the Kauravas was like that of the lord of the Daityas.
As if by Devendra himself, a favorable wind blew from behind the Pāṇṇḍavas;
while jackals howled at the Dhārtarāṣṭras.
The elephants of your son could not endure the intense scent of rut from those lordly elephants;
Duryodhana [mounted] an elephant the color of a lotus.
Seated upon his elephant, which was adorned with a golden girth and possessed the strength of its noble breed, he stood at the center of the Kurus,
being praised by bards and panegyrists.
His white parasol has the radiance of the moon,
and a golden garland shines upon his head;
Śakuni surrounded him on all sides with mountain-dwellers.
The King of Gandhāra protects [the army] together with the Gandhāras. Bhīṣma, the elder of the entire host, stands at the front,
with his white umbrella, his white bow, and his conch shell.
Wearing a white turban and a pale white banner,
with white horses, he shone like a white mountain.
His army and all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra followed him.
A portion of the Bāhlīkas and the Śalas (06.020.010c), as well as the Ambaṣṭhas who are Kṣatriyas, those along the Sindhu,
and likewise the heroic Sauvīras and Pañcanadas.
The high-souled Drona, mighty-armed and of undaunted spirit, sits upon his golden chariot drawn by chestnut horses—
the preceptor renowned among all kings.
Thereafter, like Indra protecting his army,
Vārddhakṣatri, Bhūriśravas, Purumitra, and Jaya stood in the midst of the entire host.
The Śālvas, Matsyas, and Kekayas— all these brothers, together with their elephant divisions, were about to fight;
and the high-souled son of Śaradvat was at the northern yoke.
The great archer Gautama, a warrior of diverse skills,
protects the army from the north together with the Śakas, Kirātas, Yavanas, and Pahlavas.
Accompanied by great chariot-warriors— the Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas,
Saurāṣṭrakas, and Nairṛtas— all bearing weapons,
Bṛhadbala was protected by Kṛtavarman.
Your army protects from the right side the ten thousand chariots of the Saṃśaptakas,
who have been dispatched with the thought, "Either death or victory shall be Arjuna's."
O King, those heroes of the Trigartas, skilled in weapons, set out toward where Arjuna was;
and your elephants, O Bhārata, numbered more than a hundred thousand.
For every elephant there were a hundred chariots, and for every chariot a hundred horses;
for every horse there were ten archers, and for every archer ten shield-bearers. Thus, O Bhārata, were your armies arrayed by Bhīṣma.
O King, even by the gods it would not be possible to shake his strength,
for Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, was the leader who day after day drew up the human, celestial, Gandharva, and Asura arrays.
Vast as the ocean on a full-moon day with its multitude of great chariots,
the array of the Dhartarashtras under Bhishma was turned westward in battle; yet your army appeared of diverse forms.
O King, though formidable, they are not equal to those of the Pāṇḍavas;
indeed, I consider that [army] alone to be vast and invincible,
whose leaders are Keśava and Arjuna.
Saṃjaya said:
Having seen the vast army of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra arrayed for battle,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, fell into despair.
Beholding the battle array formed by Bhīṣma, which was impenetrable, the son of Pāṇḍu,
seeing it as if truly unbreakable, became despondent and said to Arjuna:
"O Dhanañjaya, how is it possible for us to fight in this battle?"
O mighty-armed one, this army of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— whose warrior is the Grandfather—
is unshakeable and impenetrable, having been arrayed by Bhīṣma,
the scorcher of foes and possessor of vast splendor, according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures.
"O crusher of enemies, we and our armies have fallen into doubt: how shall our escape from this great military array be accomplished?
Then Arjuna, the slayer of foes, spoke to Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira.
O King, seeing your army despondent—
though it consists of many heroes who are superior in wisdom, endowed with virtues, and numerous—
learn from me, O lord of men, the reason why those far fewer in number are victorious.
O King, I shall explain that cause to you, for you are free from malice;
O Pāṇḍava, the seer Nārada knows it, as do Bhīṣma and Droṇa.
Relying on this very matter, he spoke thus during the war between the gods and the asuras.
In ancient times, it is said that Pitāmaha told Mahendra and the other denizens of heaven:
"Those who desire victory do not conquer through strength and heroism as much as they do through truth, compassion, righteousness, and exertion."
"Abandoning unrighteousness, greed, and delusion, and relying on exertion, fight without egoism; where there is dharma, there is victory.
Know this, O King: our victory in battle is certain."
"Just as Nārada told me: 'Where Kṛṣṇa is, there is victory.
Where Kṛṣṇa—the soul of the Vedas, the Lord of all, and Hari—is present, there is victory, O mighty-armed one; just as Nārada told me."
Victory is subordinate to Kṛṣṇa; it follows behind Mādhava.
Otherwise, victory would belong to him, while submissiveness would be his other quality. Govinda possesses infinite splendor and remains unperturbed even amidst hosts of enemies.

Since Kṛṣṇa is the most eternal of persons, therefore victory belongs to him. For in ancient times, this Hari, having become Vaikuṇṭha with his unimpeded arrows, thundering against the gods and demons, asked: "Who shall be victorious?"
"By those who said, 'May we conquer following Kṛṣṇa,' victory was won there;
for by his grace, the three worlds were obtained by the gods, headed by Śakra.
Therefore, O Bhārata, I do not see any cause for distress in you here."
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, the consumer of all, he who hopes for your victory...
Sañjaya said:
"Then King Yudhiṣṭhira urged on his own army."
O bull of the Bharatas, arraying his divisions against Bhīṣma,
the Pāṇḍavas,
those leaders of the Kurus, desiring the highest heaven through fair combat, deployed their forces according to the instructions given.
In the center was the division of Śikhaṇḍin, protected by Savyasācin;
the army led by Bhīmasena was guarded by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
whose forces were protected in all directions by Bhīmasena and the others.
O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s own division was protected by Bhīma himself,
while the southern wing was protected by Yuyudhāna—
the illustrious foremost of the Sātvatas, who was like Śakra among those armed with bows.
Yudhiṣṭhira [received] a chariot resembling the vehicle of Mahendra, equipped with all its furnishings, variegated with gold and jewels, and with golden trappings and yokes.
Seated in the midst of the elephant herd,
his uplifted goad-staff shines brightly,
and his exceedingly white parasol gleams most radiantly.
The great seers and the domestic priests attend upon this lord of men with circumambulations and hymns of praise,
proclaiming the destruction of his enemies.
The aged great seers, who were indeed learned,
performed rites for his well-being on all sides with prayers, mantras, and medicinal herbs.
For indeed, the study of the Vedas is a great means for victory;
thus Dhaumya and others, having assembled together, surrounded Yudhiṣṭhira with mantras for the sake of victory.
Then that high-souled best of the Kurus gave garments, as well as cows, fruits, flowers, and gold coins to the Brahmins.
Distributing among the brahmins a great variety of precious things— gold, gems, pearls, gold, silver, and so forth— he proceeded like Śakra among the immortals.
With a thousand suns and a hundred small bells,
adorned with the finest Jāmbūnada gold,
Arjuna’s chariot was like a fire wreathed in flames.
The white-horsed chariot with its beautiful wheels shines brilliantly;
mounted upon it, with the monkey-bannered standard held by Keśava, he holds the Gāṇḍīva bow and arrows in his hands.
There is no archer equal to him on earth,
nor has there ever been one, nor will there ever be one;
he shall utterly rout your son’s army.
He bears an exceedingly fierce form;
though unarmed, he who possesses strong arms could reduce men, horses, and elephants to ashes in battle with his two arms alone.
Accompanied by the twins, that Bhimasena,
Vṛkodara, was the protector of the hero’s chariot;
beholding him, who moved with the playful gait of an intoxicated bull or a lion, [he approached].
Beholding him standing at the head of the army— unassailable and resembling Mahendra himself—
the world trembled like camels stuck in the mud.
Seeing Vṛkodara, who possessed the pride of a king of elephants,
your warriors— the leaders of the Kuru army— had their hearts agitated by fear and appeared dejected in form.
Their throats became parched and they were disfigured. Then Janārdana spoke to Guḍākeśa, the best of the Bharatas, that unassailable prince who stood in the midst of the army.
Vāsudeva said:
"This one who stands as a protector, blazing with power,
and who gazes upon our army like a lion— "
This is Bhīṣma, the banner of the Kuru lineage,
by whom thirty horse-sacrifices were performed;
these armies [belong] to that one of great majesty.
They conceal [the sun] like clouds hiding the heat-rayed one.
Having slain these, O hero among men,
seek battle with the bull of the Bharatas.
Saṃjaya said:
Having seen the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons standing ready for battle,
the Blessed Lord spoke.
For the benefit of Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed one, having purified yourself and standing facing the battle,
recite the hymn to Durgā for the defeat of your enemies."
06,022.016d@001_0005 Having been thus addressed in the battle by the wise Vāsudeva,
Having descended from his chariot, Pārtha, with palms joined in reverence, uttered this hymn of praise:
"Oṃ! Homage to you, O leader of the Siddhas, Noble One who dwells on Mount Mandara!
O Kumārī, Kālī, Kāpālī, Kapilā, and Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā!"
O Bhadrakālī, homage to you; O Mahākālī, let there be salutation to you! O Caṇḍī, O Caṇḍā, homage to you; O Tāriṇī, O lady of excellent complexion!
O Kātyāyanī, O highly fortunate one, O Karālī, O Vijayā, O Jayā!
O bearer of the peacock-feather banner, adorned with various ornaments;
O wielder of the sharp trident, bearing sword and shield;
O younger brother of Gopendra, the eldest one born in the lineage of the cowherd Nanda!

O you who always delight in the blood of buffaloes, O Kauśikī, O wearer of yellow garments; O Aṭṭahāsā, O Kokamukhī, salutations be to you, O lover of battle! O Umā, O Śākaṃbharī, O White One, O Black One, O destroyer of Kaiṭabha!
O Hiraṇyākṣī, Virūpākṣī, Sudhūmrākṣī, homage be to you! O Vedaśruti, of great merit, devoted to Brahman, Jātavedas,
whose abode is eternally present in the sacred shrines of Jambūkaṭaka!
You are the knowledge of Brahman among all sciences, and the great sleep of embodied beings;
O Blessed Durgā, Mother of Skanda, dweller in the wilderness,
you are Svāhākāra, Svadhā, Kalā, Kāṣṭhā, and Sarasvatī.

Sāvitrī is the mother of the Vedas, and likewise she is called the Vedānta. O Great Goddess, you have been praised by me with a pure inner self. May victory be mine eternally through your grace in every battle.

In wildernesses, fearsome places, and fortresses, as well as in the dwellings of your devotees, you dwell eternally in Pātāla; in battle, you conquer the Dānavas. You are Jambhanī, Mohinī, Māyā, Hrī, and likewise Śrī.
You are the twilight, Prabhāvatī, and likewise Sāvitrī, the Mother;
you are contentment, nourishment, fortitude, and splendor, who increase the moon and the sun.
You are prosperity, O you who possess prosperity, and you are beheld in battle by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Saṃjaya said: Then,
having perceived the devotion of Pārtha, she who is compassionate toward humanity,
standing in the sky before Govinda, spoke.
The Goddess said:
"O Pāṇḍava, you shall conquer your enemies in a very short time. You are a man, O invincible one, and you have Nārāyaṇa as your ally."
"You are invincible in battle even by your enemies, including the wielder of the thunderbolt himself. Having spoken thus, the granter of boons vanished in an instant.
Having obtained the boon, the son of Kuntī considered victory already his own.
Then Pārtha ascended that most excellently joined chariot.
Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, together upon a single chariot, blew their divine conchs. The man who, having risen at dawn, recites this hymn—
There is never any fear from yakṣas, rākṣasas, or piśācas;
nor do enemies, serpents, or other fanged creatures pose a threat to them. Furthermore, there is never any fear for him even from the royal court.
In dispute one attains victory; one who is bound is released from bondage.
One necessarily crosses over difficult terrain and is likewise liberated from thieves.
One always triumphs in battle and attains exclusive prosperity.
Endowed with health and strength, one shall likewise live for a hundred years;
this was seen by me through the grace of the wise Vyāsa.
Out of delusion, people do not recognize these two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

Your sons are all wicked-souled and subject to the power of wrath; enveloped by the noose of Time, they have uttered these words appropriate for the occasion. [So too did] Dvaipāyana, Nārada, Kaṇva, and the sinless Rāma.
They tried to restrain your son, but he did not accept it;
for where there is dharma, there is splendor and beauty, where there is modesty, fortune, and likewise intelligence—where there is dharma, there is Kṛṣṇa; and where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is victory.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Sañjaya, which warriors among them fight at the front with joy? Who here are high-spirited, and who are dejected and bewildered?
"Who struck first in that heart-trembling battle, O Sañjaya—were they my men or the Pāṇḍavas? Tell me that.
From whose assembled army did the fragrance of perfumes and garlands arise?"
And there were shouts of "Victory! from the warriors as they roared.
Sañjaya said:
"The warriors of both armies there rejoiced with joy."

O bull of the Bharatas, there arose on both sides the scent of garlands, incense, and drinks; and as the compacted armies were drawn up in battle array and advanced in their exaltation, a truly great slaughter occurred.
A tumultuous sound of musical instruments, mingled with conchs and kettledrums,
arose from the heroes, those champions of battle, as they roared at one another;
O King, a great clash occurred between the two armies.
O bull of the Bharatas, as the warriors gazed at one another,
while the elephants trumpeted and the armies rejoiced,
[they beheld] Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals, the hearing and praising of whose name is meritorious.
I bow to Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
On the field of dharma, at Kurukṣetra, the two armies have gathered, desiring to fight.
06,023.001c What did my sons and the Pāṇḍavas do, O Saṃjaya?
06,023.001d Homage to Śrī Rāmacandra!
Homage to Śrī Kṛṣṇa! Om, homage!
Of this *Śrī Bhagavadgītā-mālā-mantra*, the blessed Vedavyāsa is the seer (*ṛṣi*); the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chanda*);
and the Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is the deity (*devatā*).
"You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom"— this is the seed [of the teaching].
"Having abandoned all duties, take refuge in me alone."
"Come to me for refuge" (Gītā 18.66ab)—this is the power; "I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve" (Gītā).
Thus is the *kīlaka*.
For the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and for the sake of virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), desire (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*),
this is the application (*viniyoga*) in recitation (*japa*).
"Neither do weapons cut this,
nor does fire burn it" (Gītā 2.23ab)—
[thus he touches] with the two thumbs.
Salutations! "Neither do the waters moisten it, nor does the wind dry it" (Gītā 2.23cd); thus, salutations with both index fingers. This [Self] is indestructible.
"06,023.001d@002_0013 This [Self] is unburnable, undissoluble, and indeed undrying" (Gītā 2.24ab); salutation to the two middle [fingers].
"Eternal, omnipresent, stable, and immovable is this..."
"To the eternal one" (Gītā 2.24cd)— homage with both ring fingers.
"Behold my forms, O Pārtha, by the hundreds and by the thousands" (Gītā).
"Salutations with the two little fingers" (referring to *Gītā* 11.5ab).
"Various divine [forms], of various colors and shapes" (*Gītā* 11.5cd).
"Salutation to the palms and backs of the hands.
Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*).
The Assignment of Limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
"Heads do not cut him; fire does not burn him" (Gītā 2.23ab).
*Namaḥ* to the heart. Nor does he...
"Waters do not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it" (Gītā 2.23cd).
*Svāhā* to the head!
This [Self] is indestructible, this is unburnable, this is unmoistenable, and this is undryable.
And likewise: "Even as... [Gītā 2.24ab]," for the *śikhā*, *vauṣaṭ*. [Offer] various divine [substances], of diverse colors and forms.
"06,023.001d@002_0026 (Gītā 11.5cd) *ity astrāya phaṭ* / Thus is the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).”
Now, concerning meditation:
Oṃ! [This work] was awakened for Pārtha by the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa himself, and was composed in the midst of the Mahābhārata by Vyāsa, the sage of the Purāṇas.

I shall study the *Bhagavadgītā*, which rains down the nectar of non-duality (*advaita*), consists of eighteen chapters, and liberates one from worldly existence (*bhava*), by means of its recurring cycles of meaning. (1) Oṃ! In the heart is a blossomed lotus, the orb of the sun, moon, and fire.

May that Vāsudeva, who is the firm foundation, grant me auspiciousness— he whose expansion consists of the *praṇava*, who is indeed free from conceptual construction, immovable, supremely tranquil, light, and the essence of space. (2)
All the Upaniṣads are the cows; the milker is the son of Gopāla;
Pārtha is the calf; the wise one is the enjoyer; and the milk is the great nectar of the Gītā. (3) Oṃ, salutations be unto you, O Vyāsa of vast intellect!
O you whose long lotus-eyes are like full-blown lotuses,
by you the lamp consisting of wisdom has been ignited, filled with the oil of the *Bhārata*. (4)

Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, who has brought the celestial *pārijāta* tree to those who have sought refuge, who holds a goad and a staff in one hand, who bears the *mudrā* of knowledge, and who yields the nectar of the *Gītā*.
(5) Saṃjaya said:
Then, having seen the Pandava army drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached the Teacher and spoke these words:
"Behold, O Teacher, this great army of the sons of Pandu."
It was arrayed by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
Herein are heroes, great archers equal to Bhīma and Arjuna in battle:
Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the heroic King of Kāśī;
Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, that bull among men;
the valiant Yudhāmanyu, and the powerful Uttamaujas.
The son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī are all indeed great chariot-warriors (mahāratha).
But as for those among us who are distinguished, learn of them, O best of the twice-born;
I shall name to you those leaders of my army for the sake of identification.
Among all those leaders in the great army who are esteemed as heroes— yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, the victor in assembly,
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and likewise the son of Somadatta— [they are all here].
Moreover, many other heroes have risked their lives for my sake;
equipped with various weapons and missiles, they are all experts in warfare. That army of ours, protected by Bhīṣma, is not insufficient.
This force of theirs, protected by Bhīṣma, is sufficient;
stationed as you are in all the strategic positions according to your respective shares,
let all of you indeed protect Bhīṣma alone.
Then the powerful grandfather, the elder of the Kurus, raising his joy for him,
let out a lion’s roar and blew his conch shell loudly.
Thereupon, conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns [resounded].
They were struck down all at once, and that sound became tumultuous.
Then, standing upon a great chariot yoked with white horses,
Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava blew their divine conchs.
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta,
and Vṛkodara, the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew the Anantavijaya.
Nakula and Sahadeva, Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka, the king of Kāśī with his supreme bow, the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki.
O lord of the earth, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī,
and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, all blew their conchs individually.
That roar rent the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Making both the sky and the earth resound with a tumultuous roar,
the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bears the monkey, then raised his bow as the clash of weapons began and saw the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra standing firm in their positions.
Then, O lord of the earth, he spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies,
so that I may behold those who stand here desiring to fight."
"With whom must I fight in this undertaking of war? I shall observe those who have gathered here,
desiring to do what is pleasing to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as they prepare for battle."
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa,
having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies,
in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and before all the lords of the earth, spoke.
"O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here," he said.
There, Pārtha beheld standing his fathers, grandfathers,
teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends as well.
Seeing his fathers-in-law and friends, as well as all those kinsmen stationed in both armies, that son of Kuntī,
overcome by supreme compassion and despondent, spoke these words.
O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these kinsmen standing here eager for battle,
my limbs fail me and my mouth becomes parched;
a trembling comes over my body and my hair stands on end.
The Gāṇḍīva bow slips from my hand and my skin burns all over; I am unable to stand steady, and my mind seems to reel. O Keśava, I see these portents that are adverse.
And I do not perceive any good in slaying my own kin in battle. I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor sovereignty, nor pleasures.
Of what use is sovereignty to us, O Govinda? Of what use are enjoyments or even life itself?
For whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures—
these very people stand here in battle, having renounced both their lives and their wealth:
teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers.
"O Madhusūdana, even if they were to kill me, I do not wish to kill these— my maternal uncles, my fathers-in-law, my grandsons, my brothers-in-law, and my other kinsmen—
even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, let alone for the sake of the earth."
"O Janārdana, what joy could there be for us even after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra? By killing these aggressors, only sin would take hold of us.
Therefore, we ought not to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their kinsmen."
For how, O Mādhava, could we be happy after killing our own kin?
Even if these men, their minds overwhelmed by greed, do not perceive the evil caused by the destruction of the family and the sin in betraying friends.

O Janārdana, how could we— not perceiving the evil caused by the destruction of the lineage— fail to turn away from this sin? Upon the destruction of the lineage, the eternal family traditions perish.
When dharma is destroyed, unrighteousness (adharma) overcomes the entire family.
O Kṛṣṇa, through the prevalence of unrighteousness, the women of the family become corrupted.
O Vārṣṇeya, when women are corrupted, the intermixture of castes (varṇasaṃkara) arises.
The intermixture of castes leads to hell for both the destroyers of the family and the family itself;
indeed, their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
By these faults of the family-destroyers, which cause the intermingling of the social orders (varṇas), [the world is corrupted].
The eternal laws of birth and the laws of the family are destroyed. O Janārdana, we have heard that for those men whose family laws are destroyed, residence in hell is inevitable.

"Alas! We have resolved to commit a great sin, in that out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen. If they, with weapons in hand, were to kill me while I am unarmed and unresisting—"
"It would be more secure for me if the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were to slay me in battle.
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna, his mind agitated by grief, cast aside his bow and arrows and sat down upon the seat of the chariot.
Saṃjaya said:
To him who was thus overcome with compassion, whose eyes were clouded and filled with tears,
and who was despondent, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Arjuna, from where has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis? It is un-Aryan, it leads away from heaven, and it brings infamy."
"Do not yield to unmanliness, O Pārtha; it does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe!
Arjuna said:
"O Madhusūdana, O slayer of enemies, how shall I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are worthy of worship? For it would be better not to slay these high-souled gurus."
It is better to subsist on alms even in this world than to enjoy pleasures stained with blood by slaying one's elders for the sake of wealth and desire.
And we do not know which of these two is better for us:
whether we should conquer them, or whether they should conquer us;
for we do not desire to live after having slain those very people.
Those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand arrayed before me,
their very nature impaired by the defect of compassion;
with my mind bewildered regarding dharma, I ask you.
Tell me decisively that which is the highest good;
I am your disciple, instruct me who have sought refuge in you.
Indeed, I do not perceive [any other way] that might dispel my grief.
That which withers the senses—
having obtained on earth a prosperous kingdom without rivals, even the sovereignty over the gods— is sorrow.
Saṃjaya said:
Having thus spoken to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes,
said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and became silent.
O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies. The Blessed Lord said:
"You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom;
the wise do not mourn for the dead nor for the living. Your inner self has been struck down by human frailty."
Overcome by despair and delusion, he lost consciousness;
yet, seized by compassion, he gazed upon his kinsmen who had fallen into the very jaws of Death.
Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these rulers of men;
nor shall any of us ever cease to be hereafter.
Just as the embodied soul in this body passes through childhood, youth, and old age, so too does it enter another body.
In the same way, the attainment of another body occurs; the steadfast man is not deluded by this.
But the contacts with the senses, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are fleeting, coming and going, and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata.
For that man whom these do not disturb, O bull among men—
the wise one who is equal in pain and pleasure— is fit for immortality. There is no being for the non-existent, nor is there non-being for the existent.
The end of both of these has been perceived by those who see the truth. But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this imperishable.
"These bodies are said to have an end, belonging to the eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable embodied self; therefore, fight, O Bhārata!
He who thinks this [self] is a slayer, and he who thinks it is slain—"
Both of them do not understand this: that it neither kills nor is killed;
it is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will never cease to be again.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient,
this Self is not slain when the body is slain. He who knows this Self as indestructible, eternal, unborn, and immutable—
O Pārtha, how can that person cause anyone to be killed or kill anyone?
Just as a man, casting off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new; so does the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enter into others that are new.
Likewise, casting off worn-out bodies,
the embodied self enters into others that are new.
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it.
Water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it;
this is indivisible, this is unburnable, indeed neither moistenable nor dryable. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
This Self is said to be unmanifest, inconceivable, and unchangeable;
therefore, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.
Yet, if you consider this Self to be constantly born or constantly dying, [you still ought not to grieve].
Nevertheless, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve for him.
For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died;
therefore, you ought not to grieve over this inevitable matter.
Beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
Someone perceives this as a marvel.
One speaks of him as a marvel,
and likewise another hears of him as a marvel;
yet even having heard of him, no one at all truly knows him.
This embodied soul in the body of everyone is eternally indestructible, O Bhārata;
therefore, you ought not to grieve for any living beings.
Furthermore, considering your own duty, you ought not to waver.
For there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war;
such a battle, arrived by chance, is an open door to heaven. O Pārtha, happy are those Kṣatriyas who obtain such a war as this.
If, however, you do not engage in this righteous battle,
then, having abandoned your own duty and fame, you will incur sin;
and people will speak of your eternal infamy.
For one who has been highly esteemed, infamy is worse than death.
The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from battle out of fear; and having once been held in high regard by them, you will now fall into contempt.
Your enemies will speak many unspeakable words, reviling your prowess; what indeed could be more painful than that?
Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth.
Therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle;
having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same,
then engage in battle, and thus you shall not incur sin.

This wisdom has been declared to you from the standpoint of Sāṃkhya; now hear this [wisdom] regarding Yoga, O Pārtha, by which wisdom you shall cast off the bondage of action. In this, there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist.
Even a very small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear.
O joy of the Kurus, in this world the intellect characterized by resolute determination is single; for the intellects of those lacking such determination are indeed many-branched and infinite.

O Pārtha, those who are unwise, who delight in the ritualistic recitations of the Vedas and proclaim that "there is nothing else," utter this flowery speech which is devoted to desire, focused on heaven, and yields the fruit of rebirth through action.
Abounding in various ritual acts directed toward the attainment of enjoyment and power,
the resolute intellect is not established in meditative concentration for those who are deeply attached to enjoyment and power, whose minds have been carried away by such pursuits.

"The Vedas concern the realm of the three qualities; be free from these three qualities, O Arjuna. Be free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, beyond the acquisition and preservation of possessions, and self-possessed.
As much purpose as there is in a small reservoir when there is a flood of water everywhere,"
That much alone is the entitlement of a discerning Brahmin across all the Vedas:
your authority lies in action alone, never in its fruits.
Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment to inaction.
Established in yoga, perform your actions, O Dhanañjaya, having abandoned attachment; becoming the same in success and failure, equanimity is called yoga.
He whose undertakings here are all free from the bonds of desire—

He who has offered everything in renunciation is a true renouncer and he is wise. For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya; seek refuge in wisdom. Miserable are those whose motive is the fruit of action.
One endowed with wisdom casts off both good and evil deeds in this very world;
therefore, apply yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in action. Indeed, the wise who are endowed with wisdom, having abandoned the fruit born of action, [attain liberation].

Freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the state that is free from all suffering. When your intellect has transcended the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what has been heard and what is yet to be heard.
"When your intellect, which has been perplexed by the scriptures, shall stand unshakable and immovable in meditative concentration, then you will attain yoga. Arjuna said:
"What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, O Keśava, when he is established in samādhi?
What does the man of steady intellect speak, how does he sit, and how does he move?
The Blessed Lord said:
When one abandons all desires residing in the mind, O Pārtha,
and is satisfied by the Self alone through the Self, then one is said to be of steady wisdom.
One whose mind is unperturbed in sorrows and who is free from longing amidst pleasures— [is called steadfast].
Free from passion, fear, and anger, he is called a sage of steady wisdom.
He who is everywhere without attachment, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering various good and evil things— his wisdom is firmly established.

When one withdraws the senses from the objects of the senses, as a tortoise draws in its limbs from all sides, his wisdom is firmly established. The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied soul who abstains from food.
Except for taste, even taste itself ceases for him upon seeing the Supreme. For,
O son of Kuntī, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind of even a wise man who strives with diligence.
Restraining all these, one should sit disciplined, intent on Me;
for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established. In a person who dwells upon sense-objects, attachment to them arises.
From attachment arises desire; from desire, anger is born.
From anger comes delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory. From the loss of memory comes the destruction of discernment, and from the destruction of discernment, one perishes.

But one who moves among sense objects with the senses free from passion and hatred, being self-controlled and having a disciplined mind, attains serenity. With serenity, the destruction of all his sufferings arises.
For the intellect of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes established.

There is no wisdom for the undisciplined, nor is there meditative cultivation for the undisciplined; for one who does not cultivate, there is no peace, and for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness?
For when the mind follows after the wandering senses,
it carries away one's wisdom, just as the wind sweeps a boat upon the waters.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, [one must restrain them] in every way.
The wisdom of that person is firmly established who has withdrawn the senses from the objects of the senses.
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in immobility,
even so all desires enter him.
He attains peace, not the seeker of desires; that man who, having abandoned all desires, wanders free from longing,
without the sense of "mine," and without egoism— he attains peace.
"This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Abiding in this even at the time of death, one attains the liberation of Brahman.
Arjuna said:
"If you consider knowledge to be superior to action, O Janārdana,
then why do you urge me toward this terrible deed, O Keśava? With these seemingly contradictory words, you are, as it were, confusing my understanding."
"Therefore, tell me that one thing with certainty, by which I may attain the highest good.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O sinless one, in this world, a twofold path was declared by Me in the past."

For the Sāṃkhyas, it is through the yoga of knowledge; for the Yogis, it is through the yoga of action. A person does not attain freedom from action by merely abstaining from actions, nor does he achieve perfection simply through renunciation.
For indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action;
for everyone is driven helplessly to act by the qualities born of material nature.
He who sits restraining the organs of action while dwelling on them with the mind...
He whose soul is deluded regarding the objects of the senses is called one of false conduct. But he who, O Arjuna, restraining the senses by the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action without attachment— he is preeminent.
Perform your prescribed duty, for action is indeed superior to inaction;
even the mere maintenance of your body would not be possible through inaction. Apart from action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.
In the beginning, having created all beings together with sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures said:
"By this shall you propagate; let this be the cow of plenty that grants your desires."
"Nourish the gods with this; let those gods nourish you. Nourishing one another, you shall attain the highest good.
For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you the enjoyments you desire."
He who enjoys what has been given by them without giving to them in return is indeed a thief.
The virtuous who eat the remnants of sacrifice are freed from all sins;
but those sinful ones who cook for their own sake eat only sin.
From food all beings come into existence; from rain comes the production of food. From sacrifice comes rain, and sacrifice originates from action.
Know that action arises from the Veda (Brahman), and the Veda arises from the Imperishable (Akṣara).

Therefore, Brahman is omnipresent and eternally established in sacrifice. He who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion here on earth— sinful, delighting in the senses— he lives in vain, O Pārtha.
But for that man who finds delight only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self,
and who is content in the Self alone— for him there is no duty to be performed. He has no interest whatsoever here in what is done, nor in what is left undone.
And he has no dependence on any object for the sake of any living being.
Therefore, always perform the action that must be done without attachment; for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme.
"For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone. You ought to act as well, considering the necessity of maintaining the world;
for whatever a great man does, that very thing other people do."

Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that. O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by me; there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action.
For if I were not to engage in action tirelessly,
O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect. These worlds would perish if I did not perform action.

I would be the author of confusion and I would destroy these creatures. As the ignorant act with attachment to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.

One who is disciplined and acting with wisdom should not create a disturbance in the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should encourage them toward all actions, while himself performing them with detachment.
For it is the qualities of material nature that perform all actions in every way.
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer. But the knower of truth, O mighty-armed one, regarding the divisions of the qualities and their actions,
does not become attached, realizing that it is the qualities acting upon the qualities.
Those deluded by the qualities of *prakṛti* become attached to the actions of those qualities;
one who knows the Whole should not unsettle those dull-witted people who do not know the Whole.
Having renounced all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Supreme Self, [one should act].
Free from desire and free from the sense of "mine," fight with your fever dispelled. Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine,
full of faith and free from carping, they too are liberated from the bonds of action.
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—
know them to be deluded in all knowledge, lost, and devoid of discernment. Even a man of wisdom acts in accordance with his own nature.
All beings return to their own nature; what can restraint accomplish?
Attachment and aversion are established toward the objects of each sense-organ;
one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries.
Better is one’s own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed.
Death in one’s own duty is better; the duty of another is fraught with fear.
Arjuna said:
"Then by what impelled does this man commit sin,
O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force?
The Blessed Lord said:
"This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of *rajas*;
it is insatiable and most sinful—know this to be the enemy here in this world.
Arjuna said:
"How does this come to be, O Kṛṣṇa, and how does it increase? What is its nature and what is its conduct? Tell me, who am asking you, O Blessed Lord. The Blessed Lord said:
[Tell me] what its essence is and what its practice is, as I ask you.
This subtle and supreme enemy of embodied beings, together with the senses,
remains seated as if established in happiness, deluding [people], O Pārtha;
it consists of desire and anger, is terrible, and arises from arrogance and joy.
The ego, whose nature is self-conceit, is difficult for those of evil deeds to overcome;
it turns away his joy and bestows sorrow upon him,
and repeatedly deluding him, it causes him fear.
O Dhanañjaya, this is that turbid, base, and harmful influence among men— active with passion (rajas), deluded in nature, and ever watching for a flaw— which,
like smoke veiling fire or dust obscuring a mirror, shrouds the light of wisdom.
Just as an embryo is enveloped by the womb, so is this [world] enveloped by that;
knowledge is covered by this eternal enemy of the wise,
O son of Kuntī— [the enemy] whose form is desire, which is difficult to satisfy and like a fire.
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat;
through these, it deludes the embodied soul by veiling its knowledge.
Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, you must first restrain the senses.
Abandon this evil which destroys both knowledge and realization. They say that the senses are superior; the mind is superior to the senses;
the intellect is superior to the mind; and he who is beyond the intellect is the Supreme.
"Thus, having known that which is beyond the intellect and having steadied the self by means of the self,
slay the enemy, O mighty-armed one, who takes the form of desire and is difficult to overcome.
The Blessed Lord said:
I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat;
Vivasvat told it to Manu, and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
Thus, transmitted through this succession, the royal seers have known it.
"O scorcher of the foe, through the long course of time, this Yoga was lost here on earth.
That very same ancient Yoga has been declared by me to you today, for you are my devotee and my friend; indeed, this is the most supreme secret."
Arjuna said:
"Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier. How am I to understand this—that you taught [this] in the beginning?"
The Blessed Lord said:
Many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna. I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe.
Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, though I am the Lord of all beings, yet by presiding over my own material nature, I manifest myself through my own divine power (māyā).
For whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata...
Whenever there is a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself for the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness; I come into being age after age.

He who thus knows in truth my divine birth and action, upon leaving the body, does not undergo rebirth; he comes to me, O Arjuna. Those whose passion, fear, and anger have departed, who are absorbed in me, and who have taken refuge in me—

Many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained My state. In whatever way people approach Me, in that very same way do I reward them; O Pārtha, human beings follow My path in every respect.
Desiring the success of their actions, people here worship the gods;
for in the world of men, success born of action is quickly attained.
The fourfold order of society was created by me according to the distribution of qualities and actions.
Know Me also as the author of that [work], yet the unchanging non-agent.
Actions do not smear Me, nor do I have any desire for the fruit of action. He who understands Me thus is not bound by actions.
Knowing this, even the seekers of liberation of old performed action;
therefore, you too perform action alone, as it was performed by those of old, even more so than before.
Even the wise are bewildered as to what is action and what is inaction.

I shall declare that action to you, by knowing which you will be liberated from the inauspicious. For one must understand action, and one must understand improper action (*vikarman*), and one must also understand inaction (*akarman*); the course of action is profound.

He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions. He whose undertakings are all free from the will for desire and from purposeful intention—
The wise call him a scholar whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge;
having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent,
he does nothing at all even though fully engaged in action.

Free from desire, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions, performing action that is merely physical, he incurs no sin. Contented with whatever comes by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, and free from envy—
Remaining the same in both success and failure, one is not bound even after acting;
for one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge,
and who performs action for the sake of sacrifice, his entire karma is utterly dissolved.
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is absorbed in the work of Brahman, Brahman alone is to be attained. Other yogis worship sacrifice as the gods alone.
Others offer the sacrifice with the sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman;
others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint;
and others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses.
Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths as oblations into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge;
likewise, others perform sacrifices of material possessions, sacrifices of austerity, and sacrifices of yoga.

And ascetics of firm vows, for whom study and knowledge constitute sacrifice, offer the out-breath into the in-breath; others likewise offer the in-breath into the out-breath. Having restrained the movements of the out-breath and in-breath, they are devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Others, restricted in their food, offer the life-breaths into the life-breaths;
all these are knowers of sacrifice, whose taints have been destroyed by sacrifice. Partaking of the nectar that remains from the sacrifice, they go to the eternal Brahman.
This world does not belong to one who performs no sacrifice; how much less another, O best of the Kurus?
Thus, various kinds of sacrifices are spread out at the mouth of Brahman;
know them all to be born of action, and by knowing this, you shall be liberated.
O scorcher of the foe, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects;
for all action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge.
Know that [knowledge] by prostration, by inquiry, and by service.
The wise who perceive the truth will instruct you in that knowledge,
O Pāṇḍava, by knowing which you shall no longer fall into such delusion; through it,
