you shall see all beings without exception within yourself, and then within me.
Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners,
you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone,
O Arjuna; just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes.
Just as a fire reduces all fuel to ashes, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes. Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge;
one who is perfected through yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time.
The man of faith, devoted to it and with senses restrained, attains knowledge;
having attained knowledge, he reaches supreme peace without delay.
But the ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish.
For one whose mind is full of doubt, neither this world nor the next exists, nor is there happiness.
But for one who has renounced actions through yoga, whose doubts have been severed by knowledge, and who is self-possessed— O Dhanañjaya, actions do not bind him.
"Therefore, having severed with the sword of self-knowledge this doubt residing in your heart, which has arisen from ignorance, take refuge in yoga and arise, O Bhārata!
Arjuna said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions, and again you praise the yoga of action.
Tell me with certainty which one of these two is the better.
The Blessed Lord said:
Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good;
however, of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.
He who neither hates nor desires should be known as a perpetual renunciant.
For one who is free from dualities, O mighty-armed one, is easily liberated from bondage.
The ignorant, but not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct;
even by being properly established in only one, one obtains the fruit of both.
The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the practitioners of Yoga.
He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees. But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to achieve without Yoga.
The sage disciplined in yoga attains Brahman before long.
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has mastered the self and conquered the senses,
whose self has become the self of all beings— even while acting, he is not tainted.
"Even while seeing,
hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing,
speaking, releasing, grasping, opening, or closing his eyes, the disciplined knower of reality should think: 'I do nothing at all.'"

Holding the conviction that "the senses move among the objects of the senses," he who performs actions by placing them in Brahman and abandoning attachment is not tainted by evil, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
With body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone,
yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification. One who is disciplined, having renounced the fruit of action, attains peace that is final.
One who acts impelled by desire, being attached to the fruit, is bound.
Having renounced all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied soul dwells in happiness within the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action to be done.
The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor does He create the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is inherent nature that operates.
The All-pervading One accepts neither the sin nor the merit of anyone.
Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded. But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self, that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun.
With their intellects fixed on That, their selves identified with That, established in That, and having That as their supreme goal,
they go to the state from which there is no return, their impurities shaken off by knowledge—
even while repeatedly remembering This and engaging in their own duties.

Though they come into contact with them, they do not become attached, like the rays of the sun upon the mud. The wise perceive with equanimity a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste.
"Even here, rebirth has been conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity;

for Brahman is flawless and equal, and therefore they are established in Brahman. One should not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant, nor should one be agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant."
Steady-minded, undeluded, a knower of Brahman established in Brahman,
with his self unattached to external contacts, he finds that happiness which is in the Self;
with his self united in yoga with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable bliss.
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed sources of suffering;
they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī, and the wise man does not delight in them.
He who is able to endure them even here, before liberation from the body—
That man is disciplined and happy who has stilled the impulse arising from desire and anger.
He who finds happiness within, whose recreation is within, and whose light is indeed within—
that yogi, having become Brahman, attains the extinction of Brahman.

The sages, whose taints are exhausted, who have severed all duality, who are self-controlled, and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the Brahman-nirvāṇa— those ascetics who are free from desire and anger and whose minds are restrained.
For those who have realized the Self, the state of Brahman-nirvāṇa lies all around them. Having cast external objects of touch outside and having fixed the eyes between the eyebrows,
one should make the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the nostrils.
The sage who has restrained his senses, mind, and intellect, who is devoted to liberation,
and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed— he is indeed always liberated. [He is] the enjoyer of sacrifice and austerity, the Great Lord of all worlds.
Knowing me as the friend of all beings, he attains peace. The Blessed Lord said: He who performs the duty that must be done without depending on the fruit of action—
He is both a renunciant and a yogi, neither one who has abandoned the sacred fires nor one who is inactive.
Know that, O Pāṇḍava, what they call renunciation is itself yoga;
for no one becomes a yogi without having renounced all purposeful intention.

For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same person once he has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means. For when he is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, [he is established in yoga].
When one has renounced all volitional constructions, one is then said to have ascended to yoga. One should uplift oneself by means of the self; one should not let the self sink down.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
The self is the kinsman of that person by whom the self has been conquered by the self;
but for one who has not conquered the self, the self itself would act as an enemy in the state of enmity.
For one who has conquered the self and is tranquil, the supreme self is fully composed.
One whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realization, who remains unshakable amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honor and dishonor, whose senses are conquered,
and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal— such a yogi is said to be disciplined (yukta).
One who possesses an even mind toward friends, allies, enemies, neutrals, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen— toward the virtuous as well as the sinful— is preeminent.
Let the yogin, established in solitude, constantly discipline the self.

Solitary, with mind and self restrained, free from desire and possessions, having established a firm seat for himself in a clean place— neither too high nor too low, covered with kusha grass, a deerskin, and a cloth, one over the other— ;

There, having made the mind one-pointed and restraining the activities of the heart and senses, one should sit upon a seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self. Holding the body, head, and neck erect, motionless and steady.
Gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction,
with a tranquil self, free from fear, and established in the vow of celibacy,
he should sit disciplined, with his mind fixed on Me, intent on Me, and regarding Me as the Supreme Goal.

Thus constantly disciplining himself, the yogin of restrained mind attains the peace that culminates in nirvāṇa and abides in Me. Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all.
But for one who is not habituated to excessive sleep, nor for one who stays perpetually awake, O Arjuna— for one whose food and recreation are regulated, whose exertion in actions is regulated,
and whose sleep and waking are regulated— yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone,
free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be "yoked. Like a lamp set in a windless place that does not flicker— this is the simile taught.
When the mind of the yogin, restrained and practicing yoga upon the Self, comes to rest through the cultivation of yoga; when,
beholding the Self by means of the Self, he finds satisfaction in the Self alone.
That absolute happiness which is beyond the senses and perceivable by the intellect— abiding in which, one does not deviate from reality;
having gained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it.
That state established in which one is not shaken even by heavy suffering—
know that to be the dissociation from the union with suffering, designated as yoga. That yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency.
Having abandoned all desires born of volitional thought without exception, and having restrained the entire collection of senses on all sides by the mind alone,
one should gradually attain tranquility through the intellect held with firm resolve.
Having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone.

For supreme happiness comes to this yogin whose mind is perfectly tranquil, whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from taint. Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogin becomes cleansed of all impurity.
Through this happiness, he experiences the touch of Brahman, which is ultimate bliss.
With his self disciplined by yoga, he perceives the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self, seeing the same everywhere.
He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me—
for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me.
He who, established in unity, worships Me as abiding in all beings,
In every way, even while acting, that yogi dwells in Me;
O Arjuna, he who sees with equanimity everywhere by means of the analogy of himself—
whether it be pleasure or pain— that yogi is considered supreme.
Arjuna said:
"O Madhusūdana, regarding this yoga of equanimity which has been taught by you,
I do not perceive its steady persistence because of the mind's restlessness."
"O Kṛṣṇa, the mind is indeed restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind.
The Blessed Lord said:
Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain;
yet, O son of Kuntī, it is mastered through practice and dispassion.
Yoga is unattainable by one whose self is unsubdued—this is my conviction.
"But by one who has mastered the self and strives through the proper means, it can be attained.
Arjuna said:
"One who is endowed with faith but lacks discipline, whose mind has strayed from yoga—"
Desiring the path of the virtuous, yet bewildered on the way to Brahman,
with a distracted mind, wandering, and fallen under the sway of delusion—
having failed to attain perfection in yoga, O Kṛṣṇa, what goal does such a person reach?

O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, I pray that you completely sever this doubt of mine: does one who has fallen away from both paths perish like a scattered cloud, finding no support and utterly bewildered on the path of Brahman?
"For there is no one other than you who can truly resolve this doubt.
The Blessed One said:
"O Pārtha, neither in this world nor in the next does destruction exist for him."
For no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever goes to an evil state;
having attained the worlds of the merit-makers and dwelt there for eternal years,
he who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous.
Or else he is born into a family of wise yogis;
for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in the world.
There, he regains the connection with the wisdom acquired in his previous body.
And from that point, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even further toward perfection;
for by that very same prior practice, he is drawn forward even against his will.
Even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Brahman of sound.

But the yogi who strives with effort, having purified all taints and perfected himself through many births, then attains the supreme goal. The yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge.

The yogi is superior even to the performers of action; therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi. And among all yogis, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me, full of faith—he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined.
"O Blessed One, by the mere attainment of [this] name, everything is obtained;
just as rice crops fully ripen when a timely rain is merely seen.
The Blessed One said:
With your mind attached to me, O Pārtha, practicing yoga and taking refuge in me,
listen to how you shall know me fully and without doubt. I shall declare to you this knowledge, together with realized wisdom, in its entirety.

Having known which, nothing further remains here to be known. Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and attain perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect,
and likewise ego— this is my material nature (prakṛti) divided eightfold. But know that there is another, higher nature of mine, distinct from this.
O mighty-armed one, know that she is the life-force by which this world is sustained; all beings have her as their source. I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe.

There is nothing else whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya; all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread. I am the taste in water, O Kaunteya, and I am the radiance in the moon and the sun.
The syllable *praṇava* among all the Vedas, the sound in space, and the virile power (*pauruṣa*) among men; the pure fragrance in the earth, and I am the radiance in the fire;
the life-force in all beings, and I am the austerity in ascetics.
O Pārtha, know Me to be the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid. And I am the strength of the strong, devoid of desire and attachment.
"O bull among the Bharatas, I am desire that is not contrary to dharma among living beings.
Know that all states of being—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me."

Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities (*guṇas*), this entire world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable. For this divine illusion (*māyā*) of Mine, composed of the qualities, is difficult to overcome.
Those who take refuge in me alone cross over this illusion.
The foolish doers of evil, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in me;
their wisdom has been carried away by illusion, and they have resorted to a demonic nature.

O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom. Among them, the man of wisdom, who is constantly disciplined and devoted to the One alone, is preeminent.
For I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me.
All these [others] are indeed noble, but the man of knowledge, I am of the opinion, is My very Self; for, with a disciplined mind, he is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in Me, realizing that Vāsudeva is everything; such a great-souled person is very rare.
Those whose wisdom has been carried away by various desires take refuge in other deities.
Adhering to their respective disciplines according to their own innate natures,
whatever form each person desires to worship with faith,
I ordain that very same unwavering faith for them.
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that deity;
and from that, he indeed obtains his desires, which are ordained by me alone.
However, the fruit of those of small intelligence is finite.
Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me as well. Those who have perfected their vows go to the Siddhas; those who sacrifice to the spirits go to the spirits.
Those who follow the rites for the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits. The unintelligent think of me, who am unmanifest, as having attained manifestation.
Not knowing my supreme nature, which is immutable and unsurpassed, this world—
deluded by the yoga-māyā that veils me— does not recognize me as the unborn and imperishable; for I am not manifest to everyone.
"I know all beings of the past, O Arjuna, as well as those of the present and the future; but no one knows me. By the delusion of the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion, O Bhārata,"
O scorcher of the foe, at the time of creation all beings fall into delusion;
however, those people of meritorious deeds whose sin has come to an end,
being freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, worship Me with firm resolve.
Those who strive for liberation from old age and death by taking refuge in me,

they know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self (adhyātma), and all action (karman) in its entirety; and those who know me as the presiding deity of beings (adhibhūta), the presiding deity of the divine (adhidaiva), and the presiding deity of sacrifice (adhiyajña).
And even at the time of departure, those whose minds are disciplined know me;
clearly, the Kalpamañjarī has been offered as devotion to the Blessed One,
which fulfills every hope appropriate for one’s desire for spiritual practice.
Arjuna said:
"What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action (karma), O Supreme Person?
And what is declared to be the elemental (adhibhūta)? What is called the divine (adhidaiva)?"
"Who is the Lord of Sacrifice here in this body, O Madhusūdana?
And how are You to be known at the time of death by those of self-restraint?
The Blessed Lord said:
The syllable *oṃ* is the supreme Brahman; its inherent nature is called the inner self (*adhyātma*).
The emission that brings about the origin of beings is designated as action (*karman*).
The perishable state is the objective world (*adhibhūta*), and the Person (*puruṣa*) is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*).

O best among those who bear a body, I alone am the Adhiyajña here in this body. And at the time of death, he who departs casting off the body while remembering me alone attains my own state; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever state of being one remembers when one finally leaves the body,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, for one is constantly permeated by that state of being. Therefore, at all times, remember Me and fight.
With mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt.
By means of a mind disciplined through the yoga of practice, not wandering elsewhere,
one who contemplates Me, O Pārtha, attains the supreme, divine Person.
He who would meditate upon the ancient seer, the ruler, subtler than the subtle,
the sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable;
At the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga, [one should meditate on Him] who is of solar hue, beyond darkness.
Having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows,
he attains that divine Supreme Person,
whom those who know the Vedas call the Imperishable (akṣara).
That which ascetics free from passion enter,
and desiring which they lead the life of celibacy—
that state I shall declare to you in brief.
That state which all the Vedas declare, which all austerities proclaim, and desiring which they lead a life of celibate studentship— [that state I shall tell you briefly].
I shall tell you that state in brief:
having restrained all the gates of the senses and fixed the mind within the heart,
placing the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the head, one remains established in the practice of yoga-concentration (*yogadhāraṇā*).
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om" and remembering Me,
he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal. He who, with mind undistracted, remembers Me constantly and perpetually—

O Pārtha, I am easily attained by that ever-disciplined yogin. Having come to Me, those great-souled ones who have reached supreme perfection do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering.

All worlds, O Arjuna, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return; but having attained Me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist. Those who know the day of Brahmā to last for a thousand yugas, [know that his night is of the same duration].
Those people who know day and night understand that the night ends at the conclusion of a thousand yugas.
At the arrival of the day, all manifest entities emerge from the unmanifest;
at the arrival of the night, they dissolve back into that very same state known as the unmanifest.
This very same collection of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves helplessly at the arrival of night, O Pārtha; it comes forth again at the arrival of day.
But beyond that unmanifested state, there is another, eternal being, unmanifested and distinct from the unmanifested.
He who does not perish even when all beings perish is called the unmanifest and the indestructible; they say that is the supreme goal,
reaching which they do not return— that is My supreme abode.
That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion alone;
having attained Him, O Arjuna, yogis are not born again—
He within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded.

I shall now describe that time, O bull of the Bharatas, departing at which yogis go to the state of non-return, as well as to the state of return. Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice— 06,030.023a At what time yogis, having departed, go to the state of non-return, and likewise to the state of return, 06,030.023c that time I shall declare, O bull of the Bharatas.
06,030.024a Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—

Departing there, people who know Brahman go to Brahman. Smoke, night, the dark fortnight, and the six months of the sun’s southern course— having attained the lunar light during that time, the yogin returns.
These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are considered eternal.
By one a man goes to non-return; by the other he returns again.
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, O Arjuna, be ever disciplined in yoga at all times;
for whatever meritorious fruit is prescribed in the Vedas, in sacrifices, in austerities, and in acts of charity— [all that is attained by the yogi].
Having understood all this, the yogin transcends it all and attains the supreme, primordial state,
once the Supreme Lord has been realized through the penetration of all principles (*tattva*).
There is no state, whether internal or external, in which the All-pervading Lord does not shine.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall declare this most secret [knowledge] to you, who are free from malice.
This knowledge, together with realized wisdom (vijñāna), knowing which you shall be liberated from evil—
this is the royal science, the royal secret, this supreme purifier;
it is directly perceivable, in accordance with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable.
O scorcher of foes, those persons who lack faith in this dharma do not reach Me, but return to the path of the mortal cycle of rebirth.
By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded.
All beings dwell in Me, yet I do not dwell in them; nor do beings dwell in Me—behold My divine yoga! My Self, the sustainer of beings and the creator of beings, does not dwell within beings.
All-pervading, all-powerful, the primordial one, the creator of all, the seer of all;
omniscient, the beholder of all, the self of all, facing every direction—
just as the great wind, though eternally abiding in space, is omnipresent.
In the same way, understand that all beings abide in Me;
for thus do I move among all beings, unperceived,
having entered into the very nature of beings, both together with them and yet distinct from them.
O Kaunteya, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature; again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth. Taking hold of my own nature, I manifest them again and again.
This entire multitude of beings, being powerless under the sway of nature, acts;
yet those actions do not bind me, O Dhanañjaya,
for I sit as if indifferent, unattached to those actions.
Under my supervision, nature (prakṛti) produces the world of the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves. Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form.
Not knowing my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings,
they are of vain hopes, vain actions, and vain knowledge, devoid of discernment;
they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and titanic.
But those great-souled ones, O Pārtha, who have taken refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undivided minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings;
they constantly glorify me, striving with firm vows.
And others, ever-disciplined, worship Me with devotion, bowing down to Me;
yet others, sacrificing through the sacrifice of knowledge, worship Me as the One,
as the distinct, and as the manifold whose face is everywhere.
I am the ritual act, I am the sacrifice, I am the ancestral offering, and I am the medicinal herb.
I am the mantra, I alone am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation. I am the father of this world, its mother, its creator, and its grandfather.
He is the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Om, and indeed the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas;
He is the goal, the sustainer, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend;
He is the source of origin, the dissolution, the station, the treasure-house, and the imperishable seed.

I heat [the world], I withhold the rain, and I send it forth. I am both immortality and death, O Arjuna, and both being and non-being. Those who know the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin—
Having sacrificed with rituals, they pray for the path to heaven;
having attained the merit of the world of the lord of gods, they enjoy divine celestial pleasures in heaven.
Having enjoyed that vast world of heaven,
they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted;
thus do they follow the dharma of the three Vedas.
Those people who worship Me, thinking of no other, and who are ever-devoted, obtain what they desire, both here and hereafter; for them,
I provide security and well-being.

"Even those who are devotees of other deities and worship them, endowed with faith, they too, O son of Kuntī, worship Me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule. For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices."
But they do not know Me in truth; therefore they fall.
Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors. Those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to Me come to Me.
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water— that offering of devotion from one of purified soul, I accept.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, and whatever you give;
Whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī, do that as an offering unto Me;
thus you shall be liberated from the bonds of action consisting of good and evil fruits. With your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, being liberated, you shall come unto Me.
I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear. But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I am also in them.
Even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, [he is to be regarded as righteous].
He indeed should be considered virtuous, for he has rightly resolved;
he quickly becomes righteous in soul and attains eternal peace.
O Kaunteya, declare this with certainty: my devotee never perishes.

For even those who may be of low birth— women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras— by taking refuge in me, O Pārtha, they too attain the supreme goal. How much more so, then, the meritorious Brāhmaṇas and devoted royal sages?
Having reached this world which is impermanent and full of suffering, devote yourself to me.
Fix your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, and bow down to me. Thus, with your self disciplined and having me as your supreme goal, you shall come to me alone.
The Blessed Lord said: O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word,
which I shall speak to you, who are dear to me, out of a desire for your welfare.
Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin;
for I am the source of the gods and the great seers in every respect.
He who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—
He who is undeluded among mortals is liberated from all sins.
Intellect, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, tranquility,
pleasure, pain, birth, non-existence, fear, and even fearlessness— these belong to him.
Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—
these various states of beings arise from me alone.
So too did the seven great seers of old and the four Manus.
Those born of my own being from my mind— of whom these creatures in the world are the offspring—
know this majesty and power of mine in its true essence;
he is joined by unwavering yoga, of this there is no doubt.
"From me all proceeds; I am the source of all"—
thinking thus, the wise, endowed with devotion, worship me, their minds fixed on me and their lives surrendered to me, enlightening one another.
Speaking of me constantly, they find contentment and delight. To those who are ever-devoted and worship me with love, I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to me.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge. Arjuna said:
"You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the highest purity.
All the sages, as well as the celestial sage Nārada, call you the eternal, divine Puruṣa, the primordial God, the unborn and all-pervading Lord."
Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa have said so, and you yourself tell me this;
O Keśava, I consider all that you say to me to be the truth.
For neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know your manifestation.
O Supreme Person, O Source of beings, Lord of beings, God of gods, Master of the universe, You alone know Yourself by Yourself.
You ought to describe, without omission, Your divine self-manifestations.
By which manifestations you remain pervading these worlds—
O Yogi, how may I know you while constantly meditating upon you?
And in what various states, O Blessed One, are you to be contemplated by me?
"O Janārdana, tell me again in detail of your own yoga and your divine manifestations; for there is no satiety for me as I listen to this nectar. The Blessed Lord said:

Come now, I shall declare to you my divine self-manifestations, O best of the Kurus, according to their principal ones; there is no end to my expansion. I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings.
I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings.
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among luminous bodies I am the radiant Sun. Among the Maruts I am Marīci; among the stars I am the Moon.

Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, I am Vāsava. Among the senses, I am the mind; among beings, I am consciousness. Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am the Lord of Wealth.
Among the Vasus I am Pāvaka, and among the peaked mountains I am Meru.
Know me, O Pārtha, to be Bṛhaspati, the chief of the household priests;
among army commanders I am Skanda, and among bodies of water I am the ocean.
Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; among words, I am the single syllable Om.
Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa-yajña); among immovable things, I am the Himalaya. Among all trees, I am the Aśvattha; and among the divine seers, I am Nārada.
Among the Gandharvas, know me to be Citraratha; among the Siddhas, the sage Kapila; among horses, Uccaiḥśravas, born of the nectar of immortality;
among lordly elephants, Airāvata; and among men, the king of men.
Of weapons, I am the thunderbolt; of cows, I am the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhuk. I am Kandarpa, the progenitor of offspring; of serpents, I am Vāsuki.
Of the Nāgas, I am Ananta; of aquatic creatures, I am Varuṇa.

Among the ancestors I am Aryaman; among those who restrain, I am Yama. Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who calculate time, I am Time (Kāla). Among beasts I am the king of beasts; and among birds, I am Vainateya.
Of purifiers I am the wind; among those who bear weapons, I am Rāma.
Of sea-monsters I am the makara; of flowing streams I am the Gaṅgā.
Of creations, O Arjuna, I am the beginning, the end, and the middle as well.
Of the sciences, I am the science of the Self; of those who debate, I am the logic.
Of letters, I am the letter *a*; and of compound words, I am the copulative compound (*dvandva*). I alone am inexhaustible time; I am the Ordainer whose face is turned everywhere.
I am death, the destroyer of all, and I am the origin of those things yet to be.
Among women, I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness.
Likewise, among the Sāmans I am the Bṛhat-sāman, and among meters I am the Gāyatrī.

Among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons, the flower-bearing spring. Among plants I am barley; among metals, I am gold. Among cattle I am the bull of Surabhi; and among unguents, I am clarified butter.
O son of Pāṇḍu, among all species of grass I am the *darbha*;
among those who practice deception I am gambling; among the radiant I am splendor; I am victory, I am resolve, and among those possessed of strength I am strength.
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya.
Among the sages I am Vyāsa; among poets, I am Uśanas the poet. Among those who subdue, I am the rod of punishment; among those who seek victory, I am policy.
I am the silence among secrets, and I am the knowledge of those who possess knowledge. Moreover, O Arjuna, I am that which is the seed of all beings;
there exists no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without me.
O scorcher of foes, there is no end to my divine manifestations;
this detailed expansion of my manifestations has been declared by me only in brief.
Whatever being possesses majesty, splendor, or power—
Understand that each of these has arisen from but a fraction of my splendor. Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge to you, O Arjuna?
Sustaining this entire universe with but a single portion of myself, I stand as the world.
Arjuna said: By those words which you have spoken for my benefit— the supreme secret known as the Adhyātma— this delusion of mine has been dispelled.
O lotus-eyed one, the origin and dissolution of beings have indeed been heard by me in detail from you, as well as your imperishable majesty. O Supreme Lord, it is exactly as you describe yourself.
O Supreme Person, I desire to see your divine form,
O Lord; if you think it is possible for me to see it,
then, O Lord of Yoga, show me your imperishable self.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and thousands—
divine, of various kinds, and of diverse colors and shapes."
Behold the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts;
behold, O Bhārata, many wonders never seen before.
Behold today, all here together, the entire universe with its moving and unmoving beings.
O Guḍākeśa, whatever else you wish to see within my body, you are not able to see me with these very eyes of yours. I shall give you a divine eye; behold my sovereign yoga.
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great lord of yoga,
then revealed his supreme sovereign form to Pārtha.
Having many mouths and eyes, he was a sight of many wonders; he wore many divine ornaments and wielded many uplifted divine weapons;
he was clad in divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes.

The god consists entirely of wonders; he is infinite and has faces on every side. If the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth simultaneously in the sky, that might resemble the splendor of that Great-Souled One.

Then the son of Pāṇḍu beheld the entire universe, though manifoldly divided, situated within the single body of the God of gods. Thereupon, Dhanañjaya was overcome with wonder, and his hair stood on end.
Having bowed his head to the God with palms joined in reverence,
Arjuna spoke:
"O God, I behold the gods within Your body."
Likewise, all the hosts of various supernatural beings, Brahmā the Lord seated upon his lotus-throne,
all the sages, and the divine serpents.
I see you with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes,
possessing infinite forms on all sides; I see neither your end, nor your middle, nor again your beginning.
O Lord of the Universe, O Universal Form, I behold you wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a discus—
a mass of splendor blazing on all sides.
I behold you, difficult to gaze upon from every side,
possessing the immeasurable radiance of blazing fire and the sun;
you are the supreme, imperishable reality to be known.
You are the supreme repository of this entire universe;
you are the imperishable protector of the eternal dharma;
you are considered by me to be the ancient Puruṣa.
I behold you, who are without beginning, middle, or end, possessed of infinite vigor, with infinite arms and eyes like the moon and sun,
and whose mouths are like blazing fires.
For this entire space between heaven and earth, as well as all the directions, is pervaded by you alone, who scorch this universe with your own splendor.
"O Great-Souled One, seeing this wondrous and fierce form of yours, the three worlds are deeply distressed; indeed,
these hosts of gods are entering into you."
Some, filled with fear, utter "Svasti" with palms joined in reverence;
the hosts of great seers and perfected beings praise you with abundant hymns of praise.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are Sādhyas; the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās;
the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas.
And they all gaze at you in amazement,
O mighty-armed one, at your great form with many mouths and eyes, and many arms, thighs, and feet.
Seeing that [form] with many bellies and many formidable fangs, the worlds, as well as I, were struck with terror—
[that form] which touched the sky, was blazing, and possessed many colors.
O Viṣṇu, seeing you with your mouth wide open and your large eyes blazing, my inner self is deeply distressed; I find neither fortitude nor peace.
Having seen your mouths, terrifying with tusks and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction,
I no longer know the directions and find no peace.
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe!
And here are all these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with the hosts of earthly rulers.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer,
together with our own foremost warriors,
are swiftly entering your mouths.
With fangs formidable and terrifying,
resembling a thousand suns,
they were poised at that moment to devour the world.
Being slain by men of various forms, those warriors—
the followers of Yudhiṣṭhira and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— enter your inconceivable mouth.
Though all these have been cut by various weapons,
they have surely been struck down by your splendor;
for thus they have entered your body.
Some were seen caught between the teeth with their heads crushed,
like the many torrents of water in rivers.
Just as rivers rush toward the ocean,
so do these heroes of the world of men enter your blazing mouths.
Just as moths, with full force, enter a blazing fire for their own destruction,
even so do worlds enter [it] for their destruction.
With your blazing mouths, you lick and devour all the worlds on every side, possessing full force even as you do so.
O Viṣṇu, having filled the entire world with your splendors, your fierce radiances scorch everything;
tell me, who are you of such formidable form?
Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious. I desire to know you, the primordial one, for I do not understand your activity.
The Blessed Lord said:
I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown great;
I have begun here to gather in the worlds.
Even without you, all these warriors who stand arrayed in the opposing armies shall cease to exist; therefore,
arise and win glory.
"Having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
These have already been slain by me alone;
be merely the instrument, O Savyasācin."
"Droṇa and Bhīṣma, Jayadratha and Karṇa, as well as other heroic warriors—
slay them when they have already been slain by me; do not be distressed."
"Fight, and you shall conquer your enemies in battle.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard these words of Keśava;
With palms joined in reverence and trembling, the diadem-wearing Arjuna,
bowing down again and again, spoke to Kṛṣṇa with a faltering voice, utterly terrified.
Arjuna said:
"It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that by Your glorification the world rejoices and becomes devoted."
The *rakṣasas* flee in terror in all directions,
and all the hosts of *siddhas* pay homage.
And why, O Great-Souled One, should they not bow down to you?
To the one greater even than Brahmā, the original creator; O infinite Lord of gods, abode of the universe,
you are the imperishable, that which is both being and non-being, and that which is beyond them.
You are the primordial god, the ancient Puruṣa; you are the supreme repository of this universe. You are the knower and that which is to be known, and the highest abode.
By you the universe is pervaded, O you of infinite forms;
you are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, and the Moon;
you are Prajāpati and the Great-Grandfather.
Homage, homage be to you a thousand times;
and yet again, further still, homage, homage to you— O you who are without beginning and of incomparable power!
O Lord of All, O You of all great manifestations!
Homage to You from the front and from behind;
let there be homage to You from every side, O All-encompassing One.
O Lord, indeed no one else in this world, nor even in the three realms, is seen to possess such inconceivable deeds; you alone possess infinite power and immeasurable valor.
You pervade everything, therefore You are everything.
Whatever was said rashly, thinking "O friend"—
"O Kṛṣṇa," "O Yādava," "O friend"— [for that I seek Your forgiveness].
Whether out of ignorance regarding this greatness of yours,
or through negligence, or even out of affection,
or if you were treated with disrespect for the sake of jest;
Whether alone, O Acyuta, or even in the presence of others regarding dwellings, beds, seats, and food,
I now ask forgiveness from you, the immeasurable one.
"You are the father of this world, both moving and unmoving; you are its object of worship, its teacher, and its most venerable elder.
There is no one equal to you, much less anyone superior."
Since your power is peerless even throughout the three worlds, I bow down, prostrating my body, and seek to propitiate you, the Lord worthy of praise.
O God, as a father toward his son, as a friend toward a friend, and as a lover toward his beloved, you ought to endure [this];
for your divine deeds are wondrous.
The ancient seers of old also remember this:
there is no other creator of the world; you alone are the sustainer, the ordainer, the all-pervading lord, and existence itself.
What indeed could be a wonder for you that is unendurable, or what could be impossible for you that I shall proclaim from others? For you yourself are truly the creator of all.
O All-pervading One, therefore all this is you alone;
this most wonderful deed is not difficult for you,
for indeed no comparison for your deeds exists.
There is no limit to your virtues—
neither to your splendor, nor to your strength, nor to your prosperity;
these deeds of yours are truly marvelous.
The sages of old have declared that there is no limit to your virtues,
nor to your splendor or your power, O Viṣṇu.
Having seen what was never seen before, I am thrilled;
yet my mind is distressed with fear. O Lord, show me that very same form!
Be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Abode of the Universe!
I wish to see you just as before— wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with a discus in hand.
"In that very form with four arms,
become thousand-armed, O you whose form is the universe!
The Blessed Lord said:
O Arjuna, being pleased with you, I have through my own yoga shown you this supreme form—
effulgent, universal, infinite, and primordial.
That which has never been seen by me before through anything other than you—
neither by the study of the Vedas and sacrifices, nor by gifts,
nor by ritual acts, nor by fierce austerities.
"O hero of the Kurus, it is impossible for anyone other than you to behold me in such a form in the world of men;
let there be no distress in you, nor any state of confusion."
Having seen this terrible form of mine,
you are now free from fear and your mind is joyful; behold once more this very same form of mine.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva again showed his own form.
And the Great-souled One, assuming once more his gentle form, comforted him who was terrified;
Arjuna said:
"O Janārdana, having seen this gentle human form of yours,
I have now become composed in mind and have returned to my natural state.
The Blessed Lord said:
"You have seen this form of mine which is so very difficult to behold;
even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can it be attained."
It is indeed possible to see Me in such a form as you have seen Me; however,
O Arjuna, it is only by means of undivided devotion that I can be known and seen in this way in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe.
"He who performs my work, who regards me as the supreme goal, who is devoted to me, who is free from attachment,
and who is without enmity toward all beings— he, O Pāṇḍava, comes to me.
Arjuna said:
"Among those who, thus constantly disciplined, worship you with devotion,
and those who worship the imperishable and unmanifest— the former, which group is most skilled in yoga? The Blessed Lord said:
Those who, fixing their minds on me, worship me with constant discipline,
endowed with supreme faith— they are considered by me to be the most perfectly disciplined.
But those who worship the Indestructible, the Undefined, the Unmanifest—
All-pervading, inconceivable, immutable, immovable, and eternal— those who,
having restrained the entire collection of their senses, possess a mind of equanimity toward all things and are devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain Me alone.

The affliction of those whose minds are attached to the unmanifest is greater; for the goal that is unmanifest is attained with difficulty by embodied beings. But those who, having renounced all actions in Me, are devoted to Me—
Those who worship me, meditating on me with an undivided yoga,
for them— whose minds are absorbed in me— I become the deliverer from the ocean of the mortal cycle of rebirth, O Pārtha; this happens before long.
Fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me.
Thereafter, you shall dwell in Me alone; of this there is no doubt. But if you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me, [then practice yoga].
Therefore, O Dhanañjaya, seek to attain Me through the yoga of constant practice. If you are unable even to practice, then be intent on My work;
by performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection.
But if you are unable even to do this, take refuge in my yoga and then renounce the fruits of all actions with a self-controlled mind.
For knowledge is better than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge.
From meditation comes the renunciation of the fruits of action; from renunciation follows peace immediately thereafter.
One who is not hostile toward any living being, but is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, equal in pleasure and pain, and patient—[he is a yogi].

The yogi who is always contented, self-controlled, and firm in resolve; who has dedicated his mind and intellect to Me—he, my devotee, is dear to Me. He from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world;
He who is free from joy, impatience, fear, and agitation; he who is unattached, pure, skillful, indifferent, and free from distress;
he who has renounced all undertakings—he who is my devotee is dear to me.
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and who is full of devotion— he is dear to Me.
He who is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor;
He who is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and free from attachment; to whom blame and praise are equal, who is silent, content with whatever comes,
homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion— that man is dear to Me.
But those who worship this immortal nectar of dharma as it has been taught, full of faith, regarding Me as the supreme goal— they, being devoted, are exceedingly dear to Me.
Arjuna said:
"Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the field and the Knower of the field—O Keśava, I desire to know this: knowledge and the object of knowledge. The Blessed Lord said:

I shall explain to you, O Bhārata, this knowledge and the object of knowledge: namely, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), as well as the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
This body, O son of Kuntī, is designated as the "field."
Those who know this call him the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). And know me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata.
That which is the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field—that, in my opinion, is true knowledge.

Listen to me in brief concerning that field— what it is, of what nature, what its modifications are, from whence it arises, and who it is, as well as his powers; [this] has been sung by the seers in many ways, separately, through various Vedic meters.
And by means of the words of the Brahma-sūtras, which are logical and definitive:
the great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest;
the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five objects of the senses.
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate [of the body], volition, and fortitude—
this is declared to be the field (kṣetra) in brief, along with its modifications. Humility, freedom from hypocrisy, non-violence, forbearance, and uprightness;
Service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, self-restraint, dispassion toward the objects of the senses, as well as freedom from egoism,
and the contemplation of the evils of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering.
Non-attachment and absence of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth; constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant;
and unswerving devotion to Me through the yoga of undivided concentration.
Frequenting solitary places, a distaste for the assembly of people, constant devotion to the knowledge of the inner self, and the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality—
this is declared to be knowledge; that which is contrary to this is ignorance.
I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality:
the beginningless Supreme Brahman is said to be neither being nor non-being.
It has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all;
appearing to possess the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses; unattached, yet the sustainer of all; free from the *guṇas*, yet the experiencer of the *guṇas*.
It exists both outside and within all beings, both unmoving and moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near. It is undivided among beings, yet it appears as if divided.
That which is to be known is the sustainer of beings, the devourer, and the source of all;
it is said to be the light of even the lights, beyond darkness.
It is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge, seated in the heart of every being.
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been briefly described. Having understood this, my devotee attains to My state of being.
Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless.
Know that both transformations and the qualities (guṇas) arise from primordial nature (prakṛti).
Primordial nature is said to be the cause in the agency of action and its instruments;
the person (puruṣa) is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain.
For the person, situated in material nature, experiences the qualities born of nature;
attachment to these qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. He is the witness, the permitter, the supporter, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord.
And he is also called the Supreme Self, the supreme Person within this body. He who thus knows the Person and Prakṛti along with its qualities,
no matter how he may conduct himself, is not born again.
Some perceive the Self within themselves by means of meditation through the self;
others by the yoga of Sāṃkhya, and still others by the yoga of action.
But others, not knowing this, worship having heard it from others.
Even they, being devoted to sacred revelation, surely transcend death. Know,
O bull of the Bharatas, that whatever being is born, whether stationary or moving, it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field.
He who sees the Supreme Lord dwelling equally in all beings,
remaining undecaying while they perish— he truly sees.
For seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, he does indeed see.

He does not destroy himself by himself; therefore, he goes to the supreme goal. And he who sees that actions are being performed in every way by nature alone, and likewise sees the self as a non-agent—he truly sees.
When one perceives the diversity of beings as abiding in the One,
and likewise perceives their expansion from that very source, then one attains Brahman.
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this Supreme Self is immutable.
O son of Kuntī, although situated within the body, it neither acts nor is it tainted;
just as space, being all-pervading, is not tainted because of its subtlety,
so too the Self, though dwelling everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
Just as the one sun illuminates this entire world, so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illuminate the entire field. Thus,
by means of the eye of knowledge, one perceives the distinction between the field and the Knower of the field.
Those who know the liberation from the nature of the elements go to the Supreme.
The Blessed Lord said:
Once more I shall declare that knowledge, the best of all forms of knowledge.

Having known this, all the sages have attained supreme perfection beyond this world; having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have come to a state of similarity with me. Even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer.
My womb is the Great Brahman; in it I place the germ. From that, O Bhārata, occurs the birth of all beings.
Whatever forms are produced in all wombs, O Kaunteya, they arise from that.

Of these, the Great Brahman is the womb; I am the seed-bestowing Father. Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities born of material nature (prakṛti), O mighty-armed one, bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body.
Therein, sattva, being stainless, is illuminating and free from affliction; O sinless one, it binds by attachment to pleasure and attachment to knowledge.
Know that rajas is of the nature of passion and arises from thirst and attachment.
O son of Kuntī, it binds the embodied soul through attachment to action.
Know that *tamas* arises from ignorance and deludes all embodied beings;
O Bhārata, it binds them through negligence, laziness, and sleep.
Sattva attaches one to happiness, O Bhārata; rajas to action;
and tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence. Rajas and tamas, having overcome sattva, prevail, O Bhārata.
When passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas) prevail over darkness, goodness,
and passion respectively, and when illumination arises through all the gates of this body, then one should know that goodness has increased.
Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing—
these arise when rajas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas. Lack of light, inactivity, negligence, and even delusion [arise when tamas has increased].
O joy of the Kurus, when darkness has increased, these qualities arise;
but when one who bears a body meets death while goodness has increased, then he attains the stainless worlds of those who know the highest.
Having gone to dissolution in *rajas*, one is born among those attached to action;
likewise, having dissolved in *tamas*, one is born in the wombs of the deluded. They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by *sattva*.
Suffering is the fruit of *rajas*, while ignorance is the fruit of *tamas*.
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas* arises greed;
from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance itself.
Those established in *sattva* go upward; those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle; and those of *tamas*, abiding in the conduct of the lowest quality, go downward.
When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities (*guṇas*), [he attains liberation].
And he who knows that which is beyond the qualities attains My state. Having transcended these three qualities, which arise from the body,
the embodied soul, liberated from birth, death, old age, and suffering, partakes of immortality.
Arjuna said:
"By what marks, O Lord, does one transcend these three qualities?
What is his conduct, and how does he go beyond these three qualities?"
The Blessed Lord said:
O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, or even delusion when they arise, nor does he long for them when they cease.

Sitting like one who is indifferent, he who is not shaken by the qualities (guṇas), who remains established in the thought "it is only the qualities that are moving," and does not waver; who is equal in pain and pleasure, self-abiding, and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same.
He who is steady-minded, to whom the pleasant and unpleasant are equal, for whom censure and self-praise are the same,
who is equal in honor and dishonor, equal toward the factions of friend and foe,
and who has renounced all undertakings— he is said to have transcended the qualities.
And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion,
having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman;
for I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the immutable.
[Regarding] the eternal Dharma and absolute bliss,
the Blessed One said:
"They speak of the imperishable Aśvattha tree as having its roots above and its branches below."
The Vedas are its leaves; he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
Its branches spread below and above, nourished by the qualities (guṇas) and having sense-objects as their sprouts.
And its roots extend downward, trailing through the world of men as they follow after karma;
its form is not perceived here in such a way.
It has no end, no beginning, and no foundation—
this *aśvattha* tree with its deeply rooted roots;
having cut it down with the firm weapon of non-attachment, [one must then seek that goal].
Therefore, that goal must be sought,
reaching which they do not return again;
to that very Primal Person I resort.
From whom this ancient course of action has proceeded— those who are free from pride and delusion, who have conquered the fault of attachment,
who are ever devoted to the supreme self, and whose desires have ceased.
Freed from the dualities known as pleasure and pain,
those who are undeluded go to that imperishable state.
Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that.
That supreme abode of Mine, having gone to which they do not return,
is My very own eternal portion, which has become the individual soul in the world of living beings;
it draws toward itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in material nature.
Whatever body the Lord (Īśvara) acquires, and whatever body he departs from,
he goes forth taking these [senses] with him, just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.
These are the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the sense of taste, and the sense of smell.
Having presided over the mind, this [Self] experiences sense objects—whether departing, staying, or enjoying while endowed with the qualities (guṇas).
The deluded do not perceive it; those who possess the eye of knowledge perceive it.
Striving yogis behold Him established within themselves;
yet those of unrefined self, though striving, do not behold Him, being devoid of wisdom. That splendor residing in the sun which illumines the entire world—
Know that the splendor which is in the moon and that which is in fire is my own. Entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my vital energy;
and becoming the sap-filled Soma, I nourish all medicinal herbs.
Becoming the Vaiśvānara fire and taking refuge in the bodies of living beings, joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I digest the four kinds of food.
And I am seated in the heart of everyone.
From Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss; by all the Vedas I alone am to be known;
I am the author of the Vedanta and the knower of the Vedas as well.

There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. All beings are the perishable; the one who stands firm (the unchanging) is called the imperishable. But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self.
The imperishable Lord, having entered the three worlds, sustains them;
since I transcend the perishable and am even superior to the imperishable,
I am therefore celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
He who, undeluded, thus knows me as the Supreme Person— he,
O Bhārata, being all-knowing, worships me with his whole being.
Thus has this most secret teaching been declared by me, O sinless one.
Having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done. The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge—
Generosity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, austerity, uprightness,
non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of malice,
compassion for all beings, lack of covetousness, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness;
Energy, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from malice, and lack of excessive pride—
these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with divine fortune.
Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, and harshness likewise [belong to the other].
And ignorance belongs to one born to the demoniacal nature, O Pārtha;
the divine nature is considered to lead to liberation, while the demoniacal leads to bondage.
Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava, for you are born to the divine nature.
In this world, there are two types of creation of beings: the divine and the demonic.
The divine has been described at length; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demonic.
People of demonic nature do not understand the path of action nor the path of renunciation.
In them, neither purity nor right conduct nor truth is found. They say that this world is without truth, without foundation, and without a Lord;
it is produced by mutual union, having nothing else as its cause but desire.

Holding fast to this view, their souls ruined and their intellects small, they exert themselves in fierce deeds for the destruction of the world, being enemies of all; relying on insatiable desire, they are possessed by hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance.
Out of delusion, having grasped false attachments, they engage in impure observances;
relying on immeasurable anxieties that end only with death,
they are devoted solely to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, convinced that "this is all there is."
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and devoted to desire and anger, they strive for the sake of sensual enjoyment, accumulating wealth by unjust means, thinking:
"This has been gained by me today; this desired object I shall obtain."
"This exists, and this wealth shall be mine again;
that enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy."
"I am wealthy and well-born; who else is equal to me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, I shall rejoice"—thus are they deluded by ignorance.
Confused by manifold thoughts, they are enveloped in the snare of delusion.
Addicted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, they fall into an impure hell. Self-conceited, arrogant, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride,
they perform sacrifices under the name of sacrifice, yet out of hypocrisy and contrary to the prescribed rules.
Taking refuge in egoism, power, arrogance, lust, and wrath—
envious and hating Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others—
I cast those hateful, cruel, and lowest of men into cycles of worldly existence.
I incessantly hurl the inauspicious ones into demonic wombs alone.
Having entered a demonic womb, deluded from birth to birth,
they fail to reach me, O son of Kuntī, and from there they go to the lowest state.
This threefold gate of hell, which leads to the ruin of the self—
namely, lust, anger, and greed— one should therefore renounce these three.
O son of Kuntī, a man who is liberated from these three gates of darkness [is freed].
He who practices what is for his own welfare thereby attains the supreme goal. But he who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims,
achieves neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
"Therefore, let scripture be your authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
having ascertained what is prescribed by the ordinances of scripture, you should perform your duty here.
Arjuna said:
"Those who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, worship with faith—what is their standing, O Kṛṣṇa? Is it in goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), or darkness (tamas)?
The Blessed Lord said:
Faith is of three kinds among embodied beings; it arises from their own nature.
It is *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*—hear now about that. O Bhārata, the faith of every person is in accordance with their inner disposition (*sattva*).
This person consists of faith; whatever his faith is, that he truly is.
Those of sattvic nature worship the gods, those of rajasic nature worship the yakṣas and rākṣasas, and other people of tamasic nature worship the spirits of the dead and hosts of elemental beings.
Those people who perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures— being possessed of hypocrisy and egoism, and impelled by the force of desire and passion—
torment the aggregate of elements within their own bodies, being devoid of wisdom.
And know those who harbor me within their bodies to be of demonic resolve. Furthermore, food is dear to everyone in three ways;
likewise, sacrifice, austerity, and charity—listen now to this distinction between them.
Foods that increase longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy,
which are savory, unctuous, substantial, and pleasing to the heart, are dear to those of sattvic nature.
Those that are pungent, sour, salty, excessively hot, sharp, dry, and burning—
The foods favored by those of passionate nature (rājasa) bring about suffering, grief, and disease; food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, and left over,
as well as that which is impure and the leavings of others— such food is dear to those of dark nature (tāmasa).
That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits,
with the mind composed in the thought "sacrifice must indeed be performed," is *sāttvika*.
But that which is performed aiming for a fruit, and even for the sake of ostentation, is [rajasika].

O best of the Bharatas, know that sacrifice to be *rājasa* which is performed [with such motives]. That sacrifice which is devoid of scriptural injunctions, where no food is distributed, which lacks mantras and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
and is bereft of faith, is declared to be *tāmasa*.
Worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, and non-violence—this is called bodily austerity.
Speech that causes no agitation, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial—[this is called austerity of speech].
The practice of private Vedic recitation is said to be austerity consisting of speech. Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint,
and purity of intention— this is called mental austerity.
That threefold austerity which is performed by men with supreme faith, by those who are disciplined and free from desire for fruit, is declared to be *sāttvika*.
But that austerity which is practiced for the sake of gaining respect, honor, and worship, and which is motivated by hypocrisy—
That which is performed here [in this world] as unstable and impermanent is declared to be *rājasa*.
That austerity (*tapas*) which is performed with a deluded grasp out of self-inflicted pain,
or for the sake of destroying another, is described as *tāmasa*.
That gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given," to one who cannot return the favor,
at the right place, at the right time, and to a worthy recipient— that gift is declared to be *sāttvika*.
But that which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again, with a view toward a fruit;
That gift which is given with distress is declared to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients,
without respect and with contempt, is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

"Oṃ tat sat"—this is declared to be the threefold designation of Brahman. By means of this, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were ordained in ancient times. Therefore, having uttered "Oṃ," the acts of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity [are performed].
These proceed constantly, as prescribed by the rules, for those who discourse on Brahman.
Thus, without aiming for a fruit, acts of sacrifice, austerity,
and various acts of giving are performed by those desiring liberation.
The word "sat" (existent) is employed in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness;
likewise, O Pārtha, the word "sat" is applied to a praiseworthy action.
Furthermore, steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and charity is called "sat."
And action performed for that purpose alone is called "good" (sat).
O Pārtha, whatever is offered in sacrifice, given in charity, or performed as austerity without faith is said to be "evil" (asat); it yields no fruit either after death or in this world.
Arjuna said:
O mighty-armed one, I desire to know the true nature of renunciation (saṃnyāsa),
and also of relinquishment (tyāga), separately, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of Keśin.
The Blessed Lord said:
The wise know the renunciation of actions performed for the sake of desire as *saṃnyāsa*. The discerning call the relinquishment of the fruits of all actions "tyāga."
"Some wise men have said that action should be abandoned as if it were full of fault;
others, however, say that the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity should not be abandoned. Hear from me my definitive conclusion regarding this renunciation, O best of the Bharatas."
O tiger among men, renunciation is indeed proclaimed to be of three kinds.
Sacrificial rites, acts of charity, and ascetic practices must not be abandoned; they must certainly be performed.
For sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the means of purification for the wise.

But even these actions, O Pārtha, must be performed after abandoning attachment and the fruits; this is my firm and supreme conviction. However, the renunciation of obligatory action is not appropriate.
The abandonment of action out of delusion is proclaimed to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). He who abandons action merely because it is painful, out of fear of physical hardship,
performs an abandonment that is of the nature of passion (rājasa) and shall not obtain the fruit of renunciation.

O Arjuna, when action is performed as a duty, necessarily, having abandoned attachment and the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). One does not hate unwholesome action, nor does one become attached to wholesome action.
One who is renounced, endowed with purity, wise, and whose doubts are severed— indeed,
it is impossible for one who bears a body to abandon actions entirely;
however, he who renounces the fruits of action is called a "renouncer."
The threefold fruit of action— unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—
accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have renounced.
O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes.
In the Sāṃkhya and the Kṛtānta, these are declared for the accomplishment of all actions:
the locus, the agent, the various instruments,
the diverse activities, and destiny as the fifth factor therein.
Whatever action a person undertakes through body, speech, or mind—
whether it be righteous or its opposite— these five are its causes.
This being so, he who regards the self alone as the sole agent...
Because his intellect is unrefined, that evil-minded person does not see;
he who has no sense of "I" and whose intellect is not defiled—
even having slain these worlds, he neither slays nor is he bound.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—this is the threefold impulsion to action. The instrument, the action, and the agent—this is the threefold aggregate of action.
Knowledge, action, and the agent are each of three kinds according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas).
It is described in the enumeration of the qualities; hear those [qualities] as they truly are:
know that knowledge to be *sāttvika* by which one perceives the one imperishable essence in all beings, undivided among the divided.

But know that knowledge to be *rājasa* which perceives various distinct entities as separate from one another among all beings. However, that which is attached to a single task as if it were the whole, and is devoid of reason—
That action which is inconsistent with reality, limited in scope, and performed out of ignorance is declared to be tāmasa.
But that action which is performed as a matter of duty, free from attachment, without desire for reward, and devoid of passion and hatred, is said to be sāttvika.
But that action which is performed by one desiring rewards, or again with egoism,
involving great exertion— that is declared to be rajasic. Furthermore,
that which is done without regard for consequences, loss, injury, or one's own human capacity, is likewise so described.
Action that is undertaken out of delusion is said to be tāmasa.
One who is free from attachment, devoid of egoism, endowed with fortitude and perseverance,
and remains unchanged in success or failure, is called a sāttvika agent.
One who is passionate, desirous of the fruits of action, greedy, violent by nature, impure,
and possessed by joy and sorrow— such an agent is proclaimed to be *rājasa*.
One who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, and lazy [is known as a *tāmasa* agent].
One who is full of envy and procrastinating is said to be a doer of the nature of *tamas*.
Now hear, O Dhanañjaya, the threefold division of the intellect and of fortitude according to the *guṇas*, as they are being described exhaustively and individually.
O Pārtha, that intellect which understands engagement and withdrawal, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, as well as bondage and liberation, is sattvic.
That [intellect] by which one perceives dharma and adharma, and what ought to be done and what ought not to be done— [is rajasic].
O Pārtha, that intellect which perceives things incorrectly is of the nature of passion (rājasa).
That intellect which, shrouded by darkness (tamas), regards unrighteousness as righteousness,
O Pārtha, and perceives all objects in a perverted manner, is of the nature of ignorance (tāmasa).

That steadfastness by which one maintains the functions of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses through unswerving yoga— that, O Pārtha, is Sāttvika steadfastness. But that steadfastness by which one holds fast to duty, pleasure, and wealth, O Arjuna—
That resolve by which one, through attachment, desires the fruit of action— that, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
That resolve by which the dull-witted man does not abandon sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and even pride— that, O Pārtha, is tāmasa.
Now hear from me, O bull of the Bharatas, about the three kinds of happiness:
that in which one finds delight through practice and reaches the end of suffering—
that which is like poison at first but like nectar in its result.
That happiness which arises from the clarity of one's own intellect is declared to be *sāttvika*. That happiness which,
at first, is like nectar due to the contact of the senses with their objects,
but in its transformation is like poison— that is remembered as *rājasa* happiness.
That pleasure which, both at the beginning and in its consequence, deludes the self and arises from sleep, laziness, and negligence, is declared to be *tāmasa*.
There is nothing on earth, nor again among the gods in heaven, that is not composed of these three qualities.
O scorcher of foes, when a being is freed from these three qualities born of nature, [he attains liberation]. For the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
their duties are divided according to the qualities arising from their own natures.
Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness;
