as well as knowledge, realized wisdom, and faith in the Vedas—these are the duties of a Brahmin, born of his own nature. Valor, majesty, firmness, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle;
Giving, sovereignty, and leadership are the duties of the Kṣatriya born of his own nature;
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of the Vaiśya born of his own nature;
and service is the duty of the Śūdra, born of his own nature.
A man who is devoted to his own specific duty attains perfection. Listen to how one who is intent on his own work finds success—
that from which all beings proceed and by which all this is pervaded.
By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. One's own duty, even if imperfectly performed, is better than the duty of another well-performed;
death in the fulfillment of one's own duty is better than the successful accomplishment of the duty of another.
One who performs action determined by one's own nature incurs no sin.
O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon innate action even if it is accompanied by fault;
for all undertakings are enveloped by defect, just as fire is covered by smoke.
With a mind unattached everywhere, having conquered the self and being free from longing,
one attains the supreme perfection of actionlessness through renunciation. Learn from me how, having attained that perfection, one reaches Brahman.
In brief, O Kaunteya, that which is the supreme consummation of knowledge is as follows:
endowed with a purified intellect and having restrained the self through fortitude,
one should abandon objects of sense such as sound and cast off both passion and hatred.
Frequenting solitary places, eating sparingly, with speech, body, and mind restrained, constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation, and having fully relied upon dispassion,
[he abandons] egoism, power, pride, desire, anger, and possessiveness.
Being liberated, free from the sense of "mine," and tranquil, he is fit for becoming Brahman. Having become Brahman, with a serene self, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me.
Through devotion one comes to know Me in truth—both who I am and what My nature is.
Then, having known Me in truth, one enters into Me immediately thereafter.
Even while constantly performing all actions, one who takes refuge in Me [attains this].
By my grace, one attains the eternal, imperishable state.
Having surrendered all actions to me with the mind and regarding me as the supreme goal, take refuge in the yoga of discernment and be ever-minded of me.
With your mind fixed on Me, you shall cross over all difficulties by My grace;
but if, out of egoism, you do not listen, you shall perish.
Relying on egoism, you think, "I will not fight."

This resolve of yours is false; nature will compel you. Bound by your own action born of your inherent disposition, O son of Kuntī, you shall do—even against your will—that which you do not wish to do because of delusion.
The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine.
Seek refuge in Him alone with your whole being, O Bhārata.
"By His grace, you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than the secret, been declared by Me to you. Having reflected upon this in its entirety, do as you wish.
Listen again to my supreme word, the most secret of all.
Because you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall speak what is for your benefit. Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
"You shall come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me. Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone.
I shall deliver you from all sins; do not grieve."

This should never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who is without devotion, nor to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who finds fault with me. But he who shall declare this supreme secret to my devotees—
Having established supreme devotion toward me, he will come to me alone, without a doubt. Among men, there shall be no one who does what is more pleasing to me than he,
nor shall there be anyone else on earth dearer to me than he.

And whoever shall request this righteous dialogue between us, by him I shall be worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction. Even that man who merely hears it, being full of faith and free from malice, [attains the same].
He too, being liberated, shall attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds.
O Pārtha, has this been heard by you with a one-pointed mind?
O Dhanañjaya, has the delusion of ignorance been destroyed within you?
Arjuna said:
"O Acyuta, through your grace, my delusion has been destroyed and I have regained my memory.
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I shall do as you command."
Saṃjaya said:
Thus have I heard this wonderful conversation between Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha, which causes the hair to stand on end.
By the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard this supreme secret,
the Yoga, directly from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, as he himself was speaking it.
O King, remembering again and again this wonderful dialogue, I am filled with wonder.
I rejoice again and again in the merit of Keśava and Arjuna; and as I recall again and again that most wonderful form of Hari,
my amazement is great, O King, and I rejoice over and over.
Wherever there is Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, and wherever there is Pārtha, the wielder of the bow, there will surely be prosperity, victory, splendor, and sound policy; this is my conviction.
Through devotion to the Blessed One, and by means of self-knowledge arising from His grace—
"May there be liberation from bondage through happiness"—this is the summary of the meaning of the Gītā.
Keśava spoke six hundred and twenty verses;
Arjuna spoke fifty-seven, and Saṃjaya spoke sixty-seven.
06,040.078d*0112_03 Dhṛtarāṣṭra says: One verse of the Gītā is said to be its measure.
06,040.078d*0113_00 Vaiśampāyana said:
06,040.078d*0113_01 The Gītā should be well-sung; what need is there for other extensive treatises?
And this Gītā, which has issued from the lotus-mouth of Padmanābha, consists of all the śāstras; Hari consists of all the gods;
the Gaṅgā consists of all sacred fords; and Manu consists of all the Vedas.
When Gaṅgā, Gītā, Gāyatrī, and Govinda are established in the heart,
conjoined with the four *ga* sounds, there is no rebirth. Of the Gītā, which is like the churned essence of the nectar of the Mahābhārata—
Having extracted the essence, Kṛṣṇa offered it into the mouth of Arjuna.
Arjuna said:
"That which is this Brahman, partless, beyond the ether, and stainless..."
Isolation is absolute, peaceful, pure, and utterly stainless;
(1) it is beyond ratiocination, unknowable, and devoid of both destruction and origination.
The Blessed One said:
O Keśava, tell me that knowledge which is devoid of the yoga of [empirical] knowledge. (2) It is the light everywhere, like space, endowed with the qualities of all beings;
it is the Supreme Self everywhere, the imperishable, supreme state. (3)
The god who is without beginning or end, the great light, most steadfast,
the ultimate supreme state, devoid of qualities such as sound and the rest—
that which is the furthermost light, situated beyond the eternal.
Even until the end of the four ages, this has not been told to anyone. (5) Within my own body, I have created both Nature and the Field;
indeed, the Field is the differentiated whole, while the supreme state is the undifferentiated. (6)

O Arjuna, by your grace, let these best of sages hear [this]. O mighty-armed Dhanañjaya, today we have been liberated through your favor. The Sāṃkhya and other systems are the authoritative means for those devoted to the true principles of the Vedas.

(8) No finality exists for them, along with all the heretics. (9) And this knowledge, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, consisting of the universal form, divine, and characterized by the knots, points, and *bindu* of Bhairava, has been taught by me.
The Suṣumṇā has been shown on the right path by the one who possesses all forms.
This question which I have explained to you is not manifest;
it is neither fire, nor wind, nor space, nor earth, nor even water.
I have not explained to you the hidden meaning regarding the mind, intellect, and ego.
(11) When one does not perceive any entity, the impermanent attains permanence;
[one realizes] Nirvana, which is empty, stainless in form, eternal, and immutable. (12)
The Person, who is devoid of qualities, stands directly and indeed everywhere;
all that is the Supreme Brahman, yet his intellect does not perceive it.
Through the effort of intuitive realization, one perceives Hari, the kinsman of the three worlds.
Pervading the tenth finger-breadth, it is situated beyond the quarters of space.
(14) That wherein the individual soul (jīva) is dissolved is known as the sixteenth digit (kalā). By it, this entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is pervaded. (15)
That which is to be contemplated is indeed knowledge; that is what the primordial ones worship here.
For it is celebrated by Brahmā himself and revealed in the Vedāntas. In the Vedas they call it "the Veda," considered the supreme abode of the Vedas.
He by whom that supreme [reality] is known is a Brahmin who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
(17) That is to be known as the supreme oblation; it is established as the *saṃdhyā*.
(18ab) It is to be known as the supreme *gāyatrī*, renowned by the name *ajapā*. (18cd)
Now, that which is thus practiced by sages in asceticism as well as in the Veda— that part (*kalā*) which one fully understands is called "one who knows the part.
Having known that, a living being is liberated from the womb, birth, old age, and so forth.
Through complete knowledge, men are liberated from the taints of sin.
(20) The goddess Iḍā is the Gaṅgā, and Piṅgalā is the river Yamunā; one should remember that Prayāga as the third [channel] situated between those two. (21)
The *iḍā* is indeed the channel of Viṣṇu, while the *piṅgalā* is the channel of Brahmā;
the *suṣumṇā* is the channel of Īśvara. These three are known as the carriers of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva correspond respectively to the exhaling (*recaka*), the inhaling (*pūraka*), and the retention (*kumbhaka*) of breath. (22)
He who understands the transits, the equinoxes,
and the conjunction (*vigraha*), that master of yoga, ever-disciplined, attains the knowledge of Brahman.
(23) Indeed, the *iḍā* is the *gārhapatya* fire, while the *piṅgalā* is the *āhavanīya* fire.
The *suṣumṇā* is the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*); indeed, these are remembered as the three fires. In the center of that is situated the light, which is the lunar orb (*somamaṇḍala*).
Situated within the lunar orb is the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*) in its center.
Situated in the center of the solar disk, he is the blazing fire of radiant energy.
In the midst of that fire, however, is one with the luster of smokeless embers.
Abiding there, that Great-Souled One is celebrated by the yogis.
One should perform the beautiful song with a one-pointed mind.
(27) Śiva is the Bindu; Śiva is the deity who, with the luster of the nectar of the *gharghara* sound, fills the entire body and removes poison, burning fever, and affliction. (28)
Having encircled the body with the Suṣumṇā, which is coiled like a serpent and curved in form,
and having encircled it with the syllable *Makāra*, one should bind it as if to a mother.
It has three locations, three measures, the three Brahmas, and three syllables.
And he who knows even half a mora becomes one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
(30) That [Self] has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides.
Arjuna said:
Stainless, possessing a pure form, resembling clear crystal.
(31) The living soul lives by means of the life-force; there is no life-force that is without a living soul.
The Blessed One said:
(32) Having emerged together with the aggregate, by what does that living being live?
(33) Between the mouth and the nose, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) always circulates;
it constantly drinks space (*ākāśa*), and by that, the living being lives.
The syllable *kākīmukha* ends with the letter *ka*, while the letter *ma* follows consciousness.
But when the letter *a* has been elided, what meaning is understood?
For that duration, one should perceive the form of the sky (*kha*) and contemplate the letter *kha*.
Place yourself in the midst of space, and place space in the midst of yourself.
One must enter into the midst of space, for space is the eternal Brahman. Having made oneself of the nature of space, one should not think of anything at all.
The upper is empty, the lower is empty, and the middle is empty—the stainless void.

He who thoroughly understands this triple emptiness shall be the delighter of the family. For that which is the essential nature of existence, the act of meditative cultivation is not at all applicable.
The movement of that unobstructed sound, of that very sound—
by him who has realized that state (*pada*), that yogin has severed all doubt.
And those others who are the five deities, who indeed remove merit and sin— (38–39)
Living beings go together [with their karma] as long as they do not find the ultimate reality.
The fire of knowledge burns away evil; through merit, one attains the state of the moon and the sun. This liberation from both merit and evil is what is called Yoga.

One who performs sacrifice by making the senses the sacrificial animals— offering the fuel of contentment and the clarified butter of mental wisdom that sustains fortitude— is truly consecrated. By contemplating the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), they attain the Supreme Brahman.
Even though one has seen the further shore in its entirety, one repeatedly applies oneself to existence (*bhāva*).
In the partless (*niṣkala*), there is no vision; it is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that applies itself to existence.
(43) At the root of the palate is Lampā; Trikūṭa is the interval between the three paths.
One should understand that there is a single reality which is the great abode of obstacles.
(44) Just as a tree whose roots have been severed has no further birth, so for one whose body is consumed by knowledge, a body does not arise again. (45)
The Gītās should be well-sung; what is the use of other compendia of scriptures?
For these [Gītās] issued forth in ancient times from the lotus-mouth of Padmanābha.
Having drunk the water of the Gaṅgā that is the Gītā, there is no rebirth.
The Gītā consists of all scriptures; Hari consists of all dharmas. (47) The Gaṅgā consists of all sacred fords and brings about the destruction of all sins.
This [Gītā] consists of all enjoyments, and indeed, it consists of all liberation. (48)
The *Gītā*, the Gaṅgā, the *Gāyatrī*, and Govinda reside within the heart;
by remembering these four "Ga"s, rebirth no longer exists. He who recites the essence of the *Gītā* in the presence of Acyuta [attains the same].
Therefore, just as the definition of Viṣṇu is established through his thousands of qualities,
so too is this supreme majesty of Viṣṇu meritorious, a destroyer of sins, auspicious, and a dispeller of evil dreams for those who read or even hear it. (50–51)
Arjuna said:
That which is this partless Brahman, beyond the ether, stainless,
absolute, solitary, peaceful, pure, and utterly immaculate— (1)
"Beyond reasoning and unknowable, devoid of destruction and origination—
the Blessed Lord said:
O Keśava, tell me that knowledge which is liberated from the yoga of [empirical] knowledge."
Space is light everywhere, endowed with the qualities of all beings;
it is the Supreme Self everywhere, the imperishable, supreme state—
the God who is without beginning or end, the great light, most steadfast.
The ultimate, supreme state is devoid of qualities such as sound and the rest.
(4) That which is the highest light, situated beyond the eternal pole (dhruva), has not been told to anyone even until this day, throughout the four ages. (5)
Within my own body, Prakṛti and the Field (kṣetra) were created by me;
indeed, the entire Field is the partless supreme state.
O Arjuna, by your grace, let these best of sages hear this.
"O mighty-armed Dhanañjaya, today we have been liberated through your grace.
(7) The Sāṃkhya and other systems are the standard authorities for those devoted to the true principles of the Vedas;
yet, no finality is found in them, along with all the heretics. (8)
And this knowledge, difficult even for the gods to obtain,
consisting of the divine universal form (*viśvarūpa*) through the knots and points (*granthi-bindu*) of Bhairava,
has been told by me; this question which I have explained to you is not to be disclosed.
The verbal essence of all scriptures, most subtle and encompassing all that moves and is stationary—
neither fire, nor wind, nor space, nor earth, nor even water;
neither mind, intellect, nor ego— it has been declared to you as a profound and hidden meaning.
When one does not perceive any entity, the impermanent attains permanence;
[one realizes] Nirvana, which is empty, of the nature of the stainless, constant, and undecaying. The Person (puruṣa), free from qualities, stands directly and indeed everywhere.
All that would be the Supreme Brahman, yet his intellect does not perceive it.
(13) Through the effort of focused intuition, one perceives Hari, the kinsman of the three worlds, who pervades ten finger-breadths and remains situated beyond the reach of the senses. (14)
That wherein the individual soul (*jīva*) is dissolved is known as the sixteenth digit (*kalā*).
By it all this triple world, including the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded. That is to be meditated upon; by that indeed is knowledge attained, and therein the primordial ones worship.
For this has been proclaimed by Brahmā himself and revealed in the Vedāntas.

(16) In the Vedas they call him "the Veda," for he is considered the supreme abode of the Veda. He by whom that supreme [reality] is known is a true Brahmin who has reached the further shore of the Vedas. (17)
That is to be known as the supreme oblation (*āhuti*); it is established as the *saṃdhyā*.
That is to be known as the supreme *gāyatrī*, renowned by the name *ajapā*. It is thus worshipped by sages both in ascetic practice (*tapas*) and in the Veda.
He who thoroughly understands that digit is called a knower of the digit.
(19) Having known it, a living being is liberated from the womb, birth, old age, and so forth;
through full comprehension, men are released from the taints of sin. (20)
The goddess Iḍā is the Gaṅgā, and the Piṅgalā is the river Yamunā;
one should remember that Prayāga is the third, situated between those two.
Indeed, the channel Iḍā belongs to Viṣṇu, while the channel Piṅgalā is the channel of Brahmā.
The *suṣumṇā*, the sovereign channel, is known to carry the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in three ways;
it is [the locus of] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva, as well as exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*).
He who understands this very form, along with the transits and the equinoxes, [attains liberation].
That lord of yogis, ever-disciplined, attains the knowledge of Brahman.
(23) The *iḍā* is indeed the *gārhapatya* fire, while the *piṅgalā* is the *āhavanīya*; the *suṣumṇā* is the *dakṣiṇāgni*—this is remembered as the triad of fires. (24)

In its center stands the light, the lunar orb itself; situated within the lunar orb is that [light], and in its center is the solar orb. Residing within the solar orb is the blazing radiance, the sacrificial fire.
In the midst of the sacrificial fire, he possesses the luster of smokeless embers. Seated there, that Great-Souled One is praised by the yogis;
and one should sing well of him with a mind of one-pointed concentration.

Śiva is the Bindu; Śiva is the deity who, with the luster of the nectar of the *gharghara* [sound], fills the entire body and removes poison, burning fever, and illness. (28) The body is encircled by the Suṣumṇā, which has a coiled form like a serpent.
Having encircled it with the letter *m*, one should apply it like a mother.
(29) He who knows the three places, the three measures, the three Brahmas, the three syllables, and the half-measure—he shall be one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas. (30)
"Having hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
Arjuna said:
"It is stainless, of pure form, resembling clear crystal. (31)

Whatever exists, whether stationary or moving, including all that is animate and inanimate—the Blessed Lord said: "The living being lives by means of the life-force; by what does that life-force live? (32)
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) always circulates between the mouth and the nose;
it constantly drinks space (*ākāśa*), and by that, the living being (*jīva*) lives.
(33) The "crow's mouth" (*kākīmukha*) ends with the letter *ka* and follows the letter *ma*, which is accompanied by consciousness (*cetanā*).
But when the letter *a* has been elided, what meaning is understood?
(34) For that long, one should visualize the form of space; one should contemplate the letter *kha*.
Place yourself in the midst of space, and place space in the midst of yourself. (35)

One should enter into the midst of space, and space is the eternal Brahman. Having made the self identical with space, one should not think of anything at all. It is empty above, empty below, and empty in the middle—free from all affliction.
He who thoroughly understands the triple emptiness shall be the delighter of his lineage.
(37) He who knows that which is devoid of the sound of measure, free from vowels and consonants, and transcends the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*—he is a knower of the Veda. (38)
When knowledge and discernment have been fully attained, and the object of knowledge is established within the heart;
when the state of peace has been reached in existence, there is neither yoga nor meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
He who was proclaimed as the God at the beginning of the Vedas is firmly established at the end of the Vedas.
For him who is dissolved in primordial nature (*prakṛti*), he who is beyond that is Maheśvara.
(40) A person seeking the boat does not cease their search until they reach the further shore;
once the further shore has been crossed, what indeed is the use of the boat? (41)
Neither standing afar nor standing near, abiding in the body yet devoid of the body;
Arjuna said:
He is stainless, pure, subtle, all-pervading, and untainted. (42)
The syllables, together with their prosodic measures, are all dependent upon the *bindu*.
The Blessed One said:
"The *bindu* is split by the *nāda*; by what is that *nāda* split? (43)
By the resonance of the sound of *oṃ*, the vital air (*vāyu*) is withdrawn until its end;
it becomes supportless and bodiless where the *nāda* has gone to dissolution.
(44) Arjuna said:
The external space is pervaded [by it], and that space is non-nasalized. The Blessed One said: How is it below, how above, and how indeed in the throat—the stainless one? (45)

That which is without heat (*anūṣman*), without manifesting [articulation], and without vowel-sound (*asvara*), as well as that which is nasalized (*anunāsika*) in the palate and throat, free from the *repha* (the letter *r*), auspicious, and devoid of the *ūṣman* sounds— [this is the nature of the *śiva-mantra*].
He never performs difficult deeds.
(46) Even space, though formless, is established within the state of the Person;
like sound is a quality of space, Brahman is said to be soundless. (47)
All-pervading, the source of all awakening and so forth, and free from the web of latent impressions—
by the cessation of the senses within the body, human beings perceive this. When the body has perished, whence could there be intellect, knowledge, or even discernment?
Knowledge conjoined with discernment must be guarded with great effort.
(49) Just as a tree whose roots have been severed cannot grow again, so for one whose body has been consumed by knowledge, a body does not arise again. (50)
The Gītās should be well-sung; what is the use of other compendia of scriptures?
These [Gītās] were formerly issued from the lotus-mouth of Padmanābha.
Having drunk the water of the Gaṅgā that is the Gītā, there is no further rebirth.
The Gītā consists of all scriptures; Hari consists of all dharmas. (52) The Gaṅgā consists of all sacred fords and brings about the destruction of all sins.
This [Gītā] consists of all enjoyments, and indeed, it consists of all liberation. (53)
The four [mantras] beginning with the syllable *ga* protect one from great fear:
Gītā, Gaṅgā, Gāyatrī, and Govinda, who abide within the heart.
Whether one has bathed or not bathed, whether one is pure or impure—
Whoever remembers the Lotus-Eyed One is pure both internally and externally. (55) He shall go at that very moment, O Embodiment of Brahman; salutations be to you!
Whoever recites the Essence of the Gītā is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (56)
This supreme majesty of Viṣṇu is meritorious, destructive of sin, auspicious, and a destroyer of evil dreams for those who read or even hear it. (57) Saṃjaya said:
Then, awakened by Viṣṇu, whose form is the universe,
Phālguna beheld his own indestructible nature as it truly is;
realizing that the form of the world was artificial, he became intent on battle.
Having joined with Devadatta, he took up his weapons once more.
Then, seeing Dhanañjaya bearing arrows and the Gāṇḍīva bow,
the great car-warriors again let out a mighty roar.
The Pāṇḍavas, the Somakas, and those who were their followers—
those heroes, filled with joy, blew their conchs born of the ocean. Then there arose the sounds of kettledrums, cymbals, saws, and cow-horns.
Suddenly they were struck down, and from that a great sound arose.
Then, O lord of men, the gods along with the gandharvas, the ancestors,
and the hosts of siddhas and cāraṇas assembled there, desiring to see.
The highly fortunate ṛṣis, placing Śatakratu at their head,
gathered together there to witness that great slaughter. Both armies stood motionless, gazing at one another.
Just as the currents of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā flow together with one another,
so did those two armies advance, silent amidst the assembly of people,
beautiful and auspicious like two wonderful paintings on a canvas.
Then, O King, seeing those two armies, resembling oceans, fully prepared for battle and repeatedly surging forward, the heroic Yudhiṣṭhira cast off his armor and laid aside his excellent weapons.
Quickly descending from the chariot, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, with palms joined in reverence, looked toward his grandfather and,
restraining his speech, proceeded on foot toward the enemy host facing the east.
Beholding him departing, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī,
quickly descended from his chariot and followed after him along with his brothers.
Thinking Yudhiṣṭhira was afraid, the powerful Bhīmasena [also pursued him].
The blessed Vāsudeva followed behind him,
as did Sātyaki, Arjuna, and the heroic Abhimanyu;
and the foremost kings, filled with eagerness, followed after him.
Arjuna said:
"O King, what is your resolve, that having indeed abandoned us,
you have set out on foot toward the enemy host with your face turned toward the east?"
Bhīmasena said:
"O king of kings, O monarch, where are you going, having cast off your armor and weapons and abandoned your brothers while the enemy forces are clad in mail?"
Nakula said:
"O Bhārata, since you, my eldest brother, have come to such a state, fear pains my heart; tell me, where indeed will you go?"
"O best of men, where will you go like this, abandoning us as if you were weak?
For you are a king, O mighty-armed one, yet you speak thus as if possessed by anger.
Sahadeva said:
"While this great and terrifying mass of battle is underway,
where indeed will you go, O King, facing the enemy in combat? Sañjaya said:

O descendant of Kuru, though addressed in this manner by his brothers, Yudhiṣṭhira remained silent and spoke nothing at all; he simply continued on his way. Then the immensely wise and high-minded Vāsudeva said to them:
"His intention has been understood by me," he said, as if smiling;
"this king, having paid due honor to all his elders— Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Gautama, and Śalya alike— will fight with his enemies."
For it is heard that in a former age, he who fights without having first obtained the consent of his elders will clearly be cursed by those superior to him; indeed,
there is no victory in battle for one who descends to fight under such circumstances.
But he who, when battle has arisen and sees his elders clad in armor,
shows them due respect according to the scriptures and then fights with those even greater than himself—
for him, victory in battle is certain; this is my conviction.
While Kṛṣṇa was speaking thus toward the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, everyone gazed at Yudhiṣṭhira with unblinking eyes;
there was a great cry of "Alas! while others became silent.
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira from afar, the soldiers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son conversed among themselves: "That disgrace to his lineage is not dead;
clearly, this king approaches Bhīṣma as if terrified."

Yudhiṣṭhira, along with his brothers, comes as a petitioner seeking refuge. Even though Dhananjaya, Vṛkodara the Pāṇḍava, Nakula, and Sahadeva are his protectors, how is it that this son of Pāṇḍu approaches in fear?
"Surely he was not born into a kṣatriya lineage renowned upon the earth,
since his heart is so terrified in battle like that of one of little courage.
Thereupon, all those kṣatriyas praised the Kauravas.
Becoming joyful and cheerful, they each waved their garments separately. Then, O lord of the people, all those warriors there censured Yudhiṣṭhira along with his brothers and Keśava.
Then, O lord of the people, having censured Yudhiṣṭhira, that Kuru army quickly became silent once again;
they wondered, "What indeed will this king say, and what will Bhīṣma reply?"
"What indeed will that King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, say?
What indeed will Bhīṣma, the bearer of the burden of the Bharatas, say?
And what will Bhīma, who delights in battle, say? And what indeed will Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna say?"
"O King, a very great doubt then arose in both armies regarding Yudhiṣṭhira’s intent;
having plunged into the enemy host, which was thick with arrows and spears,"
Surrounded by his brothers, he quickly approached Bhīṣma. Then the Pāṇḍava king, pressing Bhīṣma Śāṃtanava’s feet with his hands as he stood ready for battle, spoke to him.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I bid you farewell, O invincible one; I shall fight with you, my dear brother.
Grant me your permission, father, and bestow upon me your blessings."
"O sinless one, permitted by you, may I conquer all my enemies;
O hero, it behooves you to grant me leave as I fight in battle.
Bhīṣma said:
"O lord of the earth, if you had not thus approached me in battle, O great king, descendant of Bharata, I would have cursed you to your defeat.
I am pleased, my son; fight and obtain victory, O Pāṇḍava!"
"Whatever else you desire, obtain that in this encounter;
choose a boon, O Pārtha—what do you seek from us?
Since things have come to this pass, O Great King, there shall be no defeat for you."
"A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one"—this is the truth, O Great King; I am bound by wealth on behalf of the Kauravas.
Therefore, O joy of the Kurus, I speak these words to you like a eunuch.
"I have been captivated by wealth, O Kauravya; what else do you desire from me other than battle?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O one of great wisdom, always advise me as one who desires my welfare."
"Fight for the sake of the Kaurava; this has always been my wish.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, O delighter of the Kurus, what assistance can I provide you in this matter?"
"O King, I shall advise you regarding that which is for your supreme benefit. I will certainly fight for the sake of the enemy; tell me what you wish to say.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How may I conquer you, who are unconquered, in battle? Counsel me on this for my benefit, if you perceive any means to my welfare.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Kaunteya, I do not see any man whatsoever— even Indra himself in person— who could defeat me while I am fighting in battle. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Come now, I shall ask you this, O Grandfather; salutations be unto you! Tell me the means by which you may achieve victory over your enemies in battle.
Bhīṣma said:
"O dear one, I see no enemy who could defeat me in battle— me who am not fighting, who am united with them, overwhelmed by affection,
who have laid down my weapons, and who am devoid of effort; yet such enemies might slay me in combat."
Toward one who has laid down his weapons, one who has fallen, or one whose armor has been removed; toward one who is fleeing or terrified, or one who says, "I am yours";
toward a woman, one bearing a woman's name, one who is disabled, or one who is an only son—[toward these, one should not strike].
"I do not favor battle with those who have not yet borne children or with those who are inferior.
And this, O Pārtha, has been declared as the supreme vow in combat:
'The time for my death has not yet come; return once more.'"
06,041.044 Saṃjaya said:
06,041.044a Then Yudhiṣṭhira, O descendant of Kuru, received the words of Bhīṣma with his head bowed, and having saluted him once more, [he departed].
The mighty-armed one set out once more toward the preceptor’s chariot,
proceeding through the midst of all the armies while his brothers looked on;
having then saluted Droṇa and performed a circumambulation of him.
He spoke these words for his own ultimate welfare to the invincible one:
"O Blessed One, I bid you farewell; freed from all taint, I shall fight. Permitted by you, O twice-born one, I shall conquer all my enemies."
Droṇa said:
"O great king, had you not come to me, having resolved upon battle, I would have cursed you for your total defeat."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, O sinless one, I am pleased and honored by you. I grant you leave: fight and attain victory!
I shall also fulfill your desire; tell me what you long for."
"Since things have come to this pass, O Great King, what do you desire other than war? A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one;
this is the truth, O Great King, and I am bound by wealth to the Kauravas."
"Therefore, we speak to you like a eunuch: what do you desire other than battle?
I shall fight for the sake of the Kaurava; victory is to be hoped for by me from you.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Brahmana, pray for victory for me; counsel me for my benefit. Fight on behalf of the Kaurava; this is the boon chosen by me.
Drona said:
"Victory is certain for you, O King, you who have Hari as your counselor;
and I recognize that you shall conquer your enemies in battle. Where there is Dharma, there is Kṛṣṇa; where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is victory."
"Fight! Go, O Kaunteya! Ask me; what shall I say to you?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I ask you, O best of the twice-born; hear what I wish to say."
"How may I conquer you, who are unconquered, in battle?
Droṇa said:
"As long as I am fighting in this conflict, there can be no victory for you."
"O King, strive together with your brothers for my swift destruction.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Ah, therefore, O mighty-armed one, tell us the means for your own death."
"O Teacher, having prostrated before you, I ask you this; homage be unto you!
Droṇa said:
"O dear one, I see no enemy who could slay me while I stand in battle."

O King, I tell you this truth: among warriors, one might slay me in battle while I am fighting with great fury, raining down a torrential shower of arrows; however, one could not slay me when I have retired from the field, having laid down my weapons and become unconscious, except by means of fasting unto death.
"I would even cast away my weapon in battle upon hearing very great and unpleasant news from a man whose word is trustworthy; I tell you this truth. Sañjaya said:

Having heard this from the wise Bhāradvāja, O Great King, and having paid his respects to that teacher, he set out toward the son of Śaradvat. Having saluted Kṛpa and circumambulated him, the king departed.
Skilled in speech, he addressed these words to that most invincible one:
"O Preceptor, I infer your intent; freed from all taint, I shall fight. O sinless one, with your permission, I shall conquer all my enemies."
Kṛpa said:
"O great king, had you not approached me, having resolved upon battle, I would have cursed you for your total defeat."
"O delighter of the Pāṇḍavas, tell me what desire I may fulfill for you.
O Great King, since things have come to this pass, what do you wish for other than war? A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one."
"O Great King, this is the truth: I am bound by my duty to the Kauravas.
It is my conviction, O Great King, that I must fight for their sake.
Therefore, I speak to you like a eunuch; what else do you desire besides battle?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Ah, therefore I ask you, O Teacher; listen to my words. Tell me the means by which you might be slain by enemies in battle."
06,041.069 Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus, the king, distressed and deprived of his senses, said nothing.
Gautama, perceiving what he intended to say, replied to him.
"I am not to be slain, O protector of the earth; fight and obtain victory!
I am pleased by your approach, O lord of men;
rising every day, I shall pray for your victory—I tell you this as the truth."
Having heard these words of Gautama at that time, O great king,
the king paid his respects to Kṛpa and proceeded toward where the King of Madra was.
Having then saluted Śalya and performed a circumambulation of him, he approached.

The king spoke these words, beneficial for his own welfare, to the invincible one: "O Preceptor, I seek your permission; free from sin, I shall fight. And with your leave, O Great King, may I conquer my enemies."
Śalya said:
"O great king, had you not approached me, having resolved upon battle, I would have cursed you for your defeat in the fray."
"I am pleased and I have been honored; let that which you desire be yours. I grant you leave: fight and attain victory!
Speak further, O hero; what is your purpose? What shall I give to you?"
"Such being the case, O Great King, what do you desire other than war? A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one;
this is the truth, O Great King, and I am bound by wealth to the Kauravas."
"O Great King, it is my conviction that I must fight for their sake.
Indeed, O nephew, I shall fulfill your desire exactly as you wish.
Therefore, I speak to you like a eunuch; what else do you desire other than battle?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Great King, always deliberate for my supreme welfare;
fight at will for the sake of the enemy—I choose this as my boon."
Śalya said:
"Tell me, O best of kings, what assistance may I provide you here?
I shall certainly fight for the sake of the enemy, for I have been chosen by the Kauravas for their purpose."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"That very boon which was granted by you during the Udyoga is true for me;
you must effect the destruction of the Sūtaputra's prowess in battle."
"For Duryodhana, O maternal uncle of the Sūta's son, will appoint you as charioteer in battle for that hero; this is my firm conviction. Śalya said:
"O son of Kuntī, this desire of yours shall be fulfilled exactly as you wish. Go and fight with confidence; I promise you victory.
Sañjaya said:
Then, having taken leave of his maternal uncle, the lord of the Madrakas, the son of Kuntī emerged from the great army, surrounded by his brothers;
Vāsudeva, however, indeed approached the son of Rādhā on the battlefield.
Then the elder brother of Gada spoke this to him for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas:
"I have heard, O Karṇa, that you will indeed not fight out of hatred for Bhīṣma. Choose us as your allies, O son of Rādhā, as long as Bhīṣma has not been slain."
"O son of Rādhā, once Bhīṣma is slain, you shall come again to the battle if you consider it equal to providing assistance to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Karṇa said:
"O Keśava, I shall do nothing displeasing to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
know me as one who has renounced his life, seeking only the welfare of Duryodhana.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard those words, O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa turned back and joined with the Pāṇḍavas, led by Yudhiṣṭhira. Then, in the midst of the army, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas cried out:
"Whichever among us chooses [the other], that I shall choose for the sake of assistance.
Then, looking toward them, Yuyutsu, with a joyful heart, spoke thus to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and King of Dharma.
"O sinless Great King, if you choose me, I shall fight against the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle while they look on, for your sake. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Come, come! We shall all fight your unwise brothers.
O Yuyutsu, Vāsudeva, and we—all of us say this:
those foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will cease to exist; of this there is no doubt."
"I choose you, O mighty-armed one; fight for my sake.
In you alone are seen the funeral cake and the lineage of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
therefore, you must likewise perform the water-libation rites for him."
"O prince of great splendor, favor us who favor you;
the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, so intolerant of others, shall no longer exist.
Saṃjaya said:
Then Yuyutsu, the descendant of Kuru, having abandoned your sons and considering Yudhiṣṭhira’s words to be the truth,
went forth to the army of the sons of Pāṇḍu after sounding his drum.
The powerful son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, censuring that evil deed, [was overcome].
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his younger brothers, was filled with joy;
he once again took up his armor, radiant and blazing with gold.
Those bulls among men all mounted their own chariots;
then they once again formed their battle array as it was before.
They sounded kettledrums and hundreds of drums.
And those bulls among men uttered various lion-roars;
seeing the Pāṇḍavas, those tigers among men stationed upon their chariots, all the kings,
including Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the others, rejoiced once more with delight.
Seeing the respect shown by the sons of Pāṇḍu— who themselves honor those worthy of honor— the lords of the earth there paid them great reverence;
and they likewise displayed friendship and compassion toward those high-souled ones, as was appropriate for the occasion.
The kings proclaimed their supreme compassion toward their kinsmen;
everywhere there issued forth auspicious words of praise, accompanied by cries of "Excellent! Excellent!", which gladdened the minds and hearts of those possessed of renown.
The Mlecchas and Aryas who were there, having seen and heard that conduct of the sons of Pāṇḍu, wept with choked voices. Then they beat great kettledrums and hundreds of *puṣkara* drums.
And the wise, joyful ones blew conchs that were as white as cow’s milk.
The Blessed One said:
[to] Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals, the hearing and chanting of whose name is meritorious.
I bow to Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When my armies and those of the others were thus arrayed..."
"Who struck first there—the Kurus or the Pāṇḍavas?
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, your son Duryodhana, together with his brothers..."
Placing Bhīṣma at their head, he set forth with his army;
likewise, all the Pāṇḍavas, led by Bhīmasena,
marched forward with joyful hearts, desiring battle with Bhīṣma.
O King, amidst the sounds of *kṣveḍās*, shouts of joy, *krakacas*, and *goviṣāṇikas*,
as well as the noise of *bherīs*, *mṛdaṅgas*, and *murajas*, and the cries of horses and elephants,
those [warriors] from both armies then rushed toward us.
And as we were shouting back, there arose a great and tumultuous din among the vast armies in that great encounter between the hosts of the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras.
They trembled at the sounds of conchs and drums,
like forests shaken by the wind; [the earth] was crowded with the elephants, horses, and chariots of the lords of men.
At that inauspicious moment,
as the armies advanced, there arose a tumultuous roar like that of oceans tossed by the wind.
When that tumultuous and hair-raising noise had arisen,
the mighty-armed Bhīmasena roared like a bull. Amidst the sound of conchs and drums and the trumpeting of elephants, he let out his cry.
The roar of Bhīmasena surpassed the lion-like shouts of the armies;
amidst the neighing of thousands of horses in the ranks,
the sound of Bhīmasena overwhelmed all other noises.
Hearing that roar of his, which was like the sound of a thundercloud rumbling with the crash of Śakra’s lightning bolt, your troops were struck with terror;
and all their mounts discharged excrement and urine.
With his roar, like other beasts before a lion,
that hero displayed his terrible self and, sounding like a great cloud,
he advanced against your army, terrifying your sons.
As that great archer approached, his uterine brothers surrounded him,
shrouding him with volleys of arrows like clouds obscuring the sun—
your son Duryodhana, Durmukha, Duḥsaha, and Śala.
And Duḥśāsana, an atiratha, as well as Durmarṣaṇa, O King; Vivimśati, Citrasena, and the great car-warrior Vikarṇa;
Purumitra, Jaya, Bhoja, and the heroic son of Somadatta.
Brandishing great bows like clouds flashing with lightning,
and taking up iron shafts resembling venomous snakes that have cast off their skins,
the sons of Draupadī and the great car-warrior Saubhadra then [assailed] them.
Nakula, Sahadeva, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
advanced against the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, afflicting them with sharp arrows like high-velocity thunderbolts striking the peaks of mountains.
In that first clash, amidst the roar of terrible bowstrings and palms,
neither among your men nor among the enemies was there anyone who turned his back. O bull of the Bharatas, I beheld the dexterity of Droṇa’s disciples.
O King, as those who strike by sight discharged their arrows incessantly,
the roar of the twanging bows did not cease;
blazing arrows issued forth like luminous bodies from the vault of the sky.
But all the other kings, O Bhārata, looked like mere spectators as they beheld that formidable gathering of kinsmen, so worthy of being seen. Then,
their fury aroused, they began to reproach one another for the wrongs they had done to each other.
O King, those great car-warriors exerted themselves in mutual rivalry; those two armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
shone exceedingly in battle like figures depicted on a painting.

Then all those kings, having grasped their bows and accompanied by their armies, rushed forward at the command of your son. As they charged there, a great tumult arose, thick with elephants and horses.
Mixed with the roar of lions and filled with the sound of conchs and kettledrums, that tumultuous noise— possessing arrows for its grapples, the bow for its elephant, and the sword for its tortoise—
was like the sound of a turbulent ocean with its preceding winds blowing.
Commanded by Yudhiṣṭhira, those thousands of kings rushed roaring toward the army of your son;
that encounter between the soldiers of both armies was fierce.
The sun vanished, shrouded by the dust raised by the army;
among those who were fighting, those who were broken, and those who were returning once more,
no distinction could be made between one's own side and that of the enemy.
While that tumultuous battle, fraught with great terror, was raging,
your father shone forth, surpassing all the armies.
Sañjaya said:

O lord of the people, in the forenoon of that day, a most terrible battle commenced between that fierce one and the kings, a conflict that mangled the bodies of both Kurus and Pāṇḍavas as they sought victory.
Like the roar of lions, it made both heaven and earth resound;
there arose a tumultuous clamor along with the sounds of hand-clapping and conch shells,
as the shouting heroes let out lion-like roars in response.
O bull of the Bharatas, there were the sounds of bowstrings struck by hand-guards,
the footfalls of infantry, and the great roar of horses;
as well as the strikes of goads and hooks, and the clashing of weapons.
And amidst the sound of the bells of the elephants as they rushed at one another,
when that tumultuous and hair-raising noise had arisen,
there arose the roar of chariots like the rumbling of rain clouds.
Having set their minds on cruelty and having renounced all regard for their lives,
they all advanced against the Pāṇḍavas with their banners raised high.
O King, the son of Śaṃtanu himself rushed toward Dhanañjaya.
Grasping his terrible bow, which resembled the staff of Death in battle,
Arjuna also took up the world-renowned Gāṇḍīva bow;
then the radiant hero rushed toward the son of Gaṅgā at the forefront of the fray.
Both those tigers among the Kurus, each desiring to slay the other—
the mighty son of Gaṅgā having pierced Pārtha in battle, yet failed to shake him;
and likewise, O King, the son of Pāṇḍu failed to shake Bhīṣma in the fray.
The great archer Sātyaki advanced against Kṛtavarman,
and between them there occurred a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end;
Sātyaki fought Kṛtavarman, and Kṛtavarman fought Sātyaki.
They struck each other with terrible arrows, carving one another;
those two of great strength, their entire bodies covered in shafts,
shone like two blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees variegated with flowers in the springtime.
The great archer Abhimanyu fought against Bṛhadbala.
Then, O lord of the people, the king of Kosala cut down the standard of Subhadrā’s son in battle and struck down his charioteer.
Then, O great king, the son of Subhadrā, enraged that his charioteer had been struck down, pierced Bṛhadbala with nine arrows; thereafter,
that crusher of enemies struck him again with two other yellow-tufted broad-headed shafts.
With one [arrow] he cut down the standard, and with another the charioteer;
O King, enraged, they both struck each other with sharp shafts—
that proud and arrogant great car-warrior who had harbored enmity in battle.
Bhimasena fought against your son Duryodhana;
those two tigers among men, the mighty leaders of the Kurus,
showered each other with volleys of arrows upon the field of battle.
Those two heroes, highly enraged, skillful, and stationed on uneven ground—
seeing those two high-souled ones, so skilled and fighting with such wonderful maneuvers,
O Bhārata, all living beings were filled with amazement.
Duḥśāsana, however, advancing against the great car-warrior Nakula,
pierced him with many sharp arrows capable of penetrating the vital organs.
Then the son of Mādrī [pierced] his standard, as well as his bow along with its arrow.
O Bhārata, as if laughing, he cut [them] down with sharpened arrows;
then he struck him with twenty-five small shafts.
But your son, difficult to overcome, [attacked] Nakula in that great battle.
With his arrows, he cut through their yokes and brought down their standards as well.
Then Durmukha, advancing against the mighty Sahadeva,
pierced him— who was striving in that great battle— with a shower of arrows.

Then, in that great battle, the heroic Sahadeva struck down Durmukha’s charioteer with an exceedingly sharp arrow. Those two, both intoxicated by the fight, having encountered one another in the fray, [continued their struggle].
Seeking to retaliate for each other's deeds, the two terrified one another with terrible arrows;
then King Yudhiṣṭhira himself advanced against the King of Madra and assailed Śalya, who possessed great strength and prowess.
O noble one, the lord of the Madras cut his bow in two.
Casting aside that severed bow, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
took up another bow that was more powerful and forceful.
Then the king, filled with rage, covered the lord of the Madras with straight-jointed arrows and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Thereupon, O Bhārata, Dhṛṣṭadyumna rushed against Droṇa.
Highly incensed, Droṇa cut into three pieces in that battle the firm bow of his striving opponent— a weapon capable of ending life—
as well as a most terrible arrow that resembled a second staff of Death.
He discharged it in battle, and it sank into his body. Then, taking up another bow and fourteen arrows,
the son of Drupada pierced Drona in return during the encounter.

Highly enraged with one another, those two waged a most intense battle. O great king, Śaṅkha, impetuous in combat, rushed against the son of Somadatta, who was likewise impetuous in war, and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"
In that battle, the hero pierced his right arm,
and the son of Somadatta likewise struck Śaṅkha in the region of the collarbone.
O lord of the people, a battle of terrible form ensued between those two.
Like Vṛtra and Vāsava swiftly engaged in battle,
O lord of the people, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭaketu, of immeasurable soul and wrathful appearance, rushed against the enraged Bāhlīka in the fray.
Then, O King, Bāhlīka struck the impatient Dhṛṣṭaketu with many arrows and let out a lion’s roar;
but the King of the Cedis, filled with rage, pierced Bāhlīka with nine shafts.
In that battle, he quickly pierced him, like one rutting elephant attacking another;
those two, enraged in that combat, roared again and again and encountered each other in great fury,
like the planets Mars and Mercury.
The one of cruel deeds, Ghaṭotkaca, advanced against the Rākṣasa Alambuṣa of cruel deeds,
as Śakra advances with his host in battle.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, filled with rage, [encountered] that exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa.
O Bhārata, he pierced him with ninety sharp arrows. But Alambuṣa, in that battle, warded off the mighty son of Bhīmasena in many ways with straight-knotted shafts.
Then, wounded by arrows in that encounter, those two shone forth like the mighty Bala and Śakra in the war between the gods and the asuras.
O King, in that battle, the powerful Śikhaṇḍin advanced against the son of Droṇa.
Then Aśvatthāman, filled with rage, pierced Śikhaṇḍin— who stood firm before him—
with an exceedingly sharp iron arrow and made him tremble.
O King, Śikhaṇḍin then struck the son of Droṇa in return.
With a well-polished, sharp, and whetted arrow,
those two then struck each other with various kinds of shafts in the fray;
Virāṭa, the commander of the army, [attacked] the heroic Bhagadatta in battle.
He rushed forward in haste, O King, and then the battle commenced.
Virāṭa, struck by Bhagadatta with a shower of arrows,
being highly enraged, rained [arrows] upon him like a cloud raining upon a mountain.
Then Bhagadatta quickly covered Virāṭa, the lord of the earth, in battle, just as a cloud covers the risen sun. Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, then advanced against Bṛhatkṣatra of the Kaikeyas.
O Bhārata, Kṛpa covered him with a shower of arrows;
the enraged Kekaya prince overwhelmed Gautama with a rain of shafts.
Having slain each other’s horses and indeed cut asunder their bows, they [remained] facing one another.
Deprived of their chariots, the two impatient warriors encountered each other for a sword-fight;
between them there occurred a battle of terrible form and extreme cruelty.
Then King Drupada [attacked] Jayadratha, the ruler of the Sindhus.

O scorcher of foes, he, being greatly delighted, advanced toward him who was likewise joyful in appearance. Then the King of the Sindhus struck Drupada with three arrows in that battle, and he in turn pierced him back.

Between those two there occurred a battle of terrible form and extreme ferocity, which produced delight in the spectators, like the encounter between Venus and Mars. But your son Vikarṇa [assailed] the mighty Sutasoma.
He charged with swift horses, and then the battle commenced.
Vikarṇa, having pierced Sutasoma with arrows, could not make him waver;
and Sutasoma [did the same] to Vikarṇa—this was like a marvel.
The great car-warrior Cekitāna, a tiger among men, rushed with great fury against Suśarman for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas;
O great king, Suśarman [then rushed] against the great car-warrior Cekitāna.
With a great shower of arrows, he warded him off in the encounter;
Cekitāna, also enraged in that great battle,
covered Suśarman with shafts like a massive cloud covering a mountain.
O king of kings, the powerful Śakuni rushed against the valiant Prativindhya, like one rutting elephant charging another; meanwhile,
the son of Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with rage, [assailed] the son of Subala with sharpened arrows.
In that battle, he tore [his opponent] apart like Maghavan tearing asunder a Dānava;
and Śakuni,
the highly wise one, tore Prativindhya— who was himself piercing him in the fray— with straight-jointed arrows.
O Indra among kings, Śrutakarman rushed in battle against the valiant Sudakṣiṇa, that great car-warrior of the Kambojas.
Sudakṣiṇa, however, [assailed] the great car-warrior, the son of Sāhadeva, in the encounter.

Having pierced him, he did not cause him to tremble, just as one cannot shake Mount Maināka. Then Śrutakarman, filled with rage, struck the great car-warrior of the Kambojas with many arrows, as if tearing him apart on all sides.
Then Irāvat, filled with rage, exerted himself and advanced against the impatient Śrutāyus in battle, displaying even greater prowess than before. Thereupon,
that great car-warrior, the son of Arjuna, having slain his horses in the encounter, [proceeded further].
That great army let out a tremendous roar, filling the air.
Then Śrutāyu, enraged in battle, struck Phālguni’s horses with the tip of his mace; thereupon, the combat resumed.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti engaged the great car-warrior Kuntibhoja, along with his army and his heroic son, in battle. There we witnessed the extraordinary prowess of the two princes of Avanti.
Having become firm, they fought with a great army;
Anuvinda, however, struck Kuntibhoja with a mace,
whereupon Kuntibhoja quickly covered him with a shower of arrows.
The son of Kuntibhoja also pierced Vinda with arrows, and he in turn pierced him back; that was like a marvel.
O noble one, the five Kekaya brothers [pierced] the five Gandharas.

Accompanied by their armies, they engaged those who were likewise accompanied by their armies in battle. And your son Vīrabāhu fought with Uttara, the son of Virāṭa and best of chariot-warriors, piercing him with sharpened arrows.
Śatānīka covered Ulūka with many arrows,
and Uttara also pierced that steadfast warrior with sharpened shafts;
O King, the ruler of the Cedis then rushed against Ulūka in the battle.
In that very same way, he pierced Ulūka with a shower of arrows;
and Ulūka also struck him with sharp, feathered shafts.
O lord of the people, a battle of terrible form took place between the two of them.
Highly enraged and undefeated, the two of them tore at one another;
likewise, the King of Cedi also pierced Ulūka in return.
In this manner, there were thousands of duels between chariot-warriors, elephants, and horses.
In that battle,
the melee between your foot soldiers and theirs lasted for about a moment, and that combat was pleasant to behold;
but thereafter, O King, it became like a frenzy, and nothing could be discerned.
In that battle, elephant met elephant, chariot-warrior went against chariot-warrior,
horse charged at horse, and foot-soldier at foot-soldier;
then a most difficult-to-restrain and chaotic combat ensued.
There, having encountered one another in battle, the heroes [fought];
there the celestial rishis, siddhas,
and cāraṇas assembled and beheld that terrible combat, which was like the war between the gods and the asuras.
Then, O noble one, thousands of elephants, chariots,
floods of horses, and throngs of men turned back in every direction;
here and there, chariots, elephants, and infantry were seen in utter confusion.
And the horsemen, O tiger among men, fought again and again.
Sañjaya said:
"O King, hundreds of thousands [of them] were there at various places, from time to time."
O Bhārata, I shall describe to you how they fought without restraint:
there, the son did not recognize his father, nor the father his own legitimate son;
there, the brother did not acknowledge his brother, nor did the maternal cousin his uncle.
Neither maternal uncle nor sister’s son, neither friend nor comrade—
possessed as if by a spirit, the Pāṇḍavas fought with the Kurus.
Some of those tigers among men rushed against the chariot-array with their own chariots.
O bull of the Bharatas, the yokes were joined with yokes,
the chariot-poles with chariot-poles, and the poles with the chariot-shafts;
some, united with the united, sought to slay one another.
Some chariots, having collided with other chariots, were unable to move; likewise,
massive-bodied elephants with temples bursting with rut, having collided with other elephants, furiously tore at one another in many ways with their tusks.
O Great King, elephants equipped with maces and banners, having charged against opposing elephants with great speed,
were struck there by their tusks and cried out in extreme agony.
Trained by their instructors and struck by goads and hooks like well-broken elephants facing other well-broken ones, they advanced head-on;
even among them, some great elephants became entangled with those already engaged in combat.
Letting out cries like those of cranes, they fled here and there;
and the well-trained elephants, their temples and faces streaming with rut-fluid, those excellent tuskers were pierced by double-edged swords, javelins, and iron arrows.
With their vital organs pierced, some cried out and fell down lifeless;
others fled in all directions, uttering terrifying shrieks.
As for the elephant-foot-guards, they were broad-chested strikers.
With spears and bows, and with stainless battle-axes; with maces and pestles, and with slings together with javelins;
and with iron clubs and bright, sharp swords.
O great king, with weapons firmly grasped and highly agitated, they were seen running here and there, each desiring to slay the other;
their swords shone brightly, drenched with the blood of men.
As the heroes rushed at one another,
a tumultuous sound arose from their swords— hurled and brandished by the arms of the warriors— as they fell upon each other’s vital organs.

There, amidst the throngs of men crying out to one another, some were shattered by maces and clubs, others were split apart by excellent swords, some were pierced by the tusks of elephants, and others were crushed by those very elephants.
O Bhārata, they heard terrible cries like those of the departed;
even the horse-riders, bearing chowrie-topped headdresses,
rushed at one another with horses as swift as swans.
Released by them, those great arrows— adorned with gold,
swift, stainless, and sharp— fell like serpents.
Some, having leaped upon great chariots with horses of supreme speed, [fled].

The heroic horsemen seized the heads of the chariot-warriors; having come within range of his arrows, the charioteer struck down even many horse-riders with straight-jointed *bhalla* shafts as they approached.
Resembling clouds over the mountains, the elephants— intoxicated and adorned with golden ornaments— seized the horses and crushed them with their very feet;
even as their frontal globes and flanks were being split open, the elephants [continued their assault].
Some, struck down by spears, shrieked in extreme agony;
others, those excellent elephants, having trampled horses along with their riders,
suddenly cast them aside there in that terrible tumult.
Lifting horses along with their riders by the tips of their tusks, the elephants moved about,
crushing multitudes of chariots together with their banners;
for some among those great elephants were overcome by both their masculine vigor and their state of rut.
With their trunks and feet, they slew horses along with their riders;
likewise, in that battle, they struck down horsemen and elephant-riders as well.
Some, having seized elephants with their trunks, even pulled down chariots together with their horses.
Tearing through all directions, they converged, following every sound;
[they struck] the elephants upon their frontal globes, their limbs, their flanks, and their temples.
Released by the chariot-warriors were arrows with golden shafts and well-sharpened points.
Those arrows, with unblunted points, swift, stainless, and sharp, fell upon the elephants and horses; like serpents, they sped forth,
piercing through the bodies of men and horses as well as their iron armor.
O lord of the people, spotless *śakti* spears, hurled by the arms of heroes and resembling great meteors, fell here and there—
some bound with leopard skins and others resting in tiger-skin sheaths.
With unsheathed and stainless swords, they struck down their enemies in battle; displaying their prowess as they leaped forward in fury, with one side of their bodies gashed open,
they rushed together with swords, shields, and battle-axes.
Some were torn apart by spears and others cut down by battle-axes;
some were trampled by elephants, while others were crushed by horses;
some were sliced by the rims of chariot wheels, and others were mangled by sharpened arrows.
O King, in various places the men there cried out to their kinsmen—
some to their sons, others to their fathers, and others to their brothers along with their kin;
they called to their maternal uncles, their nephews, and even to strangers in the midst of the battle.
O Bhārata, many were seen with their entrails scattered and their thighs broken;
with their fine arms severed and their sides torn open,
they cried out, parched with thirst and longing for life.
O Lord of the People, some of those of little strength, overcome by thirst,
fell upon the ground in battle and begged only for water,
O Bhārata, while drenched in streams of blood and suffering.
They severely censured themselves and your sons gathered together;
other heroic Kṣatriyas, who had harbored mutual enmity,
O noble one, neither released their weapons nor uttered cries of lamentation.
Exultant, they threatened one another here and there;
biting their own lips out of rage with their teeth,
they glared at one another with faces contorted by frowns.
Having threatened him, they were greatly delighted as long as he remained alive;
yet others, though suffering, pained by wounds, and tormented by arrows,
became silent— those of firm resolve and great strength.
But other heroes, deprived of their chariots in the battle, fell down seeking the chariot of another; crushed by excellent elephants,
O great king, they shone like blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
Many terrifying sounds arose amidst the ranks as that most fearsome slaughter of the best of heroes proceeded;
in that battle, the father struck the son, and the son struck the father.
O King, the nephew fought the maternal uncle, and the maternal uncle likewise fought the nephew; friend fought friend, and kinsman fought kinsman—
thus did the Kurus fight there with the Pāṇḍavas.
While that lawless and great battle raged,
O bull of the Bharatas, the army of the Pārthas trembled upon encountering Bhīṣma,
who was distinguished by his five-starred palm-tree banner.
O King, with his great standard raised aloft on his great chariot, the mighty-armed Bhīṣma then shone like the moon beside Mount Meru. Saṃjaya said:
When the greater part of that dreadful day had passed, while that most terrible slaughter of the foremost of great heroes was proceeding,
Durmukha, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Vivimśati—
Urged by your son, they approached and protected Bhīṣma.
Guarded by these five great car-warriors (*atiratha*s), O bull of the Bharatas,
that great car-warrior (*mahāratha*) penetrated the armies of the Pāṇḍavas.
O Bhārata, among the Cedis, Kāśis, Karūṣas, and Pañcālas,
Bhīṣma’s palm-tree standard was seen moving in many directions;
and then Bhīṣma [severed] heads as well as arms still grasping weapons.

With broad-headed arrows of great velocity and straight joints, Bhīṣma cut down the bows of the chariot-warriors, their uplifted heads, as well as their arms, thighs, and chariots with their massive banners.
But each one of those elephants, though as large as mountains, was suddenly struck by a single iron shaft from that great-souled one and fell to the earth,
O bull of the Bharatas, as Bhīṣma danced along the tracks of his chariot.
Some elephants, struck in their vital organs, let out cries of distress;
yet he, invincible to his enemies, caused their very hearts to tremble,
and with his arrows, he felled both horses and their riders.
Moving about in many ways with his chariot, that mighty and great archer, O Bhārata, skilled in the art of charioteering, performed circles, straight paths, and "cow-urine" maneuvers,
as well as many other tracks with his chariot.
Causing amazement among the hosts of enemies, Abhimanyu, the son of Jahnavī’s daughter,
moved about highly incensed; mounting a chariot yoked with excellent tawny-colored horses, he advanced toward the chariot of Bhīṣma.
With his banner adorned with golden *jāmbūnada* and featuring a *karṇikāra* flower,
he showered down iron-tipped arrows upon the chariots bearing banners of palm trees;
he rained them down upon Bhīṣma and those very best of car-warriors.
Having struck down the standard of Tālaketu with a sharp feathered shaft,
that hero fought with Bhīṣma and his followers;
he pierced Kṛtavarman with one iron arrow and Śalya with five.
Having pierced his great-grandfather with nine sharp-pointed arrows,
he struck his gold-adorned banner with one arrow released from a fully drawn bow and perfectly aimed.
With a straight-knotted *bhalla* arrow capable of piercing all armor, he struck off from the body of Durmukha’s charioteer his head; meanwhile,
Vivimshati [struck him] with three arrows capable of piercing all armor.

With a broad-headed arrow of sharpened tip, he cut through Kṛpa’s bow adorned with gold; then, as if dancing, that great car-warrior, filled with supreme rage, struck them down with sharp-pointed shafts.
Beholding his agility, even the gods were gratified;
and all the chariot-warriors, headed by Bhīṣma, considering Kṛṣṇa’s son to have attained his mark,
regarded him as the very embodiment of the courageous Dhanañjaya.

His bow, possessing a brilliance like that of a whirling firebrand and standing on the path of swiftness, flew through the quarters with a roar like the Gāṇḍīva. Having reached him, Bhīṣma struck him with nine swift arrows of great velocity.
In that battle, the slayer of enemy heroes swiftly pierced the son of Arjuna;
with three broad-headed arrows, he of rigid vows cut down the standard of that one of supreme energy,
and struck his charioteer with three shafts.
Likewise, O noble one, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Vivimśati— O King, all those great car-warriors having pierced him,
could not make the son of Kṛṣṇa tremble, just as they cannot move Mount Maināka.
Surrounded by those great car-warriors, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the heroic son of Kṛṣṇa rained down showers of arrows upon the five car-warriors.
Then, having warded off their great weapons with showers of arrows, he...
The powerful son of Kṛṣṇa roared as he discharged arrows at Bhīṣma;
there, O King, the immense strength of his arms was seen as he strove in battle to afflict Bhīṣma with his shafts.
Even Bhīṣma discharged arrows at him as he exerted his prowess;
however, in that battle, he cut down those arrows shot from Bhīṣma’s bow.
Then, with nine unerring shafts, he struck Bhīṣma’s banner.

The hero cut it down in battle, and then the people raised a loud cry. O Bhārata, that silver-skinned palm tree, adorned with gold and possessing a massive trunk, fell to the earth, severed by the arrows of Subhadrā’s son.
O bull of the Bharatas, seeing the standard fallen by the arrows of Subhadrā’s son, Bhīma roared joyfully, gladdening the son of Subhadrā. Then Bhīṣma [discharged] many great divine weapons.
At that moment, the exceedingly fierce and mighty one manifested his great power;
then the Great-Grandfather, whose soul is immeasurable, covered the son of Subhadrā with a hundred thousand straight-knotted arrows.
Then ten great archers, the mighty chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas,
rushed swiftly with their chariots to protect the son of Subhadrā;
they were Virāṭa with his son and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata.
O lord of the people, as Bhīma, the Kekayas,
and Sātyaki were charging forward with speed, Bhīṣma the son of Śāntanu struck the Pāñcālya king with three arrows and Sātyaki with sharpened shafts in that battle.
With a single sharp, feathered arrow released from a fully drawn bow, he cut down the banner of Bhīmasena; that standard,
O best of men, was made of gold and bore the emblem of a lion.
Shaken from his chariot by Bhīṣma, he fell down before Bhīmasena.
Having pierced Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, with three arrows in that battle,
Bhīmasena struck Kṛpa with one and Kṛtavarman with eight.
With the tip of his trunk raised high,
Uttara, the son of Virāṭa, also rushed toward the king, the lord of Madra,
on that elephant. As that king of elephants charged with speed, the charioteer—
Śalya warded off that incomparable force in battle;
then that enraged lord of elephants, who was large and well-trained,
planting his foot upon the yoke, struck down the four horses.

Standing on his chariot whose horses had been slain, the lord of the Madras hurled an iron spear, resembling a serpent, which was destined to bring about Uttara's end. With his armor pierced by it, he entered into a vast darkness.
He fell from the elephant’s shoulder, his goad and lance having been cast away; and Śalya, seizing a sword and leaping down from his excellent chariot,
displayed his prowess and severed the great trunk of the lordly elephant.
With his vital organs pierced by showers of arrows and his trunk severed,
that elephant let out a terrible cry of distress, fell down, and died.
Having performed such a feat, the great car-warrior, the King of Madra—
Seeing his handsome brother Uttara slain, and seeing Śalya standing there together with Kṛtavarman, the son of Virāṭa quickly mounted the radiant chariot of Kṛtavarman.
Śveta blazed with rage like a fire-god fed with oblations;
drawing his great bow, which resembled the bow of Indra, the powerful hero charged forward,
desiring to slay Śalya, the lord of Madra.
Surrounded on all sides by a great multitude of chariots,
he advanced toward the chariot of Śalya, discharging a rain of arrows;
beholding him approaching with the prowess of an elephant in rut, [the enemy prepared for battle].
Seven chariots of your side surrounded him from all sides,
desiring to rescue the King of Madra who had fallen into the very jaws of death:
Bṛhadbala of Kosala and Jayatsena of Magadha.
Likewise, O King, the powerful Rukmaratha, the son of Śalya;
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti; Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja;
and Jayadratha, the Sindhu king and heir of Bṛhatkṣatra.
The bows of those great-souled ones, variegated with many colors,
were seen drawn like flashes of lightning amidst the clouds;
they rained down a shower of arrows upon Śvetamūrdhan.
Like clouds driven by the wind at the end of the summer heat discharging water upon a mountain,
the enraged great archer, the commander of the army, then severed their bows with seven well-sharpened broad-headed arrows and crushed them.
O Bhārata, those [arrows] were seen as if already severed; then,
within half a blink of an eye, they took up their bows and loosed seven arrows at Śveta.

Then again, the immeasurable-souled one of mighty arms, with seven swift, broad-headed arrows, cut off the bows of those archers. With their great bows severed, those great car-warriors acted with haste.

Grasping their chariot-spears, they uttered terrible roars and pursued the seven white chariots, O best of the Bharatas; then those seven blazing spears, sounding like the thunderbolt of the great Indra, [fell].

The supreme master of weapons, having failed to reach his mark, cut [the opponent's bow] with seven broad-headed arrows. Then, O best of the Bharatas, taking up an arrow capable of rending any body, Śveta discharged it toward Rukmaratha.
That great arrow, surpassing the thunderbolt, fell upon his body; then,
O King, Rukmaratha, struck firmly by that shaft,
sank down upon the seat of his chariot and was overcome by a great faint.
But the charioteer, acting with haste and deeply agitated, carried away the unconscious and despondent prince while all the world looked on;
then he took up six other horses, white and adorned with gold.

The mighty-armed one, the scorcher of foes, struck down the tops of the banners of those six; having pierced their horses and charioteers with his arrows and covered them all with shafts, he proceeded toward the chariot of Śalya.
Then, O Bhārata, a tumultuous roar arose among your troops upon seeing the commander-in-chief quickly advancing toward Śalya’s chariot;
thereafter, your mighty son placed Bhīṣma at the head [of his army].
Surrounded by his entire army, he advanced toward Śvetaratha and rescued the King of Madra, who had fallen into the jaws of death. Then a tumultuous battle ensued, hair-raising and fierce.
The chariots and elephants of your men and those of the enemy were intermingled among the son of Subhadrā, Bhīmasena, the great car-warrior Sātyaki,
the Kaikeya, Virāṭa, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata.
Among these lions among men, the Cedis and the Matsyas,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"The aged grandfather of the Kurus rained down showers of arrows."
When the great archer Śveta had thus approached Śalya’s chariot,
what did the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas do, O Sañjaya?
Sañjaya said:
"Tell me, who am asking you, what did Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, do?
O King, then hundreds of thousands of bulls among Kṣatriyas,
those great chariot-warriors, placing the heroic Śveta at their head as their commander-in-chief,"
Displaying their strength to the king, O Bhārata, those great car-warriors, placing Śikhaṇḍin at their head, desired to protect your son;
they advanced against Bhīṣma’s gold-adorned chariot.
As he sought to slay that best of warriors, a great and tumultuous battle then ensued; O Acyuta, I shall describe to you that great carnage,
how the combat between your men and the enemy unfolded.
There, the son of Śantanu rendered many chariot-seats empty;
he lopped off heads with his arrows and struck down the best of car-warriors.
Possessing prowess equal to the sun, he shrouded the sun itself with his shafts.
Driving them away on all sides in battle, like the rising sun dispelling darkness,
he dispatched arrows by the hundreds of thousands in that conflict, O King—
arrows of great speed and great power that brought an end to the kṣatriyas in the fray.
They struck off the heads of hundreds of heroes in battle,
like thunderbolts felling mountain peaks; they crushed elephants armored in thorny mail,
and chariots were seen entangled with other chariots, O lord of the people.
O King, some horses carried away the chariot along with the horse-yokemate;
they bore the youthful hero, who had been slain and was hanging down from it, still clutching his bow,
as the spirited steeds galloped here and there.
With swords and quivers still fastened, their heads shattered and slain,
they fell by the hundreds upon the earth and lay there upon the beds of heroes;
running against one another, they fell down only to rise up again.
Rising up and rushing forward, they engaged in dual combat;
oppressed by one another, they rolled about on the front lines of the battle,
still clutching their gold-adorned bows and quivers.
