O Bhārata, with their heroes slain and themselves utterly crushed by the hundreds, they fled in every direction while discharging their weapons; intoxicated elephants turned back,
and horses were left with their riders killed.
Charioteers and chariot-warriors, crushing one another on all sides, [fell]; one man, struck by the arrows of another, fell from his chariot;
and even a chariot, its driver slain, fell high like a log of wood.
While fighting in battle as the dust arose and the ranks were arrayed,
the knowledge of the twang of the bow served as the means of recognition for the combatant;
by the touch of the bodies of the warriors, he could discern his adversary.
O King, as they fought with arrows amidst the rattling of bowstrings and the roar of banners, the shouts of "hero!
uttered by the warriors could no longer be heard;
for the battle resounded with the ear-piercing beat of the drums.
While they were fighting in battle, exerting their own manly prowess, they did not hear the mention of each other's names and lineages, nor their mutual proclamations,
as they fought in the fray, afflicted by the arrows shot from Bhīṣma’s bow.
They caused the hearts of the warriors to tremble against one another. In that exceedingly tumultuous, fierce, and hair-raising battle,
no father recognized his son in the fray.
The wheel was broken, the yoke severed, and one of the lead horses slain;
the hero, along with his charioteer, was cast down from the chariot by straight-flying arrows.
And thus, in that battle, all the heroes were deprived of their chariots.
They were seen running in every direction—
elephants slain, heads severed, vital organs pierced, and horses killed; indeed,
there was not a single one who remained unhurt while Bhīṣma was slaughtering the enemies.
In that great battle, Śveta himself slew hundreds of noble princes and chariot-warriors of the Kurus;
O bull of the Bharatas, he severed the heads of those car-fighters with his arrows.
O lord of the people, there were arms still clutching their ornaments, as well as bows on all sides;
there were chariot-poles, chariot-wheels, quivers, and yokes;
and costly umbrellas and banners.
O Bhārata, multitudes of horses, multitudes of chariots, and multitudes of men,
as well as hundreds of elephants, were slain by Śveta, O Bhārata;
we too, terrified by the fear of Śveta, abandoned that best of car-warriors.
Then,
O joy of the Kurus, having moved beyond the range of the arrows,
we Kauravas, remaining fearless, beheld from all sides the all-pervading Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, as he stood in battle.
Undaunted in a time of distress, Bhīṣma, that tiger among men, stood alone in our great battle like the immovable Mount Meru;
he was like the sun at the end of winter, as if drawing away the very lives of his enemies.
Like the sun with its rays, he stood there, possessing arrows for his beams; that great archer released multitudes of arrows innumerable times,
slaying his enemies in battle like the wielder of the thunderbolt against the asuras.
Being slaughtered by Bhīṣma, they abandoned that mighty warrior,
like herds of animals deserting their leader when he has been released from the herd and is acting cruelly upon the ground.
Finding him alone, one [warrior], joyful and emboldened, [attacked] that scorcher of foes.
Devoted to the welfare of Duryodhana and causing the Pāṇḍavas to grieve,
O lord of the people, he cast down the armies of the Pāṇḍavas in that great battle, having abandoned his life— which is so difficult to give up— and all fear.
Seeing the divisions striking him, your father Devavrata Bhīṣma, the commander-in-chief, quickly advanced against Śveta and covered him with a great net of arrows.
And Bhīṣma likewise covered Śveta with showers of arrows.
Roaring like two bulls or like two elephants in rut,
they struck one another like two highly enraged tigers.
Having warded off weapons with their own weapons, those two bulls among men—
Bhīṣma and Śveta— then fought, each desiring the other's death;
Bhīṣma could have consumed the army of the Pāṇḍavas in a single day.
If Śveta had not protected him with arrows while he was exceedingly enraged,
then, seeing the Grandfather turned away by Śveta,
the Pāṇḍavas would have been filled with joy and your son would have become despondent.
Then Duryodhana, enraged and surrounded by kings,
rushed with his army against the Pandava host in battle,
O lord of men— along with Durmukha, Kritavarman, Kripa, and Shalya.
Urged on by your son, they approached Bhīṣma and protected him; indeed,
all the kings led by Duryodhana beheld the armies of the Pāṇḍavas being slaughtered in the battle.
Having bypassed the son of Gaṅgā, Śveta, O King, violently destroyed your son’s army with his might, like the wind destroys trees with its force;
having routed the host, the son of Virāṭa was frantic with rage.
Rushing forward once more with great speed toward the place where Bhīṣma was stationed, those two mighty and high-souled warriors, blazing with arrows, encountered him there, O King,
like Vṛtra and Vāsava.
O Great King, seeking to slay one another,
Śveta seized his bow and pierced Bhīṣma with seven arrows; then that valiant warrior, having displayed his own prowess, [assailed] his opponent’s valor.
With speed, Śveta warded off the son of Śantanu as one intoxicated elephant wards off another; he then pierced him again with twenty-five straight-knotted arrows, and that was like a marvel.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, pierced him in return with ten arrows.
Though pierced by him, that powerful Vairāṭi did not tremble, remaining like a mountain,
as he drew his bow back fiercely in the battle.
Then Śveta, the joy of the Kṣatriyas, struck Bhīṣma;
then Śveta, laughing and licking the corners of his mouth,
cut Bhīṣma’s bow into ten pieces with nine arrows.
Having aimed a feathered arrow with its shafts aligned,
he then struck down the palm-tree banner at the top of the high-souled one’s standard;
seeing Bhīṣma’s ensign fallen, your sons...
They considered Bhīṣma as already slain, having fallen under the power of Śveta;
and the Pāṇḍavas, filled with joy,
blew their conchs with great delight upon seeing the palm-tree standard of the high-souled Bhīṣma fallen.
Then Duryodhana, out of anger, urged on his own army:
"With all effort, strive to protect Bhīṣma from every side;
let him not meet his death while we are looking on."
"Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, is a hero; thus I speak the truth to you.
Having heard the king's words, the great car-warriors, acting with haste, protected the son of Gaṅgā with their fourfold army.
O Bhārata, Bāhlīka, Kṛtavarman, Śala, and Śalya,
along with Jalasandha, Vikarṇa, Citrasena, and Vivimśati,
hastened at that time of urgency and surrounded him on all sides.
They rained down a most tumultuous shower of weapons upon Śveta;
but the great car-warrior of immeasurable soul, acting with haste and displaying his lightness of hand, warded them off with sharpened arrows in his wrath.
Having warded off all of them like a lion warding off elephants,
he severed Bhīṣma’s bow with a great shower of arrows. Then, in that battle, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, took up another bow.
O Indra among kings, he pierced Śveta with sharp arrows feathered with heron plumes;
then, O King, the enraged commander-in-chief pierced Bhīṣma in battle with many iron shafts while all the world looked on.
Then the king was deeply distressed upon seeing Bhīṣma,
the pre-eminent hero of all the world, held back in battle by Śveta;
and a great slaughter occurred among your troops.
Seeing that hero checked by Śveta and wounded by his arrows,
they thought him slain by Śveta and fallen under Śveta’s power;
thereupon, your father Devavrata was overcome by rage.
Seeing his standard shattered and his army held in check,
O Great King, he discharged many arrows at Śveta. Having warded them off in battle, Śveta, the best of chariot-warriors, [assailed] Bhīṣma.
With a broad-headed arrow, he once again severed your father’s bow;
casting aside that bow, O King, the son of Gaṅgā, overwhelmed with rage,
took up another bow that was massive and more powerful.
Aiming there, he loosed seven broad-headed arrows sharpened on stone;
with four he struck the horses of Śveta, the commander of the army,
and with two he cut down the standard, while with the seventh he struck the charioteer.
Enraged and acting with swift prowess, he severed [his] head with a broad-headed arrow. Having leaped down from that chariot whose horses and driver were slain, the mighty one,
overcome by indignation, became agitated.
Seeing Śveta, the best of chariot-warriors, deprived of his chariot, the Grandfather struck him from all sides with multitudes of sharpened arrows.
Being thus struck in battle by the arrows discharged from Bhīṣma’s bow, he...
Casting aside his bow from his own chariot, he seized a golden spear. Then,
in the battle, Śveta grasped that fierce and terrifying spear,
which was like the staff of Time and as formidable as the very sister of Death, while he himself was breathing heavily.
And then Śveta spoke to Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, on the battlefield:
"Stay now, highly provoked; behold me and be a man!
Having spoken thus to Bhīṣma in the fray, that great archer of prowess—

Then, O lord of the people, the one of immeasurable soul, exerting his prowess for the sake of the Pāṇḍava and desiring your misfortune, hurled a spear resembling a serpent; a great cry of "Alas! arose among your sons.
O King, seeing that most terrible spear released from Śveta’s hand— resembling the staff of Death and like a sloughed-off serpent— it fell suddenly from the sky like a great meteor.
O King, your father Devavrata Bhīṣma, remaining unperturbed, then cut that spear— which was blazing in the sky as if enveloped in flames— with eight or nine feathered arrows.
O bull of the Bharatas, seeing that exquisite golden spear severed by his sharp arrows, all your men cried out;
and the son of Virāṭa, overwhelmed with rage upon seeing the spear destroyed, [rushed forward].
But his mind struck down by fate, O King, the son of Virāṭa did not recognize what ought to be done; overwhelmed by anger, as if laughing,
he joyfully seized a mace for the purpose of slaying Bhīṣma.
With eyes red with rage, like the Destroyer himself with staff in hand,
he rushed toward Bhīṣma like a torrent of water against a mountain. Perceiving his irresistible momentum, the powerful Bhīṣma—
In order to escape the blow, Śveta suddenly descended to the earth; overcome with rage, he whirled that mace and hurled it at Bhīṣma’s chariot, like the god Dhaneśvara.

By that [missile] which felled Bhīṣma, that chariot— along with its banner, driver, horses, yoke, and frame— was reduced to ashes. Seeing Bhīṣma, the best of chariot-warriors, deprived of his chariot, the foremost of car-borne warriors [advanced].
The chariot-warriors led by Śalya rushed forward together;
then, mounting another chariot and stretching his bow with a heavy heart,
the son of Gaṅgā slowly advanced toward Śveta as if smiling.
In that interval, Bhīṣma heard a vast, divine voice uttered from the sky, which brought about his own welfare: "Bhīṣma,
Bhīṣma, O mighty-armed one, exert yourself with speed!"
"For this is the time ordained by the Source of the Universe for his defeat.
Having heard these words spoken by the messenger of the gods,
he became joyful in heart and set his mind upon slaying him.
Seeing Śveta, the best of chariot-warriors, deprived of his chariot and standing on foot,
the great car-warriors turned back together, desiring to rescue him— Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata.
Kaikeya, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the heroic Abhimanyu—
all these as they rushed forward— were held back by him of immeasurable soul, along with Droṇa, Śalya, and Kṛpa, like mountains resisting the force of water.
When all those high-souled Pāṇḍavas had been held in check,
Śveta drew his sword and severed Bhīṣma’s bow.
Casting aside that broken bow, the grandfather acted with haste.
Having heard the words of the divine messenger, he set his mind upon his slaughter. Then your father Devavrata, that great car-warrior, moving about and taking up another bow, acted with haste.
In an instant, O best of the Bharatas, your father made his bow ready, which shone like the rainbow of Indra; he saw him surrounded by great car-warriors,
those tigers among men led by Bhīmasena.
The son of Gaṅgā swiftly turned toward Śveta, the commander of the army;
then the powerful Bhīṣma,
that great car-warrior, struck the attacking Bhīmasena, the general, with sixty arrows.
And in that battle, your father Devavrata,
the best of the Bharatas, struck Abhimanyu with three straight-knotted arrows;
likewise, the grandfather of the Bharatas struck Sātyaki with a hundred in the fray.
Having checked Dhṛṣṭadyumna with twenty arrows and the Kaikeya prince with five,
your father Devavrata, having held back all those great archers with his terrible shafts, rushed toward Śveta alone.
Then the powerful Bhīṣma, having drawn back that supreme arrow— which was like Death itself, capable of achieving a great burden, and difficult to withstand— fitted it to his bowstring,
an arrow feathered with hair and joined with the Brahmā weapon.
The gods, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas beheld it;
having pierced the armor and the heart of that one of immeasurable energy,
the arrow, blazing like a great thunderbolt, entered the earth.
Just as the setting sun quickly withdraws its radiance,
so did [Death] depart, taking away the life from Śvetadeha.
Thus was that tiger among men struck down by Bhīṣma in battle.
We beheld him falling like a peak fallen from a mountain;
there the Pāṇḍavas and the great car-warriors among the Kṣatriyas lamented,
while your sons and all the Kurus were filled with joy.
Then, O King, seeing Śveta struck down,
Duḥśāsana danced on all sides to the terrible sounds of musical instruments,
now that that great archer Bhīṣma, the ornament of battle, had been slain.

The great archers, the chariot-warriors led by Śikhaṇḍin, trembled. Then, O King, once the commander of the army had been slain, Dhanañjaya and the descendant of Vṛṣṇi gradually ordered a withdrawal from all sides.
Then, O Bhārata, there was a withdrawal of your troops and theirs,
while both your men and the enemy were shouting again and again;
and the great car-warriors of the Pārthas, becoming dejected in spirit, took up their positions.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dear one, while the scorchers of the foe were contemplating that terrible slaughter in single combat after their commander-in-chief Śveta had been slain by the enemies in battle,"
What did the great archers, the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas,
do upon hearing that Śveta had been struck down in battle,
while they were striving for his sake and the enemies were fleeing?

My heart rejoices as I hear of the victory, O Sañjaya; as I contemplate the counter-strategy, my noble kinsmen flow forth toward me. For he was indeed a hero, devoted and aged, the lord of the Kurus at that time.
That wise son of his father has always harbored enmity toward him;
out of fear and agitation regarding that [enmity], he previously sought refuge with the Pāṇḍavas,
abandoning all his forces and remaining in a stronghold.
Having established his camp in a difficult region through the prowess of the Pāṇḍavas,
and constantly harassing his enemies while adhering to noble conduct,
that evil-minded one was indeed always a marvel among those kings of old.
O Sañjaya, how was he who was devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira slain? How was my esteemed son, that base man, cast down— he who,
in no way whatsoever, would have favored battle against Bhīṣma or the Teacher?
Neither Kṛpa, nor Gāndhārī, nor I myself, O Saṃjaya, find this pleasing; nor does Vāsudeva of the Vṛṣṇi clan, nor the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja,
nor Bhīma, nor Arjuna, nor the two Yamas, those bulls among men.
O Sañjaya, although Duryodhana was constantly restrained by me, by Gāndhārī, by Vidura,
by Rāma the son of Jamadagni, and by the high-souled Vyāsa,
he persisted in fighting.
Adopting the counsel of Karṇa, the son of Subala, and likewise that of the evil-doing Duḥśāsana, he reviled the Pāṇḍavas;
O Sañjaya, I believe he has now met with a terrible calamity.
With Śveta having been destroyed and Bhīṣma victorious,
what did Pārtha, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, do in battle when he was enraged?
For my fear of Arjuna is great, O dear one, and it does not subside.
For that son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava, is indeed a hero and one who acts with swiftness;
I believe he will crush the bodies of his enemies with his arrows.
The son of Indrāṇī is equal to the younger brother of Indra and like Mahendra himself in strength.
Upon seeing that manifestation of infallible wrathful resolve, what was the state of your minds? Likewise, there was the hero learned in the Vedas, possessing a splendor equal to fire and the sun,
skilled in the weapons of Indra, immeasurable in soul, and victorious in battle as he leaped forward.
He performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of weapons whose forms were like the touch of a thunderbolt;
then that great car-warrior, sword in hand, raised a roar.
O Saṃjaya, he was the powerful son of Drupada, possessed of great wisdom.

When Śveta had been struck down in battle, what did Dhṛṣṭadyumna do? I believe that the minds of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were set ablaze by the former transgression and by the slaughter of the commander of the army.
Reflecting upon their wrath day and night, [Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I find no peace; tell me everything, Sañjaya. Sañjaya said: [Tell me everything, Sañjaya.]
When the greater part of that dreadful day had passed,
the battle between your men and the enemy broke out once more;
for they saw that Śveta, the commander of Virāṭa’s army, had been slain.
Seeing Śalya standing there together with Kṛtavarman,
Śaṅkha blazed up in anger like a sacrificial fire fed with oblations.
Stretching his great bow, which was adorned with gold, he—
Desiring to slay Śalya, the lord of Madra, the powerful warrior,
surrounded on all sides by a great multitude of chariots,
rushed forward, discharging a rain of arrows toward Śalya’s chariot.
Beholding him charging forward with the prowess of an elephant in rut,
seven chariot-warriors from your side surrounded him on all sides,
seeking to rescue the King of Madra who had fallen into the very jaws of death.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīṣma, roaring like a rain-cloud,
took up a bow as long as a palm tree and rushed toward Śaṅkha in battle.
Beholding that great archer of immense strength thus prepared for combat, [the enemy]—
The Pāṇḍava army was terrified, like a ship struck by the force of the wind;
there, Arjuna moved with haste, taking the lead before Śaṅkha,
thinking, "He must be protected from Bhīṣma today," and then the battle commenced.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the warriors fighting in the fray;
they were struck with wonder, thinking, "Energy has been met with energy.
Then Śalya, mace in hand, descended from his great chariot.
O bull of the Bharatas, he slew the four horses of Śaṅkha.
Having his horses killed, he quickly took up a sword and fled from the chariot;
reaching the chariot of Bībhatsu, he then found peace.
Then, from Bhīṣma’s chariot, feathered arrows flew forth swiftly,
by which the sky and the earth were completely covered on all sides.
Then [he attacked] the Pañcālas and Drupada of the Matsyas, who was surrounded by his army.
Then Bhīṣma, the best among strikers, felled the Pañcālas, the Matsyas, the Kekayas, and the Prabhadrakas with his arrows,
swiftly abandoning the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin in the midst of battle.
O King, he rushed toward Drupada, the Pāñcālya king surrounded by his army,
scattering many arrows at his dear kinsman,
like forests consumed by fire at the end of winter.
The armies of Drupada appeared as if scorched by autumnal fires; Bhīṣma stood in the battle like a smokeless flame,
like the sun at midday scorching with its brilliance.
The warriors of the Pāṇḍava could not even look at Bhīṣma;
afflicted by fear, those Pāṇḍavas cast their eyes in every direction,
yet they found no protector, like cows tormented by the cold.
That army of Yudhiṣṭhira, afflicted by the arrows of Gāṅgeya,
was like a white cow belonging to the Lord of Cattle pierced by a lion;
when the host was slaughtered, fled, dispirited, and crushed, [the battle ceased].
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Pāṇḍava troops, O Bhārata.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, whose bow was always drawn into a circle, released arrows with blazing tips like venomous serpents.

Making all directions a single path with his arrows, he of firm vows struck down the Pāṇḍava chariot-warriors, naming each one as he did so, O Bhārata. Then, when the armies were broken and crushed on every side,
When the sun had set, nothing could be discerned;
and seeing Bhīṣma still exerting himself in that great battle, O bull of the Bharatas, the sons of Pṛthā ordered the withdrawal of their troops.
Saṃjaya said:
O bull of the Bharatas, when the withdrawal of the armies had been made on that first day,
and while Bhīṣma was enraged in battle and Duryodhana was likewise joyful, [the night passed].
Then Dharmarāja, accompanied by all his brothers and all the lords of men, quickly approached Janārdana;
filled with supreme grief and reflecting upon his defeat.
O King, having witnessed Bhīṣma’s prowess, he spoke to the descendant of Vṛṣṇi:
"Kṛṣṇa, behold the great archer Bhīṣma of terrible valor,
consuming my army with his arrows like a fire consuming dry grass in the summer."
Then, O Great King, Yudhiṣṭhira, having seen Kṛṣṇa, spoke:
"How shall we be able to look upon this high-souled one,
as he licks up my army like a fire fed with oblations?"

For having seen this tiger among men, armed with a bow and possessed of great strength, my army— struck by his arrows— has fled in all directions; yet even a wrathful Yama or the wielder of the thunderbolt could be conquered in battle [by him].
Even Varuṇa, the bearer of the noose, or Kubera, the wielder of the mace,
could not defeat Bhīṣma, who possesses great splendor and immense strength. Such being the case, I am submerged in the fathomless waters of Bhīṣma like one without a boat.
"O Keśava, due to the weakness of my own intellect, having encountered Bhīṣma,
O Govinda, I shall go to the forest; it is better for me to live there than to give these protectors of the earth over to Bhīṣma as death."
"O Kṛṣṇa, Bhīṣma, who is skilled in great weapons, will destroy my army;
just as moths rushing toward a blazing fire go only to their own destruction, so do the men of my host."
"O Vārṣṇeya, for the sake of the kingdom, I, though full of prowess, have been brought to exhaustion;
and my heroic brothers too have been worn out and tormented by arrows. On my account, out of brotherly affection, they have likewise been deprived of their kingdom and their happiness."
"I hold life in high esteem, for life is indeed difficult to obtain today.
With whatever remnant of my life remains, I shall perform ascetic penances that are hard to practice. O Keśava, I will not cause these friends to be slain in battle."

"O Mādhava, the mighty Bhīṣma incessantly causes my many thousands of chariots to be slain with celestial weapons—those foremost among strikers. What indeed must I do so that my purpose may be accomplished? Tell me without delay."
I see Savyasācin standing as if indifferent in this battle;
this mighty-armed Bhīma alone fights with his utmost power,
relying solely on the strength of his arms and mindful of the duty of a Kṣatriya.
With his hero-slaying mace, that high-minded one performs difficult deeds according to his resolve against elephants, horses, chariots,
and infantry; yet, O noble sir, he is not capable of bringing about the total destruction of the enemy host.
O hero, even in a hundred years, through fair combat alone,
this single friend of yours, though skilled in weapons, looks on with indifference as we are being consumed by Bhīṣma and the high-souled Droṇa.
The divine weapons of Bhīṣma and the high-souled Droṇa,
when discharged again and again, will consume all the Kṣatriyas,
O Kṛṣṇa; for Bhīṣma is highly incensed and joined by all the kings.
"Surely he will destroy us, given such is his prowess.
Therefore, O great archer, lord of yogis, behold that great car-warrior who might quell Bhīṣma in battle, just as a rain-cloud extinguishes a forest fire."
"O Govinda, through your grace, the Pāṇḍavas, having slain their enemies,
have regained their own kingdom and will rejoice together with their kinsmen.
Having spoken thus, the high-minded Pārtha then sat in meditation.
Having remained inwardly troubled for a long time, his consciousness struck by grief,
Govinda, perceiving the Pāṇḍava afflicted by sorrow and his mind overwhelmed by distress,
spoke there to gladden all the Pāṇḍavas.
"Do not grieve, O best of the Bharatas; you ought not to mourn, for you have brothers who are heroes and archers renowned throughout all the world,
as well as I, O King, who am your well-wisher, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki."
The aged Virāṭa and Drupada, as well as Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
and likewise all the kings with their armies, O best of kings, wait for your favor and are devoted to you, O lord of the people.

"This son of Pṛṣata, the mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who is always desirous of your welfare and devoted to what is pleasing to you, has now attained the command of the army. And Śikhaṇḍin, O mighty-armed one, shall indeed bring about the death of Bhīṣma."
"O tiger among men, you whose prowess is equal to that of a tiger,
O Indra among kings, appoint Dhṛṣṭadyumna to the command of the army.
Having heard this, the king then [addressed] the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
In that assembly, while Vāsudeva was listening, he said:
"O Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O noble one, listen to this which I shall say to you;
these words spoken by me must not be transgressed."
"You, O general, are esteemed by Vāsudeva for me,
just as Kārttikeya was eternally esteemed by the gods in ancient times;
so too, O bull among men, are you the commander of the Pāṇḍavas."
Therefore, O tiger among men, exerting your prowess, slay the Kauravas!
I, Bhīma, and Kṛṣṇa shall follow you, O noble one,
as will the two sons of Mādrī together and the sons of Draupadī, all clad in armor.
"And those other eminent rulers of the earth, O bull among men.
Having said this much, the king spoke to Sahadeva:
"Bring the materials for the consecration quickly and with all speed!"
Then, O Bhārata, Dhaumya appeared, taking the sacrificial materials with him;
accompanied by Sahadeva, he presented them to the son of Pāṇḍu.
Then, [he addressed] that tiger among men, the son of Drupada, in the midst of the assembly.
Having seated him comfortably upon a noble throne, Acyuta performed his consecration. Thus consecrated, the powerful son of Drupada shone resplendently,
just as Kārttikeya shone during the war between the gods and the asuras.
Then, heartening them all, Dhṛṣṭadyumna addressed him:
"O Pārtha, I was ordained of old by Śambhu as the slayer of Droṇa;
likewise, in battle, [I shall face] Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Jayadratha."
"O King, today I shall fight against all those who are arrogant in battle.
Then a great shout was raised by the Pāṇḍavas, those mighty archers intoxicated with the desire for war.
Hearing that, the sons of Pṛthā and the great car-warriors among the kings rejoiced.
When the lord of kings, the son of Pṛṣata—the slayer of enemies—had prepared himself, Pārtha then spoke to that son of Pṛṣata, the commander of the army:
"This array is named Krauñcāruṇa; it is the destroyer of all enemies."

O kings, together with the Kurus, behold that formation which destroys the enemy host— a formation never seen before— which Bṛhaspati then spoke to Indra during the war between the gods and the asuras, and which I shall now duly deploy.
Thus addressed by that god among men, as Viṣṇu was by the wielder of the thunderbolt,
he placed Dhanañjaya at the head of all the armies at dawn;
his banner, moving along the path of the sun, was wonderful and beautiful to behold.
By the command of Indra, it was fashioned by Viśvakarman;
adorned with banners having the colors of Indra’s bow,
it moved through the sky like a traveler in the air, resembling a city of the Gandharvas.
O noble one, he appeared as if dancing during the maneuvers of the chariot. With that jewel-encrusted [bow], Pārtha, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva,
became supremely endowed with it, like the Self-existent One with the sun.
King Drupada, surrounded by a vast army, was the head;
O lord of men, Kuntibhoja and the king of Cedi were the two eyes.
The Dāśārṇakas and the Prayāgas, together with the hosts of Dāśerakas, [formed the rest].
O bull of the Bharatas, the Anūpagas and Kirātas were at the neck; and O King, Yudhiṣṭhira, together with the Paṭaccaras, Huṇḍas, Pauravakas, and Niṣādas, formed the rear.
Bhīmasena and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
the sons of Draupadī and Abhimanyu, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki formed the two wings;
as did the Piśācas, the Daradas, the Puṇḍras, along with the Kuṇḍīviṣas.
The Maḍakas, Laḍakas, Taṅgaṇas, Parataṅgaṇas,
Bāhlikas, Tittiras, Colas, and Pāṇḍyas, O Bhārata—
these peoples, O King, are situated on the southern wing.
O Bhārata, the Agniveśyas, Jagattuṇḍas, Paladāśas,
Śabaras, Tumbupas, and Vatsas, along with the Nākulis—
Nakula and Sahadeva— occupied the left flank.
Ten thousand chariots formed the two wings, and likewise a hundred thousand (*niyuta*) formed the head;
the back consisted of ten million (*arbuda*) and twenty thousand,
while the neck consisted of a hundred thousand and seventy thousand.
O King, at the tips of the wings, on the flanks, and at the ends of the wings,
the elephants marched surrounded like moving mountains;
Virāṭa, together with the Kekayas, protected the rear.
The King of Kāśī and Śaibya, with thirty thousand chariots— having thus formed this great array, O Bhārata, the Pāṇḍavas stood armored for battle, awaiting the rising of the sun.
And there, O best of the Bharatas, a tremendous sound arose that touched the very heavens.
Thus those tigers among men, the Pāṇḍavas, intoxicated for battle,
stood arrayed after having counter-arrayed the army of your son.
"O bull of the Bharatas, the hearts of the warriors seem to tremble indeed.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Having seen Bhīmasena standing before him with mace in hand..."
O Sañjaya, at sunrise, who were those eager for battle and joyful in appearance? Did my men, led by Bhīṣma, advance first?
Were the Pāṇḍavas, with their terrifying eyes, present at that time?
For whom were the moon and the sun inferior?
And for whom would the beasts of prey howl against the army?
"Whose facial complexions among the youths are serene?
Saṃjaya said:
"Tell me all this in truth, exactly as it is."
Both armies appeared exactly alike;
both armies were likewise filled with joy,
and both were as variegated as rows of forest trees.
Both armies were filled with elephants, chariots, and horses;
both armies were terrible in appearance, O lord of men;
and likewise, both were difficult to withstand, O Bhārata.
Thus both were intent on conquering heaven; thus both were frequented by virtuous men;
the Kauravas, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, turned their backs.
Likewise, the Pāṇḍavas, facing eastward and intent on battle,
were like the army of the lord of the Daityas for the Kauravas,
and like the army of the lord of the gods for the Pāṇḍavas.
A favorable wind blew from behind the Pāṇḍavas, while the wind blew against the faces of your men;
the scent of rutting ichor issued from the lordly elephants.
The elephants could not endure your son;
Duryodhana [urged] his excellent elephant, lotus-colored,
with golden girths, possessed of innate strength, and with temporal juice flowing.
Stationed in the midst of the Kurus,
being praised by chariot-warriors and bards,
his white parasol, radiant as the moon, was held over him.
Likewise, a golden garland shines upon his head;
the king of Gāndhāra protects him from all sides, along with Śakuni and the mountaineers (Pārvatīyas) of Gāndhāra.
Bhīṣma, the aged leader of the entire army, stood at the front with a white umbrella, white hair, and a conch shell;
he wore a white turban and possessed a pale banner.
The white chariot, shining like a mountain,
was likewise [surrounded] by the entire army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son and the great-souled Atiratha of the Bāhlikas.
Those great archers of noble fortune stood armored for battle;
their large, stainless white umbrellas, radiant as the sun, shone resplendently upon their elephants and chariots.
Saṃjaya said: Then,
seeing that the son of Pṛthā, of immeasurable splendor, had formed the great and most terrible Krauñca array, which was impenetrable, your son [ordered his own forces].
Having approached the preceptor, O noble one, as well as Kṛpa, Śalya, the son of Somadatta, Vikarṇa, Aśvatthāman,
and all his brothers beginning with Duḥśāsana, O Bhārata—
At that time, your son, gladdening them, spoke these words to many other heroes who had arrived for battle—
all of whom were armed with various weapons and missiles, and were experts in the use of all arms and weaponry.

"Indeed, each one of you great car-warriors (*mahāratha*) is individually capable of slaying the sons of Pāṇḍu along with their armies in battle; how much more so when united? Yet that army of ours, though protected by Bhīṣma, is insufficient."
"O best of kings, this force of theirs is sufficient:
the Saṃsthānas, Śūrasenas, Veṇikas, Kukuras,
Ārevakas, Trigartas, Madrakas, and Yavanas."
Together with Śatruñjaya, as well as Duḥśāsana,
the heroic Vikarṇa, Nanda and Upananda,
and accompanied by Citrasena and the Pāṇibhadrakas, they were all assembled there.
"Let them protect Bhīṣma alone, preceded by their armies. Then, O sire, Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and your son formed a great battle array to repel the Pāṇḍavas.
Bhīṣma, surrounded on all sides by a vast army, advanced,
leading that great host like the king of the gods;
the powerful and mighty archer, the son of Bharadvāja, followed him.
O lord of the people, together with the Kuntalas, the Daśārṇas, the Māgadhas, the Vidarbhas,
the Mekalas, and the Karṇaprāvaraṇas,
along with their entire army, [they approached] Bhīṣma, who shines in battle.
The Gāndhāras, the Sindhusauvīras, the Śibis, and the Vasātis,
along with Śakuni and his own army, protected the son of Bharadvāja.
Then King Duryodhana, together with all his brothers, [stood by him].
With the Aśvatakas, the Vikarṇas, as well as the Śarmilas and Kosalas, with the Daradas, the Cūcupas, and likewise the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas,
he joyfully protected the army of Saubaleya.
O Sire, Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, and Bhagadatta,
along with Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, protected the left flank. Saumadatti, Suśarman, and Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja [protected the right].
Śatāyu and Śrutāyu were stationed on the right flank;
while Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata stood at the rear of the army together with a vast host.
His rear-guards, however, were lords of men from various lands:
Ketumān, Vasudāna, and Abhibhū, the son of Kāśya.
Then, O Bhārata, all those on your side rejoiced for battle.
Filled with joy, they blew their conchs and let out lion-like roars. Hearing those joyful sounds, the grandfather, the elder of the Kurus,
the powerful one, let out a loud lion-roar and blew his conch shell.
Then conchs, kettledrums, and various other musical instruments were sounded by the enemies, as well as large drums; that noise became tumultuous.
Then [the two heroes] stood upon a great chariot yoked with white horses.
They both blew their excellent conchs, adorned with gold and jewels:
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya blew the Devadatta,
and Vṛkodara, the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew the Anantavijaya;
Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka respectively.
And the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, as well as the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī, [blew their own conchs].
The valiant Abhimanyu, the heroic Uttamaujas, the King of Kāśī, Śaibya, the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the highly illustrious Sātyaki.
The great archer Pāñcālya and the five sons of Draupadī all blew their great conch shells and uttered lion-like roars. That immense clamor was raised there by those heroes.
The tumultuous noise resounded through both the sky and the earth. Thus, O great king, these delighted Kurus and Pāṇḍavas came together once more for battle, scorching one another.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When my armies and those of the others were thus arrayed,
how did those best among strikers engage in the combat?
Saṃjaya said:
When the armies were drawn up in equal array, your men, clad in armor and bearing beautiful banners, fought together with the Pāṇḍavas; hear now how that occurred.
Beholding that army, which resembled the ocean and seemed as if it had no shore,
your son King Duryodhana stood in their midst and said to all your men, "Fight, clad in armor!"
Adopting a cruel resolve and having renounced their very lives,
all of them, with their banners raised high, advanced against the Pāṇḍavas.
Then a tumultuous battle took place, one that made the hair stand on end.
In that battle where the chariots and elephants of your men and the enemy were intermingled,
gold-tufted, well-sharpened arrows released by the chariot-warriors fell with unblunted points upon both the elephants and the horses.
While the battle was thus proceeding, the mighty-armed Bhīṣma, of terrible prowess, clad in armor and raising his bow, rushed forward against the son of Subhadrā,
Bhīmasena, and the great car-warrior Śaineya.
Upon the Kekayas and Virāṭa, upon Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
and upon these heroic men— the Cedis and Matsyas on all sides—
the aged grandfather of the Kurus rained down showers of arrows.
In that assembly of heroes, the great array trembled;
there was a massive commotion among all the troops.
Their banners and elephants were struck down, and their finest horses were slain.
The Pāṇḍavas, their ranks of chariots scattered, fell into disorder.
But Arjuna, that tiger among men, beholding the great car-warrior Bhīṣma, spoke angrily to the descendant of Vṛṣṇi: "Proceed to where the Grandfather is."
"O Vārṣṇeya, this Bhīṣma, highly incensed and devoted to the welfare of Duryodhana, will clearly destroy my army.
O Janārdana, here are Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Vikarṇa."
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, united and led by Duryodhana,
will slay the Pañcālas while protected by the wielder of the firm bow;
therefore, O Janārdana, I shall go to Bhīṣma for the sake of the army.
Vāsudeva said to him, "Be vigilant, Dhanañjaya!
O hero, I shall bring you before the chariot of the Grandfather.
Having spoken thus, Śauri then [directed] that world-renowned chariot.
O lord of men, he brought him toward Bhīṣma’s chariot—
a chariot with many fluttering banners, drawn by horses the color of cranes, and bearing a raised, great, and terrifying banner of a roaring monkey.
Making the vault of heaven resound with the sound of his tail-lashing,
terrifying the enemy soldiers with his tawny-eyed glances,
he advanced in a great chariot that possessed the brilliance of the sun and the roar of a thundercloud.
Slaying the Kaurava host and the Śūrasenas, the Pāṇḍava,
the destroyer of the grief of his friends, advanced swiftly while discharging arrows.
As he rushed forward with speed like an elephant in rut, [he was met by the enemy].
Terrifying the heroes in battle and felling them with his arrows, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, protected by the kings led by the ruler of the Sindhus, along with the Prācyas, Sauvirakas, and Kekayas,
suddenly advanced against Arjuna.
"For who else besides the grandfather of the Kurus, or indeed Droṇa and Vaikartana, is worthy to encounter the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva in battle?
Then, O great king, Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kauravas— "
Arjuna covered him with seventy-seven iron shafts;
Drona with twenty-five, Kripa with fifty arrows,
Duryodhana with sixty-four, and Shalya with nine arrows.
The son of Droṇa, that tiger among men, pierced him with sixty arrows; Vikarṇa with three shafts;
the ruler of the Sindhus with nine; and Śakuni also with five.
O King, Vikarṇa then struck the Pāṇḍava with ten broad-headed arrows.
Pierced on all sides by those sharp arrows,
that great archer of mighty arms did not waver, like a mountain being split asunder.
He struck Bhīṣma with twenty-five arrows and Kṛpa with nine.
That tiger among men struck Droṇa with sixty arrows, Vikarṇa with three,
Śalya with ten shafts, and Jayadratha with as many; he also struck Ārtāyani with three arrows and the king with five.
O bull of the Bharatas, the diadem-wearing one of immeasurable soul pierced him in return;
then Sātyaki, Virāṭa, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
the sons of Draupadī, and Abhimanyu surrounded Dhananjaya.
Then the Pāñcālya king, joined by the Somakas, showered arrows upon Droṇa, that great archer who was intent on the welfare of Gāṅgeya.
But Bhīṣma, the best of chariot-warriors, quickly pierced the Pāṇḍava.
Then, with eighty sharpened arrows, your men raised a great shout;
hearing the roar of those who were exultant,
that powerful lion among chariot-warriors entered their midst with great joy.
Having reached the midst of those lions among chariot-warriors, O King, Dhanañjaya sported with his bow, making those great car-warriors his targets;
that great car-warrior severed the heads of the kṣatriyas with his fierce weapons.
Having rendered the seats of his chariot empty, Phalguna then moved about;
then King Duryodhana, the lord of men, spoke to Bhīṣma,
seeing his own army being oppressed by Pārtha in the battle.
"O dear one, this mighty son of Pāṇḍu, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa,
is cutting down our very root as all our armies strive against him,
even while you, O son of Gaṅgā, and Droṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, are still alive."
"Indeed, because of you, even this great car-warrior Karṇa has laid down his weapons and does not fight Pārtha in battle, for he always desires my welfare. Therefore,
O son of Gaṅgā, act in such a way that Phalguna may be slain."

O King, having been addressed thus, your father Devavrata exclaimed, "Fie on the duty of a Kṣatriya! and proceeded toward the chariot of Pārtha. O King, seeing both those with white horses engaged in combat, the monarchs [watched].
O Bhārata, they uttered loud lion-roars and blew their conchs; O Sire,
the son of Droṇa, Duryodhana, and your son Vikarṇa,
having surrounded Bhīṣma in battle, stood ready for combat.
In the same way, all the Pāṇḍavas, having surrounded Dhanañjaya, stood ready for a great battle; then the combat commenced. And Gāṅgeya struck Pārtha in the battle with nine arrows.
Arjuna pierced him in return with ten arrows that struck his vital spots;
then, with a thousand well-aimed shafts, the Pāṇḍava Arjuna,
who delights in battle, blocked all directions from Bhīṣma.
Then, O Kaurava, Bhīṣma the son of Śāntanu likewise warded off that net of arrows from Pārtha with his own net of arrows;
both were exceedingly delighted, and both rejoiced in the battle.
They fought without distinction, each seeking to counter the other's actions; the masses of arrow-nets released from Bhīṣma’s bow were seen being shattered and broken apart by Arjuna’s shafts.
In the same way, the nets of arrows released by Arjuna fell one by one upon the surface of the earth, struck down by the arrows of Gāṅgeya;
then Arjuna pierced Bhīṣma with twenty-five sharp shafts.
Bhīṣma also pierced Pārtha in battle with thirty arrows;
having struck each other’s horses and banners, those two of great strength and subduers of enemies sported with the poles and wheels of their chariots.
Then, O great king, Bhīṣma, the best among strikers, filled with rage,
struck Vāsudeva in the middle of the chest with three arrows.
Pierced by the arrows discharged from Bhīṣma’s bow, Madhusūdana was deeply wounded.

O King, he shone in battle like a *kiṃśuka* tree in full bloom. Then Arjuna, seeing Mādhava deeply pierced, became violently incensed and struck the charioteer of Gāṅgeya in the fray with three arrows.
Striving for each other's death, those two heroes were unable to overcome one another in that battle;
they performed various circular maneuvers, advancing and retreating.

By the swiftness of their skill as charioteers, those two great car-warriors displayed many maneuvers, constantly calculating the openings for their blows; O King, they repeatedly stood poised within the paths of each other's intervals.
Both of them produced the sound of conchs mingled with the roar of lions;
likewise, those two great car-warriors produced the thunderous twang of their bows. By the blaring of their conchs and the rattling of their chariot wheels, [the earth shook].
The earth was suddenly rent asunder, and it trembled and roared;
O bull of the Bharatas, no one could perceive any difference between those two,
for both were equally powerful heroes in battle, each the match of the other.
There, the Kauravas recognized Bhīṣma by his distinctive mark alone,
and likewise the sons of Pāṇḍu recognized Pārtha by his mark alone.
O King, having witnessed such prowess from those two best of men, they [recognized them].
O Bhārata, all beings were struck with wonder in that battle;
O Bhārata, no one could perceive any opening between those two in combat,
just as no one can ever find a flaw in one who stands firm in righteousness.
For both of them became invisible due to that net of arrows,
yet in an instant, both became visible once again on the battlefield.
There, the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and the Ṛṣis—
Beholding the prowess of those two, they addressed one another:
"These two great chariot-warriors, when enraged in battle, cannot be conquered by any means,
even by the worlds including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas."
This battle is a source of wonder in the worlds, a great marvel;
such battles will never occur again in any way.
Furthermore, Bhīṣma cannot be conquered in combat by the wise Pārtha.

Standing upon his chariot with his bow, scattering arrows in battle, Bhīṣma would not venture to conquer that wielder of the bow, the Pāṇḍava, who is likewise difficult even for the gods to assail in combat.
"Even in the light of day, this battle will be equal"—
such words were heard being uttered here and there,
O lord of the people, as they praised the encounter between the son of Gaṅgā and Arjuna in the fray.
Then, O Bhārata, your warriors and those of the Pāṇḍavas struck one another in that battle during the display of prowess by those two,
using sharp-edged swords as well as bright battle-axes.
With arrows and many other various weapons in the battle,
the heroes of both armies hacked at one another while that terrible and most dreadful combat was thus proceeding.
O King, there was a great encounter between Droṇa and the Pāñcālya, the son of Pṛṣata.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How did Droṇa, the great archer, and the Pāñcālya, the son of Pṛṣata, [meet]?"
Tell me, Sañjaya, how those two, exerting themselves, encountered each other in battle.
I consider destiny alone to be superior even to human effort, O Sañjaya,
since Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, could not overcome the Pāṇḍava in combat.
"For Bhīṣma, enraged in battle, could destroy the worlds, both moving and unmoving;
how then, O Sañjaya, did he not overcome the Pāṇḍava in combat by his prowess?
Sañjaya said:
"Listen, O King, and remain steadfast; this battle is most terrible.
The Pāṇḍava cannot be conquered even by the gods led by Indra himself.
Droṇa, however, fought Dhṛṣṭadyumna with sharpened arrows."
And with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he felled his charioteer from the seat of the chariot;
then, O noble one, being enraged, he afflicted Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s four horses with four excellent shafts.
Then the heroic Dhṛṣṭadyumna, laughing, pierced Droṇa with ninety sharpened arrows and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Thereupon, the son of Bharadvāja, of immeasurable soul and great prowess, [acted again].
He covered the indignant Dhṛṣṭadyumna with arrows and took up a terrible shaft for the sake of slaying the son of Pṛṣata—
a weapon whose touch was like Śakra’s thunderbolt, resembling a second staff of Death.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the entire army, O Bhārata, upon seeing that arrow aimed by the son of Bharadvāja in the battle. There we beheld the wonderful prowess of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
That lone hero stood in battle like an immovable mountain;
and he cut down that blazing, terrible arrow— which was his own death— as it approached,
while simultaneously discharging a rain of arrows at the son of Bharadvāja.

Then all the Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, raised a great shout upon seeing that most difficult feat performed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna. Then [he took] a spear of great velocity, adorned with gold and lapis lazuli.
Desiring the death of Droṇa, that valiant warrior hurled it;
but as that gold-adorned spear came rushing suddenly toward him,
the son of Bharadvāja, as if smiling, split it into three pieces in the battle.
Seeing his spear destroyed, the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna rained showers of arrows upon Droṇa, O lord of men. Then, having warded off that shower of arrows, the highly illustrious one—

In the midst of the battle, Droṇa cut the bow of Drupada’s son. With his bow severed in that encounter, the highly illustrious and powerful warrior hurled a heavy mace made of the essence of stone at Droṇa.
Released with great force, that mace sped forth with the intent to slay Droṇa;
there we beheld the wonderful prowess of Bhāradvāja’s son,
for by his dexterity he baffled the gold-adorned mace.
Having warded off that mace, he dispatched well-sharpened,
polished, gold-feathered arrows whetted on stone at the son of Pṛṣata;
having pierced his armor, they drank his blood in the battle.
Then the high-minded Dhṛṣṭadyumna, taking up another bow,
displayed his prowess against Droṇa in battle and pierced him with five arrows.
Then those two bulls among men, smeared with blood, shone resplendently.

O King, in that spring season, they were like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom. Then, O King, filled with indignation, Droṇa advanced at the head of the army and once more severed the bow of Drupada’s son.
Then, with straight-knotted arrows, that one of immeasurable soul overwhelmed him whose bow had been severed, just as a cloud covers a mountain with rain;
yet Drona cut that bow, along with the arrow, from him in the battle.
With a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he felled his charioteer from the seat of the chariot;
then, with four sharpened arrows,
he struck down his four horses in battle and let out a lion’s roar.
Then, with another broad-headed arrow, he severed the bow from his hand.
With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
he descended with mace in hand, displaying great prowess.
O Bhārata, he swiftly struck him down from his chariot with arrows while he had not yet descended; that was like a marvel. Then he [took] a massive shield, radiant and adorned with a hundred moons.
Grasping a vast and divine sword, the strong-armed and powerful one rushed forward with speed, desiring the slaughter of Droṇa,
like a lion seeking prey or like [an elephant] toward a rutting elephant in the forest.
There, O Bhārata, we beheld the wonderful prowess of Bhāradvāja— his agility, his mastery of weapons, and the strength of his arms—
as he warded off the son of Pṛṣata with a shower of arrows.
Even though he was powerful in battle, he was unable to advance further.
There we beheld the great chariot-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna standing firm,
warding off the showers of arrows with his shield like one of practiced hand.
Then the mighty-armed and powerful Bhīma suddenly rushed forward in battle to provide assistance to the high-souled son of Pṛṣata. O King, he pierced Droṇa with seven sharp arrows.
Then he quickly placed the son of Pṛṣata upon another chariot.
Thereupon King Duryodhana urged the King of Kaliṅga,
accompanied by a great army, to protect the son of Bharadvāja.
Then, O lord of men, that great army of the Kaliṅgas,
at the command of your son, quickly advanced against Bhīma;
and Droṇa also, the best among chariot-warriors, having abandoned the Pāñcālya, [proceeded].
He engaged in battle the two elders, Virāṭa and Drupada, who had come together;
meanwhile, Dhṛṣṭadyumna also advanced against the King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) in the encounter.
Then there commenced a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
In the battle between the Kaliṅgas and the high-souled Bhīma, there occurred a terrible,
fearsome, and world-destroying conflict of horrific form.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Thus commanded, Kaliṅga, the commander of the army,
[approached] the heroic Bhīmasena of great strength and wondrous deeds,
who was moving about with his mace like Antaka himself bearing the staff of punishment.
The King of Kaliṅga, together with his army, fought in the encounter.
Sañjaya said:
"O Indra among kings, having been thus addressed by your son, that one of great strength..."

Protected by a vast army, he advanced toward Bhīmaratha. That great host of the Kaliṅgas, thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, and bearing mighty weapons, suddenly fell upon him as it charged forward.
O Bhārata, Bhīmasena advanced against the army of the Kaliṅgas,
as well as Ketumān the Naiṣādin who was approaching with the Cedis.
Then Śrutāyus, together with King Ketumān, became enraged.
When the Cedis had drawn up their battle arrays,
the lord of the Kaliṅgas,
Ketumān, together with the Niṣādas, approached Bhīma in battle with many thousands of chariots and ten thousand elephants.
O King, they surrounded Bhīmasena on all sides in battle;
meanwhile, the Cedis, Matsyas, and Karūṣas, led by Bhīmasena,
suddenly advanced against the Niṣādas along with the other kings.
Then there commenced a battle of terrible form and fearsome aspect; when the Cedis had rallied, all the Kalingas,
relying on the strength of their own arms, advanced against the son of Pāṇḍu.
Knowing full well his own warriors, yet with no desire to slay one another,
a terrible battle then ensued between Bhīma and his enemies all at once,
O great king, like that of Indra against the vast army of the Daityas.
O Bhārata, as that army fought in battle,
a tremendous roar arose like the thundering of the ocean;
at that time, O lord of the people, the warriors were cutting one another down.
They covered the entire earth with a layer resembling the blood of a hare;
in their desire to kill, they could no longer distinguish between their own warriors and those of the enemy.
Even their own kin, those heroes invincible in battle, fell upon one another.

O lord of the people, there was a very great slaughter of the few by the many— the Cedis together with the Kaliṅgas and the Niṣādas. Yet those of great strength exerted their manly effort to the best of their ability.
Abandoning Bhīmasena, the Cedis retreated;
but when the Cedis had turned back, the Pāṇḍava, having encountered all the Kaliṅgas, did not retreat, relying instead on the strength of his own arms.
The mighty Bhīmasena did not stir from the seat of his chariot;
instead, he covered the army of the Kaliṅgas with sharp arrows.
The great archer, the King of Kaliṅga, and his son, a great car-warrior, [stood firm].
The two known as Śakradeva struck the Pāṇḍava with arrows. Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, brandishing his beautiful bow and relying on the strength of his own arms, fought against the Kāliṅgas.
But Śakradeva, discharging many arrows in the battle,
slew Bhīmasena’s horses in the encounter with his shafts.
Seeing that Bhīmasena, the subduer of foes, was there deprived of his chariot—
Śakradeva,
possessed of great strength, O king of kings, rushed upon Bhīma,
scattering sharp arrows over him; he rained down showers of shafts like a cloud at the end of the summer heat.
Standing on the chariot whose horses had been slain, the mighty Bhīmasena hurled a mace made entirely of iron at Śakradeva. Struck by it, O King, the son of the Kaliṅga king fell from his chariot.
Together with his charioteer, he whose banner was the sacrificial stake fell to the surface of the earth.
Seeing his own son slain, the lord of the Kaliṅgas blocked all directions around Bhīma with many thousands of chariots.
Surrounded by ten thousand elephants and their riders,
the mighty-armed Bhīma then cast aside his heavy great mace and drew his sword,
desiring to perform a terrible deed.
O King, O bull among men, he took up an incomparable shield made of bull-hide,
adorned with stars and half-moons fashioned of gold.
Then Kaliṅga, filled with rage, rubbed his bowstring.
And grasping a single terrible arrow, resembling the venom of a serpent,
the lord of men, desiring his death, discharged it at Bhīmasena.
That sharp arrow, impelled with great force, was rushing toward him.
O King, Bhīmasena, with his massive sword, cut him in two;
and filled with joy, he let out a roar, terrifying the army.
Then Kaliṅga, enraged in that battle against Bhīmasena, [attacked].
He swiftly hurled fourteen arrows, whetted on stone; but before they had reached him, O King, the mighty-armed Pāṇḍava,
remaining unperturbed, suddenly cut them down in mid-air with his excellent sword.
Having cut down fourteen lances in battle, Bhīma,
that bull among men, beheld Bhānumat and charged toward him.
Then Bhānumat covered Bhīma with a shower of arrows.
He let out a powerful roar, making the vault of heaven resound;
Bhīma could not endure that lion-like roar in the great battle,
and so he roared back with a mighty voice of great sound.
Terrified by that sound, O bull of the Bharatas, the army of the Kaliṅgas did not regard Bhīma in battle as a mere human being. Then,
O great king, Bhīma let out a tremendous roar.
O noble one, that sword-wielder, having leaped with speed from his horse, then mounted the middle of that best of elephants, the king of the *nāgas*. Thereupon,
the King of Kaliṅga released that spear, but [Arjuna] split it in two.
Then, with his broad sword, he cut Bhānumant in the middle.
Having slain that prince who fought from within [the elephant's trunk], that tamer of foes brought his sword down upon the neck of the elephant, which was capable of bearing a heavy burden.
With its trunk severed, that leader of the elephant herd fell down crying out,
like a mountain peak shattered by the force of the Sindhu river.
Then, O Bhārata, the descendant of Bharata leaped down from that elephant.
With sword in hand, undaunted in spirit and clad in armor, he stood upon the earth;
fearless, he moved through many paths, felling elephants,
appearing like a whirling circle of fire seen on all sides.
Overpowering the throngs of horses, elephants, and chariot divisions,
and slaughtering the multitudes of foot soldiers,
Bhīma— drenched in blood and fierce against the enemy forces— roamed through the battle like a hawk.
Moving with great speed, he severed the bodies and heads of those elephant-warriors in battle with his sharp-edged sword;
alone on foot and filled with rage, he increased the terror of his enemies.
Then, resembling Kāla, Antaka, and Yama, that powerful one caused confusion;
with foot soldiers he struck down foot soldiers, horses with horses, elephants with elephants,
and chariots with chariots in many ways, slaughtering them in battle.
Deluded, they rushed toward him in battle, shouting;
like hungry [beasts] letting out a roar, they fled in the ten directions upon seeing the mighty Bhīmasena wandering there in the form of Death.
Moving with supreme speed through that great battle with his sword,
that powerful crusher of enemies cut down the chariot-poles and yokes of the car-warriors in the fray, and slew the warriors themselves.
Wandering through many paths, Bhīmasena was seen displaying the movements known as *bhrānta*,
*udbhrānta*, *āviddha*, *āpluta*, *prasṛta*, *sṛta*, *saṃpāta*, and *samudīrya*.
Thus did the Pāṇḍava manifest his prowess.
Some were cut down by the high-souled Pāṇḍava with his sword;
with their vital organs pierced, they shrieked and fell down, deprived of life.
Others had the tips of their tusks and trunks severed, and likewise others had their temples split open.
O Bhārata, the elephants, fighting against their own ranks, slaughtered one another;
crying out with great roars, they fell upon the earth.
O Bhārata, [they likewise struck] the elephants, the elephant-drivers, and the trunks of the elephants.
He saw severed lances, bows, and the heads of elephant-riders;
variegated housings, golden-gleaming girths, neck-ornaments, as well as spears, banners, and *kaṇapa* missiles.
Quivers, various mechanical devices, and bows;
bright sacrificial fire-pits, as well as goads together with hooks;
and various bells, O King, as well as sword-hilts inlaid with gold.
We saw them falling and already fallen along with their riders; with elephants whose limbs and trunks were severed and who had been slain,
the earth was strewn in that place like it were covered with mountains.
Having thus crushed those great elephants, that bull among men crushed the horses as well,
O Bhārata, and he also struck down the foremost of horsemen.
That battle between him and them was terrible, O Bhārata.
Then there were bits, yokes, and whips shining with gold;
costly saddle-cloths, spears, and double-edged swords; as well as armor, shields, and variegated rugs.
In that great battle, here and there were seen discarded [weapons]:
various types of prothas, engines, and stainless weapons;
he made the earth strewn with them as if with variegated flowers.
Having leaped up and seized some chariot-warriors, the one of great strength threw them down;
having dragged others away, he cast them to the ground,
and with his sword, he cut down yet others.
With his sword, the Pāṇḍava struck down even those with their standards;
as the illustrious warrior repeatedly leaped up and rushed in all directions,
performing various maneuvers in battle, the people were filled with wonder.
He struck some with his feet, and having seized others, he crushed them;
he cut down others with his sword and terrified others with his roar.
And by the force of his thighs, he cast others down upon the ground.
Others, beholding him, met their death from fear;
thus that vast army of the swift Kalingas,
having surrounded Bhīṣma in battle, rushed toward Bhīmasena.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, beholding Śrutāyus at the head of the Kaliṅga forces, Bhīmasena advanced against him. Seeing him approaching, the King of Kaliṅga pierced him with nine arrows.
The one of immeasurable soul pierced Bhīmasena between the breasts;
struck by the Kalinga’s arrows like an elephant tormented by a goad,
Bhīmasena blazed up with rage like fire fed with fuel.

Then Aśoka, the charioteer of the chariot-warrior, took up a chariot adorned with gold and made it ready for Bhīma. Having quickly ascended that chariot, the son of Kuntī, the slayer of enemies, [proceeded].
He rushed toward Kaliṅga and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Then the powerful Śrutāyu, filled with rage, dispatched sharpened arrows at Bhīma, displaying his lightness of hand.
O King, struck severely by nine sharp arrows released from the excellent bow of the Kalinga king,
the highly illustrious Bhima became violently incensed, like a serpent struck by a staff.
Enraged, that best of the strong drew his bow with great force; Bhīma Pārtha slew Kaliṅga with seven iron arrows,
and with two razor-sharp shafts, he killed the two mighty protectors of Kaliṅga’s wheels.
He dispatched both Satyadeva and Satya to the abode of Yama.
Then, O one of immeasurable soul, Bhima once again sent Ketumat to the abode of Yama in battle with three sharpened iron arrows.
Then the Kalingas, filled with rage, obstructed the impatient Bhimasena with many thousands of divisions of kṣatriyas. They did so with spears, maces, swords, *tomaras*, spears, and battle-axes.
Then, O King, the Kaliṅgas showered Bhīmasena with arrows;
but that mighty hero, having warded off that terrible rain of shafts that had arisen, swiftly leaped up and seized his mace.
Like a mighty lion, Bhīma fell upon the enemy hosts;
that crusher of foes sent seven hundred heroes to the abode of Yama,
and furthermore, two thousand Kaliṅgas as well.
He dispatched him to the realm of death; that was like a marvel.
O King, with the mace released, he struck down the elephant;
likewise, he sent the elephant itself to the abode of Yama by means of another elephant.
Having crushed chariot against chariot and horse against horse, he sent the foot-soldier against death with the foot-soldier;
again and again he fell upon horses and again and again upon elephants.
Like a great fire driven by the wind among chariots and foot soldiers,
or like a lion with its claws amidst a herd of deer,
Vṛkodara, the doer of terrible deeds, thus roamed through the armies.
Thus the hero repeatedly shattered those divisions of the Kaliṅgas in battle, having beheld Bhīṣma of the great vows;
and the elephants had their riders slain by the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
They scattered across the ranks like clouds driven by the wind;
crushing their own troops and crying out in the agony of their wounds,
they wandered here and there, being driven about by that great-souled one.
Then the mighty-armed and powerful Bhīma blew his conch shell;
with his great arms still grasping his sword,
he was filled with joy and blew it with a tremendous sound.
O King, as Bhīma moved suddenly through the fray, he caused the hearts of all the Kaliṅga troops to tremble;
and a great delusion, O scorcher of foes, took possession of the Kaliṅgas.
O King, the armies and all the mounts trembled on every side as Bhīma moved through many paths in the battle, rushing here and there like a lordly elephant.
As they repeatedly leaped up and ran along the elephant paths, falling down again and again,
a state of utter confusion came over the Kalingas and their army.
Trembling with fear of Bhīmasena, the army shook like a vast,
unconfined lake being agitated by a great crocodile;
and while the heroes were being terrified by Bhīma of wondrous deeds, [the battle continued].
While the Kalinga warriors were repeatedly returning and fleeing in throngs, the son of Pṛṣata,
the commander of the Pandava host, spoke to his own divisions, saying, "Fight!"
Having heard the words of the commander-in-chief, the hosts led by Śikhaṇḍin advanced against Bhīma with their striking chariot-divisions;
and the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja supported them all.
With a vast army of elephants, dark as clouds, following behind him,
the son of Pṛṣata, having thus urged on all his own divisions,
took up the rear guard of Bhīmasena in a manner befitting a noble man.
Indeed, there is no one in the world who is dearer to the King of Pañcāla than Bhīma and Sātyaki, even more so than his own life. He saw that slayer of enemies wandering among the Kaliṅgas.
O King, the son of Pṛṣata, that slayer of enemy heroes and scorcher of foes, roared many times at the mighty-armed Bhīmasena; filled with joy,
he blew his conch in battle and let out a lion’s roar.
And Bhīmasena, seeing the Kovidāra banner upon the gold-adorned chariot of Pārāvatāśva, took heart.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, seeing him pursued by the Kaliṅgas, [rushed to his aid].
The one of immeasurable soul advanced against Bhīmasena in battle for his protection.
Seeing from afar those two high-minded heroes, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Vṛkodara, fighting the Kaliṅgas in the fray, Sātyaki [proceeded].
Having gone there with speed, that descendant of Śini, the best among victors and a bull among men,
took up the rear guard of both Pārtha and Pārṣata.
And it was in this fourteenth year that Bhīma beheld the field of battle.
O King, he attained supreme satisfaction, especially regarding the elephants;
having caused a carnage there while grasping his bow, he,
assuming a fierce form, struck down his enemies in battle.
There Bhīma set flowing a river originating from Kaliṅga, with flesh and blood for its mud and streaming with gore,
between the host of the Kaliṅgas and that of the Pāṇḍavas.
The mighty Bhīmasena crossed over that river so difficult to cross.
O King, seeing Bhīmasena in such a state, your men cried out:
"This is Kāla himself in the form of Bhīma, fighting with the Kaliṅgas!"
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, hearing that roar in battle,
quickly advanced toward Bhīma with his army arrayed on all sides. Satyaki, Bhīmasena, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, [followed him].
They rushed toward Bhīṣma’s gold-adorned chariot;
and having surrounded the son of Gaṅgā impetuously in battle,
they all struck Bhīṣma directly with three terrible arrows each.
Your father Devavrata pierced all of them as they exerted themselves, those great archers, with three straight-flying arrows each. Then,
having checked those great car-warriors with a thousand arrows...

With his arrows, he struck down Bhīma’s horses, which were clad in golden armor. Standing on that chariot whose horses had been slain, the powerful Bhīmasena swiftly hurled a spear toward the chariot of Gāṅgeya.

Before that spear could even reach him, your father Devavrata cut it into three pieces in the battle, and it shattered upon the earth. Then, seizing a heavy mace made of śaikya-iron, he took it up with great force.
06.050.104c Bhīmasena, that bull among men, quickly leapt from his chariot;
06.050.104d*0180_01 that bull among the Pāṇḍavas swiftly advanced toward Bhīṣma, desiring to slay him.
06.050.105a Then Sātyaki also, out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Bhīma, quickly [proceeded].
Dashing forward again and again with speed, brandishing his shield repeatedly,
and cutting down the warriors in that great battle with his sharp-edged sword,
he struck down the charioteer of the elder of the Kurus with his arrows.
But when that charioteer had been slain, Bhīṣma, the best among car-warriors,
was carried away from the field of battle by those horses moving like the wind.
Then, O King, once the one of great vows had been removed, Bhīmasena—
He blazed like a fire kindled while burning through dry undergrowth;
having slain all the Kalingas, he stood in the midst of the army.
O bull of the Bharatas, none among your men dared to advance against him.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the best among chariot-warriors, having placed that illustrious man upon his own chariot while all the troops looked on, carried him away,
O bull of the Bharatas, being honored by the Pāñcālas and the Matsyas.
Having embraced Dhṛṣṭadyumna, he then approached Sātyaki.
Then Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth, gladdening Bhīmasena while Dhṛṣṭadyumna looked on, spoke as follows.
By good fortune, the King of Kaliṅga, Prince Ketumān,
Śakradeva the Kāliṅga, and the Kaliṅgas themselves have been slain in battle by the strength and heroism of his own arms— this host crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
"The great array of the Kaliṅgas, abounding in great men and frequented by heroic warriors, was crushed by you alone.
Having spoken thus, the long-armed descendant of Śini, the subduer of enemies, [proceeded].
Rushing from his chariot to the other’s chariot, he embraced the Pāṇḍava.
And Bhīma, O best of men, being once again possessed by the Sātvata spirit,
experienced incomparable joy together with Sātyaki.
Then, mounting his own chariot once more, that great car-warrior,
filled with rage, began to slay your men, augmenting the strength of Bhīma.
Saṃjaya said:
O Bhārata, when the afternoon of that day had mostly passed,
and there was a great slaughter of chariots, elephants, horses, infantry, and cavalry,
[the battle continued] by the son of Droṇa, Śalya, and the high-souled Kṛpa.
The Pāñcālya prince engaged with these three great chariot-warriors;
that one of mighty strength struck down Drauṇi’s world-renowned horses with ten sharp, swift arrows.
Then, having quickly mounted Śalya’s chariot after his own steeds had been slain,
the son of Droṇa showered arrows upon the heir of the Pañcālas.
O Bhārata, seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna thus engaged with the son of Droṇa, [he rushed forward].
The son of Subhadrā, scattering sharpened arrows, rushed forward swiftly;
that bull among men pierced Śalya with twenty-five arrows, Kṛpa with nine, and Aśvatthāman with eight.
Then the son of Droṇa quickly pierced the son of Arjuna with a feathered shaft,
Śalya with twelve, and Kṛpa with three sharpened ones. Your grandson Lakṣmaṇa, however, [pierced] your grandson who stood before him.
He turned back with great joy, and then the battle commenced.
O King, the son of Duryodhana, filled with rage, pierced the son of Subhadrā with nine arrows in that encounter; it was like a marvel.
But Abhimanyu, O bull of the Bharatas, being enraged,
quickly pierced his brother with fifty arrows, O King.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, with a feathered shaft, cut off his bow.
O great king, when it was severed at the grip, the people raised a loud cry;
then the son of Subhadrā, the slayer of enemy heroes, casting aside that broken bow,
took up another variegated bow of even greater power.
In that battle, those two bulls among men, joyful and seeking to counter each other's deeds, struck one another with sharp arrows.
Then King Duryodhana, seeing his son, the great car-warrior—
O lord of men, when your grandson had thus afflicted him,
that ruler of people departed; and once your son had returned, all those lords of men surrounded the son of Arjuna on every side with a multitude of chariots.
Surrounded by those heroes who were difficult to defeat in battle, that hero, whose prowess was equal to Kṛṣṇa’s, did not waver, O King. Then, seeing the son of Subhadrā engaged there, Dhanañjaya—
Enraged and desiring to protect his own son, he rushed forward.
Then the kings, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, together with their chariots, elephants, and horses, turned as one against Savyasācin.
Suddenly stirred up by elephants, horses, chariots, and riders,
a thick cloud of dust was seen reaching the path of the sun;
those thousands of elephants and hundreds of lords of the earth [were covered].
Having come within the range of his arrows, they could not advance from any side;
all living beings cried out, and the quarters of the sky became shrouded in darkness.
A fierce and terrible misfortune for the Kurus was clearly seen.

Neither the atmosphere, nor the directions, nor the earth, nor the sun could be discerned, O best of the Bharatas, due to the showers of arrows from Kirīṭin. The chariot-warriors were utterly overwhelmed; their banners and elephants were struck down, and their horses slain.
Some leaders of chariot-divisions were seen with their chariots scattered;

others, though still warriors on horseback, were now without their chariots and were running in every direction, their arms still bearing weapons and adorned with armlets. Here and there they were seen, clutching their arms with their bracelets.
O King, out of fear of Arjuna, the horse-riders abandoned their horses and the elephant-riders their elephants, and they fled in every direction from their chariots, elephants,
and horses.
Struck by Arjuna, they were seen fallen and falling;
O lord of the people, their arms were seen raised with maces, with swords,
with spears, with quivers, with arrows, and with bows.
Then Arjuna, assuming a fierce form, used his terrible arrows to sever from here and there the goads and banners of the men;
O noble one, he likewise cut down their massive iron clubs and mallets.
O Bhārata, there were spears, slings, and swords in the battle, as well as sharp axes, javelins, discarded shields,
and armor strewn upon the ground.
O Bhārata, there were banners, shields, and fans of every kind; umbrellas with golden handles, yak-tail whisks, and, O noble one, goads, whips,
and yokes.
Heaps of corpses were seen scattered here upon the field of battle;
there was not a single man among your army, O Bhārata,
who could by any means advance against the heroic Arjuna in combat.

O lord of the people, whoever indeed advanced against Pārtha in battle was surely sent to the other world by means of his sharp arrows. While those warriors of yours were thus fleeing in every direction, [Arjuna pursued them].
Arjuna and Vāsudeva blew their excellent conchs;
on the tip of the banner, the lord of monkeys was seen crying out repeatedly,
that great ape terrifying his enemies with his sight and his ears pricked up.
Seeing that army shattered, your father Devavrata,
as if smiling, spoke in the midst of battle to the heroic son of Bharadvāja:
"This powerful hero, the son of Pāṇḍu, is accompanied by Kṛṣṇa."
He directs his armies in such a manner as Dhananjaya himself would do;
for he cannot be conquered in battle today by any means whatsoever,
since his form appears like that of Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
"Even this great army cannot be turned back;
behold, this host is fleeing as they look at one another.
And we have been pierced by weapons in battle by kings who are equal to Indra."
Terrified by the array, no one desired to stand their ground anywhere; showers of arrows, resembling serpents, were seen on all sides,
for the cardinal and intermediate directions were indeed pervaded by Arjuna’s shafts.
And now this sun is reaching the best of mountains,
the setting peak, as if withdrawing the forms of all the world in every way; therefore,
O bull among men, I consider it the time for withdrawal.
"Our warriors are exhausted and terrified; they will not fight by any means.
Having spoken thus, the great car-warrior Bhīṣma then ordered the withdrawal of your troops from Droṇa, the best of teachers.
Then, having achieved victory along with their chariots, elephants, horses, and the Somakas,
the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas shouted again and again and proceeded toward their camp, with Dhanañjaya at their head.

Delighted by the sounds of musical instruments, those great chariot-warriors began to dance. Then, O Bhārata, as the sun was setting and the time of twilight arrived, there occurred the withdrawal of your troops and theirs.
Saṃjaya said:
O Bhārata, when the night had turned to dawn, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, then gave orders for the armies to advance in battle formation.
Then Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus and son of Śantanu, desiring victory for your sons, formed the great Garuḍa array;
your father Devavrata himself stood at the beak of that Garuḍa.
Bharadvāja and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata were the two eyes;
and the illustrious Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa were the head,
joined by the Trigartas, Matsyas, Kaikeyas, and Vāṭadhānas.
O venerable one, Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, and Bhagadatta—
along with the Madrakas, the Sindhusauvīras, and those from the land of the five rivers—
were stationed at the neck together with Jayadratha.
On the back [of the formation] was King Duryodhana, surrounded by his brothers and followers;
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, along with the Kambojas and the Śakas, and all the Śūrasenas, O great king, formed the tail.
The Magadhas and the Kalingas, together with the hosts of Dasherakas,
stood armored on the right wing of the formation. Likewise,
the Kananas, the Vikunjas, and the Muktas from the Pundra country were stationed there.
Accompanied by Bṛhadbala, they took their position on the left wing. Having seen that army thus arrayed, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes,
together with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, formed a counter-array in the battle.
But the Pāṇḍavas arrayed their forces against that formation of yours;
with a crescent-shaped array, they countered that most terrible formation.
Standing upon the southern horn, Bhīmasena shone forth.
Surrounded by kings from various lands equipped with a multitude of diverse weapons,
