Virāṭa and the great car-warrior Drupada followed immediately after him; and right behind them was Nīla, together with those who bear blue weapons.
Immediately following Nīla was the great chariot-warrior Dhṛṣṭaketu, surrounded by the Cedis, Kāśis, Karūṣas, and Pauravas;
as well as Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, the Pañcālas, and the Prabhadrakas.
O Bhārata, standing in the midst of that great army for the sake of battle,
Dharmarāja likewise stood surrounded by a division of elephants; then, O King,
did Sātyaki and the five sons of Draupadī follow.
Then Abhimanyu quickly advanced, followed by Irāvat; then, O King, the son of Bhīmasena and the great car-warriors of the Kekayas followed.
Then the best of men took his position on the left flank.
Janārdana is the protector of the entire world, and he whose protector he is—
there, the best of chariot-warriors stood upon Vāmaśṛṅga.
Thus did the Pāṇḍavas counter-array this great battle formation.
For the sake of slaying your sons and those who had joined their side,
a battle then commenced between your men and the enemies as they struck one another down, with chariots and elephants entangled.
O lord of the people, here and there, throngs of horses and throngs of chariots were seen rushing together, slaughtering one another;
and as the multitudes of chariots ran about, they struck down each other individually.
A tumultuous sound arose, mingled with the blasts of kettledrums,
reaching to the very heavens as those heroic men struck one another in that most fierce encounter between your troops and theirs, O Bhārata.
A terrible river flowed toward the other world, O Bhārata.
Sañjaya said:
Then, when your armies and those of the others had been drawn up in battle array...
O Bhārata, Dhanañjaya, that great car-warrior (*atiratha*), slaughtered your division of chariots in battle with his arrows,
felling the leaders of chariot-hosts;
they were being slain by Pārtha like [beings] by Time at the end of an eon.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, prepared for battle, fought against the Pāṇḍavas,
seeking radiant glory and making death their only means of retreat.
With single-minded focus, they attacked the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
O King, they broke many times and were themselves broken in that battle;
with the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas fleeing, being shattered, and even turning back, nothing at all could be discerned.

A cloud of dust arose from the earth, shrouding the sun; neither the cardinal nor the intermediate directions could be discerned there in any way. In that battle, [the warriors] were identified only by inference, through signs, names, and lineages.
O lord of the people, the battle then raged here and there;
yet the array of the Kauravas was not broken in any way,
for it was protected by the wise son of Bharadvāja, who is true to his promise.
In the same way, the great array of the Pāṇḍavas, protected by Savyasācin and well-guarded by Bhīma, could not be breached;
yet, emerging from the front of the army, those men fought there.
O King, in that great battle, the chariots and elephants of both armies became entangled;
horsemen were struck down by horsemen with spears of polished tips and also with lances in the encounter.
In that most terrifying battle, a chariot-warrior, having approached another chariot-warrior, struck him down with gold-adorned arrows;
likewise, elephant-riders [struck] elephant-riders with iron shafts, arrows, and lances.
Locked together in groups, they brought down both you and them;
then one man, leaping up in the midst of battle and mounting a choice elephant,
seized [an opponent] by the hair and carried off his head in the fray.
Others, their hearts pierced by the tips of elephants' tusks in battle,
those heroes sighed and vomited blood on all sides;
one hero, skilled in combat, stood upon the tusk of an elephant.
One man, pierced by a dart, quivered violently as he was struck down by one skilled in the training of elephants and weapons. In the battle, throngs of foot soldiers,
exultant and having committed offenses against one another, felled their fellow infantrymen with slings and battle-axes.
O King, in that battle, a chariot-warrior, having encountered an elephant-fighter, brought him down along with his elephant;
and an elephant-rider brought a chariot-warrior down from his chariot; and a horseman, O bull of the Bharatas, struck down a chariot-warrior with a lance.
In that battle, the chariot-warrior struck down the horseman;
the foot-soldier struck down the chariot-warrior in the fray, and the chariot-warrior likewise struck down the foot-soldier,
felling them with sharpened weapons upon both armies alike.
Then, elephant-riders brought down horse-riders,
and horse-riders brought down those mounted on elephants; it was like a marvel as they leaped again and again in the battle.
With sharp, keen, and whetted swords,
the best of elephant-riders struck down foot soldiers here and there,
and the elephant-warriors were likewise seen being felled by them.
Foot-soldiers were seen being struck down by horsemen, and cavalry by foot-soldiers, by the hundreds and thousands; likewise,
standards, bows, and lances were seen cast away there.
With spears, as well as maces, iron clubs, and kampanas;
with javelins, variegated armor, and even kaṇapas and goads;
with stainless swords and likewise with gold-feathered arrows.
O best of the Bharatas, with blankets, rugs, and costly woolen cloths, the earth shines as if variegated with garlands of flowers;
so it does with the fallen bodies of men and horses, and with elephants, in that great battle.
The earth, with its mire of flesh and blood, became impassable;
the dust of the ground was laid to rest, drenched by the blood of battle,
and all the quarters of the sky became clear, O lord of men.
Countless headless trunks rose up on all sides as omens for the destruction of the world, O Bhārata,
while that most fierce and terrible battle was raging.
Charioteers were seen running about in every direction.
Then Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha the king of the Sindhus,
Purumitra, Vikarna, and Shakuni the son of Subala [all advanced].
These warriors, invincible in battle and possessing prowess equal to that of lions,
repeatedly shattered the ranks of the Pāṇḍavas;
likewise did Bhīmasena and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca.
Sātyaki, Cekitāna, and the sons of Draupadī, O Bhārata,
put to flight your men and your sons, together with all the kings in battle,
just as the gods routed the Dānavas.
Thus those bulls among the Kṣatriyas, striking one another in battle,
smeared with blood and terrible in appearance, shone like Dānavas;
having utterly defeated their enemies, the heroes of both armies [stood forth].
The great ministers appeared like planets in the vault of the sky.
Then, with a thousand chariots, your son Duryodhana advanced in battle against the Pāṇḍavas and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca.
In that very manner, all the Pāṇḍavas, together with a vast army,
advanced in battle against the two heroic subduers of enemies, Droṇa and Bhīṣma.
But the Diademed One (Arjuna), filled with rage, went forth against the capable and preeminent kings.
The son of Arjuna and Sātyaki both advanced against the army of Subala’s son.
Then there once again commenced a hair-raising battle between your men and the enemy, as they sought victory in the encounter.
Saṃjaya said:
Then those kings, enraged upon seeing Phalguna in the battle,
surrounded him on all sides with many thousands of chariots.
Then, O Bhārata, having hemmed him in with a multitude of chariots,
they surrounded him on all sides with many thousands of arrows,
as well as with bright, sharp spears and maces together with iron clubs.
Enraged, they hurled spears, battle-axes, mallets, and even clubs toward Phalguna’s chariot in the battle; then,
that shower of weapons came on like a flight of locusts.
Pārtha obstructed [the enemy] on all sides with arrows adorned with gold.
Seeing there that superhuman lightness of hand belonging to Bībhatsu,
the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas—
"Excellent! Excellent!"— thus did the Gandhāras, those heroes in battle accompanied by the son of Subala, honor Phalguna, Sātyaki, and Abhimanyu, along with their great army, O Indra among kings.
There, the enraged followers of Saubala, out of fury, hacked the excellent chariot of the Vārṣṇeya into pieces as small as sesame seeds with various weapons in the battle.
But Sātyaki, abandoning his chariot while that great terror prevailed, [fled].
The scorcher of foes quickly mounted Abhimanyu’s chariot;
joined together upon that single vehicle, they swiftly shattered the army of Saubaleya with sharp, straight-jointed arrows.
Droṇa and Bhīṣma, exerting themselves in battle, were destroying the army of Dharmarāja with sharp arrows fletched with heron feathers.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī [advanced].
While all the troops looked on, they rushed against Drona’s division;
there occurred a great battle, tumultuous and hair-raising,
as fierce as the ancient war between the gods and the asuras.
Performing great deeds in battle, Bhīmasena and Ghaṭotkaca— the father and son— executing difficult feats,
advanced against the king.
Then Duryodhana, approaching, warded off both of them. There we beheld the wonderful prowess of the son of Hiḍimbā,
O Bhārata, in that he fought in battle surpassing even his father.
But Bhīmasena, the son of Pāṇḍu, filled with rage, as if laughing, pierced the impatient Duryodhana in the heart with a stone-tipped arrow. Then King Duryodhana was stunned by that excellent blow.

He sat down on the floor of the chariot and fell into a swoon. Then, O King, perceiving him to be unconscious, his charioteer quickly bore him away from the battlefield; thereupon the army broke apart.
Then Bhīma, striking that Kaurava army as it fled in every direction with his sharp arrows, pursued them from behind;
so too did the son of Pṛṣata, that best of chariot-warriors, and the Pāṇḍava, the son of Dharma.
While Droṇa looked on and while the son of Gaṅgā looked on,
they struck down the enemy host with sharp arrows capable of shattering opposing armies;
yet that army of your son continued to flee in the battle.
The great car-warriors Bhīṣma and Droṇa were unable to check him. O lord of the people, even as they tried to restrain him,
that army continued to flee while Droṇa and Bhīṣma looked on.
Then, while thousands of chariots were fleeing here and there, those two— the son of Subhadrā and the bull among the Śinis— mounted upon a single chariot,
began to slaughter Saubala’s army on all sides in that battle.
Then those two, the descendant of Śini and the bull of the Kurus, shone resplendently like the moon and the sun meeting in the vault of heaven on the night of the new moon.
But then, O lord of the people, Arjuna became enraged at your army.
Like a rain-cloud with its torrents, he rained down a shower of arrows.
Then, being struck by those arrows of Pārtha in the combat,
the Kaurava army fled, trembling with despair and fear.
O Great King, although they were being restrained by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and others,
the two great car-warriors Bhīṣma and Droṇa, seeing them fleeing,
became enraged and, desiring the welfare of Duryodhana, checked their retreat.
Then, O lord of the people, King Duryodhana, having regained his composure,
turned back that army which was fleeing in every direction;
wherever anyone among your sons saw him, O Bhārata, [they rallied].
In various places, the great car-warriors among the kṣatriyas turned back;
seeing them thus retreated, O King, other men also stood their ground, some out of mutual rivalry and others out of shame.
O lord of the people, as they turned back again, their momentum was like that of the ocean swelling at the rising of the moon. Then,
seeing them thus returning, King Suyodhana—
Having gone quickly, he spoke these words to Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu:
"O Grandfather, O Bhārata, listen to this which I shall say to you;
O Kaurava, I do not consider it fitting that this should happen while you are still alive."
With Droṇa— the best among those skilled in weapons— along with his son and his circle of friends,
and with Kṛpa the great archer, this army is fleeing;
O King, the Pāṇḍavas are by no means a match for you in any way.
Likewise, O grandfather, the sons of Pāṇḍu must surely have been favored by Droṇa, by the son of Droṇa, and by Kṛpa, since you, O hero,
tolerate this army being slaughtered.
"O King, you should have told me this very thing at our first meeting:
'I will not fight the Pāṇḍavas in battle, nor the son of Pṛṣata, nor Sātyaki.
Had I heard these words from you and from the teacher Kṛpa..."
Accompanied by Karṇa, he was indeed reflecting on his duty at that very moment:
"If I am not to be abandoned by you two here in this battle,
then let those two bulls among men fight with corresponding prowess."
Having heard these words, Bhīṣma, laughing again and again,
spoke to your son, his eyes rolling in anger:
"O King, many times indeed have I spoken truthful and beneficial words to you."
The Pāṇḍavas are invincible in battle even by the gods led by Vāsava.
However, O best of kings, that which can still be done by me, an old man, today, I shall perform to the best of my ability; behold it now along with your kinsmen.
"Today, while all the world looks on, I shall hold back all the sons of Pāṇḍu together with their armies and kinsmen. When Bhīṣma had spoken thus, O lord of men, your sons—
Filled with joy, they blew their conchs and struck their kettledrums most vigorously.
Then, O King, the Pāṇḍavas too, hearing that great clamor,
blew their conchs and sounded their kettledrums and drums.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When Bhīṣma had pledged himself to that most terrible battle,
intending to hold back the Pāṇḍavas, how did those kings fight?
"Enraged by my son, and especially distressed, what did Bhīṣma do there toward the Pāṇḍavas, O Saṃjaya? Or what did the Pañcālas do to the Grandfather? Tell me that, Saṃjaya."
Saṃjaya said:
O Bhārata, when the greater part of that day had passed and the sun was situated in the western quarter, [the battle continued].
When the high-souled Pāṇḍavas had attained victory and were filled with joy,
your father Devavrata, who is conversant with the distinctions of all duties,
advanced against the army of the Pāṇḍavas on swift horses.
Protected on all sides by a great army and by your sons,
O Bhārata, a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end then ensued between us and the Pāṇḍavas due to your misconduct.
There, the great sound of twanging bows and the slapping of palms arose like the crashing of mountains being rent asunder.
"Stay! "I am standing firm! "Pierce him! "Turn back! "Be steady!"—such were the cries heard there.
"Stay! Strike!"—such cries were heard on all sides.
Upon the golden armor, crowns, and banners, there arose a sound like that of boulders falling upon mountains.
Severed heads and adorned arms fell by the hundreds and thousands, writhing upon reaching the earth;
some, though their heads had been taken away, remained with their bows still raised.
And those best of men stood with their weapons raised;
a river of great velocity began to flow, carrying blood,
fierce with the rocks that were the limbs of elephants, and possessing mud of flesh and gore.
Then, arising from the bodies of excellent horses, men, and elephants,
that river flowed toward the mouth of the ocean of the next world, delighting vultures and jackals;
O King, such a battle had never been seen nor even heard of before.
O Bhārata, just as there was no path for chariots there among your sons and the Pāṇḍavas,
the ground was covered with warriors struck down in battle and with fallen dark elephants like mountain peaks.
O noble one, with scattered variegated armor, banners, and umbrellas,
that battlefield shone like the vault of heaven in autumn.
Some, pierced by arrows, were dragged along, suffering intense pain at their vital organs.
Fearless in battle, those clad in armor rushed toward their enemies.
Others, fallen on the field of combat, cried out: "O father! O brother! O friend! O kinsman! O companion! O maternal uncle! Do not abandon me!"
"Run toward me! Come here! Do not go! Why are you afraid? Where will you go?
others cried out, "I stand here in battle; do not fear!
There, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, with his bow drawn into a continuous circle, remained ever present.
He released arrows with blazing tips like venomous serpents;
making all directions a single path with his shafts, O Bhārata, he who was firm in his vows struck down the Pāṇḍava chariots, naming each one as he did so.
Dancing indeed upon the seat of his chariot and displaying his lightness of hand,
O King, he appeared here and there like a whirling circle of fire.
Then the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas [beheld] that lone hero in battle.
Due to his agility, they beheld him as many hundreds of thousands;
there they thought Bhīṣma was like a self created by magic.
Having seen him in the eastern quarter, people saw him in the western quarter.
O Lord, having seen him in the north, he was then seen again in the south;
thus did that heroic son of Gaṅgā appear in the battle. And not one among the sons of Pāṇḍu was able even to look at him.
They beheld only the many arrows discharged from Bhīṣma’s bow;
performing deeds in battle and slaughtering the army,
the heroes there cried out in various ways and profusely.
As your father moves about in a superhuman form,
kings, impelled by fate, fall by the thousands like locusts toward the enraged fire of Bhīṣma for their own destruction.

Indeed, not a single arrow of Bhīṣma in battle was in vain; for, being a swift archer, he pierced the bodies of men, elephants, and horses with great frequency. With a single well-aimed feathered shaft, he would pierce his mark.
Like a thunderbolt striking the finest mountain,
your father struck down two or even three elephant-riders— though they were armored in elephant-hide mail and standing shoulder-to-shoulder— with a single, exceedingly sharp iron shaft.
"Whosoever among men approaches Bhīṣma, that tiger among men, in battle,
is seen by me to be struck down to the earth within a mere moment. Thus was that great army of the King of Dharma being slaughtered."
Scorched by the rain of arrows, that great army was shattered into a thousand fragments by Bhīṣma of incomparable prowess;
it was scattered while Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha looked on.
Though those heroes exerted themselves, they were unable to restrain the great car-warriors who were fleeing, being tormented by Bhīṣma’s arrows;
for that vast army was being slaughtered by one whose prowess equaled that of Mahendra.
O great king, it broke apart, and no two men fled together;
with its men, elephants, and horses pierced, and its banners and poles fallen, the army of the sons of Pāṇḍu became senseless, crying out "Alas! Alas! in despair.
In that place, father slew son and likewise son slew father; and friend, impelled by the force of destiny, slew his dear comrade. Other soldiers of the son of Pāṇḍu cast off their armor.
O Bhārata, with their hair disheveled, they were seen running about;
then the army of Pāṇḍu’s son appeared like a bewildered herd of cattle, with its leaders of chariot-divisions distracted and crying out in distress.
Seeing that army being broken, the son of Devakī restrained the excellent chariot of Pārtha Bībhatsu and said:
"O Pārtha, that time has now arrived which was long desired by you."
"Strike him, O tiger among men, unless you are deluded by infatuation! For you have previously declared, O hero, in the assembly of kings,
that you would slay all the soldiers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa."
"I shall slay, along with their followers, those who shall fight me in battle"—
make these words true, O Kaunteya, subduer of enemies!
O Bibhatsu, behold your own army being broken on all sides.
Seeing Bhīṣma in battle like Death with his mouth wide open, all the kings fleeing within Yudhiṣṭhira’s army perished from fear,
like small animals before a lion.
Thus addressed, Dhanañjaya replied to Vāsudeva:
"Urge the horses toward where Bhīṣma is; having plunged into this ocean of an army, I shall strike down the invincible elder of the Kurus, the grandfather."
Then Mādhava urged on the silver-colored horses,
O King, toward where Bhīṣma’s chariot was— difficult to behold like the sun with its rays.
Thereupon, that great army of Yudhiṣṭhira turned back once more.
Seeing the mighty-armed Pārtha advancing against Bhīṣma in battle,
Bhīṣma, the best of the Kurus, then roared repeatedly like a lion and quickly overwhelmed Dhananjaya’s chariot with showers of arrows.
In an instant, that chariot of his, along with its horses and charioteer,
was completely covered by a great shower of arrows and was no longer visible.
But Vāsudeva, remaining unperturbed and relying on his fortitude, remained steadfast in his courage.
He urged on those horses that had been pierced by Bhīṣma’s arrows.
Then Pārtha, seizing his divine bow which resounded like a rain-cloud,
struck down Bhīṣma’s bow, cutting it with three arrows.
His bow having been cut, that Kuru prince, your father, made another great bow ready with a string in the mere twinkling of an eye;
he then drew that bow, which resounded like a thundercloud, with both his arms.
Then Arjuna, filled with rage, cut that bow of his as well. The son of Śantanu praised that lightness of hand:
"Excellent, O mighty-armed Pārtha! Excellent, O son of Pāṇḍu!"
"O Dhanañjaya, this great feat is truly worthy of you alone.
I am deeply pleased, my son; fight with me!
Having thus praised Pārtha, he then took up another great bow.
In that battle, the hero discharged arrows toward the chariot of Pārtha;
meanwhile, Vāsudeva displayed supreme skill in driving the horses,
moving in swift circles and rendering the enemy's shafts futile.
Nevertheless, O Sire, Bhīṣma pierced Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya very firmly with sharp arrows in all their limbs;
those two tigers among men shone even while mangled by Bhīṣma’s shafts.
Roaring like two bull elephants marked by the gashes of their horns,
Bhīṣma, once again violently enraged and agitated in battle, blocked out the directions with straight-jointed arrows against the two Kṛṣṇas.
Pārtha, too, enraged in battle, blocked all directions from Bhīṣma;
and Bhīṣma, the best of chariot-warriors, likewise blocked all directions from Pārtha.
Enraged, he also made the descendant of Vṛṣṇi tremble with his sharp arrows.
Then Bhīṣma, smiling repeatedly and laughing loudly, spoke; meanwhile,
the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, having witnessed Bhīṣma’s prowess in battle,
observed Pārtha’s mildness in combat.
And Bhīṣma, incessantly discharging showers of arrows in battle,
like the scorching sun situated between the two armies,
was slaying the best of the best among the soldiers of the son of Pāṇḍu.
Seeing Bhīṣma acting as if he were bringing about the end of the age within Yudhiṣṭhira’s army,
the blessed Keśava, slayer of enemy heroes and possessor of immeasurable soul, could not endure it and thought: "Yudhiṣṭhira’s army no longer exists."

For in a single day in battle, Bhīṣma could destroy even the gods and the Dānavas; how much more so the sons of Pāṇḍu in combat, along with their forces and followers? And yet, the great army of the high-souled Pāṇḍava is fleeing.

Seeing the Somakas quickly broken, these Kauravas are rushing forward in battle with joy, gladdening their grandfather. Therefore, clad in armor for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, I shall slay Bhīṣma today.
"I shall remove this burden of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.
For even Arjuna, though being struck by sharp arrows in the encounter,
does not know what ought to be done in battle out of respect for Bhīṣma."
As he was thus reflecting, the Grandfather, becoming even more enraged, again dispatched arrows toward the chariot of Pārtha. Indeed,
because of the great multitude of those arrows;
Then all the directions became shrouded;
neither the atmosphere, nor the quarters, nor the earth could be seen,
and even the sun, garlanded with rays, was no longer visible.
Tumultuous winds accompanied by smoke blew,
and all the directions became agitated;
then Droṇa, Vikarṇa, and Jayadratha [advanced].
Bhūriśravas, Kṛtavarman, and Kṛpa; Śrutāyu, the king who is lord of the Ambaṣṭhas; Vinda and Anuvinda, and Sudakṣiṇa.
All the Easterners, the hosts of Sauvīras, the Vasātis, and the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas,
rushed in haste toward Kirīṭin.
They followed the instructions of King Śāntanava,
as did your own wrathful son;
[they were covered] by networks of masses of horses, foot-soldiers, and chariots.
The grandson of Śini beheld Kirīṭin surrounded by many hundreds of thousands,
as well as by the leaders of elephant herds.
Then, seeing Arjuna and Vāsudeva being assailed from all sides by foot soldiers, elephants, horses, and chariots,
those two foremost among weapon-bearers—
The hero of the Śini clan,
that great archer, swiftly rushed against those armies, attacking them with sudden force.
Then he rendered assistance to Arjuna,
just as Viṣṇu did for the slayer of Vṛtra; [he shattered] the multitude of elephants, horses, chariots, and standards.
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira’s army charging forward, having terrified all the warriors by Bhīṣma, the hero of the Śini clan spoke.
"O Kṣatriyas, where will you go? This is not the dharma proclaimed of old by the virtuous in the presence of the wise.
O great heroes, do not abandon your own vow!"
"Protect your own heroic duty!
Thus spoke Antaraja, hearing those Vasus—
the foremost among kings— fleeing in every direction.
Seeing Pārtha’s mildness in combat and Bhīṣma being exalted in the fray,
that high-souled one could not endure it.
Seeing the Kurus attacking from all sides, the lord of all the Daśārhas spoke to the illustrious descendant of Śini, praising him:
"O hero of the Śini clan, let those who are fleeing indeed flee;
O Sātvata, let even those who stand firm depart as well—
behold Bhīṣma being struck down from his chariot!"
And today in battle, Drona along with his host shall be overcome by me; O Satvata, not a single one among the Kauravas' chariot-warriors shall escape from me when I am enraged in this fight today.
Therefore, seizing my fierce discus,
I shall take away the life-breath of that one of great vows;
having likewise slain Bhīṣma along with his hosts in battle.
And, O descendant of Śini, I shall bring joy to Dhananjaya, to King Bhima, and likewise to the two Aśvins, by slaying Droṇa, that foremost of chariot-warriors.
Having slain all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and those leading kings who were on their side,
[he established] King Ajātaśatru in the kingdom.
"Today, filled with joy, I shall accomplish this," having said this, that magnanimous one called to mind his ancient, sharpened discus.
As soon as Sudarśana was thought of,
it ascended of its own accord onto his outstretched hand;
then the son of Vasudeva took up the beautiful-navelled discus.
Raising with his arm a discus that possessed the brilliance of the sun and the power of a thunderbolt, with an edge sharp as a razor,
he leaped down from his chariot and urged on his horses.
Making the earth tremble with his feet, the high-souled Kṛṣṇa rushed with speed toward Bhīṣma,
who was blinded by intoxication and swollen with pride in battle.
Like a lion desiring to slay a lordly elephant,
that wrathful destroyer, the younger brother of Mahendra, rushed toward Bhīṣma in the midst of the army.
With his yellow bordering cloth hanging down,
he shone like a cloud in the sky enveloped by lightning;
and the Sudarśana discus of that Śauri gleamed.
That lotus of a wheel, with his beautiful arms as its stalk,
shone like the primordial lotus born from the navel of Nārāyaṇa, possessing the color of the rising sun.
That [arrow], its blade well-formed with a sharp tip as keen as a razor’s edge, was produced from the sun that arose from the wrath of Kṛṣṇa,
having grown from the great lake of his own body.
Beholding that younger brother of Mahendra, who was enraged, roaring loudly, and grasping his discus, the lotus-stalk-like arm of Nārāyaṇa shone forth.
All living beings shrieked aloud,
thinking that the destruction of the Kurus was at hand;
then Vāsudeva, grasping his discus, [advanced].
As if about to dissolve the world of the living,
the Teacher of the World shone as he ascended,
like the fire of time consuming all beings.
Beholding that god, the best among bipeds, rushing forward with his discus grasped, [Arjuna],
without any agitation, held bow and arrow in his hands.
Standing upon his chariot, the son of Śantanu spoke without agitation; with both arms,
he drew that great bow, which possessed a sound equal to that of the Gāṇḍīva.
With an undeluded mind, Bhīṣma spoke to Govinda of infinite prowess in the midst of the battle:
"Come, come, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe!"
Homage be to you, O wielder of the Śārṅga bow and the discus! O Lord of the World, refuge of all beings, forcibly cast me down from this supreme chariot in battle.
"O Kṛṣṇa, cut my body with your supreme discus; for me, slain by you here today,
there will be welfare both in the next world and in this one."
"O hero, lord of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, I have been honored by the three worlds through your expedition.
Having heard these words of the son of Śāntanu, Kṛṣṇa—
Running with great speed, he then addressed him:
"You are the root of this destruction here on earth;
today you shall uproot Duryodhana."
A king addicted to gambling should be restrained by a wise minister established on the path of righteousness; or else, he must be abandoned when his intellect is overwhelmed by time.
"He who transgresses the dharma would be a defiler of his lineage.
Having heard this, Bhīṣma said to that hero of the Yadus,
"The King is the supreme deity."
Kaṃsa was indeed abandoned by the Yadus for their own welfare; at that time, the king of the Kurus, though being exhorted toward righteousness,
did not awaken.
If, by fate, one possesses a perverted intellect leading to affliction,
and there is no listener for what is beneficial,
what indeed can that speaker say, however much he may strive?
Then, leaping down from the chariot with haste,
Pārtha also ran after the hero of the Yadus and seized him by his thick, excellent, and long-hanging arms.
Then that primordial deity, the yogi, though his arms were long and powerful, seized Hari by the arms and became exceedingly enraged.
Taking him up with speed, Viṣṇu departed,
just as a great wind carries away a single tree; Pārtha, however, planted his feet firmly by means of his strength.
O King, as he was rushing swiftly toward Bhīṣma,
the wearer of the diadem and garland restrained him by force at the tenth step with some difficulty.
Having prostrated before the standing Kṛṣṇa,
Arjuna, adorned with a variegated golden garland, joyfully said,
"Withdraw your anger."
O Keśava, you are the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas;
I swear by my sons and my brothers that you shall not abandon your duty according to your promise.
"O younger brother of Indra, being thus urged by you, I shall bring about the end of the Kurus.
Then he [Arjuna] made a solemn promise and an agreement to him.
Having heard this, Janārdana, his mind pleased by the dear words of the best of the Kauravas,
stood still and once again mounted his chariot along with Cakra.
Then, having fulfilled his vow, Bhīṣma, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise to the one worthy of praise,
whose body shone forth during the three strides of Viṣṇu.
Seeing him likewise blazing in that manner,
the slayer of his enemies took up those reins once more and, seizing his conch, stood ready.
Then Śauri caused the quarters to resound with the roar of the Pāñcajanya;
he [was] adorned with trembling golden neck-ornaments, armlets, and earrings.
Seeing his eyes with curved lashes covered in dust,
his pure tusks bared, and his conch held aloft,
the Kuru heroes cried out in distress.
The resounding blasts of mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, and paṭahas, the clatter of chariot rims, the booming of kettledrums,
and fierce lion-roars arose together.
Then, amidst all the divisions of the Kurus,
the roar of Pārtha’s Gāṇḍīva bow, resembling thunder, traveled through the sky and the quarters.
And spotless, radiant arrows,
released from the Pāṇḍava’s bow, sped toward all directions;
[the lord of the Kauravas] by his might [assailed] him.
With Bhīṣma and Bhūriśravas,
he advanced with bow and arrow raised in hand,
like a fire wishing to consume a forest thicket.
Then Bhūriśravas struck Arjuna with seven gold-feathered broad-headed arrows (bhalla),
and Duryodhana hurled a lance of fierce velocity.

With a sharp razor-headed arrow, he shattered that lance released from Duryodhana’s arm; then,
he [faced] the beautiful spear as it came rushing toward him.
With two arrows, the hero cut down both the lightning-flash mace released by the son of Śantanu and the mace hurled from the arm of the lord of Madra.
Then, having powerfully drawn with both arms that wonderful, immeasurable bow Gāṇḍīva,
he duly invoked the most terrible Māhendra weapon.
Then that high-souled one, the great archer, manifested a wonder in the sky with that supreme weapon,
[overwhelming] all the armies.
Wearing his diadem and garland, he warded off Bhīṣma in battle by surrounding him with a net of arrow-showers, bright as the color of fire.
He severed Bhūriśravas’s bow and,
having pierced Śalya with nine arrows,
he struck Duryodhana in the chest.
The stone-tipped arrows released from Pārtha’s bow,
having severed the chariots, the tops of the banners, the bows, and the arms, entered the bodies of the enemies.
Then Pārtha, having spread out the quarters and intermediate directions with his sharp, well-edged arrows, [overwhelmed] kings, great serpents, and horses.
With the sound of the Gāṇḍīva, he who wears the diadem and garland caused their hearts to tremble;
while that most terrible [battle] was thus proceeding.
The sounds of conchs and the blasts of kettledrums were eclipsed by the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
as fierce shouts of battle arose.
Then, recognizing that sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
the heroic men led by King Virāṭa,
as well as the valiant Drupada, king of the Pañcālas, [were filled with alarm].
All your troops, undaunted in spirit, arrived at that place from wherever the sound born of the Gāṇḍīva was heard.
From that point on, they all bowed down; not one among them advanced against him in opposition,
even though all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra repeatedly [tried].
In that most terrible slaughter of kings,
great heroes were slain along with their chariots and charioteers;
and elephants were tormented by the falling of iron arrows.
Great banners with beautiful golden girths,
filled with living beings, suddenly fell down,
their bodies and armor shattered by the wearer of the diadem.
Struck firmly by Pārtha with sharp-pointed, whetted *bhalla* arrows of fierce velocity,
their mechanical fittings were severed and their mainstays destroyed.
Great banners were at the heads of the divisions,
and in the battle, the throngs of infantry, chariots,
horses, and elephants [were all overcome] by Dhanañjaya.
Struck by arrows and swiftly deprived of their life-force,
O King, they fell to the earth with their limbs paralyzed by that supreme weapon of Indra.
In that great battle, their armor and bodies shattered by the showers of sharp arrows from Kirīṭin,
they became rivers with the blood from wounds inflicted by human bodies and weapons as their water.
A most terrible river, with human bodies for its foam,
was set flowing there upon the field of battle;
then, with showers of sharpened arrows, the Diademed One—
He set flowing a most terrible river, with the blood of slaughtered men, elephants, and horses for its waters, and with the marrow, bones, and flesh of kings for its foam.
With great speed, the river flowed forth with exceedingly broad currents,
its form terrifying with its roar,
and its banks blocked by the bodies of departed nāgas and horses.
A mire of flesh filled with human entrails and marrow,
frequented by hosts of numerous *rakṣasas* and *bhūtas*,
and overgrown with moss-like hair amidst a mass of skulls.
Carrying away thousands of heaps of bodies,
it was crowded with waves of shattered diverse armor;
it had the bones of men, horses, and elephants for its gravel.
Terrifying like the abyss of destruction,
it was filled with flocks of herons and vultures,
as well as throngs of carnivorous beasts and hyenas.
They beheld it on all sides as having its banks filled out,
cruel and resembling the great Vaitaraṇī river,
set in motion by the multitudes of Arjuna’s arrows.
Then, having seen the army of the Kurus— most terrifying, flowing with marrow, fat, and blood, and likewise with its foremost heroes slain— by Phalguna;
Then those kings of Cedi, Pañcāla, Karūṣa, and Matsya,
as well as all the sons of Pṛthā united together, roared aloud— those heroes among men, bold in victory.
Scorching the Kuru warrior-heroes upon seeing the armies whose foremost champions had been slain by Kirīṭin, the bringer of fear to his enemies.
Having terrified the army of the commanders of the banner-bearing hosts,
like a lion among herds of deer,
he struck down your son's army as it fled in retreat.
Then, seeing those two lions of the Bharata and Vṛṣṇi clans,
the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow and Janārdana both roared, filled with exceeding joy.
Then, seeing the sun with its network of rays withdrawn,
and that most terrible Aindra weapon spread abroad, they— whose limbs were severely mangled by weapons— [beheld it].
Beholding that unbearable sight, which resembled the end of an eon,
the Kurus— including Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Duryodhana, and Bāhlika— then began their retreat.
Observing that the night had reached its twilight hour,
marked by streaks of red from the sun, they waited; and the intermediate quarters of the sky shone with a crimson hue.
They smeared everything with blood from their separation, as if from the heart of the one named "Exceedingly Chariot-Wheel" (Cakrātyartha), which was overflowing with streams of blood.
Having attained fame and glory in the world,
and having conquered his enemies, Dhanañjaya also departed together with the lords of men and his brothers.
Having completed his duties, Duryodhana, his inner soul deeply distressed upon beholding that [state] in the midst of the battle, then went to his camp at night.
Then, at the onset of night, a tumultuous and most terrible clamor arose from the Kurus,
after ten thousand chariots had been destroyed in battle.
Seven hundred elephants were slain by Arjuna; all the hosts of the Easterners and the Sauviras, as well as the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas, were struck down.
A great deed has been performed by Dhanañjaya, such as no one else could possibly accomplish. Śrutāyu and the king who is the lord of the Ambaṣṭhas—
Likewise, O King, Durmarṣaṇa and Citrasena,
Droṇa, Kṛpa, the ruler of the Sindhus, Bāhlika,
Bhūriśravas, Śalya, and Śala were there.
And hundreds of other warriors assembled together were defeated by the enraged Pārtha in the midst of battle through the strength of his own arms, along with Bhīṣma.
"Ah! Surrounded by throngs of lordly elephants and pierced by the arrows of the Pāṇḍava, this great chariot-warrior of the world, the Diademed One (Arjuna), is advancing."
The dull-witted Duryodhana, with a parasol as radiant as the moon held askance over him,
departed for his tents while they spoke thus.
O Bhārata, all your troops,
with thousands of well-kindled torches and likewise with brilliantly shining lamps, [shone forth].
With all its warriors terrified by Arjuna,
the army of the Kurus,
whose great car-warriors were shattered in their pride, made its camp.
And the great chariot-warriors and elephants had their faces shattered. Sañjaya said:
"O Bhārata, when the night had turned to dawn for the Bhāratas..."
The high-souled Bhīṣma, his anger aroused against his enemies, advanced at the head of the divisions, surrounded by his entire army.
Droṇa, Duryodhana, and Bāhlika,
as well as Durmarṣaṇa and Citrasena,
and the exceedingly powerful Jayadratha with his floods of troops;
O King, other kings likewise followed him from all sides—
those great chariot-warriors who were illustrious and heroic.
Surrounded by the foremost of kings, that best of monarchs shone like the wielder of the thunderbolt among the gods;
he was firmly stationed at the head of that army.
And great banners,
of deep red, yellow, black, and pale white,
being shaken as they were borne upon the backs of mighty elephants, shone resplendently.
That army, with the king Śāntanava at its head,
together with great chariot-warriors, elephants, and horses,
shone like a cloud accompanied by lightning and thunder.
Then, like the sky at the onset of the rains when clouds have gathered,
she set out for battle,
protected by the son of Śantanu, facing Arjuna.
The formidable army of the Kurus, with its sudden onset, was like the terrifying current of a river;
beyond this lay a battle array of inconceivable form.
The great archer drew up that army,
which had various hidden strengths like predatory beasts and was winged by a flood of elephants, horses, infantry, and chariots.
The great-souled one, whose banner bore the king of monkeys, saw from afar that array resembling a massive cloud;
he then set forth on his chariot adorned with banners.
That bull among men, the heroic and high-souled one, with his white horses and chariot-fender, stood at the head of the army,
resolved upon the slaughter of all his youthful rivals.
Like Indra protected by Nārāyaṇa,
or like the moon joined with the sun,
so was that Great-souled One together with Keśava.
He shone at the head of the armored hosts,
like Mahendra among the armies of the Asuras,
protected as Indra is by Nārāyaṇa.
Just as the moon meets with the sun,
so did that Great-Souled One unite with Keśava. [He beheld] that chariot, well-equipped, with its upper binding and its pole.
Seeing the ape-bannered one exert himself in battle against the bull among the Yadus,
the Kauravas, along with your sons, were despondent in the fray.
Your men beheld that king of battle arrays, protected by Kirīṭin, the great chariot-warrior of the world, who stood with his weapon raised in supreme excellence.
It was crowded with four thousand elephants of each kind,
just as the array had been formed on the previous day by the King of Dharma, the joy of the Kurus.
In that manner, having approached their respective positions,
the leaders of the Cedis stood together with the leaders of the Pañcālas; such a thing had never occurred before among men on earth.
Never seen before and never even heard of,
thousands of kettledrums, struck by a great force, resounded in the battle.
The sounds of conchs and the blasts of kettledrums arose from all the divisions along with lion-roars;
then there were great-sounding volleys of arrows.
The bows being drawn by the heroes in an instant drowned out the sounds of the kettledrums and small drums,
as well as the great blasts of the conch shells.
The atmosphere was filled with the sound of conch shells,
covered by a mass of dust swiftly raised from the earth,
and possessed a radiance spread like a vast canopy.
Beholding him, the heroes suddenly rushed forward;
a chariot-warrior, struck down by another’s chariot, fell along with his driver, his horses, his chariot, and his banner.
An elephant struck by an elephant fell;
a foot-soldier struck by a foot-soldier fell; those who were turning back were struck down by those advancing against them.
Wounds inflicted by arrows, wondrous to behold,
and those struck down by spears and swords;
herds of noble horses [clashing] with herds of noble horses.
The excellent shields, adorned with clusters of golden stars,
were hurled by the heroes and torn asunder by battle-axes.
Struck by spears and swords, they fell upon the earth; some chariot-warriors, crushed by the tusks and trunks of elephants, fell down along with their drivers.
And even the bull-like elephants, struck by arrows from that bull among chariot-warriors, fell to the earth—
those who had been brought down and crushed by the force of the surging elephant hosts.
Hearing the piteous cries of the young riders and foot-soldiers, who were struck by the tusks and bodies [of the elephants], the men sat down upon the earth.
While the young cavalrymen and foot soldiers were being born into a state of great terror amidst the panicked elephants, horses,
and chariots, he was surrounded on all sides by great car-warriors.
Bhīṣma, whose banner bore the emblem of five palm trees as tall as palmyra trees, saw him who possessed the banner of the king of monkeys,
as he advanced with prowess aroused by the speed of his excellent horses.
The son of Śantanu rushed toward Kirīṭin, whose path was ablaze with great weapons, arrows, and thunderbolts,
who was like a second Śakra in his prowess.
O King, Kṛpa, Śalya, Vivimśati, Duryodhana, and the son of Somadatta rushed against the son of Indra, Droṇa, and his followers.
Then, emerging from the front of the chariot division,
that hero skilled in all weapons, clad in variegated golden armor, rushed with speed toward them all.
Likewise, Abhimanyu, the son of Arjuna—
the son of Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are unimpeded— having destroyed the great weapons of those mighty chariot-warriors, [pierced the array].
He shone like the Lord Agni seated in the assembly hall, garlanded with the flames of great mantras offered as oblations;
then he quickly [drank] that foam of blood-water.
Having indeed created a river of slaughter for his enemies,
Bhīṣma, undaunted in spirit, bypassed the son of Subhadrā and advanced against the great car-warrior Pārtha.
Then, laughing with a wondrous appearance,
he [shattered] that great net of weapons with a net of *vipāṭha* arrows and the great sound of the twang of the *Gāṇḍīva*.
The wearer of the diadem garland, whose actions are unimpeded and who bears the banner of the king of monkeys, destroyed that foremost of all bowmen.
The high-souled one swiftly rained down upon Bhīṣma nets of arrow-showers and spotless broad-headed shafts (bhallas);
likewise, that which was struck by Bhīṣma remained suspended in the sky.
Your troops beheld the great net of arrows belonging to the one whose banner bears the king of monkeys as it was being shattered,
like darkness overcome by the sun.
The world, as well as the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas, beheld that very form, with the terrifying roar of the bow, displayed by those two best of virtuous men without any sign of dejection.
That duel between Bhīṣma and Dhanañjaya—
Saṃjaya said:
"O Sire, the son of Droṇa, Bhūriśravas, Śalya, and Citrasena..."
The son of Sāṃyamani fought against the son of Subhadrā;
people beheld that single youth,
possessed of exceeding splendor, engaged with those five tigers among men, like a lion cub with five elephants.
No one was his equal in discernment, nor in heroism, nor in prowess; none was like the son of Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna) in the use of missiles or in lightness of hand.
Thus did that subduer of enemies, his own son, display his valor in battle.
Seeing him exerting himself in battle, Pārtha then let out a lion’s roar;
and seeing him afflicting that army of your grandson, O lord of the people, your warriors, O king of kings, surrounded him on all sides.
O King, the Pāñcālya general, the subduer of enemies whose foes were dejected, beheld the army of the Dhārtarāṣṭras as if it were not dejected; he,
the son of Subhadrā, advanced against it with both brilliance and strength.
As he fought with his enemies in battle, his great bow was seen positioned along a swift path, possessing a radiance like that of the sun.
Having pierced the son of Droṇa with a single arrow and Śalya with five, [he struck them down].
With eight arrows, he also struck down the standard of Sāṃyamani. Then,
with a sharp, feathered shaft resembling a serpent, he warded off that great gold-shafted spear hurled by the son of Somadatta.
As Śalya was discharging hundreds of most terrible arrows,
the son of Phalguna cut his bow with a broad-headed shaft of fierce velocity;
having warded him off, the heir of Arjuna slew his horses in battle.
Bhūriśravas, Śalya, the son of Droṇa, Sāṃyamani, and Śala—
though enraged, they could not prevail against the strength of Kṛṣṇa’s arms.
Then, O king of kings, the Trigartas, the Madras, along with the Kekayas, [advanced].
Thirty-five thousand preeminent masters of the science of archery, invincible by enemies in battle, were urged on by your son;
they surrounded Kirīṭin as he sought to slay him along with his son.

O King, the Pāñcālya general, the conqueror of enemies, beheld there those two bulls among chariot-warriors, father and son, surrounded [by the foe]. He was himself encompassed by many thousands of hosts of elephants and chariots.
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of cavalry and infantry,
that slayer of enemy heroes mounted his chariot drawn by Pārāvata horses; then,
stretching his bow in a fury, he urged on his armored army.
That scorcher of foes advanced against that army of the Madrakas and the Kekayas.
Protected by that illustrious warrior of firm bow, the army—
arrayed with chariots, elephants, and horses— shone resplendent as it prepared for battle.
O descendant of Kuru, as Arjuna was advancing at the front, that prince of the Pañcālas struck Śāradvata in the region of the collarbone with three arrows;
then, having slain the Madrakas with ten arrows each, he [proceeded].
Delighted, that scorcher of foes struck down Kṛtavarman’s horse with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla),
and he also slew Damana, the heir of the high-souled Paurava, with a long iron shaft (nārāca) tipped with a massive point.
Then the son of Sāṃyamani pierced the Pāñcālya, who was fierce in battle,
with thirty arrows, and his charioteer with ten. Deeply pierced,
that great archer licked the corners of his mouth.
With an exceedingly sharp broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he cut his bow asunder; then,
O King, he quickly struck him with twenty-five arrows and slew both his horses and his two flank-guards (pārṣṇisārathi).
Standing on his chariot whose horses had been slain, O bull of the Bharatas,
the son of Sāṃyamani beheld the son of the high-souled Pāñcālya.
Grasping a most terrible and excellent sword made of iron, he—
On foot, he quickly rushed toward the son of Drupada, who was stationed on his chariot.
Approaching like a mighty torrent, like a serpent falling from the sky,
with his shield and sword whirling, he was like Death himself unleashed by Time.

The Pāṇḍavas and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, beheld him there, blazing as if with the luster of weapons and possessing the prowess of an elephant in rut. But the son of the Pañcālas [rushed] against him as he charged forward.
As he approached the vicinity of the chariot, sword cool in his hand and wearing a quiver of arrows, having withstood the force of the shafts,
the enraged commander-in-chief quickly struck off his head with a mace.
O King,
as he was falling, slain, his radiant sword and shield fell forcefully from his hand to the earth.
Having struck him down with the tip of his mace, he attained supreme glory.
The high-souled son of the Pāñcāla king, possessed of terrible prowess—
that great archer and prince of great chariots— having been slain,
a great cry of "Alas! arose among your troops, O honorable one.
Then Sāṃyamani, enraged upon seeing his son slain,
rushed with speed toward the Pāñcālya prince, who was fierce in battle.
Those two heroes, the best among chariot-warriors, encountered one another there in the fray.
All the kings— the Kurus as well as the Pāṇḍavas— beheld this.
Then Sāṃyamani, the slayer of enemy heroes, filled with rage, struck the son of Pṛṣata with three arrows, like a great elephant being struck with goads.
In the same way, Śalya, the ornament of the assembly, struck the heroic son of Pṛṣata in the chest in his rage; then the battle commenced.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Saṃjaya, I consider destiny alone to be superior even to human effort,
since the army of my son is being slaughtered by the army of the Pāṇḍavas. For you constantly report to me, dear one, that my men have indeed been slain."
"O Sañjaya, you always describe the Pāṇḍavas as undisturbed and joyful,
while you constantly report my own men as shattered and ruined;
today, O Sañjaya, my men have been deprived of their manly prowess."
"You report those who have fallen, those being struck down, and even those already slain—
those who were fighting to the best of their ability and striving for victory. Yet the Pāṇḍavas are truly prevailing, while my men are being defeated."
O dear one, I have constantly heard of many intense and unbearable sufferings inflicted upon me by Duryodhana. I see no means by which the Pāṇḍavas might be defeated.
"Or by what means, O Sañjaya, might my men achieve victory in battle?
Sañjaya said:
"There will be a destruction of human bodies, and a destruction of elephants, horses, and chariots."
"Listen, O King, and remain steadfast; this great transgression is yours alone.
Dhrṣṭadyumna, however, being afflicted by Śalya with nine arrows, became enraged and struck the lord of Madra with iron shafts."
There we beheld the marvelous prowess of the son of Pṛṣata,
as he swiftly held back Śalya, the ornament of the assembly. No one could perceive any opening between those two as they contended furiously in battle.
For a mere moment, that battle between the two seemed equal;
then, O great king, Śalya severed Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s bow in the encounter with a sharp, yellowed broad-headed arrow.

Then, O Bhārata, he covered him with a shower of arrows, just as water-bearing clouds cover a mountain at the onset of the rainy season. But Abhimanyu, becoming enraged when Dhṛṣṭadyumna was thus oppressed—
He rushed with speed toward the chariot of the King of Madra. Then, having reached the chariot of the lord of the Madras, the son of Kṛṣṇa,
possessed of immeasurable soul and exceedingly enraged, pierced Ārtāyani with three arrows.
Then, O King, your warriors, seeking to protect the son of Arjuna in battle,
quickly surrounded the chariot of the King of Madra and took their stand.
Duryodhana, Vikarṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Vivimśati [did likewise].
Durmarṣaṇa, Duḥsaha, Citrasena, Durmukha,
Satyavrata, and Purumitra— blessings be upon you, O Bhārata—
these stood in battle, protecting the chariot of the lord of Madra.
Enraged, Bhīmasena, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, the sons of Draupadī, Abhimanyu, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
each countered ten of the Dhārtarāṣṭra chariot-warriors.
O lord of the people, discharging various kinds of weapons,
they advanced with great joy, each seeking to slay the other;
they indeed encountered one another in battle, O King, as a result of your evil counsel.
While that terrifying battle involving the son of Daśaratha was underway,
the chariot-warriors among your men and those of the enemy became mere spectators.
The great car-warriors discharged weapons of many different forms.
Roaring at one another, they engaged in a violent clash;
all of them, striving with fury and desiring to slay each other,
roared at one another while vying with one another.
O King, out of mutual rivalry, kinsmen gathered together; O Great King, those kinsmen, weapons in hand, having assembled, fell upon one another in their indignation, discharging mighty missiles.
But Duryodhana, enraged in that great battle, swiftly and vehemently pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna with four sharpened arrows;
Durmarṣaṇa pierced him with twenty, and Citrasena with five.
Durmukha pierced him with nine arrows, Duḥsaha with seven,
Vivimśati with five, and likewise Duḥśāsana with three;
Vikarṇa struck him with ten arrows and Purumitra with five.
Satyavrata struck the son of Pṛṣata with seven arrows in that battle;
and the lord of the Madras and Vikarṇa each struck him with three and five arrows respectively.
O Indra among kings, the son of Pṛṣata, the scorcher of his enemies, pierced them all in return.
Displaying his lightness of hand by showing twenty-five [arrows] for each single one,
O Bhārata, Abhimanyu pierced Satyavrata and Purumitra in battle with ten arrows each.

But the two sons of Mādrī, the delighters of their mother, covered their maternal uncle in battle with showers of arrows; that was like a marvel. Then, O great king, Śalya [assailed] his two sister's sons, the best among chariot-warriors.
With many arrows, they struck each other, seeking to counter one another's deeds; though thus covered by shafts, the two sons of Mādrī did not waver.
Then, beholding Duryodhana, the mighty Bhīmasena—
Desirous of bringing an end to the strife, the Pāṇḍava seized his mace. Seeing the mighty-armed Bhīmasena with his mace raised, resembling the peaked mountain Kailāsa, your sons fled in fear.
But Duryodhana, filled with rage, urged on the King of Magadha,
along with a division of ten thousand swift elephants;
accompanied by that elephant force, King Suyodhana [advanced].
Placing the Magadha king at his front, he advanced against Bhīmasena.
Seeing that elephant division charging toward him, Vṛkodara,
mace in hand, descended from his chariot while roaring like a lion.
He was terrible and fearsome, like the wielder of the Pināka bow himself;
seizing a massive,
heavy mace made of the essence of stone, he brandished that great club in his wrath.
He rushed toward the elephant division like Death with his jaws wide open. Striking down the elephants with his mace,
the mighty and long-armed Bhīmasena moved through the battle like Vāsava wielding the thunderbolt.
O King, by that great roar of his, which caused the minds and hearts to tremble, the elephants were utterly thrown into confusion; abandoning their rut, they were overcome with fear.
As Bhīma roared, the elephants huddled together and struggled in distress.
Then the sons of Draupadī, the great car-warrior Saubhadra,
Nakula, Sahadeva, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
protecting Bhīma’s rear, [assailed] the elephants with a shower of arrows.
They rushed forward like clouds raining upon mountains;
then Śatānīka, the son of Nakula and slayer of enemy hosts,
[assailed them] in battle with razors, crescent-headed arrows, broad-headed shafts, yellow-tipped arrows, and even *añjalika* darts.
The Pāṇḍavas felled the heads of the elephant-warriors;
with those falling heads, the adorned arms,
and the hands still clutching their goads, it appeared like a rain of stones.
Elephant-riders, their heads severed, were seen upon the shoulders of the elephants like trees with broken tops on the summits of mountains;
we beheld other great elephants slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Then the Māgadha king, seeing those already fallen and those being felled by the high-souled son of Pṛṣata,
dispatched an elephant resembling Airāvata in battle toward the chariot of Subhadrā’s son.
Beholding that pre-eminent elephant of the Magadhan king charging toward him,
the heroic son of Subhadrā, the slayer of enemy heroes, struck it with a single arrow. As the elephant was being turned aside by the son of Kṛṣṇa, that conqueror of hostile cities—
With a silver-feathered broad-headed arrow, he struck off the king’s head.
Having plunged into that elephant division, Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava also roamed through the battle,
crushing the elephants like Indra crushing mountains.
In that battle, we beheld elephants struck down by Bhīmasena with a single blow, like mountains struck by thunderbolts;
their tusks broken, their temples shattered, and their thighs crushed.
Elephants as large as mountains—some with broken backs and shattered frontal globes, others struck down;
some trumpeting, others sinking down, still others turning their faces away from the battle; some voiding urine, others agitated and broken, and yet others discharging excrement.
Along the paths of Bhīmasena,
we saw mountain-like elephants slain and deprived of life; others were groaning, while yet other great elephants with shattered frontal globes were vomiting blood.
Reeling, they fell to the ground like mountains upon the surface of the earth;
on both sides of Bhīma as he proceeded along the path,
fallen elephants were seen like mountain peaks struck by a thunderbolt.
With his limbs smeared with fat and blood, and drenched in marrow and grease,
Bhīma moved through the battle like Death himself with staff in hand;
Vṛkodara bore that mace, which was stained with the blood of elephants.
Terrible and fearsome, he was like the wielder of the Pināka bow himself;
as the elephants were being crushed by the enraged Bhīmasena,
the survivors fled suddenly, trampling your army.
For the car-warriors led by the son of Subhadrā— those great archers—
protected that hero as he fought, just as the immortals protect the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Bearing a mace smeared with blood, he was drenched in the blood of elephants.
Bhīmasena appeared like the fierce-souled Kṛtānta himself,
O Bhārata, as he exerted himself with his mace in all directions;
we beheld him dancing, like Śaṅkara himself in his dance.
O great king, we beheld that fierce and murderous mace, heavy as the staff of Yama and sounding like Indra’s thunderbolt;
it was smeared with blood and mingled with hair and marrow.
Anointed with hair, marrow, and blood, the son of the Wind-god then bore a fierce form like that of the enraged Rudra striking down sacrificial animals,
or like the wielder of the trident striking down sacrificial animals in the past.
Just as a herdsman might drive a herd of cattle with a staff,
so did Bhīma drive back the elephant division with his mace.
Being struck on all sides by that mace and by his arrows, they were scattered.
Crushing their own ranks, your elephants fled;
yet Bhīma stood firm in that tumultuous fray like the wielder of the trident in the cremation ground, having scattered those elephants as a great wind disperses the clouds.
Saṃjaya said:
When that elephant division had been slain, your son Duryodhana urged all the troops, saying, "Slay Bhīmasena!"
Then, by the command of your son, all the divisions rushed toward Bhīmasena, who was uttering terrible roars—
that boundless flood of troops which would be difficult even for the gods to withstand.
It was like an ocean at the time of the full moon, difficult to cross as it surged forward—
a lake of kings, motionless yet vast and shoreless, thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, and resounding with conchs and kettledrums.
In that battle, Bhīmasena held back that unshakeable ocean of an army, like the shore restrains another great sea;
we beheld that wonder, which was both credible and marvelous.
O King, Bhīmasena performed a superhuman feat in that battle; with his mace,
he struck down the entire earth— swelling with its horses, chariots, and elephants—
without any agitation.
Having checked those floods of troops with his mace, Bhīma, the best of chariot-warriors, stood firm in that tumultuous fray like the immovable Mount Meru.
At that most fierce and exceedingly terrible time of great confusion, he remained steadfast.
His brothers, his sons, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
the sons of Draupadī, Abhimanyu, and the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin did not abandon the mighty Bhīmasena when danger arose.
Then, seizing his heavy and massive mace made of Śaikya iron,
he struck down your warriors like Antaka with staff in hand;
that conqueror crushed multitudes of chariots and throngs of horses.

Bhīma moved through the battle like the fire at the end of an eon, striking down all his enemies in combat like the all-pervading Time at the end of the age. Dragging along masses of chariots with the force of his thighs, the son of Pāṇḍu roamed the field.
Crushing all the elephants like a great elephant crushing a thicket of reeds, he crushed chariot-warriors from their chariots, elephant-riders from their elephants,
horsemen from the backs of their horses, and foot-soldiers upon the ground.
With his mace, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena violently scattered all those in your son’s army, just as the wind scatters trees with its power;
that mace was indeed smeared with marrow, fat, flesh, and blood.
A most terrible mace was seen, the slayer of elephants and horses;
with humans, elephants, and steeds slain here and there,
that field of battle became like the execution ground of Death itself.

They beheld Bhīmasena’s fierce and slaughtering mace, resembling the *pināka* of the enraged Rudra as he strikes down creatures, as formidable as the staff of Yama, and sounding like Indra’s thunderbolt.
As that high-souled son of Kuntī whirled his mace,
the force of the wind from the mace was like the crash of a thunderbolt;
its form appeared most terrible, like that of Time at the end of an eon.
Seeing him thus repeatedly routing that great army,
like Death himself approaching, they all became despondent;
wherever the Pāṇḍava looked while raising his mace, [there they fled].
O Bhārata, by him all the armies were torn asunder; he,
unconquered by the flood of his forces,
was rending the troops like Death himself with gaping jaws as he devoured the ranks.
Seeing Vṛkodara, whose deeds were terrible, thus grasping his great mace, Bhīṣma suddenly rushed toward him on a chariot that possessed the splendor of the sun and the roar of a mighty cloud.
Covering him with a shower of arrows like a rain-cloud pouring down its rain,
Bhīṣma advanced; seeing him thus approaching like Death with his mouth wide open, the mighty-armed and impatient Bhīma went forth to meet him.
At that very moment, Sātyaki, true to his promise and the foremost hero of the Śini clan, rushed toward the grandfather,
slaying his enemies with his firm bow.
Causing your son's army to tremble,
he advanced on horses as bright as silver,
blowing forth arrows from his firm bow.
At that time, O Bhārata, none of all your troops were able to restrain him;
he pierced him with the tips of sharpened arrows.
The heroic Alambusa, that best of kings and descendant of Ṛśyaśṛṅga,
having pierced him with four arrows,
Śini’s grandson rushed at him on his chariot.
Hearing that the best of the Vṛṣṇis had arrived,
moving about in the midst of his enemies and driving away the bulls of the Kuru race;
And as he roared again and again in battle,
your warriors showered him with volleys of arrows,
just as clouds drench a mountain with torrents of water.
They were unable to restrain that most excellent one,
who was like the sun scorching at midday;
there was no one there who did not become despondent.
Except for the son of Somadatta, O King—
for Bhūriśravas, the son of Somadatta, O Bhārata, was taking up his bow of fierce velocity.
Then, O King, Bhūriśravas,
seeing his own chariots being driven away,
advanced against Sātyaki, desiring to fight, along with the son of Somadatta.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O King, Bhūriśravas, becoming violently enraged, pierced Sātyaki with nine arrows,
like a great elephant being struck with goads.
And Sātyaki, of immeasurable soul, covered the Kaurava with straight-jointed arrows while all the world looked on. Then King Duryodhana was surrounded by his uterine brothers.
Vigilant in battle, he surrounded the son of Somadatta on all sides;
likewise, all the Pāṇḍavas of great prowess stood encircling the impetuous Sātyaki from every direction in that combat.
But Bhīmasena, O Bhārata, filled with rage and raising his mace,
hemmed in all your sons, headed by Duryodhana;
and likewise, your sons surrounded the great car-warrior Bhīmasena.
Led by Duryodhana, they all surrounded him from every side with many thousands of chariots, filled with rage and indignation;
and your son Nandaka [attacked] the mighty Bhīmasena.
He pierced him with six sharp arrows, winged with heron feathers and whetted on stone. But Duryodhana, enraged in battle, struck the mighty Bhimasena in the chest with three sharpened shafts.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, endowed with great strength,
ascended his own excellent chariot and spoke thus to Viśoka:
"These heroic and mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are great car-warriors."
"Highly enraged, they have risen up in battle to slay me alone. O charioteer, the tree of our desires, which we have nurtured for many years,
has today borne fruit here, in that I behold my brothers."
Wherever the dust is raised by the rims of chariot wheels, O Aśoka,
it shall not reach the atmosphere nor the intermediate quarters with its showers of arrows.

There stands King Suyodhana himself, fully armored; his brothers, noble sons intoxicated with pride, are likewise arrayed for battle. Today, while you look on, I shall slay them—of this there is no doubt.
"Therefore, O charioteer, restrain my horses with care in this battle.
Having spoken thus, Pārtha then pierced your son Duryodhana with ten sharp arrows adorned with gold.
And with three arrows, he pierced Nandaka in the middle of the chest.
Duryodhana, having struck the mighty Bhīma with sixty arrows,
then pierced Viśoka with three other well-sharpened shafts.
O King, as if laughing, your son, O Bhārata, with three sharp arrows drawn back to his ear, severed Bhīma’s radiant bow at the handle in the midst of the battle.
But Bhīma, seeing his charioteer Viśoka then in that battle afflicted by the sharp arrows of your son,
the archer, could not endure it; filled with rage, he grasped his celestial bow.
O great king, O bull of the Bharata race, for the sake of slaying your son, Bhīma,
filled with rage, took up a razor-edged arrow feathered with hair;
with that, he cut through the king’s excellent bow.
Casting aside his severed bow, blazing as if with rage,
he quickly took up another bow of even greater power. He fixed a terrible arrow upon it, which possessed a radiance equal to that of Time, the Destroyer.
Enraged, he struck Bhīmasena between the breasts;
deeply pierced and pained, he sank down onto the floor of the chariot. Seated there upon the chariot floor, he fell into a swoon.
Seeing Bhīma thus distressed, the great bowmen and mighty chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, led by Abhimanyu, could not endure it. Then,
they unleashed a tumultuous shower of weapons of fierce brilliance.

With unwavering focus, they struck [the mace] down upon the head of your son. Then, regaining his consciousness, the mighty Bhīmasena pierced Duryodhana with three arrows and struck him again with five.
And the Pāṇḍava, that great archer, pierced Śalya with twenty-five gold-feathered arrows; thus wounded, he fled from the battle. Then fourteen of your sons advanced against Bhīma.
The general Suṣeṇa, Jalasaṃdha, Sulocana,
Ugra, Bhīmaratha, Bhīma, Bhīmabāhu, Alolupa,
Durmukha, Duṣpradharṣa, Vivitsu, Vikaṭa, and Sama.
Discharging many arrows with eyes bloodshot with rage,
they rushed toward Bhīmasena and pierced him deeply together.
But beholding your sons, the mighty Bhīmasena—
Licking the corners of his mouth like a wolf in the midst of a flock of animals,
the long-armed hero, the son of Pāṇḍu, rushed forward with speed like Garuḍa and severed the head of the army commander with a razor-sharp arrow.
Rejoicing and with a delighted heart, the mighty-armed one pierced Jalasandha with three arrows and sent him to the abode of Yama; then,
having slain Suṣeṇa, he dispatched him as well to death.
Having slain Vicitra in that manner, he dispatched him to Death;
with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he struck down upon the earth the head of Ugra— complete with its helmet, resembling the moon, and adorned with two earrings.
And Bhīma, O noble one, dispatched Bhīmabāhu to the other world in battle with seventy arrows, along with his horses, standard, and charioteer.
Then Bhīmasena, as if laughing, [attacked] both Bhīma and Bhīmaratha.
O King, he sent those two impetuous brothers to the abode of Yama. Then,
in that great battle, Bhīma dispatched Sulocana to the abode of Yama with a razor-headed arrow while all the troops looked on.
But your sons, O King, seeing that prowess of Bhīmasena,
those others who remained there were afflicted by fear of Bhīma;
being slaughtered by that high-souled one, they fled in all directions.
Then the son of Śantanu spoke to all those great car-warriors:
"This Bhīma, enraged in battle, [is attacking] the great car-warriors among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
those who are foremost, those who are eldest, and those who are most heroic, as they stand gathered together."
"The wielder of the formidable bow brings him down; crush him, O kings!
Thus addressed, all the soldiers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son then rushed in great fury toward the mighty Bhīmasena.
O lord of the people, Bhagadatta, mounted upon a rutting elephant,
suddenly descended upon the spot where Bhīma was stationed.
Even as he was charging in battle toward Bhīmasena, [he struck him] with arrows sharpened on stone.
In that battle, he made [Bhīma] invisible like a cloud obscuring the sun;
the great car-warriors there, led by Abhimanyu, could not endure it,
relying on the strength of their own arms to counter Bhīma’s concealment in the fray.
They surrounded him on all sides with a rain of arrows,
and with that shower of shafts, they pierced the elephant from every direction.
Struck by that downpour of weapons, it fled twice as fast.
O King, the elephant of Prāgjyotiṣa, with various well-sharpened weapons and streams of blood gushing forth,
became a sight to behold in battle,
like a great cloud pierced by the rays of the sun.
Urged on by Bhagadatta,
that rutting elephant charged at them all like Death himself unleashed by Time,
doubling its speed and shaking the earth with its feet.

Seeing that exceedingly great form of his, all those great car-warriors, considering it unbearable, became dejected in spirit. Then the king, filled with rage, [struck] Bhīmasena in the middle of the chest.
O tiger among men, he struck him with a straight-knotted arrow;
that great archer and mighty chariot-warrior, deeply pierced by the king,
his limbs overcome by fainting, leaned against his flagpole for support.
Beholding them terrified and Bhīmasena unconscious,
the powerful and majestic Bhagadatta let out a mighty roar.
Bhīma, having regained his senses, then rushed forward in the battle.
Then, O King, seeing Bhīma in such a state, the terrible Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca became enraged and vanished right there. Having created a dreadful illusion that increased the fear of the timid, he—
Within half a blink of an eye, he appeared, assuming a terrible form;
having mounted Airāvata, which he himself had created through his illusory power (*māyā*),
he approached like Vajrapāṇi, resembling Mount Kailāsa.
And he had other great elephants as his followers:
Añjana, Vāmana, and the radiant Mahāpadma;
these three great elephants were presided over by Rākṣasas.
In the midst of Trigarta,
the Rākṣasīs obtain [their powers] and they flow forth; possessing the ability to assume forms at will, they become many-formed.
Then, with his hair disheveled, he prostrated himself and grasped the feet of his father;
and the supreme archer [Parasurama] also [grasped the feet] of his mother. They both gave him a name, and his mother addressed him by the name Ghatotkaca, which had been previously mentioned.
Because of that [name], he was indeed called Ghaṭotkaca.
For he was created by the high-souled Maghavan for the sake of Karṇa,
as a great car-warrior (*mahāratha*) and a counter-combatant against Karṇa of unrivaled prowess.
O King, those of massive bodies, endowed with splendor, heroism, and strength, and possessed of great power and prowess, flow with abundant rut in three ways;
and they have been dispatched, O Great King, by the *rākṣasas* in the four directions.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, the scorcher of foes, desiring to slay Bhagadatta along with his elephant, urged on his own elephant. And those other elephants were likewise urged on by those mighty Rākṣasas.
Highly enraged, those four-tusked elephants rushed from all four directions;
with their tusks, they tormented Bhagadatta’s elephant.
Being thus oppressed by those elephants, he was afflicted by pain and distressed by arrows.
He let out a tremendous roar, sounding like Indra’s thunderbolt; yet,
afflicted by Bhīmasena’s arrows,
that great clamor was turned back after he had crushed all the troops of your son, O Bhārata.
Hearing that most terrible roar of his, with its fearsome resonance,
Bhīṣma spoke to Droṇa and King Suyodhana:
"This one is fighting in battle with the evil-minded son of Hiḍimbā."
The great archer Bhagadatta is struggling with difficulty;
so too is the Rākṣasa of great illusion and that exceedingly wrathful king.
When those two of great prowess unite, they are both like Time and Death itself.
"Indeed, this great roar of the joyful Pāṇḍavas is heard,
as well as the massive sound of the terrified elephant crying out. Let us go there— may you be blessed— to protect the king."
"If he is left unprotected in battle, he will quickly lose his life. Therefore, O you of great prowess, make haste; why do we delay?
For a great, fierce, and hair-raising battle is now underway."
"He is devoted, a son of noble family, a hero, and a commander of armies;
O unshakable ones, it is fitting for us to provide him with protection.
Having heard those words of Bhīṣma, the warriors led by the son of Bharadvāja [prepared to act].
All the kings, united and desiring to rescue Bhagadatta, set out with the utmost speed toward the place where he was. Seeing them advancing, those led by Yudhiṣṭhira—
The Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, pursued the enemies from behind. Then, beholding those armies, the powerful lord of the Rākṣasas let out a tremendous roar, like the crash of a thunderbolt.
Hearing that roar of his and seeing the Nāgas fighting,
Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, spoke again to the son of Bharadvāja:
"A battle with the evil-minded son of Hiḍimbā does not please me."
Now, endowed with strength and valor and accompanied by allies,
he cannot be defeated in battle even by the wielder of the thunderbolt himself; for he is a striker who never misses his mark, while our mounts are exhausted.
Wounded and mangled by the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas throughout the day,
that Rākṣasa cannot now be conquered in battle;
for the sun is setting, and it is impossible to fight at night.
"War with the Pāṇḍavas, who appear victorious, does not please me. Let a withdrawal be proclaimed today; we shall fight with the enemies tomorrow.
Having heard the words of the grandfather, the Kauravas did exactly so.
Afflicted by the fear of Ghaṭotkaca, they retreated through a stratagem.
When the Kauravas had turned back, the Pāṇḍavas, appearing victorious,
let out lion-roars along with the sounds of conchs and flutes.
Thus, O bull of the Bharatas, that battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus continued for the entire day, with Ghaṭotkaca placed at their forefront. Then,
O King, the Kauravas retired to their own camp.
Feeling ashamed at the time of night, having been defeated by the sons of Pāṇḍu,
their bodies mangled by arrows, those great car-warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu,
became cheerful in spirit after the battle and departed for their camp.
O Great King, placing Bhīmasena and Ghaṭotkaca at their head,
they then honored one another, filled with supreme joy,
uttering various shouts mingled with the sounds of musical instruments.
Uttering lion-like roars mingled with the blasts of conchs,
those high-souled warriors, shouting aloud and making the earth tremble,
struck at the vital organs of your son, O honorable one.
O lord of the earth, O Indra among kings, shaking the hearts of your sons, those subduers of enemies, likewise wounded by arrows,
departed for their camp at the hour of night.
But King Duryodhana, dejected by the slaughter of his brothers and overwhelmed with tears and grief, reflected for a moment. Then,
