having performed all the prescribed rites for the camp according to tradition, he departed.
Tormented by grief and emaciated by the calamity that had befallen his brother, he fell into deep reflection.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, a very great fear and even a sense of wonder have arisen within me."
O Sañjaya, having heard of the deeds of the Pāṇḍava princes, which are so difficult even for the gods to perform,
and having heard in every detail of the defeat of my sons,
O Sūta, a great anxiety has arisen within me as to what will happen next.
"Surely the words of Vidura will burn my heart,
O Sañjaya, for everything is seen to happen through the power of destiny—
how it is that the heroes, those best of warriors skilled in weapons, with Bhīṣma at their head,"
The strikers are fighting against the armies of the Pāṇḍavas;
by whom are those high-souled and mighty sons of Pāṇḍu unslayable? By whom, dear one, were boons granted to them, or what knowledge do they possess?
By which they do not go to destruction, like the hosts of stars in the sky;
yet again and again, I cannot endure my army being slaughtered by the Pāṇḍavas. By fate, this most terrible punishment falls upon me alone.

"Tell me all this according to the facts, O Sañjaya: how it was that the sons of Pāṇḍu were not to be slain, and how my own sons were to be slain. For I do not see any end to this suffering in any way whatsoever."
Like a man crossing the great ocean with his two arms,
I believe a most terrible calamity has surely befallen my sons;
Bhīma will slay all my sons, there is no doubt.
"I do not see that hero who might protect my sons in battle;
surely, O Sañjaya, the destruction of my sons in the encounter is certain. Therefore, O Sūta, tell me the reason and especially the means [for their safety]."
"Since I ask you today, you ought to relate everything according to the truth:
what Duryodhana did upon seeing his own men turning away in battle,
and what Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Jayadratha the son of Subala did."

O Sañjaya, O man of great wisdom, what was the resolve of those high-souled ones— whether it was the son of Droṇa, the great archer, or the mighty Vikarṇa— at that time when my sons had turned their backs in flight?
"You ought to tell me what occurred there in that battle.
Sañjaya said:
"Listen attentively, O King, and having heard, take it to heart."
"O King, the Pāṇḍavas do not employ any spells, nor such illusions, nor any kind of intimidation. They fight according to the rules of righteousness and with full prowess in battle."

"O Bhārata, it is said that all undertakings should be carried out according to dharma; thus the sons of Pṛthā always begin their endeavors, seeking great renown. Endowed with righteousness and possessed of great strength, they never retreat from battle."

"Endowed with supreme glory, where there is dharma, there is victory. Therefore, O King, the sons of Pṛthā are invincible in battle and possessed of victory; whereas your sons are evil-minded and always delighting in sinful deeds."
Cruel and of base deeds, they were defeated in battle by him. O lord of men, many acts of cruelty were committed here against the Pāṇḍavas by your sons, just as low men might act toward others.
O elder brother of Pāṇḍu, lord of the people, disregarding all that transgression of your sons, the Pāṇḍavas have always remained free from reproach;
nor do your sons hold them in high regard, O ruler of men.
The extremely terrible fruit of that evil deed which was constantly being performed— resembling the *kiṃpāka* fruit—
has now arrived; eat it, O Great King, together with your sons and your circle of friends.
O King, you did not perceive this even though you were repeatedly warned by your well-wishers—
by Vidura, Bhīṣma, and the high-souled Droṇa;
likewise, though warned by me as well on many occasions, you did not accept it.
Just as a mortal accepts wholesome and beneficial medicine, you have accepted the advice that is both beneficial and salutary;
by relying on the opinion of your sons, you consider the Pāṇḍavas already conquered. Listen further to the truth regarding that which you ask me.
O best of the Bharatas, O subduer of enemies, I shall relate to you the reason for the victory of the Pāṇḍavas exactly as I have heard it,
concerning that matter which was asked of the Grandfather by Duryodhana.
Seeing all his brothers, those great chariot-warriors, defeated in battle,
the Kaurava, his heart bewildered by grief at the time of night,
approached the highly wise grandfather with humility.
"O lord of men, hear from me what that son of yours said.
Duryodhana said:
'You, Droṇa, Śalya, Kṛpa, and likewise the son of Droṇa...'"
Kṛtavarman Hārdikya, Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja,
Bhūriśravas, Vikarṇa, and the heroic Bhagadatta—
these are celebrated as great car-warriors (mahārathas), sons of noble lineage who were ready to sacrifice their lives.
"It is my opinion that they are sufficient for all three worlds;
yet all the Pāṇḍavas together do not stand firm against his prowess.
A doubt has arisen in me regarding this; explain it to me as I ask."
"Relying upon whom the sons of Kuntī conquer us at every step.
Bhīṣma said:
"Listen, O King, to my words, which I shall speak to you, O Kaurava."
"Many times have you spoken to me, yet you have not acted according to my words.
O best of the Bharatas, let peace be made with the Pāṇḍavas;
O Lord, I consider this to be for the benefit of both the earth and yourself."
"O King, enjoy this earth together with your brothers in happiness, tormenting all your enemies and delighting your kinsmen. Yet,
O dear one, you did not listen to me when I cried out to you in the past."

That which you have disregarded by showing contempt for the Pāṇḍavas has now come upon you. O Great King, O Lord, listen as I proclaim to you the reason why those performers of untainted deeds are incapable of being slain.
"There is nothing in the worlds that has been, nor is there, nor will there ever be,
anyone who could defeat the Pāṇḍavas in battle while they are protected by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
But as for what was told to me, O dear one, by the sages of purified souls— "
O knower of dharma, listen to this ancient song exactly as it was sung.
Long ago, it is said, all the gods and sages gathered together and waited upon the Grandfather on Mount Gandhamādana.
Seated in their midst, Prajāpati beheld a magnificent celestial chariot, blazing with light, stationed in the sky.
Having recognized it through meditation, Brahmā, composed and with palms joined in reverence, [gazed upon it].
With a joyful heart, he paid homage to the Supreme Lord, the Highest.
Then the sages and the gods, seeing that Brahmā had risen,
all stood with palms joined in reverence, gazing upon that great marvel.
Having duly honored him, Brahmā— the creator of the world, the best among the knowers of Brahman, and the supreme knower of dharma— spoke to the Supreme Being:
"Viśvāvasu, Viśvamūrti, Lord of the Universe;..."
You are Viṣvaksena, Viśvakarman, and the Self-controlled One;
you are the Lord of All, Vāsudeva. Therefore, I approach you, the deity whose very self is Yoga.
O Abode of All, O Embodiment of All, Viṣvaksena, Janārdana; O Creator of All, Lord of All, God of Gods, Lord of the Universe;
O Lord of Yoga, salutations be unto You, the one who carries us across the ocean of worldly existence.
Victory to you, O Viśva, Great God! Victory to you, who are devoted to the welfare of the world!

Victory to you, O Lord of Yogins, O All-pervading One! Victory to you, the supreme and inferior [master] of Yoga! Victory to you, O Lotus-wombed One, O Large-eyed One, O Lord of the Lords of the World!
O Lord of the past, the future, and the present, victory to you, O son of the son of the Gentle One!
Victory to the unconquerable one of innumerable virtues, O refuge of all!
O Nārāyaṇa, difficult to cross over, victory to you, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow!
O you who are endowed with all secret virtues, O universal form, O stainless one! O Lord of the universe, O mighty-armed one, victory to you who are devoted to the welfare of the world!
O great serpent, O Boar, O primordial one, O golden-haired one, O pervasive Lord, victory to you!

O abode of Hari, Lord of the people, dwelling in all things, immeasurable and immutable; O manifest and unmanifest one, whose station is infinite, whose senses are restrained, yet who possesses the senses; O knower of the nature of the innumerable selfs, victory to you, O profound granter of desires!
O you of infinite and known wisdom, eternally perceiving the true nature of beings; O you who have accomplished what was to be done, perfected in wisdom, knower of Dharma, victorious and unconquered;
O secret self, self of all beings, source of all that has clearly arisen.

O Lord of the World, you who manifest reality; victory to you, the creator of beings! O self-born one of great fortune, intent upon the dissolution of the eon; O source of manifestation, born of the mind; victory to you, beloved of the people of Brahmā!
O Lord who delights in the natural flow of creation, O Lord of Desire, O Supreme Sovereign; O Source of Nectar, O True Being, O Fire at the End of the Yuga, O Bestower of Victory;
O Lord of the Lords of Creatures, O Divine One, O Lotus-navelled One, O You of Great Might!
O you who have become the self, the great elements, whose essence is action, victory to you, O giver of action! The goddess Earth is your feet, the quarters are your arms, and heaven is your head.
I am your body, the gods are your limbs, and the moon and sun are your two eyes.
O Lord, strength, austerity, truth, and dharma are born from your will; fire is your splendor, the wind is your breath, and the waters arise from your sweat.
The two Aśvins are eternally your ears, and the goddess Sarasvatī is your tongue.
For the Vedas are rooted in your purificatory rites, and this entire world rests upon you.
O Lord of Yoga and master of yoga, we do not know your number, nor your measure, nor your splendor, nor your prowess, nor your strength, nor your origin.

"O God, O Viṣṇu, devoted to you and concentrated upon you through religious observances, we always worship you, the Supreme Lord, the Great Sovereign. So too do the sages, gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas."
Piśācas, humans, beasts, birds, and reptiles—
these and others such as these were created by me upon the earth through your grace,
O lotus-navelled one, large-eyed Kṛṣṇa, destroyer of evil dreams.
You are the refuge of all beings; you are the leader, you are the mouth of the world. By your grace, O Lord of Gods, the deities are always happy.
By your grace, O God, the earth has always been free from fear.
Therefore, O large-eyed one, become the increaser of the Yadu lineage for the sake of establishing dharma, for the destruction of the Daityas,
and for the support of the world; O Lord, grant my request.
"O All-pervading Lord Vāsudeva, this supreme secret consisting of your grace has been sung by me to you exactly as it is. Having created the god Saṃkarṣaṇa from yourself by means of your own self,"

O Kṛṣṇa, you yourself brought forth Pradyumna from your own self; and from Pradyumna, you produced Aniruddha, whom they know as the imperishable Viṣṇu. Indeed, it was Aniruddha who created me, Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds.
"I am composed of Vāsudeva, and I have been created by you alone.
O Lord, one should know him as Vāsudeva by whom I was created. Therefore, O Lord of the World, I entreat you with your own fourfold self."
"O Lord, dividing yourself into portions, enter the human state;
there, for the sake of the happiness of all the worlds, having slain the asuras,
established righteousness, and attained glory, you shall truly attain yoga."
For you indeed, O one of immeasurable prowess, the Brahman-sages and the gods in this world sing of as the Supreme Self through various names—
the Lord of all beings, the Divine, Yoga, the Lord of Yoga, and the Sovereign.
And all the hosts of beings abide in you,
O mighty-armed one, having made you— the giver of boons, without beginning, middle, or end, and possessed of boundless yoga— their refuge.
"The Brahmins declare him to be the bridge of the world.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then that Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign of the worlds..."
He replied to Brahmā with words that were affectionate and deep:
"O dear one, all this that you desire is known to me through my yoga.
Having said, "So shall it be," he vanished right there.
Then the celestial sages and gandharvas were filled with the utmost wonder;
overcome by curiosity, they all spoke to the Grandfather:
"O Lord, who indeed is this person who, out of humility, bows down before your blessed self?"
"Praised with these most excellent words, we wish to hear from him. Thus addressed, the Blessed Grandfather replied to all the gods, brahmin-sages, and gandharvas with a sweet voice.

O bulls among the gods, I have held a conversation with him who is the Supreme, who is the future, and who is that which must come to be; he who is the soul of all beings, the Lord, and the supreme state of Brahman— him, being well-pleased, I have conversed with.
"For the sake of favoring the world, the Lord of the World was entreated by me:
'O Vāsudeva, renowned as such, descend into the human realm;
take birth upon the surface of the earth for the purpose of slaying the asuras.'"
Known as Vāsudeva,
he appeared in person in the house of Vāsudeva.
Those Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas who were slain in battle—
These beings, born among men, are of terrible form and great strength;
for their destruction, the Blessed One, the self-controlled one, having entered a human womb together with Nara,
will wander upon the surface of the earth.
Those two ancient and most excellent sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
of immeasurable splendor, were born together in the world of men;
when united, they are invincible in battle even by the immortals.

But the deluded do not recognize these two as the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa; we, however, O bulls among the gods, know them to be the two deities who are the first-born of the universe. Of that [universe], I am the son, Brahmā, the lord of the entire world.
Vāsudeva, the Great Lord of all the worlds, is to be worshipped by you.
O best of gods,
he must never be disregarded as a mere mortal, for he is possessed of great heroism and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
This indeed is the ancient, supreme form known as Puruṣa;
this is the highest secret, this is the supreme state,
this is the supreme Brahman, and this is the supreme glory.
This is the unmanifest syllable; this is that eternal and great. It is indeed designated as the Puruṣa; it is sung of, yet it is not known.
This is the supreme splendor; this is the supreme bliss.
This supreme truth has been proclaimed by Viśvakarman:
therefore, Vāsudeva— the Lord of immeasurable prowess— must not be disregarded by any of the gods led by Indra, nor by any in the worlds, on the grounds that he is merely a human being.
And that person of very dull intellect who would say,
"This one is merely human," out of contempt for Hṛṣīkeśa, is called the lowest of men;
[for he fails to recognize] that great-souled yogin who has entered a human body.
Those people who would despise Vāsudeva—
the god who is the soul of all moving and unmoving beings, marked with the Śrīvatsa, possessed of great splendor,
and lotus-navelled— those people are called *tāmasa*.

"He who disregards the Great-Souled One, who wears the diadem and the Kaustubha gem and grants fearlessness to his friends, sinks into terrible darkness. Having thus understood the true nature of things, [one should worship] the Lord of the lords of the worlds."
"Vāsudeva, O best of gods, is to be saluted by all the worlds.
Having spoken thus to all the hosts of gods in the past, the Blessed One,
the soul of all the worlds, dismissed them and went to his own abode.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, sages, and even the apsarases,
having heard that story sung by Brahmā, departed for heaven in great joy.
This, O dear one, was heard by me from the sages of purified souls.
O you who are expert in sacred learning, you have heard this ancient account of Vāsudeva as it was told in the assembly of Jamadagnya Rāma, the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, Vyāsa, and Nārada.
Having understood this matter and having heard it from the imperishable Lord Vāsudeva— the Great Soul, the Lord of the lords of the worlds—
of whom Brahmā, the father of the entire universe, is the son.
"How is it that this Vāsudeva is not to be honored and worshipped by men?
O dear one, you were previously forbidden by sages who had mastered the Vedas:
'Do not enter into combat with that wise Vāsudeva.'"
"Do not [act] together with the Pāṇḍavas"— you do not understand this because of delusion.
I consider you a cruel Rākṣasa, for you are thus shrouded in darkness,
since you hate Govinda and Dhanañjaya, the son of Pāṇḍu.
"No mortal man indeed should hate the two gods, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, O King, I tell you: he is truly eternal and imperishable;
he consists of all the worlds, is constant, the teacher, the creator, the supporter, and the immovable."
He who sustains the three worlds, the Lord and preceptor of all that moves and is stationary;

he who is the warrior, the victory, and the conqueror; the Sovereign who is the source of all nature—O King, he is indeed composed of pure goodness (sattva), entirely free from darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas).

Where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is Dharma; where there is Dharma, there is victory. O King, by virtue of his majesty and through the power of his own yoga, the sons of Pāṇḍu have been sustained, and victory shall be theirs.
He who always bestows upon the Pāṇḍavas an intellect endowed with excellence, and who constantly grants them strength in battle and protects them from fears—
he is that eternal God, the auspicious one, whose nature consists of all mysteries.

"O Bhārata, you who ask me about him should know him as Vāsudeva. He is served and worshipped by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have fulfilled their defining marks and are ever-devoted to their own duties."
At the end of the Dvāpara Yuga and at the beginning of the Kali Yuga,
he who was sung by Saṃkarṣaṇa, having resorted to the Sātvata rite—
this very one [is the protector] of all the worlds of Asuras and mortals.
Vāsudeva creates again and again the cities separated by the ocean's moats and the human dwelling in age after age.
Duryodhana said:
"O Grandfather, Vāsudeva is proclaimed as a great being in all the worlds; I wish to know his origin and his establishment."
Bhīṣma said:
Vāsudeva is the Great Being who has arisen together with the gods;
O bull among the Bharatas, nothing superior to the lotus-eyed one is seen.
"O father, I have heard from Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, as he was speaking,
and from the celestial sage Nārada, and from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
and also from Asita Devala and the Vālakhilyas, whose wealth is their asceticism."
And Mārkaṇḍeya tells Govinda a great wonder:
"The Great-Souled One, the Supreme Person, the Self of all beings, fashioned these three: water, wind, and fire."
Having created the earth, that Lord, the Master of all worlds,
the Great-Souled Puruṣottama, made his bed upon the waters;
there the God, consisting of all water, slept through the power of yoga.
From his mouth he emitted fire, and from his breath the wind;
and the imperishable one created Sarasvatī and the Vedas from his mind. In the beginning, he created the worlds, as well as the gods together with the hosts of seers.
He is the end and death of all creatures, yet he is their inexhaustible source; he is righteousness itself and the knower of righteousness, the bestower of boons and the granter of all desires.
He is the agent and the action, the primordial god and the self-sovereign Lord.
Janārdana first fashioned this world— the past, the present, and the future— as well as both twilights, the quarters, the sky, and the law of restraint. Indeed,
Govinda also fashioned the sages and the practice of austerity.
The high-souled, imperishable Lord also fashioned Saṃkarṣaṇa, the creator of the world and the first-born of all beings;
from him was born Nārāyaṇa, the eternal God of gods.

In his navel there appeared a lotus, from which the origin of the entire world arose; from that was born the Grandfather (Brahmā), and from him these creatures were born. Furthermore, he fashioned the god Śeṣa, whom they know as Ananta.
The Brahmins speak of that one of great majesty who, through the yoga of meditation, sustains all beings as well as this earth with its mountains;
and [they speak of] the great Asura named Madhu, who was born from the flow of Karna’s ear.

The father of Brahmā slew him, who was fierce, whose deeds were fierce, who had established himself in a fierce intellect, and who was carrying off the Vedas of Brahmā; Puruṣottama slew him while performing an act of reverence toward Brahmā.
O dear one, because of his very slaying of him, the gods, dānavas, and humans,
as well as the sages, call Janārdana "Madhusūdana.
He is the Boar, the Lion, and the Lord who traverses the three strides.

This Hari is indeed the mother and the father of all living beings; for there has never been, nor will there ever be, anyone superior to the lotus-eyed one. From his mouth he created the Brāhmaṇas, and likewise the Kṣatriyas from his arms.
O King, from his thighs he created the Vaiśyas, and likewise from his feet the Śūdras;
the Lord, restrained by austerity, is the storehouse of all embodied beings,
having become Brahman on the new moon and likewise on the full moon.
By attending upon Keśava, who is the embodiment of yoga, one shall attain greatness.
O lord of men, the sages indeed say that Keśava is the supreme splendor and the grandfather of all the worlds;
thus they speak of Hṛṣīkeśa.
Know him thus as your teacher, father, and guru;
he with whom Kṛṣṇa is pleased has conquered imperishable worlds. And whoever seeks refuge with Keśava in a time of fear, [he too shall find safety].
If a man always recites this, he shall be possessed of well-being and happiness. Those men who take refuge in Kṛṣṇa do not become deluded;
Janārdana eternally protects those who are submerged in great danger.
Having understood this exactly as it is, O Bhārata, Yudhiṣṭhira,
with his whole being, took refuge in the high-souled Keśava, the Lord of the universe, the sovereign and master of all yogas, O King.
Bhīṣma said:
Listen to this, O great king, my hymn of praise to Brahman,
which was formerly proclaimed upon earth by the celestial rishis and the gods.
"Nārada declared that you are the Lord of the gods, the sovereign of even the Sādhyas, the creator of the worlds, and the knower of all beings.
And Mārkaṇḍeya spoke of you as the past, the present, and the future."
The venerable Bhṛgu has declared you to be the sacrifice among sacrifices, the austerity among austerities, and the god among gods; indeed,
O Viṣṇu, Lord of Beings, he has described your form as Bhairava in the Purāṇa.
"You are Vāsudeva among the Vasus, and likewise the establisher of Śakra;
you are the God of gods among the gods," so said Dvaipāyana. "In former creations of beings, they called Dakṣa the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati)."

Then Aṅgiras said to you, "You are the creator of all beings. Devala Asita, however, said, "The unmanifest arises from your body; the manifest resides in your mind; and the gods are born from your speech."
The heavens are pervaded by your head, and the earth is supported by your two arms;
the three worlds are your belly—you are the eternal Puruṣa.
Thus do men purified by austerity recognize you.
O Madhusūdana, you are the refuge of those sages who are satisfied by the vision of the Self,
of the noble royal seers who never retreat in battle,
and of all those for whom dharma is paramount.

Thus, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person Hari, is constantly praised and worshipped by those who know yoga, headed by Sanatkumāra. This Dvaipāyana spoke after having indeed praised the Supreme Person.
06,064.010a This detailed account and its summary, O dear one, have been proclaimed to you according to the truth regarding Keśava. 06,064.010c Be well-pleased with Keśava,
for such is the purpose of the Ancient Being’s manifestation among men in this world.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Great King, having heard this sacred narrative,
your son held Keśava and the great car-warriors, the Pāṇḍavas, in high esteem."
O great king, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, spoke to him again:
"O King, you have heard of the majesty of the high-souled Keśava;
indeed, the majesty of Arjuna has also been described by me according to the truth."
I shall not be defeated anywhere by that man who roams about in great battle;
nor shall I be defeated by Nārāyaṇa in combat, for those two are remembered as being invincible.
So too are Dharmarāja, Bhīma, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī.
These too have been declared inviolable in the Purāṇa by the supreme seer;
and as for that which you ask me regarding the true nature of Nara—
why both Nara and Nārāyaṇa were born among men.
And how those two heroes are invincible and cannot be slain in battles; and how the Pāṇḍavas, O King, are unassailable by anyone in war—
Kṛṣṇa is indeed deeply devoted to those illustrious sons of Pāṇḍu.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, I say: let there be peace with the Pāṇḍavas. Rule the earth together with your powerful brothers, remaining self-controlled.
By disregarding the two gods, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, you shall perish.
"If you are not the author [of these words], you will not cross over this doubt.
Having spoken thus, O lord of the people, your father remained silent;
he dismissed the king and entered his bedchamber.
The king also, having prostrated before the high-souled one, went to his tent and lay down upon a white bed for that night, O bull of the Bharatas. Sañjaya said:
When the night had passed and the sun had risen,
O great king, both armies came together for battle.
When that night had elapsed, the bulls among the Kurus marched forth.
Placing the high-souled Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, at their head in battle,
they rushed forward in great wrath, desiring to conquer one another;
and having all come together in the fight, they surveyed each other.
O King, due to your evil counsel, the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras,
having formed their battle arrays, fought furiously as warriors;
Bhīṣma, O King, protected the Makara array from all sides.
In that very manner, O King, the Pāṇḍavas protected their own formation;
Ajātaśatru himself, having arranged that formation like a hawk at the word of Dhaumya, caused the hearts of his enemies to tremble.
O Bhārata, he was indeed well-versed in the construction of fire-altars; meanwhile,
the wise son of yours formed the great array known as the Makara,
with the entire army under his own command, having been authorized by Droṇa at that time.
Śāntanava followed that very same array once again;
then your father Devavrata, the best among chariot-warriors, set forth with his division of chariots,
surrounded by a great multitude of chariots.

Stationed according to their respective divisions, the chariot-warriors, infantry, elephant-riders, and cavalrymen followed one another. Seeing them thus prepared for battle, the illustrious Pāṇḍavas [advanced].
With that invincible king of battle-arrays, the Śyena (Hawk), in the midst of the fray,
the mighty Bhīmasena shone at its beak;
while the irrepressible Śikhaṇḍin and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, were its two eyes.
The hero Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth, became its head;
then Pārtha, brandishing the Gāṇḍīva, became its neck.
That entire Akṣauhiṇī army then became its left wing.

The high-souled and illustrious Drupada, together with his son, stood on the right flank in the battle; and the Kaikeya king, the commander of an akṣauhiṇī, was on the left flank. Behind them were the sons of Draupadī and the heroic son of Subhadrā.
On the back [of the array] stood the illustrious King Yudhiṣṭhira himself,
wise and of beautiful prowess, accompanied by his two brothers, the twins. Then,
Bhīma entered the battle from the mouth of the Makara formation.
Having encountered Bhīṣma in battle, he covered him with arrows.
Then, O Bhārata, Bhīṣma unleashed great celestial weapons in that great conflict,
bewildering the arrayed army of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Then, as the army was being thrown into confusion, Dhanañjaya acted with haste;
at the head of the battle, he pierced Bhīṣma with a thousand arrows,
having warded off the weapons discharged by Bhīṣma in that encounter.
Standing ready for battle with his own joyful army,
King Duryodhana, the best among the strong, having previously witnessed the terrible slaughter of his forces, then addressed the son of Bharadvāja:
Remembering the slaughter of his brothers in battle, that great car-warrior said:
"O Preceptor, you are indeed always my well-wisher, O sinless one;
for it is by relying upon you and our grandfather Bhīṣma that we have stood firm."

We seek to conquer even the gods in battle, of this there is no doubt; how much more so the sons of Pāṇḍu, who are inferior in strength and prowess? Therefore, may prosperity be yours, act in such a way that the Pāṇḍavas are slain.
O sire, having been thus addressed by your son, Droṇa then spoke to the king there, sighing as if in great anger:
"You are a fool; you do not understand the prowess of the Pāṇḍavas."
"For the Pāṇḍavas are indeed possessed of great strength and cannot be conquered [by force alone].
Therefore, O King, I shall perform for you whatever task is within my power and according to my prowess.
Having said this, O King, he approached his son’s army.
While Sātyaki looked on, he [Droṇa] broke through the Pāṇḍava army;
but then, O Bhārata, Sātyaki held Droṇa back,
and thereupon a tumultuous battle commenced that made the hair stand on end.
Then the powerful Bhāradvāja, enraged in battle,
pierced Śaineya in the region of the collarbone with sharp arrows as if smiling;
thereupon the furious Bhīmasena pierced Bhāradvāja in return.
O King, while protecting Sātyaki from Droṇa, the foremost of weapon-bearers,
Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Śalya, O noble one,
then became enraged in battle and covered Bhīmasena with their arrows.
There, O Sire, the enraged Abhimanyu and the sons of Draupadī pierced all those warriors who stood with weapons raised, using sharpened arrows.
Then the two mighty heroes, Bhīṣma and Droṇa, also rushed forward in great wrath.
But in that great battle, the mighty archer Śikhaṇḍin advanced against him;
grasping his bow, which resounded like a rain-cloud, the hero swiftly rained down arrows, obscuring the very sun.
Having encountered Śikhaṇḍin, the grandfather of the Bharatas avoided him in battle, remembering his femininity; then,
O great king, Droṇa rushed toward him in the fight.
Then, urged by your son, Śikhaṇḍin, while protecting Bhīṣma,
encountered Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons,
and avoided him in battle as one would avoid the fierce fire at the end of an eon.
Then, O lord of the people, your son, with a great force and seeking great glory, approached and protected Bhīṣma;
likewise, O King, the Pāṇḍavas placed Dhanañjaya at their head.
Having set their firm resolve upon victory, they turned toward Bhīṣma alone;
that battle became as terrible as the one between the gods and the Dānavas,
as they constantly sought both victory and most wonderful glory.
Saṃjaya said:
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, fought a tumultuous battle,
desiring to rescue your sons from the fear of Bhīmasena.

In the forenoon, that most terrible battle between the kings of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas commenced, a conflict that destroyed the foremost heroes. While that tumultuous and greatly fearsome engagement was taking place, [the battle continued].
A tumultuous sound arose, touching the vast sky,
produced by trumpeting great elephants, neighing horses,
and the blare of kettledrums and conchs; thus a great clamor came into being.
Desirous of battle, those valiant and mighty warriors roared at one another for the sake of victory, like great bulls in cow-pens;
as their heads were being struck down in the conflict by sharpened arrows.
O bull of the Bharatas, it was like a rain of stones in the sky;
heads adorned with earrings and turbans, radiant with gold,
were seen falling, O bull of the Bharatas.
The earth became covered with limbs mangled by arrows, with arms still clutching bows, and with others bearing hand-ornaments;
it was strewn with bodies clad in armor and hands still finely adorned.
O King, in a mere moment, the entire earth became strewn with heads resembling the moon and beautiful with eyes red at the corners, as well as with all the limbs of elephants, horses, and men.
With tumultuous clouds of dust illuminated by the lightning-flashes of weapons,
the roar of the arms became like the thundering of clouds.
That tumultuous and bitter clash had blood for its water.
O Bhārata, that battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas proceeded—
a terrible, fierce, tumultuous, and hair-raising encounter—
in which the Kṣatriyas, intoxicated by war, rained down showers of arrows.
O best of the Bharatas, in that battle between your men and the enemy, the elephants cried out, tormented by showers of arrows—
those furious heroes, steadfast and possessed of immeasurable energy.
Due to the sound of bowstrings slapping against palms, nothing else could be discerned. As headless trunks rose up on all sides amidst a sea of blood,
the kings, intent on slaying their enemies, rushed about in the battle.
O scorcher of enemies, those heroes of immeasurable splendor struck one another in battle with arrows, spears, maces,
and swords; and there, elephants pierced by arrows wandered about uncontrollably.
And horses, their riders slain, galloped in the ten directions;
others, afflicted by the blows of arrows, leaped up and fell down,
O bull of the Bharatas, among the warriors of your side and those of the enemy.
Of many heads and bows,
as well as maces and iron clubs, along with hands together with thighs,
feet, ornaments, and armlets, all in great numbers.
O lord of the people, heaps of horses, elephants, and chariots were seen scattered here and there as they rushed forward with terrifying and formidable prowess.
Driven by Time, the Kṣatriyas there struck one another with maces, swords, spears, and straight-knotted arrows;
other heroes, skilled in hand-to-hand combat, fought with their bare arms in the fray.
O lord of the people, they clashed in many ways like iron clubs; with fists, knees, and palms,
your heroes struck one another along with the Pāṇḍavas.
O Lord of Men, in various places on that field of battle, as men lay fallen, were being struck down, or writhed upon the ground,
a terrible carnage ensued during that fierce gambling match with dice at the command of Duryodhana.
O Bhārata, when Bhīṣma displayed his prowess in battle,
a terrible river began to flow with waves of surging blood;
in its midst stood the great army, with hair for its moss and aquatic grass.
O King, horses whose riders had been slain and chariot-warriors who were now without their chariots roamed about in that battle, wielding excellent swords; there,
even those chariot-warriors deprived of their vehicles moved about, bearing fine blades.
Charging at one another and seeking each other's death,
King Duryodhana, surrounded by many Kaliṅgas and placing Bhīṣma at the forefront, then advanced against the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
In the same way, all the Pāṇḍavas, having surrounded Vṛkodara,
rushed furiously toward Bhīṣma in battle on their swift mounts.
Saṃjaya said:
Seeing his brothers and other kings engaged in combat with Bhīṣma,
Dhanañjaya, with weapons raised, rushed toward the son of Gaṅgā;
he was accompanied by the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Upon seeing Pārtha’s banner— with its lion-tail and its blazing form like a mountain in the sky— fear entered all of us;
it clung not to the trees, appearing like a risen comet.
O great king, we beheld the banner of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow— divine, marked with the figure of a monkey, multicolored,
and variegated— shining like lightning in the midst of clouds within the sky.
The warriors beheld the Gāṇḍīva bow with its golden back upon the great chariot;
and we heard his loud roar, like that of Śakra himself,
as he struck down your army with the most terrible sound of his palms.

Like a fierce wind-driven cloud accompanied by lightning and thunder, Dhananjaya— armed with terrible weapons— rushed toward the son of Gaṅgā, inundating all directions on every side with showers of arrows.

"Deluded by the weapon, we could no longer distinguish the eastern from the western direction; bewildered as to which way to turn, our mounts exhausted, our weapons destroyed, and our minds shattered,
those warriors, O bull of the Bharatas, clung to one another."
They sought refuge with Bhīṣma alone, together with all your sons;
in that battle, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, became their protector in distress. Then, terrified, the chariot-warriors leaped down from their chariots.
O King, riders were seen falling from the backs of their horses onto the ground, and foot soldiers likewise; elephant-warriors, terrified and bewildered by fear,
appeared distraught, no longer knowing the directions.

O Bhārata, hearing the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt, all the armies were terrified and cowered in fear. Then, [he was pursued] by the foremost Kamboja warriors, who were large and swift-moving.
Surrounded by many thousands of troops of cowherds, Govāsana was accompanied by the chiefs of the Kambojas— the Haṃsapatha and Karṇika clans—
as well as by the hosts of Gopāsanas and Gopāsanapati.
O lord of the people, the king of Kaliṅga was surrounded by the Madras, Sauviras, Gāndhāras, and Trigartas, as well as by all the chiefs of Kaliṅga;
and there were hosts of elephants and throngs of men led by Duḥśāsana.
And King Jayadratha, together with all the kings,
and fourteen thousand of the best horsemen urged on by your son, surrounded the son of Subala.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, all those on your side, having divided their chariots and mounts, advanced together against the Pāṇḍavas in battle,
accompanied by the infantry of the Cedis and Kāśis, and by the chariot-warriors of the Pañcālas and Sṛñjayas.
All the Pāṇḍavas together, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna and urged on by the son of Dharma, advanced against your men in battle;
they were accompanied by chariot-warriors, elephants, horses, and foot soldiers.
A terrible dust, resembling a massive cloud, arose from the battlefield of the warriors fighting with elephants,
horses, and chariots, using *tomaras*, *prāsas*, and *nārācas*.
With a great force, Bhīṣma engaged in combat with the Diademed One (Arjuna).
The king of Avanti was engaged with Bhīmasena, the king of Kāśī; the Saindhava with Ajātaśatru; and Śalya, together with his sons and ministers, encountered the illustrious bull among the Madras.
Vikarṇa was opposed by Sahadeva, and Citrasena by Śikhaṇḍin;
O lord of the people, the Matsyas advanced against Duryodhana and Śakuni.
Drupada, Cekitāna, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki [also joined the fray].
They engaged with the high-souled Droṇa and his son;
Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman rushed against Dhṛṣṭaketu. Thus did the horses gallop and the elephants and chariots whirl about.
The armies, engaged in combat on all sides, clashed together;
O lord of the people, intense lightning flashes appeared in a cloudless sky, the quarters were shrouded in dust, and great meteors fell with thunderous crashes.
A great wind blew and a rain of dust fell;
the sun was hidden in the sky, shrouded by the dust raised by the army.
A profound delusion came over all living beings.

They illuminated the sky with their excellent raised swords, while those who were overwhelmed by dust and pierced by nets of weapons— weapons released from the arms of heroes that penetrate all defenses— [remained there].
A tumultuous mass of arrow-nets was formed;
O bull of the Bharatas, the weapons raised by those excellent arms made the sky appear as bright as the stainless luster of the stars.
O bull of the Bharatas, variegated shields made of bull-hide, covered with networks of gold, flew in all directions;
they were struck down on every side by swords with the brilliance of the sun.
In all directions, bodies and heads were seen;
great chariot-warriors, with their wheels, axles, and seats shattered, their great banners cast down, and their horses slain, fell here and there upon the earth.
There, some horses, wounded by weapons,
bolted away, dragging behind them chariots once their warriors had been slain; those excellent steeds, struck by arrows and their bodies mangled, were still bound to their yokes.
O Bhārata, they dragged the yokes here and there; O King, chariots were seen being destroyed by a single powerful elephant, along with their drivers, horses,
and warriors.
In that clash of the masses of troops, many elephants in battle, having smelled the flow of ichor from the scent-elephant (Gandhahasti), became devoid of their vigor;
they were struck down along with their lifeless mahouts who still held their tomara-spears.
The battlefield became covered with elephants struck down by iron arrows,
as those excellent tuskers were dispatched in the clash of the vast armies;
in that combat, chariots fell broken along with their warriors and banners.

O Great King, in that battle, chariot-poles were seen shattered by elephants who, with trunks resembling the king of serpents, seized them; and those whose chariot-frames were destroyed were likewise dragged by their hair by the tuskers.
Like tree branches shaken and crushed in battle, the chariot-warriors were ground down in the fray;
and in that combat, excellent elephants dragged chariots that were entangled with other chariots,
scattering in all directions and filling every quarter with their cries.

As those elephants were thus dragging [the bodies], their appearance shone like that of those dragging a mass of lotuses stuck in the lakes. In this way, the great battlefield there became completely covered.
With horsemen, foot soldiers, and great car-warriors bearing banners— Sañjaya said:
"O lord of the people, Śikhaṇḍin, together with Virāṭa the Matsya..."
Dhananjaya quickly encountered Bhishma, the great archer who was exceedingly difficult to defeat;
he also assailed Drona, Kripa, and Vikarna— all mighty archers of great strength—
as well as many other heroic kings in battle.
O bull among kings, [you have conquered] the great archer Saindhava along with his ministers and kinsmen,
as well as the rulers of the East and the South;
and also your son, the great archer Duryodhana, who is full of indignation.
And Bhīmasena advanced against Duḥsaha in battle; Sahadeva, however, advanced against Śakuni and the great car-warrior Ulūka— those two invincible sons of a father, both mighty archers.
O great king, the great car-warrior Yudhiṣṭhira encountered the elephant division in battle,
having been treated with deceit by your son.
But Nakula, the son of Mādrī, was a hero who roared aloud in combat.
The son of Pāṇḍu engaged with the noble chariot-warriors of the Trigartas;
the invincible Śālva and the Kekayas advanced against him in battle,
as did Śatānīka, the son of Nakula and a bull among car-warriors.
Sātyaki, Cekitāna, the great car-warrior Saubhadra,
Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca—
these most invincible warriors advanced in battle against the chariot-division of your sons.

O King, the commander-in-chief Dhrishtadyumna, of immeasurable soul and great strength, encountered Droṇa— who performed deeds like those of Indra— in battle. Thus did these great archers on your side engage with the Pāṇḍavas.
Having come together in battle, the heroes engaged in a fierce encounter;
when the sun had reached the meridian and the sky had become turbid,
the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas struck one another down.
Adorned with banners and their parts decorated with gold, the chariots— furnished with flags and covered in tiger-skins— shone as they moved about the field of battle.
And so did those assembled in the encounter, each desiring victory over the other.
A tumultuous sound arose like the roar of lions;
there we beheld a wondrous and most terrible encounter,
as the heroic Sṛñjayas engaged the Kurus in battle.
O King, scorcher of enemies, we could see neither the sky nor the quarters, nor the sun, nor even the intermediate directions, because of the arrows released on all sides; likewise,
there were spears with polished points and *tomaras* being hurled.
The luster of polished swords, resembling blue lotuses,
as well as the radiance of variegated armor and ornaments,
illuminated the sky, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate points with their brilliance.
O King, the battlefield shone here and there with the bodies of the lords of men, which possessed a radiance equal to that of the moon and the sun;
and the lions among chariot-warriors, like tigers, were arriving for the encounter.
O King, they shone in battle like planets in the vault of the sky.
Then Bhīṣma, the best of chariot-warriors, filled with rage, checked the mighty Bhīmasena while the entire army looked on.
Then, released by Bhīṣma, gold-feathered arrows, whetted on stone,
cleansed with oil, and keenly sharpened, struck Bhīma in battle. Against his spear of great velocity, the mighty Bhīmasena—
O Bhārata, he dispatched that mace, which resembled an enraged venomous serpent;
as it came rushing suddenly, with its golden staff and difficult to approach,
Bhīṣma cut it apart in battle with straight-jointed arrows.
Then, O Bhārata, with another sharp, yellowed broad-headed arrow, he cut Bhīmasena’s bow in two. Casting aside his broken bow, the mighty Bhīmasena—
With many arrows, he struck Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, in battle.
Then Sātyaki, quickly approaching Bhīṣma in the encounter,
[struck him] with sharp, whetted, and fiercely pointed shafts drawn back to his ear.
O lord of men, he struck your father with many arrows.
Then, having fixed a sharp and most terrible shaft,
Bhīṣma caused the charioteer of the Vārṣṇeya to fall from his chariot.
O King, when the charioteer had been slain, his horses fled;
with the speed of thought or the wind, they ran hither and thither.
Then, a tumultuous roar arose from the entire army.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the high-souled Pāṇḍavas:
"Attack! Seize! Restrain the horses!
Run!"—such was the tumultuous noise directed toward Yuyudhāna’s chariot.

At that very time, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, once again began to slaughter the Pāṇḍava army, just as Vṛtrahaṇ (Indra) destroyed the host of Asuras. Being slaughtered by Bhīṣma, the Pañcālas together with the Somakas—
Having resolved upon a noble course in battle, they rushed toward Bhīṣma;
and the Pārthas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, also charged at the son of Śaṃtanu in the fray,
desiring to conquer the army of your son.
In the same way, O King, your warriors, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa,
rushed with speed toward the enemy, and then the battle commenced.
Saṃjaya said:
Then Virāṭa, that great car-warrior, struck Bhīṣma, the great car-warrior, with three arrows;
and he pierced Bhīṣma’s horses with three arrows as well. Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, pierced him in return with ten shafts.
The great archer, the mighty warrior of firm hand,
the son of Droṇa— whose bow was formidable and who was a great chariot-warrior— pierced the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva with six gold-tufted arrows in the middle of his chest.
Phalguna, the slayer of enemy heroes and crusher of foes, cut through his bow and pierced him deeply with sharp, feathered arrows. Enraged and frantic with fury, he took up another powerful bow.
Unable to endure the severing of his bow by Pārtha in that battle,
O King, he pierced Phalguna with ninety sharpened arrows and struck Vāsudeva with seventy excellent shafts.
Then Phalguna, his eyes copper-red with rage, together with Krishna,
sighed long and hot and reflected again and again;
that crusher of foes gripped his bow with his left hand.
Enraged, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow took up sharp, straight-jointed,
and terrible arrows capable of ending life;
with them, he swiftly pierced the son of Droṇa, the foremost among the powerful, in that battle.
Having pierced his armor, they drank his blood in the battle;
yet, though pierced by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, the son of Droṇa did not waver,
discharging showers of arrows in that same manner, undisturbed.
O King, he stood in that battle desiring to protect the one of great vows;
the bulls among men praised that truly magnificent deed of his,
in that he did not feel shame in the encounter with the two Krishnas joined together.
Though pierced by Phalguna in battle, he did not fall to the surface of the earth;
for he always fought in the ranks, established in fearlessness,
having obtained from Drona that most difficult-to-attain collection of weapons along with the methods for their withdrawal.
"This son of my preceptor Droṇa is exceedingly dear to him as a son;
moreover, he is a Brāhmaṇa and thus especially worthy of my respect. Having formed this resolve, the heroic Bībhatsu, the scorcher of his enemies, [acted accordingly].
The best of chariot-warriors felt compassion toward the son of Bharadvāja;
then the son of Kuntī, the scorcher of his enemies, leaving the son of Droṇa in the battle,
fought with haste, slaying your men with great prowess.

Duryodhana, however, struck the great archer Bhīmasena with ten gold-feathered arrows, whetted on stone and fletched with vulture feathers. But Bhīmasena, filled with rage, [discharged] a firm weapon capable of ending the life of his foe.
He took up a variegated bow and ten sharp arrows;
with those keen, swift, and fiercely pointed shafts drawn back to his ear,
he quickly and calmly pierced the Kuru king in the great chest.
The jewel on his chest, encircled by golden threads and arrows,
shone like the sun surrounded by planets;
yet your son, though full of splendor, was struck by Bhīmasena.
He could not endure it, just as an elephant cannot bear the sound of a palm-clap;
then, O great king, filled with rage and terrifying the army, he pierced Bhīma with arrows whetted on stone and fletched with gold.
Fighting fiercely in battle and deeply wounding one another,
those two sons of yours, endowed with great strength and resembling gods, shone resplendent.
Then the son of Subhadrā, that tiger among men and slayer of enemy heroes, [attacked] Citrasena.
He pierced Purumitra with ten arrows and Satyavrata with seventy; equal to Śakra in battle,
that hero, as if dancing upon the field, caused us great distress.
Citrasena pierced him with ten feathered arrows,
Satyavrata with nine, and Purumitra with seven.
Pierced thus and shedding blood, he [remained] great in his obstruction of the enemy.
The son of Arjuna cut through Citrasena’s variegated bow,
and having pierced his armor, struck him in the chest with an arrow.
Then those heroic princes of yours, the great chariot-warriors—
Having come together in battle, they, enraged, pierced him with sharpened arrows;
but he, the supreme knower of weapons, struck them all down with his own sharp shafts.
Having witnessed that feat of his, your sons then surrounded him.
Scorching your army in battle like a fierce fire consuming dry undergrowth at the end of the winter season,
the son of Subhadrā shone brilliantly as he slaughtered your troops.
O lord of the people, seeing that conduct of his, your grandson Lakṣmaṇa swiftly rushed toward the son of Sātvatī in the battle.
But Abhimanyu, filled with rage, [assailed] Lakṣmaṇa, who was endowed with auspicious marks.
He pierced him with six arrows and his charioteer with three shafts;
likewise, O King, Lakṣmaṇa struck the son of Subhadrā with sharpened arrows,
O great monarch, and that was like a marvel.
Having slain his four horses and his charioteer,
the mighty Saubhadra rushed at Lakṣmaṇa with sharpened arrows.
But Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, stood firm upon his chariot whose horses had been killed.
Enraged, he hurled a spear toward the chariot of Saubhadra. As it came rushing suddenly— terrible in form, difficult to withstand,
and resembling a serpent— Abhimanyu cut it down with sharp arrows.
Then, having placed Lakṣmaṇa upon his own chariot, Gautama carried him away from the battlefield by means of that chariot while the entire army looked on. Then,
while that great terror was prevailing in that tumultuous situation,
O Lord of the People, horsemen rushed against horsemen, elephant-riders against elephant-riders, and heroes against heroes,
seeking to slay one another and desiring each other's death.
Both your great archers and the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas engaged in the fray.
Sacrificing their lives in the encounter, they struck one another down. With hair disheveled, divested of armor, deprived of chariots, and with bows shattered,
the Sṛñjayas fought with their bare arms against the Kurus.

Then the mighty-armed Bhīṣma, possessed of great strength, being highly incensed, slaughtered the army of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas with divine weapons. There, elephants were slain along with their riders, and men and horses were struck down.
The earth was strewn with chariot-warriors and horsemen alike.
Sañjaya said:
"Then, O King, the mighty-armed Sātyaki, who is fierce in battle,"
Drawing his bow in battle— that supreme instrument for accomplishing great feats—
which he had previously learned from his friend Arjuna,
he released feathered arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Displaying his lightness of hand with weapons in a manner that was brilliant, swift, and varied— while he was drawing his bow, discharging other arrows,
taking up more, and fixing yet others to it—
As he discharged arrows in battle and struck down his enemies,
his form appeared exceedingly like a cloud pouring forth rain. Then, beholding him thus surging forward, King Duryodhana—
O Bhārata, he dispatched ten thousand chariots against him;
but the heroic Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth and who is a supreme archer, slew all those great bowmen with a divine weapon.
Having performed that terrible deed, the hero, with his bow grasped,
then advanced against Bhūriśravas in battle;
for he had seen that army struck down by Yuyudhāna.
Enraged, the enhancer of the Kurus' fame rushed forward;
drawing that great bow which was the color of Indra’s rainbow,
he released arrows resembling thunderbolts and venomous serpents.
O great king, displaying his lightness of hand by the thousands,
those followers of Sātyaki could not endure those arrows that touched the very touch of death; O King, they then fled in every direction.
O King, having left Satyaki— who was fierce in battle— behind in the fray,
[the enemy] beheld the ten mighty sons of Yuyudhana;
they were renowned great car-warriors, adorned with variegated armor, weapons, and banners.
Having encountered the great archer Bhūriśravas in battle, they all, highly incensed in that great conflict, spoke to him whose banner bore the sacrificial stake:
"Fight in this encounter today; let us behold your prowess!"
"O mighty heir of the Kauravas, come with us, O one of great strength! Fight in battle with all of us together, or even separately.
Either defeat us in combat and attain glory, or [be defeated by us]."
"Either we shall defeat you and give the pleasure to our father, or you shall do so for him.
Thus addressed by those heroes, the immensely powerful one,
that best of men who prided himself on his valor, spoke to them as they stood before him.
"O heroes, it is well said that such is your resolve today;
fight together with diligence, for I shall slay you in battle. Having been thus addressed, those heroic and swift-acting great archers [prepared themselves].

With a great shower of arrows, they rained upon the subduer of foes. O Great King, in the afternoon, a tumultuous battle took place on the field of combat between one man and many who had assembled there.
O King, they overwhelmed that sole preeminent chariot-warrior with showers of arrows,
just as clouds drench a great mountain during the rainy season. Those masses of arrows released by them were like the staff of Yama or a thunderbolt in their brilliance.
The great car-warrior swiftly cut down those arrows before they had even reached him;
there we beheld the wonderful prowess of Saumadatti,
in that he alone, fearless as he was, engaged in battle with many.

O King, having discharged that shower of arrows, the ten great car-warriors surrounded the mighty-armed one and set about to slay him. Then, O Bhārata, the son of Somadatta, filled with rage, [cut off] their bows.

In the blink of an eye, that great car-warrior cut them down with ten arrows. Then, O King, with broad-headed shafts of straight joints and sharpened arrows, he severed their heads in battle once their bows had been broken.
Slain, they fell upon the earth like trees shattered by a thunderbolt.
Seeing those mighty sons, heroes slain in battle,
O King, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi let out a roar and rushed toward Bhūriśravas.
Having crushed chariot against chariot in battle, those two of great strength,
having struck down each other’s horses in the encounter,
met as two great car-warriors leaping about, both now deprived of their chariots.
Grasping their great swords and bearing excellent shields, those two tigers among men shone as they stood ready for battle;
Bhūriśravas was unbearable in combat for sword-fighting.
Realizing this, the great car-warrior Vṛkodara quickly leaped forward;
then,
O King, Bhīmasena, acting with haste, approached Sātyaki— who was wielding an excellent sword— and lifted him onto his chariot.

O King, your son also swiftly placed Bhūriśravas upon his chariot in the midst of battle while all the archers looked on. While that battle was thus proceeding, [he placed] the great car-warrior Bhīṣma [upon his chariot].
O bull of the Bharatas, the enraged Pāṇḍavas fought on;
and as the sun turned red, Dhanañjaya, acting with haste,
slew twenty-five thousand great car-warriors.
For they, commanded by Duryodhana for the destruction of Pārtha,
perished as soon as they reached him, like moths entering a fire.
Then the Matsyas and the Kekayas, who were experts in the science of archery, [advanced].
Then they surrounded the great car-warrior Pārtha along with his son.
At that very time, as the sun was setting,
a total confusion came over all the troops.
Then,
O great king, at the time of twilight, when the mounts of the armies were exhausted,
your father Devavrata ordered a withdrawal for both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus as they met one another.
Those two armies, greatly agitated, returned to their respective encampments. Then, O Bhārata, having gone to their own camps,
the Pāṇḍavas together with the Sṛñjayas and the Kurus settled there according to the prescribed rules.
Saṃjaya said:
O King, having spent that time together, the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas,
when the night had passed, went forth once more for battle.
There, O Bhārata, a great clamor arose from both you and them:
"Let the foremost chariots be yoked! Let the elephants be equipped!
Let the foot soldiers and the horses be armored!"—so it was said, O Bhārata.
A tumultuous sound of conchs and kettledrums arose on all sides.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira addressed Dhṛṣṭadyumna:
"O mighty-armed one, form the Makara array, which scorches the enemy."
Thus addressed by Pārtha, O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
that great car-warrior and best among chariot-fighters, gave his orders to the warriors.
Drupada was at its head, and Dhananjaya the Pāṇḍava was also there.
Sahadeva and Nakula, that great car-warrior, were the two eyes;
O Great King, the mighty Bhimasena was the beak.
And Saubhadra, the sons of Draupadī, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca [were its other parts].
Sātyaki and Dharmarāja were stationed at the neck of the array;
O great king, Virāṭa, the commander of the army, was at the rear,
accompanied by Dhṛṣṭadyumna and surrounded by a vast host.
The five Kekaya brothers took their positions on the left flank;
Dhṛṣṭaketu, that tiger among men, and the heroic Karakarṣa stood taking their places on the right wing to protect the formation.
O Great King, at the two feet stood the illustrious and great car-warrior Kuntibhoja Śatānīka, surrounded by a vast army;
and there was the mighty and great archer Śikhaṇḍin, surrounded by the Somakas.
And Irāvat was stationed at the tail of that crocodile formation.
Having thus arrayed this great military formation, O Bhārata, the Pāṇḍavas,
O great king, clad themselves in armor once again for battle at the rising of the sun.
With elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, they quickly advanced against the Kauravas,
with variegated banners raised high and bright, sharp weapons.
But seeing that military array, your father Devavrata [beheld] that army.
O King, with that great *krauñca* formation, he arrayed his army.
At its beak shone the great archer, the son of Bharadvāja;
and Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, O lord of men, were its two eyes.
But Kṛtavarman, the best among all archers and the foremost of men, was at the head [of the army], accompanied by the Kambojas, Āraṭṭas, and Bāhlikas;
while Śūrasena and your son, O honorable one, were at the neck.
O great king, Duryodhana was surrounded by many kings; O best of men, the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa, joined by the Madras, Sauviras, and Kekayas,
stood at the breast, surrounded by a vast army.
And on the rear stood those two great archers from Avanti along with their followers,
and Suśarman, the lord of Prasthala, together with his own army, stood armored,
taking his position on the left wing.
O Bhārata, the Tuṣāras, the Yavanas, and the Śakas, together with the Cūcupas,
took their positions on the right wing of the array.
And Śrutāyus, Śatāyus, and the son of Somadatta, O noble sir, [stood there].
Standing at the rear of the formation, they protected one another. Then, O Great King, at sunrise, the Pāṇḍavas engaged with the Kauravas for battle, and a great conflict ensued.
Charioteers encountered elephants, and elephants advanced against charioteers; horsemen met horsemen, and chariot-warriors likewise met riders.
O King, in that great battle, a chariot-warrior attacked a charioteer, and [elephants] attacked other elephants.
O King, elephant-riders rushed against chariot-riders, and chariot-warriors against horsemen; chariot-warriors together with foot-soldiers, and horsemen together with foot-soldiers,
charged at one another in battle, filled with indignation.
Protected by Bhīmasena, Arjuna, the twins, and other great car-warriors,
the Pāṇḍava army shone like a night sky filled with stars;
likewise [did the Kaurava army] with Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, Droṇa, Śalya, Duryodhana, and the others.
Your army also shone forth like the sky covered with planets.
But the valiant Bhīmasena, the son of Kuntī, seeing Droṇa,
advanced against the host of Bharadvāja’s son with swift horses.
But Drona, enraged in battle, O King, pierced Bhima with nine iron arrows in that encounter, aiming at his vital organs; thus struck firmly by the son of Bharadvaja in the fray, Bhima—
He dispatched his charioteer toward the abode of Yama. Then the powerful Bhāradvāja himself took up the reins and scattered the Pāṇḍava army like fire consuming a heap of cotton.
O best of men, being slaughtered by Droṇa and Bhīṣma,
the Sṛñjayas together with the Kekayas became intent on flight;
likewise, your army was mangled by Bhīma and Arjuna.
O Samadeva, right there the excellent women were bewildered;
then, in that slaughter of the best of heroes, the two battle arrays broke apart,
and a terrible clash occurred between your men and theirs, O Bhārata.
O Bhārata, we beheld that wonder of your men fighting with the enemies, as they all took to a single path;
O lord of the people, they warded off one another's weapons.
The Pāṇḍavas and the Kaurava great-chariot warriors fought on.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Thus was the army possessed of many qualities, thus was it of many kinds and supreme."
O Sañjaya, this army is thus arrayed according to the scriptures and is indeed unfailing;
it is exceedingly well-nourished by us, ever devoted to our cause,
humble, free from calamities, and has previously displayed its prowess.
Neither too old nor childish, neither emaciated nor corpulent, with limbs that were mostly light, rounded, and long, possessing a body of solid substance and free from disease;
equipped with armor and weapons, and having taken up many implements of war.
He was skilled in sword-fighting, wrestling, and club-fighting; he was proficient in battle with spears, javelins, and lances, as well as with iron bludgeons,
slings, pikes, and maces in every respect.
He was skilled in all forms of archery— whether with vibrating bows, slings,
or various types of projectiles— as well as in wrestling and boxing; he possessed direct knowledge of the sciences and had exerted himself in physical training.
He was fully proficient in all the sciences of wielding weapons; he was skilled in mounting, leaping down, charging, jumping with intervals, striking accurately, advancing, and retreating.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles have been repeatedly and thoroughly examined; having been scrutinized according to the proper rule, they were provided with their wages.
This was not done out of social circles, nor through mere formal service, nor on account of kinship.
Neither by the strength of friendship nor by the inclusion of those of low birth can one overcome that city,
which is prosperous, noble, filled with contented and honored kinsmen, abounding in those who have rendered services, illustrious, and high-minded.

O dear one, it was protected by many preeminent men accompanied by their armies, who were renowned throughout the world, comparable to the guardians of the quarters, and possessed of many distinguished deeds; it was guarded by numerous kṣatriyas esteemed by the world across the earth.
It was filled on all sides by those who had approached us out of desire, together with their forces and followers—
like the great ocean overflowing with rivers from every direction— and it was crowded with chariots and elephants that, though wingless, resembled birds in flight.
Terrible with its waters of various weapons, possessing waves in the form of mounts,
crowded with slings, swords, maces, spears, arrows,
and darts, it was thick with banners and ornaments and strewn with jeweled cloths.
With its moving vehicles, shaken by the force of the wind,
it was like a vast, shoreless ocean roaring and resembling the sea itself;
it was well-protected by Droṇa and Bhīṣma, and guarded by Kṛtavarman.

It was protected by Kṛpa and Duḥśāsana, as well as by those headed by Jayadratha, by Bhagadatta and Vikarṇa, and by the son of Droṇa, the son of Subala, and Bāhlika— by these great-souled, world-renowned, and powerful pre-eminent heroes.
That he was slain in battle is an ancient destiny;
neither men nor highly blessed sages of old on earth, O Sañjaya, have ever seen such an exertion as this.
For such a flood of troops, equipped with a wealth of weapons and missiles, is being slaughtered in battle; what else can this be but fate?
O Sañjaya, all this appears to me as utterly contrary [to reason].
06,072.022c Since such a formidable force did not overcome the Pāṇḍavas in battle, 06,072.023a or perhaps the gods themselves have assembled there for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas,
06,072.023c and are fighting against my army, O Sañjaya, which is why they were not slain.
"O Saṃjaya, Vidura has indeed spoken here what is beneficial and wholesome;
yet my dull-witted son Duryodhana does not accept it.
I believe that the mind of that great-souled one, who is all-knowing, was already fixed long ago."
"It was as it came to be, dear one, according to how this was seen by him in the past.
Or rather, O Sañjaya, it had necessarily to be so in every way;
for as it was created by the Creator in the beginning, so it is, and not otherwise."
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, it is through your own fault that you have encountered such calamity;
for Duryodhana, O bull of the Bharatas, did not perceive those [consequences]."
O King, lord of the people, that gambling match which you witnessed earlier, brought about by the confusion of dharma, occurred through your own fault;
and through your fault, this war with the Pāṇḍavas has been set in motion.
"O King, you yourself must now experience the fruit, having committed this sin by your own self;
for the action performed by oneself is experienced by oneself alone,
whether in this world or after death, exactly as it was done."

Therefore, O King, having encountered this great calamity, remain steadfast and listen, O noble one, as I describe the battle exactly as it occurred. Bhīmasena, however, having pierced the great army with sharpened arrows...
Then the hero approached all the younger brothers of Duryodhana:
Duḥśāsana, Durviṣaha, Duḥsaha, Durmada, Jaya,
Jayatsena, Vikarṇa, Citrasena, and Sudarśana.
Seeing Cārucitra, Suvarmāṇa, Duṣkarṇa, Karṇa himself, and these and many other great car-warriors standing nearby— the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all highly enraged— the mighty Bhīma [prepared for battle].
He entered the great army protected by Bhīṣma in battle.
Then they called out to one another, "Vṛkodara has arrived!
And seeing that he had entered, they all spoke thus.
"O lords of men, let us seize him alive!
Thus surrounded by those brothers who were firm in their resolve,
Pārtha was like the sun encircled by cruel, great planets at the time of the destruction of all creatures.
Having reached the center of the formation, fear did not enter the son of Pāṇḍu,
just as Mahendra felt no fear upon encountering the Dānavas in the battle between the gods and the Asuras.
Then, O Lord, hundreds of thousands of chariot-warriors from all sides [surrounded him].
Covering him with terrible arrows, they surrounded that single warrior;
yet that hero, disregarding the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, slew their foremost combatants— the riders of elephants, horses, and chariots— in battle.
O King, perceiving their resolve and their desire to seize him, the high-minded Bhīmasena set his mind upon the slaughter of them all. Then the Pāṇḍava, abandoning his chariot, took up his mace.
"O Bhārata, Bhīma said to his charioteer, 'Stop!
Until I have slain these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their followers.
Having spoken thus, Bhīmasena entered the vast army."
He struck down that great ocean-like flood of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s forces.
By Bhīmasena, with his mace, those excellent elephants were struck;
their frontal globes were shattered, their massive bodies split, and likewise their backs were broken.
With their limbs mangled and their riders fallen, they lay like mountains; and chariots, along with their warriors, were shattered into pieces like sesame seeds by the hundreds in battle,
O Bhārata, as were horses and horsemen together with the foot soldiers.
There we beheld the marvelous prowess of Bhīmasena,
O King, in that he alone fought against many in battle,
like the Destroyer himself with staff in hand at the time of the end of all creatures.
When Bhīmasena had entered [the ranks], Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
also swiftly abandoned Droṇa and proceeded to where the son of Subala was;
that bull among men had torn through the vast army of your warriors.
He approached the empty chariot of Bhīmasena in the battle;
and seeing the chariot empty and looking toward Bhīma,
he lost his presence of mind upon seeing Viśoka, the charioteer of Bhīmasena, in the fray.
O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, dejected and deprived of his senses, asked with a voice choked by tears, uttering words in a low murmur:
"Where is Bhīma, who is dearer to me than my own life? Thus he spoke in his distress.
Viśoka, with palms joined in reverence, said this to Dhṛṣṭadyumna:
"Having stationed me here, the powerful and majestic son of Pāṇḍu has entered this great ocean-like army of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
Having spoken these words to me with affection, O tiger among men, he said:
"O charioteer, restrain the horses and wait for me for a moment,
while I quickly slay those who are intent on killing me."
That one of great strength, mace in hand, rushed toward that army. Then,
seeing him of great strength rushing forward with mace in hand,
a great agitation arose among all the troops.
While that tumultuous and terrifying battle was raging,
O King, your friend [Arjuna] broke through the great array and entered it.
Having heard the words of Viśoka, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, also [advanced].
Then, in the midst of the battle, the one of great strength replied to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, there is indeed no purpose for my life today,
having abandoned Bhīmasena in battle and cast aside my affection for the Pāṇḍavas."
"If I go without Bhīma, what will the warrior class say of me? While Bhīma has gone on his solitary path and I remain here in the fray,
even the gods led by Agni bring ill fortune upon him."
He who returns home safely after abandoning his companions—
his life, though lived under the contempt of the warrior class (*kṣatra*), becomes utterly meaningless;
he shall sink into the Raurava hell, which is without a raft and difficult for men to cross.

"Bhīma is my friend and my kinsman, and he is possessed of great strength. He is devoted to us, and I too am devoted to him, that slayer of enemies. Therefore, I shall go to that place where Vṛkodara has gone."
"Behold me slaying my enemies like Vāsava against the Dānavas!
Having spoken thus, the hero then proceeded through the midst of the Bharata host along the paths of Bhīmasena, which were strewn with elephants crushed by his mace.
Then he beheld Bhīma consuming the enemy host,
forcibly shattering the kings in battle like a wind breaking down trees. Those chariot-warriors and horsemen were thus being slaughtered in the conflict.
The foot-soldiers and the elephants likewise raised a great cry of distress, O Sire;
and a tumultuous clamor of "Alas! Alas! arose among your troops as they were being slaughtered by the skilled Bhīmasena, that warrior of diverse combat skills.
Then all those masters of weapons, having surrounded Vṛkodara,
fearlessly assailed him from every side with a rain of missiles.
Thus was that foremost of weapon-bearers beset.
The Pāṇḍava, the best among weapon-bearers, was assailed from all sides by world-heroes; and that hero, equal to the guardians of the world, was likewise surrounded on every side by the world-heroes.
Seeing Bhīmasena with his body mangled by arrows, the powerful son of Pṛṣata approached him, accompanied by a formidable and well-arrayed army.
Reassuring Bhimasena, who was on foot and vomiting the poison of his wrath like Death himself with mace in hand at the time of universal destruction, the son of Prishata approached.
The high-souled one quickly made him free from the arrow's barb,
and having embraced Bhīmasena tightly, he placed him upon his own chariot.
And he comforted her in the midst of the enemy; while that [battle] was proceeding with such extreme violence,
Bhīma likewise comforted Yājñasenī after she had fainted.
Then, having approached his brothers, your son also,
seeing them in that great conflict as it unfolded in battle, spoke these words.
"This evil-minded son of Drupada has encountered Bhīmasena;
go all together and slay him!"
Let not the enemy seek your army;
let this man of base deeds, who is utterly inferior,
approach them and destroy their host with his arrows.
Hearing those words, however, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, unable to endure them and urged by the command of their eldest brother,
rushed forth with uplifted weapons for the sake of slaughter.
Like fierce comets at the end of an eon,
those heroes, brandishing variegated bows,
caused the earth to tremble with the sounds of their bowstrings and the slapping of their palms.
They rained arrows upon the son of Drupada, just as clouds shower a mountain with torrents of water;
and having struck them down with his own exceedingly sharp shafts, he—
The one who fights with diverse skill did not waver in battle upon seeing your sons,
those exalted heroes, standing on all sides in the fray.
Desirous of slaying the fierce one, the youthful son of Drupada,
that great car-warrior, O King, being exceedingly enraged at your sons, invoked the Pramohana weapon.
Just as Mahendra [acts] among the Daityas in battle,
that high-souled one then [discharged] the weapon of great power called Pramohana, given by Droṇa.
O King, in that battle, he of noble deeds caused [confusion] among your army;
then the heroic men were bewildered in the fray.
Their intellects and courage struck down by the *pramohana* weapon,
all the Kurus fled in every direction, along with their horses, elephants, and chariots.
Seeing your sons as if their time were spent, deprived of consciousness, and overcome by delusion—
at that very moment, Bhīma, the best among strikers—
O King, having rested there and drunk the water that tasted like nectar,
he quickly re-equipped himself and once again fought in the battle; accompanied by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O Bhārata, he drove back the enemy.
At that very time, however, Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons,
approached Drupada and pierced him with three fierce arrows. O King, that monarch was then deeply pierced in battle by Droṇa.
O King, Drupada fled from the calamity, remembering his former enmity.
Having defeated Drupada, the powerful Drona blew his conch shell;
hearing the sound of that conch, all the Somakas were struck with terror.
Then Drona, the radiant one and best among wielders of weapons, heard that your sons had been rendered unconscious in battle by the Pramohana weapon. Thereupon,
Drona, longing for the kingdom, quickly departed from the field of battle.
There, the powerful Bhāradvāja, that great archer, beheld Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Bhīma roaming through the great battle,
and that great car-warrior saw your sons overcome by confusion.
Then, taking up the weapon of wisdom (*prajñāstra*), he neutralized the weapon of delusion (*mohanāstra*).
Thereupon, your sons, those great car-warriors, having regained their senses,
once more advanced in battle against Bhīma and the son of Pṛṣata to do battle.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, having summoned his own soldiers, said:
"Let twelve armored chariot-warriors, headed by the son of Subhadrā, follow the path of Bhīma and the son of Pṛṣata in battle according to their strength."
"Let them observe their movements, for my mind is not yet at peace.
Having ascertained the activities of Bhīmasena and the son of Pṛṣata in the encounter,
quickly enter the ocean of chariots in battle."
"Go forth with all your might; this is my resolve. Thus authorized, those heroes, valiant warriors who pride themselves on their manliness, replied, "So be it."
When the sun had reached the meridian, all of them indeed set forth—
the Kekayas, the sons of Draupadī, and the heroic Dhṛṣṭaketu—
surrounded by a vast army and placing Abhimanyu at their head.
Having formed the needle-mouthed array (*sūcīmukha*) in battle,
those tamers of foes pierced that division of chariots belonging to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the fray.
As those great archers advanced with Abhimanyu at their head, [the enemy watched them].
"O lord of men, your army— overcome by the fear of Bhīmasena and confounded by Dhṛṣṭadyumna— is unable to hold its ground;
like a young woman on a road, her soul is possessed by the fainting fit of intoxication."
Those great archers, with their banners adorned with gold, advanced,
rushing forward in a desire to rescue Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Vṛkodara;
