and they beheld those great bowmen led by Abhimanyu.
Filled with joy, they began to strike down your army;
and seeing Drona, who was skilled in archery and had reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge,
suddenly approaching, the Panchala prince [beheld] his own preceptor.
The heroic son of Pṛṣata did not hope for the slaughter of your sons;
then, having placed Vṛkodara upon the chariot of the Kekaya king,
he rushed in great fury toward Droṇa, who had reached the further shore of the science of archery and weapons.
As he was rushing forward swiftly, the powerful Bhāradvāja,
the destroyer of enemies, became enraged and cut his bow with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
He then dispatched hundreds of other arrows at the son of Pṛṣata.
Remembering the debt he owed his master for the sake of Duryodhana’s welfare, the son of Pṛṣata,
the slayer of enemy heroes, then took up another bow and pierced Droṇa with seventy gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone.
Droṇa, the crusher of enemies, once again cut his bow,
and with four excellent arrows, he swiftly dispatched his four horses to the terrible abode of Vaivasvata. The valiant one sent them to the realm of Death.
And with a broad-headed arrow, he dispatched his charioteer to death;
O King, that twice-born one indeed sent him to the city of Dharmarāja.
Then, quickly leaping down from that chariot whose horses were slain, that great car-warrior—
The mighty-armed one ascended the great chariot of Abhimanyu;
then, while Bhīmasena looked on and the son of Pṛṣata looked on, the entire army, with its chariots, elephants, and horses, trembled.
Seeing that army shattered by Droṇa of immeasurable splendor,
all those great chariot-warriors were unable to restrain it;
indeed, that host was being slaughtered by Droṇa with his sharpened arrows.
It wandered here and there like an ocean being agitated;
and seeing that army thus, your forces rejoiced,
as they beheld the Preceptor enraged, consuming the enemy host.
"O Bhārata, the warriors on all sides cried out, 'Excellent! Excellent!
Sañjaya said:
"Then King Duryodhana, having regained his composure from that delusion,"
With showers of arrows, he again warded off the unshakable Bhīma;
then once more, your sons, those great car-warriors,
having united and assembled in battle, exerted themselves to fight Bhīma.

Bhimasena also, having regained his own chariot in the battle, the mighty-armed one mounted it and proceeded toward where your son was. Grasping his firm bow of great velocity, which brings about the end of enemies, he advanced.
With his variegated bow in battle, he pierced your sons with arrows.
Then King Duryodhana struck the mighty Bhīmasena deeply in his vital organs with an exceedingly sharp iron shaft (nārāca).
Deeply pierced by your son, the great archer,
his eyes bloodshot with rage, he drew his bow with force and struck Duryodhana in the arms and chest with three arrows.
Though struck in such a manner, that king did not waver, like the king of mountains.
Seeing those two enraged in battle, striking one another,
all the heroic younger brothers of Duryodhana, having renounced their lives, [rushed forward].
Recalling their previous counsel regarding the subjugation of that one of terrible deeds,
and having made a firm resolve in their minds to capture him, they set out to seize him.
As they were rushing toward him in battle, the exceedingly powerful Bhīmasena—
O great king, like an elephant advancing against rival elephants,
he rushed forward; and the radiant and highly illustrious one, filled with intense wrath, struck your son Citrasena with a steel shaft, O great king.
Likewise, O Bhārata, he struck your other sons in battle with various kinds of gold-feathered arrows of great velocity. Then,
having stationed his own troops in their respective positions throughout the field of battle, he remained there.
Those twelve great car-warriors, headed by Abhimanyu,
dispatched by Dharmarāja as followers in the footsteps of Bhīmasena,
advanced against your mighty sons, O great king.
Having seen those heroes standing in their chariots, possessing splendor equal to the sun and fire— all of them great archers, radiant and endowed with glory,
shining in that great battle, resplendent in their golden armor—
In that battle, your mighty sons abandoned Bhīma; however,
the son of Kuntī could not endure that they had fled while still alive,
and pursuing them all once more, he afflicted your sons.
Then, seeing Abhimanyu engaged in battle with Bhīmasena and the son of Pṛṣata (Dhṛṣṭadyumna), the great car-warriors in your army—
the Kekayas and the sons of Draupadī— [rushed forward].
Seeing them in battle, Duryodhana and the others, filled with rage and grasping their bows,
rushed forward on extremely swift horses to where those chariots were.
Then, O King, in the afternoon, a great battle commenced between your powerful warriors and those of the enemy, O Bhārata. Abhimanyu, having slain Vikarṇa’s horses of great speed, [proceeded].
Then he struck him with twenty-five small arrows.
But the great chariot-warrior Vikarṇa, abandoning his chariot whose horses had been slain,
ascended, O King, the radiant chariot of Citrasena.

O Bhārata, while those two brothers, the enhancers of the Kuru race, were stationed upon a single chariot, the son of Arjuna covered them with a net of arrows. Then Durjaya and Vikarṇa struck the son of Kṛṣṇa with five iron shafts.
They both pierced him, yet the son of Kṛṣṇa did not waver, remaining as immovable as Mount Meru.
But Duḥśāsana, O noble king, fought against the five Kekayas in that battle; O Indra among kings, it was like a marvel.
The sons of Draupadī, enraged in battle, held back Duryodhana;
O lord of the people, each one of them struck your son with three arrows.
Your son, too, who was difficult to vanquish, [struck] the sons of Draupadī in the battle.
O King, he struck them individually with sharpened arrows;
and pierced by them and drenched in blood, he shone like a mountain with mineral-rich mountain springs.
O King, the powerful Bhīṣma also, like a herdsman driving his flocks, drove back the army of the Pāṇḍavas in battle. Then, O lord of the people, the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow resounded.
To the right of Varūthinī, as Pārtha was slaughtering his enemies,
headless trunks (kabandhas) rose up on all sides there in the battle,
O Bhārata, among the armies of both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
With chariots for whirlpools, elephants for islands, and horses for waves, those tigers among men crossed the ocean of the army, which had blood for its water, by means of chariots as their boats.
Those best of men were seen with severed arms, stripped of armor, and deprived of their bodies.
There they were seen fallen by the hundreds and thousands—
slain elephants in rut, drenched in streams of blood;
O best of the Bharatas, the earth shone as if covered with mountains.
There, O Bhārata, we beheld a marvel among both you and them;
there was not a single man there who did not desire to fight.
Thus did those heroes battle, seeking great glory.
Your men, together with the Pāṇḍavas, were longing for victory in battle.
Sañjaya said:
Then King Duryodhana [beheld] the sun turning red.
Eager for battle and desiring to slay Bhīma, he rushed forward.
Beholding that hero among men, his firm adversary, approaching,
Bhīmasena, greatly incensed, spoke these words.
This very moment has arrived, long desired for many years;
today I shall slay you, if you do not abandon the field of battle.
Today I shall [avert] Kuntī’s suffering and her entire exile in the forest.

"When you are slain, I shall dispel the suffering of Draupadī. O son of Gāndhārī, behold this calamity that has come upon you for that sin of yours, in that you, having become a gambler, treated the Pāṇḍavas with contempt."
Having previously ascertained the opinion of Karṇa and the son of Subala,
you disregarded the Pāṇḍavas out of desire and acted according to your own will; and out of delusion, you insulted the descendant of Daśārha when he was entreating you.
Since you joyfully gave the command to Ulūka,
today I shall slay you along with your followers and kinsmen;
I will settle that sin which you committed in the past.
Having spoken thus, he repeatedly drew and whirled his formidable bow;
then, seizing terrible arrows with the brilliance of great thunderbolts,
he furiously and swiftly released twenty-six of them at Suyodhana.
Resembling blazing crests of fire, like thunderbolts, and flying straight,
he then pierced his bow with two arrows and his charioteer with two;
with four more, he sent the swift horses to the abode of Yama.
With two well-aimed arrows,
the crusher of foes severed the king’s parasol from his excellent chariot in that battle;
and with three more, he cut down his blazing, supreme standard.
With three other arrows, that great archer likewise cut down his banner;
having severed it, he roared loudly while your son looked on.
And that glorious banner, adorned with various jewels, fell from the chariot.
All the kings beheld the severed banner of the Kuru lord— a beautiful, jewel-encrusted elephant, blazing like the sun— suddenly falling to the earth like lightning from a cloud.
Then, in that battle, the great car-warrior Bhīma, as if smiling, struck him with ten arrows, like goads used for a mighty elephant. Thus struck,
that king, the great car-warrior, remained as if smiling.
Then Jayadratha, the king of the Sindhus and the best of chariot-warriors,
took up the rear-guard position of Duryodhana, as is fitting for a virtuous man;
and Kṛpa, the foremost of car-warriors, [protected] the Kaurava of immeasurable splendor.
O King, he placed the indignant Duryodhana upon the chariot.
Deeply pierced and pained by Bhīmasena in that battle,
King Duryodhana then sank down upon the seat of the chariot.
Then Jayadratha, desiring to kill Bhīma,
surrounded him and blocked all directions with many thousands of chariots,
O King; at that time, Dhṛṣṭaketu and the heroic Abhimanyu [also advanced].
The Kekayas and the sons of Draupadī fought against your sons—
Citrasena, Sucitra, Citrāśva, Citradarśana,
Cārucitra, Sucāru, as well as Nanda and Upanandaka.
O King, these eight illustrious and delicate masters of great bows surrounded Abhimanyu’s chariot on all sides; thereupon,
the high-minded Abhimanyu swiftly struck them.
Having pierced each one with five straight-knotted arrows— arrows resembling the thunderbolt or Death itself, discharged from his variegated weapons—
all of them, unable to endure it, [assailed] the son of Subhadrā, that best of chariot-warriors.
They rained down sharp arrows upon him, like clouds showering Mount Meru;
being thus afflicted in battle, O Great King, Abhimanyu— skilled in weapons and fierce in combat— made your troops tremble.

O Bhārata, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt [Indra] struck down the great Asuras in the war between the gods and Asuras, that best of chariot-warriors then dispatched fourteen terrible broad-headed arrows, resembling venomous serpents, at Vikarṇa.
That valiant one caused him to fall from his chariot; having severed Vikarṇa’s banner, charioteer, and horses as if dancing in the fray,
he again discharged other yellow arrows with unblunted tips, sharpened on stone.
The mighty son of Subhadrā dispatched [arrows] against Vikarṇa.
Reaching Vikarṇa, those arrows, fletched with the feathers of herons and peacocks,
pierced his body and entered the earth like blazing serpents.
Those arrows with golden shafts and tips were seen upon the surface of the earth,
drenched in Vikarṇa’s blood as if vomiting gore.
Beholding Vikarṇa thus pierced through, his other brothers...
In that battle, they rushed against the chariot-warriors headed by the son of Subhadrā; having swiftly approached those warriors standing in their chariots, who were as radiant as the sun, those men—
furious and intoxicated with the pride of war— pierced one another in the encounter.
Durmukha, having pierced Śrutakarman with seven swift arrows,
cut down his standard with one and struck his charioteer with seven.
[He also struck] the horses, which were covered with nets of gold and possessed the speed of the wind.
Having approached him, he struck him with six arrows and felled his charioteer.
Standing on that chariot whose horses had been slain, the great car-warrior Śrutakarman,
filled with rage, hurled a spear that was like a blazing great meteor.
Having pierced the massive armor of the illustrious Durmukha and torn through it,
that brilliantly sharpened arrow entered the earth, blazing with light.
O Lord, Durmukha, overwhelmed there, sank down upon his chariot.
Seeing him unconscious, all those brothers surrounded him.
Seeing him there deprived of his chariot, the mighty Sutasoma,
while all the troops looked on, placed him upon his own chariot.

O King, the heroic Śrutakīrti likewise advanced in battle against your son Jayatsena, desiring to slay that illustrious one. As the high-souled Śrutakīrti was drawing his bow, [the arrows] of that great-souled one...
O King, O Bhārata, Jayatsena, your son, as if laughing, severed it in battle with a very sharp razor-headed arrow. Seeing his brother’s bow thus cut, Śatānīka—
The radiant hero, roaring repeatedly like a lion, charged forward; meanwhile,
Śatānīka, having firmly drawn his bow in battle,
let out a tremendous roar like an elephant in rut.
He quickly pierced Jayatsena with ten stone-tipped arrows; then,
with another exceedingly sharp shaft capable of piercing all armor, Śatānīka struck Jayatsena deeply in the heart.
While that was occurring, Duṣkarṇa, beside his brother,
released at him sharp, whetted arrows resembling venomous serpents; then,
overcome with rage, he severed the bow of Nākuli in the encounter.
Then, taking up another supreme bow capable of bearing a great burden, the mighty Śatānīka took up sharp arrows and,
standing before his brother, addressed Duṣkarṇa, saying, "Stay! Stay!"
He released sharpened arrows that blazed like serpents.
Then, O noble one, he swiftly cut off his bow with one arrow, his charioteer with two,
and pierced him himself with seven in that battle.
Free from all stain, he swiftly struck all twelve of his horses, which were as swift as thought and dappled in color, with twelve sharpened arrows.
Then, with another well-aimed, falling broad-headed shaft, he struck him down.
Enraged in battle, he pierced Duṣkarṇa deeply in the heart;
he then fell to the ground like a tree shattered by a thunderbolt. Distraught, your son sat down upon the seat of his chariot.
O King, seeing Duṣkarṇa slain, five great car-warriors,
desiring to kill Śatānīka, surrounded him on all sides.
The illustrious Śatānīka was being covered by volleys of arrows.
The five Kekaya brothers, enraged, rushed forward.
Seeing them charging, O great king, your sons, those great car-warriors,
went out to meet them like elephants meeting great elephants.
Durmukha, Durjaya, the youthful Durmarṣaṇa, Śatruñjaya, and Śatrusaha— all illustrious and enraged—
advanced together against the Kekayas, O great king, along with their brothers.
On chariots resembling cities, yoked with horses swift as thought and adorned with banners of various brilliant colors,
the heroes stood, wielding excellent bows and bearing diverse armor and standards.

They entered the enemy army like lions moving from one forest to another. A most tumultuous and exceedingly fierce battle took place among them as they struck one another down, with chariots and elephants entangled in combat.
O King, having committed offenses against one another, they waged a most terrible battle that increased the population of Yama’s realm when the sun had set for a mere moment;
chariot-warriors and horsemen alike were scattered by the thousands.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, filled with rage, destroyed the army of those high-souled ones with straight-jointed arrows;
he sent the troops of the Pāñcālas to the abode of Yama with his shafts.

Having thus broken the army of the Pāṇḍavas, O King, that great archer, having ordered the withdrawal of his troops, went to his own camp. The two heroes, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Vṛkodara, caused [the enemy] to be destroyed.
Having struck down the armies of the Kauravas with his straight-jointed arrows,
Dharmarāja, seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Vṛkodara,
joyfully embraced them by their heads and departed for the camp.
Arjuna and Vāsudeva, having struck down and routed the army of the Kauravas with their arrows, proceeded toward the camp. Sañjaya said:

Then, O Great King, those heroes, having committed offenses against one another and being drenched in blood, returned to their own camps. Having rested according to custom and honored one another, they remained there.
They were seen once more, fully armored and desiring further combat. Then, O King, your son, overwhelmed by anxiety and his limbs smeared with flowing blood, questioned his grandfather thus:
Having torn asunder, slain, and crushed the fierce and terrifying armies, which were properly arrayed and possessed many banners, those heroes—
Those illustrious and swift throngs of chariots belonging to the Pāṇḍavas, having confounded everyone in battle,
shattered that Makara array which was like a thunderbolt.
Having entered, I was struck down by Bhīma with terrible arrows resembling the staff of Death;
O King, beholding him enraged, I was overcome with fear.
Faint with exhaustion, I have not found peace today;
O you who are true to your promise, through your grace I desire to obtain victory and slay the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Thus addressed by him, the high-souled and wise one, perceiving that Duryodhana was filled with wrath, replied to him with a smile and an undisturbed mind.
O prince, the son of Gaṅgā, the best among weapon-bearers,
having penetrated your army with supreme effort and with all his soul, [stands ready for you].
"I wish to grant you victory and happiness;
I do not conceal myself for your sake.
However, these many fierce great chariot-warriors—"
Those illustrious and most heroic masters of weapons,
who are the allies of the Pāṇḍavas in battle,
having overcome all fatigue, vomit forth the poison of their wrath.
They cannot be conquered here by force, for they are bristling with prowess and have been made your enemies; however,
O King, I myself shall fight against them.
O hero of great majesty, having surrendered my life entirely for your sake in battle today,
my life is no longer to be protected by me.
"For your sake, O King, I could burn all the worlds, including the gods and the Daityas; how much more so your enemies here? Therefore, I shall fight against the Pāṇḍavas."
"And I shall do everything that is pleasing to you.
Upon hearing this, Duryodhana became supremely confident and his mind was filled with joy.
Then, being greatly delighted, he said to all the armies and all the kings, "March forth!
At his command, they quickly set out.
O King, those vast hosts, consisting of tens of thousands of chariots, horses, infantry, and elephants, were filled with great joy and equipped with various kinds of weapons.
O King, your forces— consisting of elephants, horses, and infantry— stood arrayed and shone resplendent in battle,
stationed in well-ordered groups.
O god among men, your troops shone on all sides, presided over by warriors skilled in the use of hand-to-hand weapons and missiles.
By the chariots and the throngs of infantry, elephants,
and horses setting out for battle as prescribed by rule,
a dust was raised that had the color of the rising sun.
Dust shone forth, obscuring the rays of the sun;
banners mounted on chariots and elephants gleamed as they were tossed and whirled about on all sides by the wind.
O King, in that battle, the bows of the monarchs as they drew them were of various colors,
just like flashes of lightning amidst clouds in the sky.
A tumultuous and most terrible sound arose from the gods and the great hosts of asuras as they were being churned,
just like that of the ocean at the beginning of the age.
That army of yours, with its fierce roar and many forms and colors, having thus risen up,
became the destroyer of the enemy host.

Resembling a mass of clouds at the end of an eon, Sañjaya then spoke again to your son, who was absorbed in meditation: Sañjaya said: "Then the son of Gaṅgā addressed your son once more as he remained in deep reflection."
The best of the Bharatas spoke these words, which caused great joy:
"I, Droṇa, Śalya, Kṛtavarman the Sātvata,
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, Somadatta, and the ruler of the Sindhus— "
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, Bāhlika with the Bāhlikas,
the powerful king of Trigarta, and the invincible king of Magadha;
Bṛhadbala of Kosala, Citrasena, and Vivimśati.
O King, Kṛpa was there along with his uterine brothers as your footmen;
and many thousands of chariots, resplendent with great banners,
were present, as were horses of noble breed, O King, well-mounted by their riders.
And lordly elephants, agitated by rut with temples and faces streaming ichor, as well as heroic foot-soldiers equipped with various weapons and missiles,
born in various lands, are prepared to fight for your sake.
"These and many others have risked their lives for your sake;
it is my conviction that they are capable of conquering even the gods in battle.
Yet, O King, I must certainly always speak what is beneficial to you."
The Pāṇḍavas cannot be conquered even by the gods led by Vāsava;
for they have Vāsudeva as their ally and possess prowess equal to that of Mahendra.
Nevertheless, O Indra among kings, I shall carry out your command in every way.

"Either I shall defeat the Pāṇḍavas in battle, or the Pāṇḍavas shall defeat me. Having spoken thus, he gave him a beautiful, potent medicinal herb called Viśalyakaraṇī; and by it, he then became free from his arrows.
Then, at the clear dawn,
the heroic Bhīṣma, skilled in the art of arraying troops, himself formed a circular formation (*maṇḍala*) with his own army,
O best of men, crowded with various weapons.
It was filled with chief warriors,
as well as elephant-riders and infantry, and surrounded on all sides by many thousands of chariots and great throngs of horses bearing spears and lances.
For every elephant there were seven chariots, and for every chariot seven horses;
following each horse were ten archers, and for every archer seven shield-bearers. Thus, O great king, was your army arrayed by the great car-warriors.
Stationed for a great battle and protected by Bhīṣma in the fray were ten thousand horses, as many elephants,
ten thousand chariots, and your sons, all clad in armor.
The heroes headed by Citrasena protected the Grandfather;
and being protected by those heroes, while they in turn protected him,
those mighty kings were seen standing ready for battle, clad in their armor.
But Duryodhana, armored and mounted upon his chariot in the battle,
shone with splendor like Śakra in Triviṣṭapa.
Then, O Bhārata, a great roar arose from your sons.
The tumultuous roar of chariots and the sound of musical instruments arose as Bhīṣma arrayed the Dhārtarāṣṭra forces in battle facing westward;
it was a vast circular formation, impenetrable for those who strike down their enemies.
O King, he who was difficult for enemies to approach shone brilliantly on all sides in battle.
Beholding that most formidable circular array (*maṇḍala-vyūha*),
King Yudhiṣṭhira himself then formed the thunderbolt array (*vajra-vyūha*).
When the armies had been thus arrayed and the chariot-warriors and horsemen were stationed in their respective places, they let out a lion’s roar;
then, desiring battle and wishing to break through the formation, they marched forth.
Brave warriors, striking with their armies, advanced against one another: the son of Bharadvāja went against the Matsya king, and the son of Droṇa against Śikhaṇḍin;
King Duryodhana himself rushed against the son of Pṛṣata.
O King, Nakula and Sahadeva advanced against the Lord of Madra;
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti rushed against Irāvat;
and all the kings fought Dhananjaya in the battle.
Bhīmasena, exerting himself in battle, held back the son of Hṛdika;
and the son of Arjuna, O King, fought against Citrasena, Vikarṇa, and Durmarṣaṇa— your sons— in the encounter, O Lord.

O King, the son of Hiḍimbā, that best of Rākṣasas, rushed with speed toward the great archer of Prāgjyotiṣa, like one rutting elephant charging another. Then Alambuṣa [rushed] at Sātyaki, who is fierce in battle.
Enraged in battle, the Rākṣasa rushed toward him along with his army;
Bhūriśravas, exerting himself in the fray, fought Dhṛṣṭaketu,
while Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, confronted King Śrutāyus.
Cekitāna, however, engaged Kṛpa alone in battle;
the rest, exerting themselves, advanced against the great car-warrior Bhīma.
Then thousands of kings surrounded Dhanañjaya.
With spears, javelins, iron arrows, maces, and clubs in their hands,
Arjuna, then exceedingly enraged, spoke this to the descendant of Vṛṣṇi:
"Behold, O Mādhava, the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in this battle!"
"Behold, O Mādhava, the arrays formed by the high-souled Gāṅgeya, who is skilled in military formations; behold the armored heroes eager for battle,
O Keśava, and see the King of Trigarta together with his brothers."
"O Janārdana, today, while you look on,
I shall strike down those who stand here on the field of battle desiring to fight me, O best of the Yadus.
Having spoken thus, the son of Kuntī rubbed his bowstring.
He rained down showers of arrows upon the hosts of kings;
they too, those supreme archers, filled him with showers of arrows,
just as clouds in the rainy season fill a lake with torrents of rain.
A great cry of "Alas! arose in your army, O lord of the people, upon seeing the two Kṛṣṇas being heavily covered with arrows in that great battle;
so too did the gods, the celestial sages, the Gandharvas, and the great serpents.
Seeing the two Kṛṣṇas arrived in such a state, they were struck with supreme wonder.
Then, O King, the enraged Arjuna invoked the Aindra weapon;
there we beheld the marvelous prowess of Vijaya.
O lord of the people, when he warded off the rain of weapons discharged by his enemies with floods of arrows, not a single person there remained unpierced;
such was the case among those thousands of kings, as well as their horses and elephants.
O noble one, Pārtha pierced others with two, three, or five arrows;
being struck by Pārtha, they fled toward Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu.
Then Bhīṣma became the protector of those who were sinking into the bottomless depths.
As they fell upon them there, O great king, your army was shattered and agitated like the great ocean by the winds. Sañjaya said:
When the battle had thus proceeded and Suśarman had retreated,
and when the heroes were broken by the high-souled Pāṇḍava,
your army— resembling the ocean— was quickly thrown into agitation.
When the son of Gaṅgā had advanced swiftly toward Vijaya,
O King, Duryodhana beheld Pārtha’s prowess in battle;
hurrying forward, he approached all those kings and spoke to them.
And at their head stood the heroic and mighty Suśarman;
standing in the midst of the entire army, he spoke these words to greatly encourage them:
"Here is Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, desirous of fighting with Dhanañjaya."
"O best of the Kurus, having renounced your own life with all your soul,
that descendant of Bharata is advancing against the enemy host with his entire army;
all of you, being prepared for battle, protect your grandfather."
Having said, "So be it," O Great King, all those armies of the lords of men gathered around the Grandfather from every side.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, suddenly advanced against Arjuna.
In battle, he encountered the mighty descendant of Bharata as he approached,
resplendent upon a great chariot that thundered like a cloud, yoked with magnificent white horses and bearing the formidable ape-banner.
When Dhananjaya approached all the troops in battle,
a tumultuous roar arose upon seeing Kiritin;
and seeing Krishna with the reins in his hand, like a second sun.
In that battle,

they were unable to look upon him who had reached the meridian; likewise, the Pāṇḍavas were unable to gaze upon Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, with his white horses and white bow, like the risen white planet [Venus].
Surrounded on all sides by the high-souled Trigartas,
by your sons, by his brothers, and by other great car-warriors,
the son of Bharadvāja, however, pierced the King of Matsya in battle with a feathered shaft.
With one arrow he cut down his banner in battle, and with another he severed his bow.
Casting aside that broken bow, Virāṭa, the commander of the army,
swiftly took up another firm bow capable of bearing a great strain.
With arrows resembling venomous serpents, blazing like hissing snakes,
he pierced Droṇa with three, his horses with four,
his standard with one, and his charioteer with five.

He pierced Dhanu with a single arrow, and thereupon that bull among the twice-born grew angry. O best of the Bharatas, Droṇa slew his horses with eight straight-knotted arrows and his charioteer with a single feathered shaft.
Leaping down from his chariot whose horses had been slain and whose charioteer was killed,
that best of car-warriors quickly mounted the chariot of Śaṅkha.
Then those two, father and son, stood upon the chariot of Bhāradvāja.
With a great shower of arrows, the two of them forcibly warded him off.
Then, O lord of men, the son of Bharadvāja, enraged in that battle, swiftly discharged an arrow resembling a venomous serpent toward Śaṅkha.
Having pierced his heart and drunk his blood in the battle,
that arrow, its surface drenched in gore, entered the earth;
struck by the shaft of Bhāradvāja, he fell swiftly from his chariot.
Casting aside his bow and arrows right before his father,
Virāṭa fled in fear upon seeing his own son slain,
abandoning Droṇa in the midst of battle as he stood like Death with a gaping maw.
Then Bhāradvāja swiftly tore apart the great army of the Pāṇḍavas in battle by the hundreds and thousands;
and Śikhaṇḍin also, O Great King, having encountered the son of Droṇa in the encounter—
He struck him between the eyebrows with three swift iron arrows;
that tiger among men shone with those three lodged in his forehead,
like Mount Meru with its three lofty golden peaks.
Then, O King, the enraged Aśvatthāman, within half a blink of an eye, struck Śikhaṇḍin’s charioteer, standard, horses,
and weapons with many arrows in that battle, felling them all.
Leaping down from his chariot whose horses had been slain, that best of car-warriors, Śikhaṇḍin— the scorcher of his enemies— took up a sharp, stainless sword and a shield,
and moved about in fury like a hawk.
O Great King, as he moved about in the battle with his sword, the son of Droṇa could find no opening; it was like a marvel.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, he [discharged] many thousands of arrows.
The son of Droṇa, exceedingly enraged,
dispatched that most terrible shower of arrows in battle; but the best among the strong cut down that oncoming rain of shafts with his sharp-edged sword.
Then, O King, the son of Droṇa cut through his spotless, beautiful shield adorned with a hundred moons,
shattered his sword in the encounter,
and pierced him repeatedly with many sharp feathered arrows.

Then Śikhaṇḍin, having whirled that sword which had been shattered by those arrows, swiftly hurled it like a blazing serpent. As it came rushing suddenly, possessing a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction—
In that battle, the son of Droṇa, displaying his lightness of hand,
cut [the weapons] asunder and pierced Śikhaṇḍin with many iron arrows.
But Śikhaṇḍin, O King, was severely struck by those sharp shafts.
He quickly ascended the chariot of the high-souled Mādhava. Then the powerful Sātyaki, enraged in battle, pierced the fierce and mighty Rākṣasa Alambuṣa with terrible arrows.
Then, O Bhārata, the lord of the Rākṣasas cut his bow with a crescent-shaped arrow in that battle and pierced him with shafts;
having employed his Rākṣasa illusion, he overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.
Then, taking up another supreme bow capable of bearing a great weight,
we beheld there the wonderful prowess of Śini’s grandson;
for even while being struck by sharp arrows in battle, he did not falter.
And the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, O Bhārata, employed the Aindra weapon,
which the illustrious Mādhava had obtained from Vijaya;
having reduced that Rākṣasa illusion to ashes with that weapon, he then [proceeded].
With terrible arrows, he overwhelmed Alambusa from all sides,
just as a cloud in the rainy season drenches a mountain with torrents of water.
Thus was he tormented by that high-souled Mādhava.
The Rākṣasa fled in fear, abandoning Sātyaki in the battle;
having conquered that lord of Rākṣasas, who was invincible in combat even for Maghavan himself,
the descendant of Śini let out a roar while your warriors looked on.
Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth, also struck down your men with many sharpened arrows; afflicted by fear, they fled.
At that very moment, however, the powerful son of Drupada [arrived].
O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna covered your son, the lord of men,
in battle with straight-jointed arrows. Being thus shrouded by the shafts of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O Bhārata...
Yet your son, O Indra among kings, lord of men, did not waver; instead,
he quickly pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle with sixty and thirty arrows, which was truly like a marvel.
O noble one, his commander-in-chief, a great car-warrior, became enraged and severed his bow;
he swiftly struck down his four horses and quickly pierced him with seven well-sharpened arrows.
His horses having been slain, the mighty and long-armed one leaped down from his chariot;
raising his sword, he rushed on foot toward the son of Pṛṣata. Śakuni, possessed of great strength and intent on capturing the king, approached him.
He caused the king of all the world to mount his own chariot;
then, having defeated the monarch, the son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of enemy heroes,
began to strike down your army like the wielder of the thunderbolt against the asuras.
In that battle, Kṛtavarman struck the great car-warrior Bhīma with arrows and completely shrouded him,
just as a massive cloud obscures the sun.
Then, laughing in the midst of the fray, Bhīmasena, the scorcher of foes—
Enraged, he dispatched arrows at Kṛtavarman; though afflicted by them, O Great King, that Atiratha of the Sātvatas, skilled in weapons,
did not waver, but struck Bhīma with sharp shafts.
Having slain his four horses, the mighty Bhīmasena struck down the charioteer and the well-adorned banner;
then that slayer of enemy heroes covered him with various kinds of arrows.
With all his limbs mangled like a porcupine, he appeared as such;
then, quickly leaping from his chariot whose horses had been slain, he fled to the chariot of Vṛṣaka,
O great king, while your son— the brother-in-law— looked on.
Bhīmasena, also filled with rage, rushed against your army;
and, enraged, he struck them down like Death himself with staff in hand.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, I have heard from your speech of many diverse single combats here between the Pāṇḍavas and my own men;
yet you do not mention even one of my men who was bold."
"O Sūta, you always report the sons of Pāṇḍu as joyful and unbroken,
while you speak of my men as being defeated, dejected, and deprived of their vigor in battle; this is undoubtedly destiny."
Saṃjaya said:
O bull among men, your warriors are striving in battle according to their strength and according to their energy, displaying the utmost manliness they possess.
Just as the water of the Gaṅgā, that divine river, though naturally sweet,
acquires salinity through contact with the qualities of the great ocean,
even so, O King, was the prowess of those high-souled men on your side.

Having encountered the heroic sons of Pāṇḍu, who are striving to the best of their ability and performing difficult deeds in battle, it becomes futile [for you]. O best of the Kurus, you ought not to blame the Kauravas for this.

"O lord of people, this great and terrible destruction of the earth, which increases the realm of Yama, has arisen from your own transgression along with that of your sons. O King, you ought not to grieve over what has been produced by your own fault."
For kings do not protect all their possessions, nor even their own lives;
desiring the worlds of the righteous after battle, these lords of the earth always plunge into the army and fight, intent upon heaven.

In the forenoon, O Great King, the destruction of men began; listen to that account, which resembles the battle between the gods and the asuras, with a focused mind. The two princes of Avanti were great bowmen, high-souled, and possessed of great strength.
Beholding Irāvant, those two fierce warriors in battle drew near;
a tumultuous and hair-raising combat then ensued between them. But Irāvant, highly incensed, [encountered] his two brothers who possessed the forms of gods.
He quickly pierced them with sharp, straight-knotted arrows;
those two, who fought with wonderful skill, pierced him in return in that battle. O King, as they thus fought, no distinction could be seen between them.
For those striving to destroy their enemies and seeking retaliation for injuries received,
O King, Irāvat then, with four arrows, sent Anuvinda’s four horses to the abode of Yama.

O noble one, with two extremely sharp bhalla-arrows, he cut down both the bow and the standard in that battle, O King; it was like a marvel. Then Anuvinda, abandoning his own chariot, mounted the chariot of Vinda.
Taking up their ninth bow, the supreme instrument for achieving great feats,
those two heroic princes of Avanti, the best among chariot-warriors, stood together on the battlefield and swiftly loosed arrows at the high-souled Irāvat.
Released by those two, arrows of great velocity adorned with gold reached the path of the sun and covered the sky.
Then Irāvat, filled with rage, [attacked] those two brothers, the great chariot-warriors.
He rained down a shower of arrows and struck down the charioteer as well. When that charioteer had fallen upon the earth, deprived of life,
the chariot then fled in all directions with its horses wandering in confusion.

O great king, having defeated those two, the son of the daughter of the Naga king quickly scattered your army, proclaiming his own prowess. That great host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons was being slaughtered in battle.
Like a man who has drunk poison, he manifested various kinds of impetuous movements;
then the mighty son of Hiḍimbā, the lord of the Rākṣasas, rushed toward Bhagadatta on a chariot as bright as the sun and adorned with a banner.
Then the King of Prāgjyotiṣa, mounted upon the king of elephants,
appeared like the wielder of the thunderbolt in the former battle against Tāraka;
there the gods, along with the Gandharvas and the ṛṣis, had assembled.
They could perceive no difference between the son of Hiḍimbā and Bhagadatta;
just as Śakra, the lord of the gods, struck terror into the Dānavas,
even so, O King, did he strike terror into the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
Being routed by him in every direction, O Bhārata, those Pāṇḍavas could find no protector among their own ranks. But there,
O Bhārata, we beheld the son of Bhīmasena standing upon his chariot.

The remaining great car-warriors, becoming despondent, fled away. But when the armies of the Pāṇḍavas had turned back again, O Bhārata, those best of the Bharatas resolved their minds upon the ultimate goal and set their hearts on heaven.
A terrible clamor arose among your troops in that battle.
Then, O King, in that great conflict, Ghaṭotkaca covered Bhagadatta with arrows,
just as a cloud covers Mount Meru.
Having struck down those arrows discharged from the Rākṣasa’s bow,
the king swiftly struck the son of Bhīmasena in all his vital parts on the battlefield.
Being thus struck by many straight-knotted arrows, he...
The lord of the Rākṣasas did not tremble, like a mountain being split asunder. Enraged, the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa hurled fourteen lances at him in battle, but the Rākṣasa cut them all down.
Having cut those lances with sharp arrows, the mighty-armed one pierced Bhagadatta with seventy heron-feathered shafts.
Then, O King, descendant of Bharata, the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa, as if laughing, [attacked].

In that battle, he struck down his four horses with arrows. Standing on his chariot whose horses had been slain, the powerful lord of the Rākṣasas hurled a spear with great force toward the elephant of the king of Prāgjyotiṣa.

As that gold-staffed spear, possessing great velocity, was suddenly rushing toward him, the king cut it into three pieces; it then fell scattered upon the earth. Seeing his spear destroyed, the son of Hiḍimbā fled in fear.
Just as in former times Namuci, the best of the Daityas, [fought] Indra in battle—
having conquered that hero, who was valiant, renowned for his prowess,
and invincible in combat even by Yama and Varuṇa, O King.

Accompanied by his elephant, he crushed the Pāṇḍava army in battle, O King, just as a wild elephant roams about trampling a lotus pond. Meanwhile, the Lord of Madra engaged in combat with the two sons of Yama.
With floods of arrows, he shielded his two sister's sons, the two sons of Pāṇḍu.
But Sahadeva, beholding his maternal uncle standing together in battle,
warded him off with a shower of arrows, just as a cloud obscures the sun.
Being covered by that shower of arrows, he became even more joyful;
and between the two of them, there arose an incomparable affection on account of their mother.
Then, laughing in the midst of battle, the great chariot-warrior [Śakuni]—
O noble one, with one arrow he cut down his banner and with another his bow;
then, O Bhārata, as if covering him who was now bowless,
he struck him in battle and felled his charioteer.
O King, with four excellent arrows, he dispatched the four horses toward the abode of Yama in that battle. Then, leaping quickly from the chariot whose horses had been slain, the great car-warrior—
Then he ascended the chariot of his illustrious brother. Standing together as two heroes on a single vehicle, they drew their firm bows and,
filled with rage, covered the chariot of the King of Madra in an instant.
Though covered by many straight-jointed arrows from his two sister’s sons, that tiger among men did not tremble, remaining as steady as a mountain; rather,
as if smiling, he struck down that shower of shafts.
Discharging thousands of arrows as if laughing,
he hemmed them in in battle, just as a cloud obstructs a mountain with rain.
Then the valiant Sahadeva, filled with rage, raised his arrow.
O Bhārata, having sighted the King of Madra, he dispatched [the arrow];
that arrow, released by him, swift as Garuḍa,
pierced through the King of Madra and fell upon the surface of the earth.
Deeply pierced and pained, that great car-warrior sat down on the floor of his chariot, O great king, and fell into a swoon. Seeing him fallen and unconscious in the battle, the charioteer [acted].
He carried away with his chariot in battle him who was being hard-pressed by the twins;
seeing the chariot of the lord of the Madras turned away, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra became despondent and thought, "This [war] is no more."
Having defeated their maternal uncle in battle, the two sons of Mādrī, those great car-warriors, joyfully blew their conchs and let out lion-like roars; then,
O lord of the people, they cheerfully charged against your army.
"O King, like the two immortals Indra and Upendra [against] the army of the Daityas.
Sañjaya said:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, when the sun had reached the meridian, [proceeded].
Beholding Śrutāyus, he urged on his horses;
then the king rushed toward Śrutāyus, the subduer of enemies,
striking him with nine sharp, straight-knotted arrows.

Having warded off those arrows dispatched by the son of Dharma in battle, that great archer, the king, struck back at the son of Kuntī with seven shafts. Piercing his armor, they drank his blood in the combat.
Searching through the body of that high-souled one as if for his very life-breaths,
the Pāṇḍava,
though severely pierced by that great king with the *varāhakarṇa* shaft in battle, struck the king in the heart.

Then, with another broad-headed arrow, Pārtha, the best of chariot-warriors, swiftly struck down the standard of that great-souled one from his chariot onto the ground. Seeing his standard fallen, King Śrutāyus—

O King, he pierced the Pāṇḍava with seven sharp arrows. Thereupon, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, blazed up in anger like the sacrificial fire at the end of an eon, as if about to consume all beings.
Seeing the Pāṇḍava enraged, O great king, the gods, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas were deeply distressed, and the entire world became agitated. This was the thought in the minds of all living beings:
"Today this king, filled with rage, will surely consume the three worlds," so saying,
the ṛṣis and the gods performed a great rite for well-being,
O King, for the sake of pacifying the worlds when the Pāṇḍava was thus provoked to anger.
Overcome by rage and licking the corners of his mouth,
he assumed a terrible form resembling the sun at the end of an eon.
Then, O lord of the people, all your troops—
O Bhārata, they there became hopeless regarding their lives. But that highly illustrious one, restraining his anger with fortitude,
severed Śrutāyus’s great bow at the handle.
Then, while the entire army looked on, the king pierced that warrior, whose bow had been severed, in the center of the chest with a steel shaft in the midst of battle. O King,
he swiftly struck down the mounts of that high-souled one in the encounter.

The exceedingly powerful [Arjuna] swiftly struck him with arrows and his charioteer as well. Seeing the king's prowess, Śrutāyus then abandoned his chariot, whose horses had been slain, and fled with great speed from the battle.
When that great archer had been defeated in battle by the son of Dharma,
O King, the entire army of Duryodhana turned its back in retreat.
Having accomplished this, O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma—
With his mouth wide open like the God of Death, he struck down your army.
Then Cekitāna of the Vṛṣṇi clan, while all the troops looked on, covered Gautama, the best of chariot-warriors, with his arrows.
Having warded off those arrows in battle, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, O King, pierced Cekitāna— who was striving in the fray— with feathered shafts;
then, with another broad-headed arrow, O noble one, he cut through his bow.
With swift hand, he struck down his charioteer in the battle;
O King, he also slew his horses and both his flank-guards. Then the Sātvata hero, quickly leaping from the chariot, seized a mace.
With that hero-slaying mace,
the best of mace-wielders killed Gautama’s horses and struck down his charioteer.
Standing on the ground, Gautama discharged sixteen arrows at him.
Those arrows, having pierced the Sātvata, entered the surface of the earth.
Then Cekitāna, enraged, again hurled that mace,
desiring the death of Gautama, just as Purandara [hurled his bolt] at Vṛtra.
As that stainless, sapphire-studded great mace came flying toward him,
Gautama warded it off with many thousands of arrows. Then, O Bhārata, Cekitāna drew his sword from its scabbard.
Resorting to extreme agility, he rushed toward Gautama.
Gautama, for his part, casting aside his bow and seizing a well-sharpened sword,
charged at Cekitāna with great speed, O King.
Both of them, endowed with great strength and wielding excellent swords,
hacked at one another with their two extremely sharp blades. Then those two bulls among men were struck by the force of each other’s swords.
They both reached the earth, which is inhabited by all living beings;
their limbs were overcome by fainting and they were rendered unconscious by the exertion. Then Karakarṣa, their friend, rushed toward them with speed.
Seeing Cekitāna in such a state, though he was fierce in battle,
[Kṛtavarman] placed him upon his chariot while the entire army looked on;
and likewise, O lord of people, your heroic brother-in-law Śakuni did the same.
He quickly placed Gautama, the best of chariot-warriors, upon his chariot;
likewise, O King, the mighty Dhṛṣṭaketu, filled with rage,
swiftly pierced the son of Somadatta in the chest with ninety arrows.
O great king, Saumadatti shone intensely with those arrows fixed in his chest,
like the sun at midday with its rays.
But Bhūriśravas, in that battle, [assailed] the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭaketu.
With his finest arrows, he deprived him of his chariot, slaying both his driver and his horses.
Seeing him thus rendered carless, with his horses and charioteer slain,
he covered him in battle with a great shower of shafts.
O noble one, having abandoned that chariot, the high-minded Dhṛṣṭaketu then ascended the vehicle of Śatānīka; and likewise,
O King, Citrasena, Vikarṇa, and Durmarṣaṇa did the same.
Chariot-warriors clad in golden armor rushed against the son of Subhadrā; then, O King,
a terrible battle took place between Abhimanyu and them,
like that of the body with the three humors— wind, bile, and phlegm.
O King, having deprived your sons of their chariots in that great battle,
that tiger among men did not slay them, remembering at that time the words of Bhīma.
Then, by hundreds of kings accompanied by elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry...
Beholding Bhīṣma— who was difficult even for the gods to approach— thus hemmed in in battle as he advanced swiftly to rescue your sons,
[the warriors] turned toward Abhimanyu, that lone great car-warrior who was but a youth.
Then the son of Kuntī, whose horses are white, spoke thus to Vāsudeva:
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, urge on the horses to where these many chariots are;
for these are numerous heroes, skilled in weapons and intoxicated with the pride of battle."
"O Mādhava, urge [the horses] in such a way that they do not strike our army.
Thus addressed by the son of Kuntī of immeasurable splendor, that descendant of Vṛṣṇi said,
"O Dhanañjaya, let us go quickly for the sake of protecting the children."
He dispatched a chariot yoked with white horses into the battle; O noble one, a great clamor arose among your troops when Arjuna, enraged in combat, advanced against your men.
Having approached those kings who were protecting Bhīṣma, O King, the son of Kuntī then addressed these words to Suśarman:
"I know you to be the foremost in battle and my most persistent enemy from former times."

Then, surrounded by many kings, you shall fight in battle; behold today the most terrible fruit that has arrived through the turn of time. Today I shall show you your ancestors who have passed away long ago.
While Bībhatsu,
the slayer of enemies, was thus speaking these harsh words, Suśarman, the leader of chariot-divisions, heard them but did not say anything to him, whether pleasant or unpleasant.

Having approached the heroic Arjuna, surrounded by many kings— encircling Arjuna on all sides, from the front, from behind, and from the flanks in that battle, O sinless one— he stood together with your sons.
With arrows he completely covered him, as clouds shroud the sun. Then, O Bhārata, a truly great battle commenced between your men and the Pāṇḍavas in that encounter, with blood for its water.
06,081.001 Saṃjaya said: 06,081.001a Being thus pierced by arrows, the mighty Dhanañjaya hissed like a snake struck by a foot.
With arrow after arrow, he forcibly severed the bows of the great chariot-warriors in battle;
having thus cut down those bows of the kings, he—
In that battle, the high-souled one simultaneously pierced those heroic warriors with his arrows in an instant,
considering them then to have been completely eliminated.
Smeared with blood, they fell in battle,
O King; struck by the son of Śakra,
their limbs were mangled and their heads fell away.
Their life-breaths departed, their armor shattered and their bodies pierced,
they fell to the earth, overcome by the power of Pārtha;
assuming various forms, they perished all at once.
Seeing those princes slain in battle,
the king of the Trigartas set out in an instant;
then, there were protectors at the rear of their chariots.
Another thirty-two descended upon Pārtha;
likewise, they surrounded Pārtha,
drawing their bows that emitted a great roar.
They rained down a great torrent of arrows, just as clouds drench a mountain with floods of water;
thus he was oppressed by that shower of arrow-storms.
Dhananjaya, his wrath kindled in battle,
struck them with sixty oil-polished arrows in the fray,
and then he also slew their rear-guards.
Having conquered those sixty chariots in battle,
the illustrious Dhanañjaya, with a joyful mind,
then urged on Jiṣṇu for the sake of slaying Bhīṣma.
Having destroyed the forces of the kings in battle,
the King of Trigarta then beheld those great car-warriors, his kinsmen, who had been slain.
Placing those lords of men at the forefront in battle,
he went swiftly toward Pārtha for his slaughter;
and as he rushed forward, [he encountered] that best among the wielders of weapons.
Beholding Dhanañjaya, those warriors led by Śikhaṇḍin,
with sharp weapons in their hands, rushed forward,
desiring to protect Arjuna’s chariot.
Pārtha, too, seeing those heroic men together with the king of the Trigartas rushing toward him,
destroyed them in battle while wielding his bow.
Desiring to advance against Bhīṣma in battle with sharp arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow, he beheld Duryodhana and the kings headed by the ruler of the Sindhus.
Having approached those who were intent on warding him off,
the hero of infinite prowess fought them with his strength for a moment and then released the king.
Then the high-spirited one of terrible strength, bow and arrows in hand, went forth against Jayadratha and the other kings,
and toward the son of Gaṅgā in battle.
Bhīṣma, too, having seen those noble chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas skilled in weapons in battle,
left Dhanañjaya at the front of the fray.
With speed he returned again toward Pārtha;
and Yudhiṣṭhira, the high-souled one of fierce strength,
arrived swiftly, filled with wrath.
Having completely abandoned the lord of the Madras in battle,
he of infinite fame,
together with the two sons of Mādrī and Bhīmasena, took his own allotted share.
He advanced for battle against Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu;
joined by those foremost of great car-warriors,
the son of Gaṅgā, a fighter of diverse skills, stood in the fray.
The high-souled son of Śantanu was not shaken,
even when all the sons of Pāṇḍu had assembled against him;
then King Yudhiṣṭhira, true to his promise, approached him in battle.
Jayadratha, possessed of exceedingly fierce strength and high spirit,
forcibly severed the bows of those great car-warriors with his own excellent bow.
Having conceived wrath in battle against Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, the twins, and likewise Pārtha,
the high-souled Duryodhana was like the poison of his own anger.
O Lord, he struck them in battle with arrows radiant as fire—
by Kṛpa, Śalya, Śala,
and likewise by Citrasena.
Just as streams of water pour down upon the king of mountains,
so do those of great majesty rain down;
they were pierced by arrows from those whose wrath had grown exceedingly fierce.
Just as the gods were [assailed] by the assembled hosts of Daityas,
so too the king, seeing Śikhaṇḍin with his weapons severed by the son of Śantanu, was filled with rage.
The high-souled Ajātaśatru, enraged in battle, spoke these words to Śikhaṇḍin:
"Having spoken thus to me in the presence of your father..."
"I shall slay that Bhīṣma of great vows with showers of arrows having the color of the stainless sun;
I speak the truth— thus was my vow made."
O hero among men, do not let your vow become false by failing to slay Devavrata in battle, so that you may make this [promise] of yours fruitful.
Protect the dharma, your lineage, and your fame;
behold Bhīṣma of terrible speed in battle,
scorching all my hosts of troops.
With nets of arrow-showers of exceeding brilliance,
he cut down his bow in an instant, like Time itself bringing about death, and became indifferent to the battle.
Defeated by King Śāntanava,
having now abandoned your kinsmen and brothers,
where will you go? This is not worthy of you.
Having seen that Bhīṣma of infinite prowess and the army thus broken and fleeing,
you must surely be afraid, O son of Drupada.
For thus is the color of your face joyless,
O hero among men, even though Dhanañjaya is being observed while the great battle is engaged.
"How is it, O hero, that you who are renowned throughout the earth, now cause fear from Bhīṣma?
Having heard these words of Dharmarāja, he [reflected].
O King, considering those harsh words and incessant reproaches as a personal insult, the high-souled one hastened toward the slaughter of Bhīṣma.
As Śikhaṇḍin was rushing toward Bhīṣma with great speed,
Śalya indeed held him back as he charged.
And he too, seeing that weapon being unleashed— terrible, exceedingly difficult to conquer, and possessing a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon— [acted].
O King, that son of Drupada, whose majesty was equal to that of Mahendra, did not lose his composure;
and that great archer remained right there.
Warding off that weapon with his arrows,
Śikhaṇḍin then took up another fierce Vāruṇa weapon to counter it.
06.081.027e The gods stationed in the sky and the kings on earth beheld that weapon being torn asunder by another weapon;
06.081.028a O King, the high-souled Bhīṣma, however, in that battle—
Having cut through the variegated bow and the standard as well, the hero roared at King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu and descendant of Ajamīḍha.
Then, casting aside his bow and arrow and beholding Yudhiṣṭhira overwhelmed by fear,
he seized a mace and rushed forward in the battle.
Bhimasena was on foot against Jayadratha;
as he rushed forward with great speed toward Bhimasena, who held his mace, Jayadratha—
He pierced him from all sides with five hundred sharp arrows, terrible as the staff of Yama;
yet that swift hero paid no heed to those shafts.
Vṛkodara, his mind overwhelmed with rage,
slew all the horses of the King of Sindhu in battle— those born in Āraṭṭa— in that conflict.
Then, beholding him, your son of incomparable prowess, hastening in his chariot,
advanced to slay Bhīmasena.
With his weapons raised, Jayadratha, who was like the king of the gods,
abandoned that chariot whose horses had been broken and went to where the king of the Kurus was.
With his mind bewildered by fear of Bhīma,
he and Saubala were terrified of the battle there;
then Bhīma suddenly let out a roar at him.
Seeing that uplifted mace,
which resembled the staff of Yama, those Kurus from all sides rushed forward, threatening him with their own maces.
Leaving behind all of them, your fierce son,
they fled from the tumultuous clash, desiring to avoid the fall of the mace.
O Bhārata, in that most terrible and bewildering moment, Citrasena, his mind undeluded,
beheld the great mace as it was descending upon him.
Abandoning his chariot in the battle, he leaped down on foot, grasping a stainless sword and shield,
like a lion from the peak of a mountain.
And she went to another region of the earth;
meanwhile, that mace, having reached the brilliantly decorated chariot along with its horses and driver, destroyed it in the battle.
A blazing great meteor fell to the earth,
like a falling star descending from the sky;
it was a most wondrous sight for your troops.
O Bhārata, upon seeing that, they were all filled with joy and, gathering together from all sides, they roared and,
along with their armies, paid homage to your son.
Saṃjaya said:
Having approached the high-minded Citrasena, who was deprived of his chariot,
your son Vikarṇa took him up onto his own chariot.
While that tumultuous and intense conflict was thus unfolding,
Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, swiftly rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then the Sṛñjayas, along with their chariots, elephants, and horses, trembled.
They considered Yudhiṣṭhira to have already entered the jaws of Death;
yet the lordly Kuru prince Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by the twins,
advanced against Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, that great archer and tiger among men.
Then, discharging thousands of arrows in battle, the Pāṇḍava covered Bhīṣma just as a cloud covers the sun. O Bhārata, those nets of arrows were skillfully discharged by him.
The son of Gaṅgā then intercepted them by the hundreds and thousands;
likewise, O noble one, the nets of arrows discharged by Bhīṣma appeared in the sky like flocks of birds in flight.

In less than half a blink of an eye, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, rendered the son of Kuntī invisible in battle by means of a multitude of arrows shot in successive volleys. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira [attacked] the high-souled Kaurava.

Enraged, he dispatched an iron shaft resembling a venomous serpent. But before it had reached him, O King, the great car-warrior Bhīṣma cut down that arrow released from his bow in battle with a razor-headed shaft.

But having cut down that iron shaft, which was like Death itself, in battle, Bhīṣma struck the gold-adorned horses of the Kuru lord. Standing on his chariot whose horses had been slain, the King of Dharma hurled a spear.
As it came rushing suddenly toward him, sharp as the noose of Death,
Bhīṣma cut it down in battle with straight-jointed arrows.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, abandoning his chariot whose horses had been slain, fled.
He quickly mounted the chariot of the high-souled Nakula;
then Bhīṣma, the conqueror of enemy cities, having encountered the twins in battle while greatly enraged, covered them with arrows.

Bhīṣma, the best among chariot-warriors, also pierced those two brothers of great heroism, who struck terror into the enemy army, with sharpened arrows. O Great King, seeing them thus afflicted by Bhīṣma’s shafts, they were overwhelmed.
Then he fell into deep reflection, desiring the slaughter of Bhīṣma.
Thereupon Yudhiṣṭhira urged those kings under his command and his circle of friends, saying, "All of you, slay Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu!"
Then all those kings, having heard the speech of Pārtha,
surrounded their grandfather with a vast array of chariots.
Thus was your father Devavrata encompassed on all sides.
O King, he sported with his bow, felling great chariot-warriors;
the Pārthas beheld that Kaurava moving about in battle like a lion cub that has entered into the midst of deer in the forest.
Seeing him threatening the heroes in battle and terrifying them with his arrows,
O great king, they trembled like herds of deer at the sight of a lion;
they beheld the movement of that lion among the Bharatas in the fray.
Just as a fire aided by the wind desires to consume a thicket of dry grass,
so did Bhīṣma strike down the heads of the chariot-warriors in battle,
like a skillful man gathering ripe fruits from palm trees.
And as those heads fell upon the surface of the earth, O great king,
there arose a tumultuous sound like that of falling stones.
While that tumultuous and most dreadful battle was thus proceeding, [the combatants fought on].
A great confusion arose among all the armies. When those battle arrays were broken, the kṣatriyas challenged one another individually and stood ready for combat.
But Śikhaṇḍin, having approached the grandfather of the Bharatas, rushed at him with speed and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Then Bhīṣma, disregarding Śikhaṇḍin in that battle, [proceeded].
Reflecting upon Śikhaṇḍin’s womanhood, he advanced toward the Sṛñjayas in a rage. Then the Sṛñjayas, seeing the great car-warrior Bhīṣma,
were filled with joy and uttered various lion-roars mingled with the sound of conchs.

Then, O Lord, while the sun stood in the western quarter, a battle commenced in which chariots and elephants were closely entangled. Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Pāñcālya, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki [advanced].
Severely afflicting the army with showers of spears, lances,
and many weapons, O King, they struck down your men in battle.
Being thus slaughtered in the encounter, O bull among men, those of your side...

Having set their minds on noble combat, those great car-warriors did not abandon the fray; according to their resolve, they struck down the world in battle. There, a great cry arose from your high-souled warriors.
"O King, let him be slain in battle by the high-souled son of Pṛṣata.
Hearing that terrible outcry of your men, the two great car-warriors Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti rushed against the son of Pṛṣata.
Having slain his horses, those two great car-warriors, acting with haste, both covered the son of Pṛṣata with a shower of arrows. Then the mighty Pāñcālya, leaping down quickly from his chariot—
He quickly ascended the chariot of the high-souled Sātyaki. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, surrounded by a vast army,
advanced in battle against those two wrathful princes of Avanti, the subduers of foes.
In the same way, O noble one, your son also, with every effort,
stood surrounding Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti.
And Arjuna, O bull among kṣatriyas, being filled with rage, [assailed] the kṣatriyas.
Like the wielder of the thunderbolt against the Asuras, he fought in battle;
and Drona, enraged in the fray and seeking to do what was pleasing to your son,
scattered all the Panchalas like fire consuming a heap of cotton.
O lord of the people, your sons, led by Duryodhana,
surrounded Bhīṣma in battle and fought with the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, as the sun turned crimson, King Duryodhana—
"O Bhārata, he said to all your men, 'Hurry!
While they were thus fighting and performing difficult deeds,
the sun ascended the western mountain and ceased to shine."

At the onset of night, in an instant, there flowed a terrible river with waves of surging blood, crowded with packs of jackals and filled with the howling of inauspicious female jackals uttering a fearsome sound.
A terrible battlefield arose, crowded with throngs of living beings;
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and other flesh-eaters were seen on all sides by the hundreds and thousands.
Intoxicated by the scent of blood and by flesh, those kings,
tasting it again and again, dance and let out terrifying cries;
and headless trunks with bows in their hands dance in the battle.
Then Arjuna, seizing a sharp spear and a large, stainless sword, defeated those kings led by Suśarman along with their followers in the midst of the army,
and proceeded toward his own camp.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the descendant of Kuru, together with his brothers,
went to his own camp at night, surrounded by his army;
Bhīmasena also, O king of kings, [pursued] the chariot-warriors headed by Duryodhana.

Having thus conquered him in battle, he then proceeded toward his own camp. King Duryodhana also, having surrounded Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, in that great conflict, quickly set out for his own camp.
Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata,
having surrounded the entire army, proceeded toward their camp;
and likewise, O King, did Sātyaki and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata.
Surrounding the warriors in battle, they both proceeded toward their camp.
Thus, O great king, those scorchers of the foe, your men together with the Pāṇḍavas, returned together at the time of night.

Then, O great king, having gone to their own camps, the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus settled down, honoring one another; those heroes, having made arrangements for their own protection, stationed outposts according to the prescribed rules.
Having extracted those arrows and bathed in various waters,
all those illustrious ones, having performed the rites for well-being and being praised by bards, sported amidst the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
For a mere moment, that entire place became like heaven;
indeed, the great car-warriors did not engage in any talk of battle there. O King, while the two armies were thus fast asleep, their people being utterly exhausted.
O King, they became a sight to behold, abounding in elephants and horses.
Sañjaya said:
Having passed that night, those lords of men slept soundly.
The Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas once again set out for battle;
then a great sound arose from both armies as they marched forth for the fray, like the vast roar of the ocean.
Then King Duryodhana, Citrasena, Vivimśati, Bhīṣma— the best of chariot-warriors— and the twice-born son of Bharadvāja,
having united and being well-prepared, [led] the great army of the Kauravas.
O King, having donned their armor, they formed battle arrays against the Pāṇḍavas.
O lord of the people, your father Bhīṣma, having constructed a great and formidable array resembling the ocean, with its mounts as its waves and billows, stood ready.
At the head of all the armies went Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu,
accompanied by the Mālavas, the Southerners, and the Āvantyas.
Immediately following him was the powerful Bhāradvāja.
O lord of the people, the powerful Bhagadatta, exerting himself, was stationed immediately after Droṇa, accompanied by the Pulindas, the Pāradas, as well as the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas,
along with the Māgadhas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Piśācas.
After the king of Prāgjyotiṣa came Bṛhadbala, the king of Kosala, accompanied by the Mekalas,
the Traipuras, and the Cicchilas;
after Bṛhadbala came Śūra, the Trigarta, the lord of Prasthala.
Together with many Kambojas and thousands of Yavanas,
O Bharata, the impetuous and heroic son of Droṇa followed behind the Trigarta king,
making the earth resound with his lion-like roar.
Then King Duryodhana, surrounded by his uterine brothers and accompanied by his entire army, advanced immediately behind the son of Droṇa;
and after Duryodhana, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, then went forth.
Thus did this great array advance, resembling the ocean.
O Lord, there the banners and white umbrellas shone,
as did the variegated armlets and the costly bows.
But seeing that great array of your men, the great car-warrior Yudhiṣṭhira quickly spoke to the son of Pṛṣata, the commander of the army: "Behold, O great archer, this array formed like the ocean."
"O son of Pṛṣata, you too must form a counter-array without delay.
Thereupon, O great king, that heroic son of Pṛṣata formed a most formidable array known as the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, which is destructive of enemy formations.
From the horns came Bhīmasena and the great car-warrior Sātyaki,
accompanied by many thousands of chariots as well as horses and foot soldiers; at the navel was that best of men, he of the white horses and the monkey-banner.
In the center stood King Yudhiṣṭhira and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī;
then the other great archers, the lords of men together with their armies—
experts in the science of military formations— filled out that array.
Then followed Abhimanyu, the great car-warrior Virāṭa,
the joyful sons of Draupadī, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca.
O Bhārata, having thus formed this great array, the Pāṇḍavas stood ready.
The heroes stood in the battle, desiring to fight and seeking victory;
the tumultuous sounds of kettledrums, mingled with the blasts of conchs, along with lion-roars,
the slapping of arms, and shouts, made all directions most terrifying.
Then, O King, having encountered one another in battle, those heroes, provoked to fury, gazed at each other with unblinking eyes;
yet first, O lord of men, they did so with their minds.
Having challenged one another, they assembled for battle;
then there commenced a battle of terrible form and fearsome nature between your men and the enemy as they struck one another down.
O Bhārata, sharpened iron arrows fell in the battle like terrifying snakes with gaping mouths, moving in swarms;
bright spears, cleansed with oil and well-tempered, flew forth.
O King, like brilliant flashes of lightning from the clouds,
beautiful maces— bound with bright bands and adorned with gold—
were seen falling there, resembling the peaks of mountains.
And swords, resembling the stainless sky, shone brightly;
and shields made of bull-hide, adorned with a hundred moons, O Bhārata,
looked magnificent in the battle as they fell in every direction, O King.
O lord of men, as lightning appears to blaze amidst the clouds,
so did those two armies shine as they fought one another in battle,
like the hosts of Daityas and Devas arrayed for combat.
In that battle, they rushed at one another from all sides; indeed,
chariots were swiftly driven by their riders in that supreme conflict,
and those bulls among kings fought, their yokes entangled with yokes.
From the friction of the tusks of the combatting elephants,
O best of the Bharatas, fire arose with smoke in every direction.
Some elephant-warriors were struck on all sides by spears.
They were seen falling like trees from mountain peaks;
and foot-soldiers were also seen striking one another— heroes assuming diverse forms, fighting with their claws and spears.
Having encountered one another, the soldiers of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies dispatched each other to the abode of Yama in battle with various kinds of terrible weapons.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, made the earth resound with the rattling of his chariot.
He advanced against the Pāṇḍus in battle, bewildering them with the sound of his bow;
and the chariots of the Pāṇḍavas, too, roaring with a terrible sound,
rushed forward prepared for combat, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Then, O Bhārata, the battle between your men and theirs commenced,
a melee of infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants, all entangled with one another.
Sañjaya said:
But the Pāṇḍavas were unable to look upon Bhīṣma as he raged in battle, scorching all around like the sun burning down;
then, by the command of the Son of Dharma, all the troops [advanced].
They rushed toward the son of Gaṅgā, who was crushing them with sharp arrows;
but Bhīṣma, who delighted in battle, struck down the Somakas along with the Sṛñjayas and the great archers among the Pañcālas with his shafts.
Being slaughtered by Bhīṣma, those Pāñcālas, together with the Somakas,
quickly rushed toward Bhīṣma himself, casting aside the fear of death.
In that battle, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, was the hero among those chariot-warriors.
O King, he suddenly severed their arms and then their heads;
your father Devavrata deprived the chariot-warriors of their chariots,
and the heads of the horse-riders fell from their horses.
O great king, we beheld elephant-riders, as large as mountains, lying there deprived of their men and rendered senseless by Bhīṣma’s weapon;
O lord of the people, there was not a single man among the Pāṇḍavas remaining there.
Except for Bhīmasena, the most powerful of chariot-warriors;
for he, having encountered Bhīṣma, struck him in the fray. Then there arose a terrible clamor at the encounter between Bhīṣma and Bhīma.
It became terrible and fearsome for all the armies; likewise, the Pāṇḍavas, filled with joy, then let out lion-like roars. Then King Duryodhana was surrounded by his uterine brothers.
While that slaughter of men was proceeding in battle, Bhīma—
the best of chariot-warriors— having slain Bhīṣma’s charioteer,
[left him] with his horses fled and his chariot fleeing in every direction.
The slayer of foes swiftly severed Sunābha’s head with a sharp, razor-edged arrow;
struck down, he fell to the earth. O great king, when that son of yours, a great car-warrior, was slain, [the army trembled].
In that battle, seven heroic brothers could not endure it in the fray:
Ādityaketu, Bahvāśin, Kuṇḍadhāra, Mahodara,
Aparājita, Paṇḍitaka, and Viśālākṣa, who was very difficult to conquer.
Wearing variegated armor and possessing diverse coats of mail and banners, those crushers of enemies, eager for battle, rushed toward the Pāṇḍava in the fray.
Meanwhile, Mahodara pierced Bhīma in the encounter with feathered shafts.
With nine arrows resembling thunderbolts, he struck Namuci as Vṛtra-slayer [Indra] did;
Ādityaketu with seventy, Bahvāśin also with five,
Kuṇḍadhāra with ninety, and Viśālākṣa with seven.
O Great King, the invincible Aparājita, a great car-warrior intent on victory,
struck the mighty Bhīmasena with many arrows;
and in that battle, Paṇḍitaka also afflicted him with three shafts.
Bhīma, the crusher of enemies, could not endure that slaughter by his foes in battle; O king of kings, the mighty Bhīmasena, the unconquered one, gripped his bow with his left hand.
In that battle, with a straight-knotted arrow, he severed the handsome nose and head of your son Aparājita;
thus defeated by Bhīma in the encounter, his head fell to the earth.
Then, with another broad-headed arrow, he dispatched the great car-warrior Kuṇḍadhāra to the world of death while all the world looked on. Thereupon,
that one of immeasurable soul, having again aimed a feathered shaft, [sent him forth].
O Bhārata, he dispatched [that arrow] at Paṇḍita in the battle.
That arrow, having slain Paṇḍita, entered the surface of the earth,
just as a serpent impelled by Time quickly kills a man.
Having severed the head of Viśālākṣa, he, undaunted in spirit and remembering his former sufferings, caused it to fall upon the earth with three arrows; then,
with a steel shaft, he struck Mahodara, the great archer, between the breasts.
O King, he pierced him in battle, and being slain, he fell to the earth.
Having severed the standard of Ādityaketu with an arrow in the encounter,
that slayer of foes cut off his head with an exceedingly sharp broad-headed shaft (bhalla).
Then Bhīma, filled with rage, dispatched that great eater with a straight-jointed arrow toward the abode of Yama. Thereupon,
O lord of the people, those other sons of yours fled away.
For they considered that which he had spoken in the assembly to be the truth;
then King Duryodhana, emaciated by the calamity that had befallen his brothers,
said to your warriors, "Let this Bhīma be slain in battle!"
"O lord of the people, thus were these great archers, your sons,
slain in battle by Bhīmasena of great heroism;
and beholding their brothers slain, they indeed remembered those words."
O lord of men, that beneficial and wholesome advice which the highly wise Kṣattṛ spoke—
those words of one with divine vision have now come to pass; for you,
O ruler, were possessed by greed and delusion through affection for your son.
You do not realize that what was said by me long ago was a great and truthful word; for indeed, the mighty Pāṇḍava, the long-armed one, has surely been born for the very purpose of slaying your sons,
as he now strikes down the Kauravas.
Then, O Sire, King Duryodhana, having approached Bhīṣma,
overcome by great sorrow and exceedingly emaciated, lamented:
"My heroic brothers have been slain by Bhīmasena in battle."
Likewise, other soldiers too, though striving, are being slain;
and you, remaining neutral, constantly disregard us. Thus I have entered upon a wrong path; behold this fate of mine.
Having heard these cruel words, your father Devavrata,
with eyes full of tears, spoke this speech to Duryodhana:
"This was said by me previously, as well as by Droṇa and Vidura."
O dear one, you did not understand the truth regarding the illustrious Gāndhārī;
moreover, O crusher of enemies, a compact was previously made by me with you all:
"I am not to be released in battle, nor is the Preceptor (Ācārya) under any circumstances."
"Whomever among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra Bhīma beholds in the encounter, him he shall slay in battle; I tell you this as the truth.
Therefore, O King, remain steadfast and firm in your resolve for the fight."
Fight the Pārthas in battle, making heaven your ultimate goal. The Pāṇḍavas cannot be conquered even by the gods and asuras led by Indra.
Therefore, O Bhārata, set your mind firmly on war and fight!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, having seen my many sons slain by a single man,
what did Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa do in the battle?"
Day after day my sons are perishing, O Sañjaya;
