I believe, O Sūta, that they are utterly and severely struck down by fate,
since all my children are being defeated and do not achieve victory.
Wherein [were gathered] Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the high-souled Kṛpa;
the heroic son of Somadatta, both Bhagadattas,
and likewise Aśvatthāman, O dear one— those heroes of most exalted soul.
My sons were slain in battle while standing in the midst of other heroes; what else can this be but destiny?
For the dull-witted Duryodhana did not understand what was told to him in the past.
Though restrained by me, O dear one, and by Bhīṣma and Vidura,
as well as by Gāndhārī— who always desired his welfare— that evil-minded man did not understand due to delusion; now this fruit of his actions has been obtained.
"Since Bhīmasena, enraged day after day in battle, sends my sons— who have lost their senses— to the abode of Yama. Saṃjaya said:
"O Lord, that supreme advice of the Steward (Kṣattṛ) has now come to pass; you did not understand it when it was being spoken for your benefit at that time—
namely, 'Restrain your sons from gambling, and do not act with malice toward the Pāṇḍavas.'"

Though your friends, desiring your welfare, have spoken those very words to you, you did not wish to hear them— just as a mortal rejects wholesome medicine. Now that well-spoken advice has come upon you.

"O Lord of the People, the Kauravas have already transgressed that very advice which Vidura, Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and other well-wishers offered for their own welfare, and thus they are heading toward destruction."
Therefore, hear from me in truth how that battle took place. At midday, O King, a most terrible conflict occurred, causing the destruction of the world; listen as I describe it to you.
Then, by the command of the son of Dharma, all the troops,
filled with fury, rushed toward Bhīṣma alone with the desire to slay him;
so too did Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki.
O great king, with their divisions arrayed, they advanced toward Bhīṣma himself; Virāṭa and Drupada, together with all the Somakas,
those great car-warriors, rushed against Bhīṣma alone in the battle.
O great king, the Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Kuntibhoja, clad in armor and with their armies arrayed, advanced against Bhīṣma himself;
likewise Arjuna, the sons of Draupadī, and Cekitāna in the battle.
Commanded by King Duryodhana, they all advanced together; likewise, the heroic Abhimanyu, the great car-warrior son of Hiḍimbā,
and the enraged Bhīmasena rushed toward the Kauravas.
Divided into three groups, the Kauravas struck at the Pāṇḍavas in battle;
likewise, O King, the enemies struck at the Kauravas in that fray.
Droṇa, however, the best of chariot-warriors, [attacked] the Somakas along with the Sṛñjayas.
Enraged and intent on sending them to the abode of Yama, he rushed forward;
there, O King, a great cry arose from the high-souled Sṛñjayas as they were being slain in battle by the archer, the son of Bharadvāja.
There, many Kṣatriyas were slain by Droṇa in battle;
they were seen writhing like men afflicted by disease,
moaning, crying out, and groaning in the conflict.
A constant sound was heard, like that of men emaciated by hunger;
even so did the mighty Bhīmasena,
enraged like a second Kāla, inflict a terrible slaughter upon the sons of Kuru.
As the armies there slaughtered one another in that great battle,
a terrible river began to flow, carrying away a torrent of blood.
That great battle, O great king, became horrific in appearance.
Increasing the population of Yama’s kingdom for both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas,
Bhīma, enraged and especially impetuous in battle,
then encountered the elephant division and dispatched it to death.
There, O Bhārata, elephants struck by Bhīma’s iron arrows fell,
sank down, shrieked, and wandered aimlessly in all directions;
their trunks were severed and their feet were cut off, O noble one.
Crying out like cranes in fear, they lay prostrate upon the earth.
Nakula and Sahadeva then rushed toward the cavalry division;
those horses were adorned with golden crests and equipped with trappings of gold.
They were seen being slaughtered by the hundreds and by the thousands;
and the earth, O King, was strewn with falling horses—
some tongueless, some gasping, and some groaning as their lives departed.
O best of men, O descendant of Bharata, lord of the people, the earth shone with horses of various forms slain by Arjuna in battle;
thus did the terrible ground appear here and there.
With broken chariots, severed banners, and highly resplendent parasols;
with necklaces, golden coins, and armlets, along with heads adorned with earrings;
and with broken fly-whisks and fans, as well as great weapons hacked to pieces.
With broken and mangled goads, with great weapons,
with discarded turbans, and with banners scattered everywhere; with beautiful chariot-poles, O King, and with yokes whose thongs and reins were torn asunder.
The earth shone as if covered with blossoms in spring;
in this manner, O Bhārata, this destruction of the Pāṇḍavas occurred when Śāntanu’s son Bhīṣma and Droṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, were enraged.
"In Aśvatthāman, in Kṛpa, and likewise in Kṛtavarman,
as well as in the others who are enraged, there is also destruction among your own men.
Sañjaya said:
O King, while that fierce slaughter of the best of heroes was thus proceeding,
the illustrious Śakuni, the son of Subala, rushed against the Pāṇḍavas;
and likewise, O King, the Sātvata Hārdikya, the slayer of enemy heroes, [rushed against them].
He charged in battle against the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
Then [he encountered] the horses of the foremost Kāmbojas, those born of the rivers,
those from Āraṭṭa, those born of the earth, and those from the Indus region, from all sides.
They surrounded him on all sides in the battle with many horses— brilliant steeds from Vanāyu as well as those dwelling in the mountains—
and others that were born of the *tittira* breed, swift and possessing the speed of the wind.
With these excellent horses— adorned with gold, well-armored, well-equipped, and swift as the wind— the powerful son of the Pāṇḍava,
that scorcher of foes, advanced against that army with a joyful countenance.
Then Arjuna’s heir, the heroic one named Irāvat,
was born to the daughter of the Naga king by the wise Pārtha.
She had been given to him by the high-souled Airāvata, as she was childless.
When her husband had been slain by Suparṇa, she was miserable and dejected in spirit; Pārtha took her as his wife, for she had surrendered herself to the power of desire.
Thus was this son of Arjuna born in the field of another.
He grew up in the world of the Nāgas and was protected by his mother;
he had been abandoned by his wicked uncle out of hatred for Pārtha.
He was handsome, endowed with heroism, virtuous, and possessed of true prowess.
Having heard that Arjuna had gone there, he quickly went to the world of Indra. O King, having approached his high-souled father, whose prowess is truth, the son of Ulūpī then spoke these words.
With composure and with hands joined in reverence, he offered his salutation;
and he announced himself to the high-souled Arjuna:
"I am Irāvān; may you be blessed, O Lord, for I am your son."
He reported everything regarding his meeting with his mother,
and the Pāṇḍava recollected all of that exactly as it had occurred;
then, he embraced his son, who was equal to himself in virtues.

Pārtha became filled with joy in the abode of the King of the Gods. O Bharata, O King, having been thus instructed by Arjuna in the world of the gods, the mighty-armed one then spoke with affection regarding his own mission.
And that tiger among men, possessing prowess equal to a tiger, then said to Pārtha, "O Lord, here I am;
I stand as your servant and your son; command me in every way."
"What desire of yours shall I fulfill? What wish do you desire?
Embracing his son with affection, the son of Vasava replied to him with love and purpose, O giver of honor: "This must be done out of affection, and it must be done for the sake of our duty."
"O Lord, you must grant us your assistance at the time of battle.
Having said, "So be it," he arrived when the time for battle had come,
O King, surrounded by many horses as swift as those of any desired color.
Those horses, adorned with golden head-ornaments, of various colors and swift as thought,
suddenly leapt up, O King, like swans upon the great ocean.
Having encountered your own hosts of horses of great speed, they [rushed forward].
Striking one another with their chests and snouts,
O King, they fell suddenly to the ground, violently impelled by their own momentum;
and likewise, as those throngs of horses fell upon one another, [the earth shook].
A terrible sound was heard, like that of a great bird’s descent;
and even so, O Great King, having encountered one another in battle,
those horsemen wrought a horrific slaughter upon each other.
While that tumultuous and intense melee was thus proceeding,
the throngs of horses on both sides were completely exhausted;
the heroes, their arrows spent and their horses slain, were overcome with fatigue.
Having reached their destruction while hacking one another down,
O Bhārata, when the cavalry force was thus depleted and only a small remnant remained,
the heroic sons of Subala’s son emerged at the forefront of the battle.
Mounting excellent horses that were endowed with good character, in their youth, and whose touch was like the force of the wind and whose speed was equal to the wind—
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Vṛṣaka, Carmavat, Ārjava, and Śuka.
These six, endowed with strength, set out from their great army;
though restrained by Śakuni and by their own mighty warriors,
they were armored, skilled in battle, fierce in appearance, and possessed of great power.
O mighty-armed one, having broken through that most invincible host,
those Gāndhāras— endowed with great strength, seeking victory, and intoxicated by battle— then entered [the fray] with joy.
Seeing them then entered, the heroic Irāvat spoke to the warriors in battle, who were adorned with various ornaments and weapons:
"Just as these warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, along with their followers and mounts..."

"All are being slain in battle; let policy be applied accordingly. Having said, "So be it," all those warriors of Irāvata struck down the enemy host, which was difficult for others to conquer in combat.
Seeing that division struck down by the opposing force in battle,
all those sons of Subala, unable to endure it,
rushed toward Irāvān and surrounded him on all sides.
Striking one another with sharp spears and goading each other on,
those heroes ran about, creating a great tumult.
Then Irāvat was pierced by the sharp spears of those high-souled warriors.
Smeared with flowing blood like an elephant pierced by goads,
and struck violently on his chest, back, and sides,
he— though alone against many— was not shaken from his fortitude, O King.
Then Irāvat, enraged, that conqueror of enemy cities, pierced all of them with sharpened arrows and confounded them in battle; that subduer of foes then drew forth all the lances from his own body.
With those very [weapons], he struck the sons of Subala in battle;
drawing his sharp sword and taking up his shield,
he advanced swiftly on foot, desiring to slay the followers of Subala in the fray.
Then, having regained their breath, all those sons of Subala,
once again overcome with rage, rushed toward Irāvant. Irāvant, for his part, displayed his lightness of hand with his sword.
Proud of his strength, he turned against all those sons of Subala; then,
as he moved with such agility, all those swift-moving sons of Subala could find no opening against him, despite their own rapid movements.

Then, seeing him standing on the ground in the midst of the fray, they all surrounded him closely once more and set about to seize him. Thereupon, that crusher of enemies, with his sword, [struck] those who had come near.
With his hands raised and lowered, he cut through their limbs,
as well as the weapons and the adorned arms of them all; with their members severed, they fell to the earth, deprived of life.
But Vṛṣaka, O great king, though severely wounded in many places, was released from that most terrible slaughter of heroes. Seeing all of them fallen, Duryodhana then became terrified.
Enraged, he addressed the Rākṣasa of terrible appearance,
the son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the great archer, the master of illusions, and the subduer of foes—
who had previously been an enemy of Bhīmasena due to the slaying of Baka.
"Behold, O hero, how this powerful son of Phalguna,
a master of illusions, has wrought a terrible and unpleasant destruction of my forces.
And you, dear one, are able to go wherever you wish and are skilled in the weapons of illusion."
"You have incurred the enmity of Pārtha; therefore, slay him in battle!
Having said, "So be it," the Rākṣasa of terrible appearance set out with a lion's roar toward where the youthful son of Arjuna was.

Mounted by those skilled in combat, warriors who fought with spotless lances— brave strikers joined by their own divisions and surrounded by two thousand of the best horses that remained after the slaughter, O great king.
Desirous of slaying the mighty Irāvant in battle,
the powerful Irāvant, filled with rage and acting with haste, checked the Rākṣasa— who was himself intent on killing him— with his own prowess, for he was a destroyer of enemies.
Seeing him rushing toward him, the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa then quickly began to employ his illusory power (māyā). By that power,
he fashioned as many horses made of illusion as there were [of the original ones].
Mounted by terrible Rākṣasas with spears and sharp-edged pikes in their hands,
those two thousand strikers, filled with fury, having come together,
soon sent one another to the world of the dead.
When that army had been slain, those two, intoxicated by battle,
stood firm in the encounter like Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Beholding the Rākṣasa, who was fierce in combat, rushing toward him—
The mighty Irāvaṇ, agitated by rage, rushed forward;
as that evil-minded one drew near in battle, he cut off his blazing bow and his five quivers with his sword.
Seeing his bow severed, he [Irāvān] entered the sky with speed,
as if bewildering the enraged [Ghaṭotkaca] with his illusory power (*māyā*).
Then, having leaped up into the air, Irāvān [attacked] the Rākṣasa as well.
Having bewildered him with illusions,
he who knew all the vital points, who could assume any form at will, and who was difficult to approach, cut his limbs with arrows.
Thus that best of Rākṣasas was repeatedly mangled by the shafts.
O great king, he grew and attained youth;
for their birth-magic (māyā) is innate, while their age and form are born of desire.
Thus, O dear one, that limb of the Rākṣasa grew back again and again whenever it was severed.
Irāvat, also filled with rage, repeatedly severed that mighty Rākṣasa with his sharp battle-axe. Under the blows of that powerful hero, he was like a tree being cut down.
The Rākṣasa let out a terrible roar, and that sound became tumultuous. Wounded by the battle-axe, the Rākṣasa bled profusely;
thereupon the powerful one grew enraged and exerted his full force in the combat.
Then, seeing his powerful enemy in battle,
the son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga assumed a terrible and massive form and proceeded to seize the heroic and illustrious Irāvān, the son of Arjuna.
In the midst of the battle, while everyone there was looking on,
Irāvān— having seen that kind of illusion created by the high-souled Rākṣasa—
also became enraged and proceeded to create an illusion of his own.

O King, his maternal lineage, which had never retreated in battles, now advanced against him who was overcome by wrath; surrounded on all sides by many elephants in that conflict, he stood firm in the fray.
He assumed a truly immense form, like the serpent Ananta with his coils;
then he covered the Rākṣasa with many kinds of serpents. Being thus covered by the serpents, that bull among Rākṣasas reflected.
Assuming the form of Garuḍa, he devoured the serpents.
When that maternal lineage had been consumed through his illusory power,
the Rākṣasa slew the bewildered Irāvanta with a sword.

The Rākṣasa struck down Irāvata’s head— adorned with earrings and a diadem, and radiant like the lotus or the moon— to the surface of the earth. When that heroic son of Arjuna had been slain by the Rākṣasa, [the battle continued].
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with the kings, became free from grief.
In that great battle, so terrible once again,
a vast and horrific carnage occurred between the two armies.
Horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers were mingled and slain by tuskers;
chariots and elephants likewise were destroyed there by foot-soldiers.
So too, in that battle, were many throngs of foot-soldiers, chariots, and horses.
O King, in that tumultuous clash between your men and theirs, many chariot-warriors were slain;
and Arjuna, unaware that his own biological son had been killed,
slaughtered those heroic kings who were protecting Bhīṣma in battle.
In that same manner, O King, your warriors and the mighty Sṛñjayas,
sacrificing their lives in battle, slaughtered one another—
some with disheveled hair, others without armor, some deprived of chariots, and others with bows broken.
Having assembled together, they fought one another with their arms;
likewise, the mighty Bhīṣma struck down the great car-warriors with arrows that pierced the vital organs,
making the army of the Pāṇḍavas tremble in battle.
By him, many men were slain in Yudhiṣṭhira’s army—
elephants, riders, chariot-warriors, and likewise horses.
There, O Bhārata, having witnessed Bhīṣma’s prowess in battle, [the troops were struck with awe].
O Bhārata, we beheld a most wonderful prowess, like that of Śakra himself, belonging to Bhīmasena, the son of Pṛṣata,
and the bowman of the Sātvatas; at that time, the battle was truly fierce.
Seeing Drona’s prowess, fear entered the hearts of the Pandavas:
"He alone is capable of slaying us along with our armies in battle;
how much more so when he is surrounded by hosts of warriors and the heroes of the earth?"
"Thus they cried out, O Great King, being oppressed by Droṇa in battle;
while that fierce combat was thus proceeding, O bull of the Bharatas,
the heroes of both armies could not endure one another."
As if possessed by Rakshasas and spirits,
O dear one, your mighty bowmen and those of the Pandavas fight with fury;
we see not a single one who seeks to preserve his life.
In that battle resembling the conflict between the Daityas, O lord of men, he was the warrior.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Having seen Irāvān slain, the great car-warriors among the Pārthas—"
"Tell me, Sañjaya, what did they do in that battle?
Sañjaya said:
"Having seen Irāvanta slain in the battle, the Rākṣasa..."
Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīmasena, let out a tremendous roar. O King,
at the sound of him roaring, the earth— clothed by the oceans,
along with its mountains and forests— trembled violently at that time.
The intermediate space, the cardinal directions, and all the subsidiary quarters likewise trembled suddenly there, resounded by that roar. Having heard that great noise from your army, O Bhārata...
Stiffness in the thighs, trembling, and perspiration arose;
and all your men, O king of kings, became dejected in heart and coiled up like snakes, or like elephants terrified by a lion.
Uttering a tremendous roar like a thunderclap,
that Rākṣasa raised a flaming trident and assumed a terrifying form,
surrounded by the foremost of Rākṣasas bearing various dreadful weapons.
He arrived, highly incensed, resembling Yama, the Ender, at the time of destruction.
Seeing him rushing forward, enraged and of terrifying appearance,
his own army for the most part turned away in fear of him.
Then King Duryodhana rushed toward Ghaṭotkaca,
grasping his massive bow and roaring repeatedly like a lion;
he pursued him from behind with mountain-like elephants that were shedding rut-fluid.
The lord of the Vaṅgas himself, accompanied by ten thousand elephants,
advanced; seeing him approaching, surrounded by that elephant division,
O great king, that night-stalker became enraged at your son.
Then, O king of kings, there commenced a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end between the Rākṣasas and the army of Duryodhana.
And beholding the elephant division rising up like a mass of clouds, [he struck it down].
Enraged, the Rākṣasas, weapons in hand, rushed forward,
uttering various cries like clouds accompanied by lightning,
striking down the elephant-warriors with arrows, spears, double-edged swords, and iron shafts.
With slings, spears, mallets, and battle-axes,
as well as with mountain peaks and trees, they struck down those great elephants; the elephants had their frontal globes split open, were drenched in blood, and their limbs were shattered.
O Great King, we beheld them being slaughtered by the night-stalkers.
As those elephant-warriors were being decimated and broken,
O Great King, Duryodhana rushed against the Rākṣasas.
Overcome by indignation and having renounced his own life,
the mighty one released sharpened arrows at the Rākṣasas;
and that great archer struck down the principal Rākṣasas there.
Enraged, O best of the Bharatas, your son Duryodhana,
that great car-warrior, struck down with four arrows the four— Vegavān, Mahāraudra, Vidyujjihva, and Pramāthin.

Then again, O best of the Bharatas, that one of immeasurable soul released an unassailable shower of arrows against the army of the night-rangers. And having seen that great feat of your son, O honorable one—
The mighty Bhaimaseni blazed up with rage;
stretching his great bow, which produced a sound like Indra’s thunderbolt,
he rushed with speed toward Duryodhana, the subduer of enemies.
Beholding him rushing forward like Death himself unleashed by Time,
O great king, your son Duryodhana did not tremble.
Then, enraged, cruel, and with bloodshot eyes, he spoke to him.
Today I shall attain freedom from my debt to my ancestors and to my mother,
who were exiled for a long time by you, cruel as you are;
and likewise, O King, regarding those Pāṇḍavas whom you defeated through a deceitful game of dice.

And because you, O evil-minded one, brought Draupadī Kṛṣṇā— while she was clad in a single garment and in her courses— into the assembly hall and tormented her in many ways, O wicked-minded one, reap now the fruit of this sin.

"O lowest of your lineage, while staying in the hermitage, she was tormented by that evil-minded Saindhava, who sought to please you and showed contempt for my fathers. Because of these and other such insults,"
"Today I shall go to my end if you do not desist from the fight.
Having spoken thus, the son of Hiḍimbā drew his great bow,
biting his lip with his teeth and licking the corners of his mouth.
With a great shower of arrows, he covered Duryodhana,
just as a cloud covers a mountain with torrents of rain during the monsoon.
Sañjaya said:
Then that shower of arrows, unbearable even for the Dānavas,
the king of kings received in battle like a great elephant receives a rain;
thereafter, overcome with rage, he hissed like a serpent.
O bull of the Bharatas, having fallen into a state of extreme peril,
your son released twenty-five sharp, whetted iron arrows;
O King, they fell suddenly upon that foremost of Rākṣasas.
Like enraged venomous serpents upon Mount Gandhamādana,
he was pierced by them; with blood flowing like an elephant in rut,
that flesh-eater set his mind upon the destruction of the king.

And the mighty-armed one, desiring to slay your son, seized a great spear capable of splitting even mountains— a blazing weapon with the luster of a great meteor, like Maghavan seizing his thunderbolt.
Beholding that [weapon] raised, the lord of the Vaṅgas quickly urged his elephant, which resembled a mountain, toward the Rākṣasa. In that battle,
he [the Rākṣasa] was mounted upon an excellent elephant, powerful and swift-moving.
Since Duryodhana’s chariot had taken that path,
he [the elephant] blocked your son’s chariot with the elephant.
Seeing the path blocked by the wise King Vaṅga, [he turned back].
O great king, Ghaṭotkaca, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
hurled that raised great spear at that elephant.
Struck by it, O king, as it was released from his arm, [the elephant fell].
With a gushing stream of blood, he fell down and died. As the elephant was falling, the powerful lord of the Vaṅgas also rushed forward with speed and reached the surface of the earth.
Duryodhana, too, beholding that excellent elephant struck down and seeing his army broken, fell into extreme distress; indeed,
he was unable to fight back upon witnessing his [the enemy's] prowess.
Placing the duty of a warrior before him and out of his own sense of self-respect,
the king remained as immovable as a mountain even when the time for retreat had arrived;
he fixed a sharp arrow upon his bow, possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
Highly enraged, he released [the arrow] at that terrible night-stalker.
Seeing that arrow, which possessed the brilliance of Indra’s thunderbolt, as it came rushing toward him,
the massive-bodied Ghaṭotkaca evaded it with great agility.
Once more, that fierce one roared, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
terrifying all living beings like a rain-cloud at the end of an eon.
Hearing that terrible roar of the rakṣasa Bhīṣma, [the monkeys were struck with fear].
Approaching his preceptor, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, said:
"Since this terrible roar is heard, uttered by the Rākṣasas,
it is certain that the son of Hiḍimbā is fighting with King Duryodhana."
Indeed, he cannot be conquered in battle by any living being;
go there— may you be blessed— and protect the king,
that highly fortunate one who is being assailed by the evil-minded Rākṣasa.
"O subduers of enemies, this indeed is the supreme duty for all of us.
Having heard these words of the grandfather, those great car-warriors, acting with haste,
exerted their utmost speed and proceeded to where the Kaurava was.
Droṇa, Somadatta, Bāhlika, and Jayadratha;
Kṛpa, Bhūriśravas, Śalya, Citrasena, and Vivimśati;
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, the prince of Avanti, and Bṛhadbala.
And many thousands of chariots followed them,
seeking to rescue your son Duryodhana as he was being pursued. That invincible army was protected by the best of men in the world.
Seeing the assailant approaching, that best of Rākṣasas,
the mighty-armed one, did not tremble, remaining as firm as Mount Maināka;
grasping his massive bow, he was surrounded by his kinsmen.
With spears and mallets in hand, and with various other weapons as well,
there then ensued a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end,
between the chief of the Rākṣasas and the army of Duryodhana.
O great king, the tumultuous sound of twanging bows arose from all sides; it was heard like the crackling of bamboos being consumed by fire,
as weapons were brought down upon the armor of the warriors.
O King, a sound arose like that of mountains splitting apart;
O Lord of the People, the appearance of the lances hurled by the arms of the heroes as they stayed in the sky was like that of slithering serpents.
Then, extremely enraged, the mighty-armed lord of the rākṣasas drew his great bow and, uttering a terrifying roar,
furiously severed the preceptor’s bow with a crescent-headed arrow.
Having struck down Somadatta’s standard with a broad-headed arrow, he let out a roar;
he pierced Bāhlīka in the center of the chest with three arrows,
struck Kṛpa with one, and Citrasena with three shafts.
With an arrow drawn to its full extent and released with perfect aim,
he struck Vikarṇa in the region of the collarbone;
drenched in blood, Vikarṇa sank down upon the seat of his chariot.
Then again, O bull of the Bharatas, the immeasurable-souled one, filled with rage, dispatched fifteen iron shafts at Bhūriśravas;
having pierced his armor, they swiftly entered the surface of the earth.
He struck the two charioteers of Vivimshati and the son of Drona;
they both fell upon the floors of their chariots, letting go of the horses' reins.
With a crescent-shaped arrow, he [struck] the boar-emblemed standard of the King of Sindhu, which was adorned with gold.
O great king, with a second [arrow] he struck him down, and with a fourth he severed his bow;
then, his eyes bloodshot with rage, he slew the four horses of the high-souled prince of Avanti with four iron shafts (nārācas).
O great king, with that sharp arrow drawn to its full extent and released, he pierced Prince Bṛhadbala. Deeply wounded and distressed, he sat down upon the floor of his chariot.
Overcome by intense rage, the lord of the Rākṣasas, standing upon his chariot,
discharged sharp, keen arrows resembling venomous serpents;
O great king, they pierced Śalya, who was skilled in battle.
O King, they entered the earth like serpents entering an anthill.
Sañjaya said:
Having turned all those on your side away in battle, the Rākṣasa—
Desirous of slaying him, O best of the Bharatas, he rushed toward Duryodhana.
Seeing that king rushing forward with great speed toward him,
your warriors, intoxicated by battle, charged at him, seeking to kill him.
Drawing bows as long as palm trees, those mighty warriors rushed toward him alone, roaring like a pride of lions;
then they surrounded him on all sides with a rain of arrows.
Like clouds in autumn drenching a mountain with torrents of water,
he was deeply pierced and pained like an elephant struck by a goad; then,
like the son of Vinatā, he leapt up into the sky from all sides.
He let out a tremendous roar like an autumnal thundercloud,
making the quarters, the sky, and the intermediate directions resound with his terrifying voice.
Hearing that sound of the Rākṣasa, King Yudhiṣṭhira—
The best of the Bharatas spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"Surely the Rākṣasa is fighting with the great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons,
for his roar is heard as he utters a terrible sound."
"O father, I perceive a heavy burden concentrated there:
the Grandfather (Bhīṣma) is enraged and intent on slaying the Pāñcālas,
while Phalguna fights against his enemies for their protection."

"O mighty-armed one, having heard this, two tasks have presented themselves: go and protect the son of Hiḍimbā, who has fallen into the greatest danger. Having received his brother’s command, Vṛkodara hurried away.

He set forth with a lion’s roar, terrifying all the kings, O King, with great speed like the ocean at the time of the new moon. Satyadhṛti, the son of Sucitti, who is difficult to vanquish in battle, followed him.
Śreṇimān, Vasudāna, and Abhibhū, the son of Kāśya;
the great chariot-warriors headed by Abhimanyu, the sons of Draupadī;
and the valiant Kṣatradeva, as well as Kṣatradharman.
Anūpādhipati, who was dark-complexioned and relied upon his own strength,
surrounded the son of Hiḍimbā with a great multitude of chariots and six thousand ever-intoxicated, striking elephants.
Together they protected Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
shaking the earth with their great lion-roars, the clatter of chariot rims, and the thundering sound of hooves.
O great king, hearing that sound of those advancing [foes], your army—
agitated by fear of Bhīmasena and with pale faces—
turned back, abandoning Ghaṭotkaca.
Then, in various places, a battle commenced between those high-souled warriors—
your own men and the enemy— who never retreated from combat.
Discharging weapons of many forms, the great car-warriors fought on.
Rushing at one another, they engaged in a fierce combat;
an intense and most terrible battle ensued, bringing fear to the timid. Horses clashed with elephants, and foot-soldiers with chariot-warriors.
Chariots encountered chariots and elephants met elephants in the battle,
O King, as they sought great glory against one another in the fray;
and from that violent collision, a thick cloud of dust suddenly arose.
A thick, smoky-red dust, raised by the feet and the rims of the wheels of chariots, horses, elephants, and infantry, completely shrouded the battlefield;
O King, neither one's own men nor the enemy could distinguish each other.

O best of the Bharatas, in that hair-raising slaughter where all bounds of propriety had vanished, fathers did not recognize their sons, nor did sons recognize their fathers; amidst the clashing of weapons and the roaring of men.
A tremendous sound arose like that of burning bamboos. There, a river of blood began to flow, with elephants, horses, and men as its current, and hair as its moss and aquatic grass.
From the bodies of men as their heads fell in battle,
a tremendous sound was heard, like that of falling stones; likewise,
with headless men and elephants with severed limbs.
The earth became strewn with horses whose bodies were mangled;
the great car-warriors, discharging various kinds of weapons and charging at one another, engaged in a fierce combat.
Horses, urged on by their riders, having encountered other horses,
struck one another in battle and fell down, deprived of life.
Men, having encountered other men, their eyes intensely red with rage, [fell upon one another].
Embracing one another chest to chest, they struck each other down;
and elephants sent forth by the mahāmātras,
those great tuskers, struck down other elephants in the battle with the tips of their tusks.
Adorned with crests of blood and decorated with banners,
they appeared joined together like clouds accompanied by lightning;
some were pierced by the tips of tusks, and others had their frontal globes shattered by *tomara* lances.
Crying out and roaring like clouds, some rushed forward;
others, with arms severed in two and their limbs likewise mangled,
fell in that tumultuous fray like mountains whose wings have been clipped.
Others, those excellent elephants, with their flanks torn open by other elephants,
shed copious blood like mountains discharging minerals. Still others were struck by iron arrows and likewise pierced by javelins.
With their riders slain, they appeared like mountains stripped of their peaks.
Some, overcome by rage, blinded by intoxication, and unrestrained,
crushed chariots, horses, and foot soldiers by the hundreds on the battlefield.

Likewise, horses struck by horsemen with spears and javelins turned back in every direction, throwing the quarters of the sky into confusion. Chariot-warriors, sons of noble lineage who were ready to cast away their lives, engaged with other chariot-warriors.
Relying upon their supreme power, they performed their deeds fearlessly;
like those at a svayaṃvara,
O King, those warriors, seeking either glory or heaven, struck one another in that crushing conflict.
While that hair-raising battle was thus proceeding,
the great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons was for the most part turned away from the fight.
Saṃjaya said:
Seeing his own army slaughtered, King Duryodhana himself,
filled with rage, rushed toward Bhīmasena, the tamer of foes,
grasping a massive bow whose sound was like Indra’s thunderbolt.
With a great shower of arrows, he overwhelmed the Pāṇḍava; then,
filled with rage, he fixed a very sharp, feathered crescent-headed arrow and cut through Bhīmasena’s bow.
Observing that interval, the great car-warrior acted with haste;
he fixed a sharpened arrow capable of splitting even mountains, and with it,
the mighty-armed one struck Bhīmasena in the chest.
Deeply pierced and pained, licking the corners of his mouth, the spirited warrior clung to his gold-adorned banner. Seeing Bhimasena thus despondent, Ghaṭotkaca—
He blazed up in fury like a fire wishing to consume everything;
and the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, led by Abhimanyu,
rushed toward the king, crying out in a state of great agitation.
Seeing them rushing forward, enraged and filled with agitation,
the son of Bharadvāja spoke these words to the great car-warriors of your side:
"Go quickly— may you be blessed— and protect the king!"
Having fallen into the utmost doubt and sinking into an ocean of calamity,
these enraged great archers, the mighty chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas,
placing Bhīmasena at their head, have rushed against Duryodhana.
Discharging various kinds of weapons and intent on victory, they uttered terrible roars, terrifying this earth. Then, having heard those words of the Preceptor, the warriors led by Somadatta—
Your warriors—
Kṛpa, Bhūriśravas, Śalya, the son of Droṇa, Vivimśati, Citrasena, Vikarṇa, the ruler of the Sindhus, and Bṛhadbala— advanced against the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
And those two great archers from Avanti surrounded the Kaurava.
Having advanced twenty paces, they began the combat—
the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— each desiring to slay the other.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one drew his great bow wide;
then the son of Bharadvāja struck Bhīma with twenty-six arrows.
Furthermore, the mighty-armed one quickly overwhelmed him again with shafts.
Like a cloud in autumn drenching a mountain with torrents of water,
Bhīmasena, the mighty archer of great strength, acting with haste, pierced him on his left side with ten stone-tipped arrows.

Deeply pierced and pained, O Bhārata, he who was advanced in years suddenly sat down on the floor of his chariot, losing consciousness. Seeing his preceptor so greatly distressed, King Duryodhana himself [acted].
The son of Droṇa and [Aśvatthāman], both enraged, rushed toward Bhīmasena. Seeing them charging like Kāla, Antaka,
and Yama, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena quickly took up his mace.
Quickly leaping down from his chariot, he stood firm like an immovable mountain,
raising his heavy mace which resembled the staff of Yama in battle;
seeing him with mace uplifted, like Mount Kailāsa with its peaks, [the enemy was struck with awe].
The Kaurava and the son of Droṇa rushed forward together.
As those two best among the strong approached together in haste,
Vṛkodara, hurrying himself, charged toward them with speed.
Beholding him rushing forward, enraged and of fearsome appearance,
all the great car-warriors of the Kauravas, led by the son of Bharadvāja, quickly charged at him with the intent to slay Bhīmasena.
They rained down various kinds of weapons upon Bhīma’s chest;
all together, they oppressed the Pāṇḍava from every side.
Seeing that great car-warrior fallen into danger and being thus afflicted, [the others rushed forward].
The great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, headed by Abhimanyu,
rushed forward, desiring to rescue him and having renounced their lives which are so difficult to give up.
The heroic lord of Anūpa, the beloved friend of Bhīma, [also joined them].
Nīla, who resembled a dark blue cloud and was ever vying with the son of Droṇa, being highly enraged, rushed toward the son of Droṇa;
stretching his great bow, he pierced the son of Droṇa with a feathered shaft.
Just as in the past, O Great King, Śakra pierced the Dānava Vipracitti—
who was difficult to overcome and a source of terror to the gods—
by whom the three worlds were struck with fear through his own splendor and wrath.
Previously defeated by Rudra and slain by Mātariśvan, and likewise pierced by Nīla and the bird Sumukha,
the son of Droṇa, with a gushing flow of blood, was filled with rage.
Stretching his variegated bow, which resounded like Indra’s thunderbolt,
that best of the wise set his mind upon the destruction of Nīla.
Then, having fixed to it stainless broad-headed arrows tempered by a smith, he drew them back.
He struck down the four horses and caused the standard to fall;
then, with a sixth broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he felled the charioteer from the chariot,
and with another single broad-headed arrow, he swept the charioteer away from the seat of the car.
And with a seventh broad-headed arrow, he pierced Nīla in the chest.
Deeply pierced and pained, he sat down on the floor of his chariot.
Seeing King Nīla, who resembled a mass of clouds, thus rendered unconscious, [he...].
Ghaṭotkaca also, filled with rage and surrounded by his brothers,
rushed with speed toward the son of Droṇa, who graces the field of battle;
likewise, the other Rākṣasas, intoxicated by war, charged forward.
The heroic Bhīmasena also, having mounted Nīla— who shone like black collyrium— upon his own chariot in the midst of battle, rushed toward Duryodhana.
Beholding that Rākṣasa of terrible appearance as he charged forward, [he...].
The radiant son of Bharadvāja rushed forward in haste and,
filled with rage, struck down the Rākṣasas of fearsome appearance who had stood before him as the angry Rākṣasa's vanguard.
Seeing them turned away by the arrows shot from the bow of Droṇa’s son, the massive-bodied Ghaṭotkaca, son of Bhīmasena, grew enraged;
he manifested a great illusion, terrible in form and most dreadful.
Deluding the son of Droṇa in battle, that lord of the Rākṣasas, a master of illusion,
then caused all your men to turn away through his magic;
they beheld one another cut down upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing them writhing piteously, drenched in blood—
Droṇa, Duryodhana, Śalya, and Aśvatthāman,
as well as most of the great archers who were the foremost among the Kauravas— [he was filled with grief].
All the chariot-warriors were shattered, the elephants were struck down,
and horses along with their riders were cut to pieces by the thousands.
Seeing that, your army fled toward the camp.
"O King, while I and Devavrata were thus crying out, 'Fight!
Do not flee! This is an illusion employed by Ghaṭotkaca in battle,' they did not stand their ground, being utterly deluded."
Terrified, they did not believe the words we two were speaking;
and seeing them fleeing and the Pāṇḍavas victorious,
accompanied by Ghaṭotkaca, they let out lion-like roars.
And the sounds of conchs and kettledrums resounded loudly on all sides. Thus, at the hour of sunset, your entire army was shattered by the evil-minded son of Hiḍimbā and fled in all directions.
Saṃjaya said:
In that great tumult, King Duryodhana,
the scorcher of foes, could not endure his defeat at the hands of the Rākṣasa.
Approaching the son of Gaṅgā and saluting him with humility,
he began to relate everything exactly as it had happened:
the victory of Ghaṭotkaca and his own defeat.
Sighing again and again, the invincible one spoke;
and then, O King, he addressed Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus:
"Having relied upon you, just as [the Pandavas] rely on Vāsudeva against their enemies..."
"O Lord, a terrible conflict has been commenced by me with the Pāṇḍavas. O scorcher of enemies, those eleven *akṣauhiṇīs* that are said to be mine stand at your command along with me."
O tiger among the Bharatas, having relied upon Ghaṭotkaca, I have been defeated in battle by the Pāṇḍavas led by Bhīmasena;
that burns my limbs like fire consumes a dry tree.
Therefore, O illustrious one, O scorcher of foes, I desire through your grace,
O Grandfather, to slay that lowest of Rākṣasas myself;
relying upon you, O invincible one, you ought to grant me the means to accomplish this.
O best of the Bharatas, having heard these words of the king,
Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"Listen, O King, to my words which I shall speak to you, O Kaurava."
"O Great King, O scorcher of foes, you must conduct yourself in such a way that your own self is protected in battle at all times, my dear,
O subduer of enemies. O sinless one, you must always engage in combat with Dharmarāja."
O King, you should not engage in combat with the evil-minded son of Hiḍimbā, even if he were to face Arjuna, the twins, or Bhīmasena again; for,
upholding the duty of a king, a king should seek out another king.
I, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata; Śalya, the son of Somadatta, and the great car-warrior Vikarṇa; and your heroic brothers, led by Duḥśāsana.
"For your sake, we shall fight that Rākṣasa of great strength.
If you have a great longing for that fierce lord of the Rākṣasas,
then let this one go to battle against that evil-minded one."
"Bhagadatta, the protector of the earth, is equal to Purandara in battle.
Having said this much to the king, he who was skilled in speech then addressed these words to King Bhagadatta in the presence of that lord of kings.
"Go quickly, O great king, and with diligence restrain the son of Hiḍimbā,
who is fierce in battle, in the midst of all the archers while they look on—
restrain that Rākṣasa of cruel deeds, just as Indra did Tāraka in ancient times."
O scorcher of the foe, you possess celestial weapons and supreme prowess;
in the past, you have encountered many asuras together. O tiger among kings, you shall be the one to fight him back in the great battle.
"O King, surrounded by your own forces, slay that bull among Rākṣasas.
Having heard these words of Bhīṣma, the commander of the army,
he quickly advanced toward the enemy with a lion’s roar.
Seeing him rushing forward like a thundering cloud,
the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas turned back in a rage:
Bhīmasena, Abhimanyu, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca.
O sire, the sons of Draupadī, Satyadhṛti, and Kṣatradeva,
as well as Vasudāna the king of the Cedis and the lord of the Daśārṇas—
Bhagadatta likewise rushed against them along with Supratīka.

Then there occurred a battle of terrible form and fearsome aspect between the Pāṇḍavas and Bhagadatta, which increased the population of Yama’s kingdom. Sharp-pointed arrows of fearsome velocity were released by the chariot-warriors.
O great king, they fell upon the elephants and the chariots; and the great elephants, with temporal lobes bursting, though well-trained by their riders,
encountered one another and charged fearlessly.
Blinded by intoxication and agitated by rage, they encountered one another in that great battle and pierced each other with the tips of their horns and their mace-like tusks.
And there were horses adorned with yak-tail plumes, ridden by men holding spears in their hands.
Urged on by their riders, they swiftly fell upon one another; and foot soldiers, struck by throngs of infantry with spears and lances,
then fell to the ground by the hundreds and thousands.

And likewise, O King, the chariot-warriors, having slain heroes in battle with barbed and reed-tipped arrows, let out lion-like roars. While that hair-raising battle was thus proceeding, [the combatants] cried out.
Then the great archer Bhagadatta rushed toward Bhīmasena on an elephant in rut,
with temporal juice flowing from seven parts of its body like water streaming from every side down a mountain.
O sinless one, stationed upon Airāvata like Maghavat pouring down torrents of rain, he who was mounted upon Supratīka’s head discharged thousands of arrows;
that king struck Bhīma with those showers of shafts.
Like a cloud in the rainy season drenching a mountain with torrents of water,
the great archer Bhīmasena, filled with rage, furiously struck down more than a hundred foot-guards with showers of arrows.
Seeing them slain, the powerful Bhagadatta became enraged and urged his lordly elephant toward the chariot of Bhīmasena. That elephant, dispatched by him, was like an arrow impelled by the bowstring.
He rushed with speed toward Bhīmasena, the tamer of foes. Seeing him charging, the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, led by Bhīmasena, advanced with force against him.
The Kekayas, Abhimanyu, and all the sons of Draupadī,
O noble one, as well as the heroic lord of the Daśārṇas, Kṣatradeva,
and Citraketu of Cedi— all of them were filled with fury.
Displaying supreme divine weapons, those of great strength,
filled with rage, surrounded that single elephant from all sides.
Pierced by many arrows, that great elephant shone resplendently.
With a gushing flow of blood, he appeared like the king of mountains variegated with mineral ores;
and the lord of Daśārṇa, mounted upon an elephant resembling a mountain,
charged toward Bhagadatta’s elephant.
As that elephant charged in battle, the lord of elephants,
Supratīka, held it back just as the shore holds back the ocean;
and Kṣatradharman, in turn, held Supratīka back with his own elephant.
Seeing the lord of the *nāgas* repulsed by the high-souled King of Daśārṇa, the Pandava troops honored him, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
Thereupon, the King of Prāgjyotiṣa, filled with rage, hurled fourteen lances.
O best of kings, he hurled it at the front of that elephant;
piercing through its armor and its mouth-protector— which was adorned with gold— it quickly entered [the beast] like serpents into an anthill.
Deeply pierced and pained, O best of the Bharatas, that elephant,
its rut suddenly subsiding, quickly turned back with speed and fled away,
uttering a terrible cry.
Crushing his own army with his might like the wind crushing trees,
that elephant was defeated; then the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas,
uttering loud lion-roars, stood ready for battle.
Then, placing Bhīma at their head, they rushed toward Bhagadatta,
scattering various arrows and diverse weapons. O King, as they were charging forward, enraged and impatient, [Bhagadatta confronted them].
Hearing that terrible roar, the great archer Bhagadatta, his fear dispelled by indignation, urged his own elephant forward in battle;
impelled by the goad and his big toe, that preeminent elephant advanced into the fray.
At that moment, he became like the fire of universal destruction;
highly enraged, he [consumed] multitudes of chariots, as well as elephants and horses along with their riders, and foot-soldiers by the hundreds and thousands.
O King, as he rushed here and there in battle, he crushed [the enemy];
and that great army of the Pāṇḍavas, being agitated by him,
O Great King, shriveled up like a piece of leather placed in a fire.
Seeing his own army broken by the wise Bhagadatta,
Ghaṭotkaca then rushed toward Bhagadatta in a great rage—
O King, a man of terrifying form, with a blazing face and flaming eyes.
Assuming a terrifying form and as if blazing with rage,
he seized a massive spear capable of splitting even mountains;
desiring to slay the naga, the one of great strength hurled it suddenly.
Seeing that [missile] suddenly approaching in battle, enveloped on all sides by flames and sparks, and filled with fire,
that king hurled a beautiful and sharp crescent-headed arrow (ardhacandra).
With that swift arrow,
he cut down the massive spear; severed in two, the gold-adorned spear fell like a great thunderbolt released by Śakra falling from the sky.
Seeing the spear fallen, cut in two, that king seized a great javelin with a golden shaft that resembled a flame of fire;
he hurled it at the Rākṣasa and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"
Seeing it falling like a thunderbolt suspended in the sky,
the Rākṣasa leaped up, swiftly seized it, and roared; then,
O Bhārata, he quickly broke it by pressing it against his knee.
As the lord of kings looked on, it was like a marvel;
seeing that deed accomplished by the powerful Rākṣasa,
the gods in heaven, along with the Gandharvas and the sages, were filled with wonder.

And the Pāṇḍavas, those great archers led by Bhīmasena, made the earth resound with the cry, "Excellent! Excellent! Hearing that great roar of the exultant high-souled ones, [Duryodhana was filled with fear].
The powerful and great archer Bhagadatta could not endure this;
stretching his great bow, which sounded like Indra’s thunderbolt,
he rushed with speed toward the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas.
Discharging stainless, sharp iron arrows with the brilliance of fire,
he pierced Bhīma with one arrow, the Rākṣasa with nine,
Abhimanyu with three, and the Kekayas with five.
With a feathered arrow, gold-tufted and released from a fully drawn bow,
he pierced the right arm of Kṣatradeva in battle;
his excellent bow, along with the arrow, suddenly fell to the ground.
Then he struck the five sons of Draupadī with five arrows each;
and out of rage, he slew Bhīmasena’s horses and cut down his lion-standard with three shafts.
With three other feathered shafts,
he pierced his charioteer; deeply wounded and pained, O best of the Bharatas, Viśoka sat down on the floor of the chariot in that battle with Bhagadatta.
Then, O great king, Bhīma— the best among chariot-warriors— being deprived of his chariot,
seized a mace and swiftly leaped down from that great vehicle.
Seeing him with his mace raised, like a mountain with its peaks, [the enemy was struck with fear].
O Bhārata, a terrible fear seized your men.
At that very moment, O great king, the Pāṇḍava with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer arrived, slaughtering enemies by the thousands.
O best of the Bharatas, he arrived there in haste, scattering arrows. Then King Duryodhana, that great car-warrior, acting with urgency,
quickly urged on his army, which was crowded with chariots, elephants, and horses.
As that great army of the Kauravas was suddenly charging forward,
the Pāṇḍava Śvetavāhana (Arjuna) rushed against it with speed,
O Bhārata; and Bhagadatta also, in that battle, [advanced] with that elephant.
Crushing the Pāṇḍava army, he rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira. Then, O sire, there occurred a tumultuous battle between Bhagadatta and the Pañcālas, Sṛñjayas, and Kekayas, who had raised their weapons.
Bhimasena also, in that battle, reported to both Kesava and Arjuna exactly what had occurred regarding the supreme slaughter of Iravat. Sanjaya said:

Having heard that his son Irāvant had been slain, Dhanañjaya, overcome with great sorrow and sighing like a serpent, O King, spoke these words to Vāsudeva on the battlefield: 06.092.001a Having heard that his son Irāvant had been killed, Dhanañjaya, 06.092.001c overcome with great grief, sighing like a snake, 06.092.002a spoke these words to Vāsudeva in the midst of battle, O King.
Surely the highly wise and great-minded Vidura foresaw long ago this terrible destruction of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas;
therefore, he sought to restrain Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men.

"O Madhusūdana, many heroes who should not have been slain were killed by the Kauravas in battle, and likewise they have been killed by us. O best of men, for the sake of wealth, a despicable deed is being committed."
"Fie on wealth, for it is for the sake of wealth that this destruction of kinsmen is being carried out! For one without wealth, death is better than wealth gained through the slaughter of kinsmen.
What indeed shall we gain, O Kṛṣṇa, by killing these assembled relatives?"
"Through the transgression of Duryodhana and Śakuni the son of Subala,
and through the evil counsel of Karṇa, the Kṣatriyas are going to their destruction;
and now, O Madhusūdana, I understand what was well done."
O mighty-armed one, the king made an offer to Suyodhana, requesting either half the kingdom or even five villages; yet that evil-minded man did not grant it.
For he saw the heroic Kṣatriyas lying upon the surface of the earth.
I severely reproach myself; fie upon the life of a warrior! These kṣatriyas will perceive me as powerless in battle;
O Madhusūdana, fighting with these kinsmen is indeed appropriate for me.
"Urge the horses quickly toward the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son!
With my two arms, I shall cross this ocean of battle, which has a vast shore.
O Mādhava, there is no time at all for faint-heartedness."
Thus addressed by Pārtha, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
urged on those white horses that were as swift as the wind.
Then, O Bhārata, a great clamor arose from your army.
Like the ocean at the time of the full moon, its force stirred up by the Maruts,
he swiftly urged on his radiant chariot with great speed.
O Great King, in the afternoon, the battle commenced.
With a roar like that of the rain-cloud, Bhīṣma [fought] together with the Pāṇḍavas;
then, O King, your sons rushed toward Bhīmasena,
surrounding Droṇa in battle just as the Vasus surround Vāsava.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, and Kṛpa, the best of chariot-warriors,
as well as Bhagadatta and Suśarman, rushed toward Dhanañjaya. Hārdikya and Bāhlika likewise charged against Sātyaki.
King Ambaṣṭhaka, however, held back Abhimanyu;
the remaining others, O great king, engaged the remaining great car-warriors. Then there commenced a battle of terrible form, inspiring fear.
But Bhīmasena, O lord of men, beholding your sons,
blazed up in battle with rage like a sacrificial fire fed with oblations.
Your sons, however, covered the son of Kuntī with their arrows.
O great king, like clouds covering a mountain during the rainy season,
he was covered in many ways by your sons, O lord of the people;
licking the corners of his mouth, the hero was as proud as a tiger.
Then, O King, Bhīma struck down Vyūḍhoraska with an exceedingly sharp razor-headed arrow; thus,
in that great battle, he was deprived of life by that well-aimed shaft.
Enraged, he struck him...
with another sharp, polished broad-headed arrow (bhalla),
he felled Kuṇḍalin like a lion brings down a small deer.
Then the mighty Bhīmasena, filled with wrath, took up many well-sharpened, yellow-feathered arrows and discharged them in that battle. Then, enraged in the fray, Bhīmasena [discharged] those shafts.
O noble one, having reached your seven sons with great haste,
those arrows dispatched by Bhīmasena, the wielder of the firm bow,
struck down your sons— those great car-warriors— from their chariots.
Anādhṛṣṭi, Kuṇḍabheda, Vairāṭa, Dīrghalocana,
Dīrghabāhu, Subāhu, and likewise Kanakadhvaja—
those heroes, as they fell, shone forth, O bull of the Bharatas.
Like mango trees variegated with blossoms in spring that have suddenly fallen,
the remaining sons of yours then fled, O lord of the people,
regarding the mighty Bhīmasena as if he were Time itself.
But the mighty-armed Droṇa, in that battle, checked the powerful Bhīmasena as he was consuming your sons,
covering him on all sides with arrows just as a mountain is drenched by torrents of rain.
There we beheld the marvelous prowess of Kuntī’s son:
that even while being restrained by Droṇa, he slaughtered your sons.
For just as a bull bears the rain falling from the sky, so did he endure [the restraint].
In that manner, Bhīma withstood the shower of arrows released by Droṇa;
closing his eyes as one might catch [a falling object], the Pāṇḍava thus received that unassailable rain of shafts produced from Droṇa’s bow.
Closing his eyes, Vṛkodara likewise grasped the arrows;
and there, O great king, Vṛkodara performed a marvel,
in that he slew your sons in battle and even fought against Droṇa.
O great king, the elder brother of Arjuna sported among your heroic sons like a mighty tiger roaming among deer;
or rather, like a wolf standing in the midst of cattle, he would drive them away.
Vṛkodara likewise put your sons to flight in battle; meanwhile,
Bhīṣma the son of Gaṅgā, Bhagadatta, and the great car-warrior Gautama held back the impetuous Pāṇḍava Arjuna in the fight.
Having warded off their weapons with his own weapons in that battle,
that great car-warrior dispatched the foremost heroes among your troops to death;
and Abhimanyu [attacked] the world-renowned king Ambaṣṭha.
With his arrows, he deprived that best of chariot-warriors of his chariot.
Deprived of his chariot and being struck by the illustrious son of Subhadrā,
that lord of men quickly leaped down from his vehicle in great shame.
In that battle, he hurled his sword at the high-souled son of Subhadrā and ascended the chariot of the high-souled Hārdikya;
however, as the sword came rushing toward him, [Kṛṣṇa], who was skilled in the ways of combat, [intercepted it].

With great agility, Saubhadra, the slayer of enemy heroes, baffled [his opponent's sword]. O lord of the people, seeing his sword thus baffled by Saubhadra in that battle, a great roar of "Excellent! Excellent! arose from the troops.
Then, O lord of men, seeing himself unarmed,
others led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna fought against your army;
likewise, all your men fought against the Pandava host.
There, O Bhārata, a great outcry arose from both you and them as they struck one another violently, performing deeds of great difficulty;
then a terrible battle commenced, like that of Hārdikya.
For in that battle, O noble one, those heroes, having seized one another by the hair,
fought with their nails and teeth, as well as with fists and knees; and with arms, palms, and even very sharp swords.
Finding openings against one another, they led each other to the abode of Yama;
in that battle, father struck son and son struck father,
as men fought there with their resolve utterly confounded.
O Bhārata, there lay on the battlefield beautiful bows with golden backs,
discarded by the slain, as well as costly quivers; and there were sharp arrows with shafts made of gold and silver.
Washed with oil, they shone like snakes that have cast off their skins;
there were swords with ivory hilts adorned with gold,
and discarded shields with golden backs belonging to the archers.
Spears fashioned from gold, *paṭṭiśas* adorned with gold, spears made of refined gold,
and javelins blazing with gold;
and heavy clubs that had been severed and fallen.
O noble one, there were iron clubs, spears, and slings;
fallen javelins, too, variegated and adorned with gold;
and blankets of many forms, as well as yak-tail fans.
Having cast aside various kinds of weapons, the fallen men—
those great car-warriors whose vital strength had departed— appeared as if they were still alive,
with their limbs crushed by maces and their heads split by clubs.
Crushed by elephants, horses, and chariots, men lay upon the earth;
likewise, O King, the ground then shone, covered on all sides with the bodies of horses, men, and elephants, as if strewn with mountains.
And with spears, double-edged swords, arrows, and *tomaras* fallen in the battle;
with scimitars, *paṭṭiśas*, darts, iron lances, and axes; as well as with clubs, *bhiṇḍipālas*, and *śataghnīs*.

O slayer of enemies, the earth was strewn with bodies pierced by weapons— some silent, some making little sound, all drenched in floods of blood; covered by these lifeless forms, the great ground shone forth.
The earth there was covered with arms adorned with armlets and smeared with sandalwood paste, still clutching firmly held clubs,
as well as with the severed thighs of the swift warriors, which resembled the trunks of elephants.

O Bhārata, the earth shone with the fallen arms of those bull-eyed warriors, still adorned with armlets and severed from their bodies; and with their heads, wearing crest-jewels and earrings, that lay scattered upon the ground.
With scattered golden armors smeared with blood,
the earth shone intensely, as if with fires whose flames have been extinguished;
likewise with quivers cast aside and bows fallen.
The ground was strewn everywhere with scattered arrows fletched with gold,
with many broken chariots adorned with networks of tiny bells,
and with slain horses covered in blood, their tongues lolling out.
The earth shone with the fallen chariot-poles, banners, quivers, and standards;
with the great white conchs of the preeminent heroes scattered about;
and with elephants lying there, their trunks hanging limp.
O King, the earth shone as if with blazing mountains;
with the fallen ornaments,
the ground then gleamed like a young woman adorned with various kinds of decorations.
And there, with other elephants in intense agony,
armed with lances and emitting cries from their trunks while repeatedly spraying ichor,
that battlefield shone like mountains being smelted.
It was covered on all sides with multi-colored woolen blankets and elephant housings, as well as variegated and outspread elephant rugs,
and beautiful goads with handles of beryl that had fallen about.
With the bells of the lordly elephants fallen on all sides,
with various colorful blankets and likewise with woolen cloths, with neck-chains of diverse forms and even with golden girths;
O lord of the people, the earth there shone most brilliantly with various kinds of shattered mechanical weapons and kampana-equipped javelins,
and with breastplates covered in gold that were turned tawny by the dust of horses.
And with the severed arms of horsemen fallen there, still adorned with armlets,
as well as with bright, sharp spears, gleaming javelins,
and turbans cut to pieces and scattered here and there.
With various crescent-shaped ornaments adorned with gold,
with crushed blankets for horse-covers made of *rāṅkava* wool,
and with diverse, highly precious crest-jewels of kings;
With discarded umbrellas and yak-tail fans as well,
and with faces possessing the luster of lotuses and moons, adorned with beautiful earrings and highly decorated with well-trimmed beards— such were the faces of the fallen heroes.
O great king, with discarded earrings blazing with gold,
the earth became like the sky variegated by planets and stars.
Thus, O Bhārata, were those two great armies crushed there.
Having encountered one another in that battle between you and them,
O Bhārata, when they were exhausted, broken, and crushed,
a terrible night set in, and we could no longer see the field of combat.

Then, at the onset of the terrible, fierce, and most dreadful night, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas ordered the withdrawal of their armies. Having thus made the withdrawal, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas remained together.
Having gone to their own camp at that time, they entered it according to the proper hour.
Then Sañjaya said:
"Then King Duryodhana and Śakuni, the son of Subala,"

Your son Duḥśāsana and the invincible Sūtaputra, O great king, having come together, held a consultation regarding their intended purpose: "How may the sons of Pāṇḍu, along with their followers, be conquered in battle?"
Then King Duryodhana addressed all those ministers,
speaking to the Sūta’s son and the mighty Saubala:
"Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, Śalya, and the son of Somadatta are in battle."
They do not oppose the sons of Pṛthā, and I know not the reason for this;
yet, remaining unslain themselves, they continue to destroy my army. Thus, O Karṇa, I am one whose strength is exhausted and whose weapons are spent in this battle.
"O son of Rādhā, while you and I were looking on, those heroic brothers of mine were slain by Bhīmasena in the very presence of Droṇa.
They were treated with contempt by the Pāṇḍavas, who are heroes that cannot be slain even by the gods."
Thus, fallen into doubt, I wonder how I shall conduct this battle,
O one of great strength and great wisdom, proficient in all the scriptures,
a knower of mantras, possessed of mantras, skillful, ethical, and an expert in policy.
"He is a hero, he is valiant, the son of the Sun, full of majesty—
how shall I cross this battle that causes such great terror? To him,
O Great King, the Sūta's son spoke to the lord of men:
"Do not grieve, O best of the Bharatas; I shall do what is pleasing to you.
Let Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, quickly withdraw from this great battle.
When the son of Gaṅgā has desisted from the fight and laid down his weapons, O Bhārata..."

"I shall slay the Pārthas, even though they are accompanied by all the Somakas, while Bhīṣma looks on in battle; I swear this to you in truth, O King. For Bhīṣma, O King, always maintains compassion toward the Pāṇḍavas."
Bhīṣma is incapable of conquering these great car-warriors in battle;
yet Bhīṣma is full of pride and is ever fond of combat. How then, my dear, will he defeat the Pāṇḍavas when they are united in war?

Therefore, O Bhārata, go quickly from here toward Bhīṣma’s camp; having obtained his consent in battle, make him lay down his weapons. Then, when Bhīṣma has laid down his weapons, behold the Pāṇḍavas as slain.
"O King, by me alone in battle [shall they be slain], along with their circles of friends and kinsmen.
Thus addressed by Karṇa, your son Duryodhana then spoke these words to his brother Duḥśāsana.
"O Duḥśāsana, ensure that the entire retinue is prepared in every respect; provide everything very quickly. Having spoken thus, O King, the lord of men then addressed Karṇa.
"O subduer of enemies, having paid my respects to Bhīṣma, the best of men, in battle,
I shall then return quickly to your side;
thereafter, O tiger among men, you shall engage in the combat."
Then, O lord of the people, your son quickly rushed forth together with all his brothers, like Śatakratu with the gods;
then [he approached] that tiger among kings, whose prowess was equal to that of a tiger.
Then his brother Duḥśāsana quickly helped the king mount the horse;
adorned with armlets, a bound crown, and hand-ornaments, O great king,
that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shone like Mahendra himself.
Anointed with the most excellent, fragrant sandalwood paste, which resembled the *bhāṇḍī* flower and was like refined gold,
the king— clothed in dustless garments and possessing the playful gait of a lion— advanced.
He shone with stainless radiance like the sun in autumn.
As that tiger among men proceeded toward Bhīṣma’s camp,
the great archers— the bowmen of all the world— followed him.
And his brothers, great archers like the thirty gods surrounding Vāsava,
surrounded him on all sides— some mounting horses, others elephants, O Bhārata, and other best of men on chariots.
And foot soldiers, swift and fighting with claws and spears,
surrounded the great archer, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that great chariot-warrior;
and his friends, having taken up their weapons, stood there for the protection of the lord of the earth.
They appeared together like the immortals with Śakra in heaven;
being honored by the Kurus, O King, that great chariot-warrior of the Kauravas proceeded to the abode of the illustrious son of Gaṅgā.
Followed on all sides by his brothers gathered together, the king, being himself skillful,
then raised his right arm at the proper time—
that arm which resembled the trunk of an elephant, was trained in battle, and was the destroyer of all enemies.
Accepting the joined palms raised by men from every direction,
he heard the sweet words of those dwelling in various lands;
the highly illustrious one was being extolled by bards and panegyrists.
And while worshipping all of them, the Lord of the lords of all worlds [was honored] there with golden lamps filled with fragrant oil;
they surrounded that Great-Souled One on all sides with those blazing lights.
Just as Indra shines amidst the gods and asuras in a terrifying battle,
so did that king, surrounded by those beautiful golden lamps,
gleam like the moon joined with blazing great planets.
There, men wearing tunics and turbans, with canes and rattles in their hands,
were slowly clearing the people away in every direction;
then the king reached the auspicious residence of Bhīṣma.
Having dismounted from his horse and approached Bhīṣma, O lord of men,
he then saluted Bhīṣma and sat down upon an excellent seat—
a golden throne, auspicious on all sides, covered with a costly carpet.
With palms joined in reverence, his throat choked with emotion and eyes filled with tears, he said to Bhīṣma:
"O destroyer of enemies, by relying upon you in battle,
we have the courage to conquer even the gods and asuras led by Indra in the field of war."
How much more so the heroic sons of Pāṇḍu, along with their circles of friends and kinsmen?
Therefore, O Lord, O son of Gaṅgā, you ought to show me mercy;
slay the heroic sons of Pāṇḍu as Mahendra slays the Dānavas.
"O mighty-armed Bhārata, it was previously said by me: 'I shall slay the Somakas, the Pāñcālas along with the Pāṇḍavas, and the Karūṣas.
Let those words come true; slay the sons of Pṛthā who have assembled here."

And [protect] the Somakas, those great archers; O Bhārata, be true to your word! Whether out of compassion, O King, or because of my state as one you detest, O Lord, or even due to my own misfortune, you are protecting the Pāṇḍavas.
"Give permission for Karṇa, the ornament of battle, to enter the fray;
he shall conquer the Pārthas along with their circles of friends and kinsmen in combat.
Having said this much, O King, your son Duryodhana—
He did not utter a single word to Bhīṣma of terrible prowess.
Sañjaya said:
"The grandfather, having been deeply pierced by the word-arrows of your son..."
Overwhelmed by great sorrow, he did not utter even the slightest unpleasant word.
Filled with grief and rage, he meditated for a very long time,
hissing like a serpent prodded by a stick.
Rolling his eyes in anger as if to consume everything, O Bhārata,
that best of those who know the world spoke these words, preceded by a conciliatory tone, to your son, including the worlds of the gods, asuras, and gandharvas.
Why indeed, O Duryodhana, do you pierce me thus with wordy shafts,
when I am striving to the best of my ability, performing what is pleasing to you,
and offering up my very life in battle out of a desire for your welfare?

When the heroic Pāṇḍava gratified the fire-god Agni at Khāṇḍava after defeating Śakra in battle— that is sufficient proof. And when you, O mighty-armed one, were forcibly carried off by the Gandharvas—
The son of Pāṇḍu liberated him; that is sufficient proof. O Lord, while his own heroic brothers were likewise fleeing, and while the Sūta’s son, Rādheya, was present—that too is sufficient proof.
And that he then advanced alone against all of us gathered together in the city of Virāṭa— that is sufficient proof. Furthermore,
having defeated both Droṇa, who was enraged in battle, and myself in combat—
He took away the garments of Karṇa, yourself, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛpa, that great car-warrior;
that was sufficient proof.
Likewise, he did so to the son of Droṇa, the great archer, and also to the son of Śaradvat.

In the past, he conquered the seizure of the cows; that is sufficient proof. Furthermore, when he defeated Karṇa—who always prided himself on his manliness—and gave him a garment for Uttarā, that too is sufficient proof.

In battle, Pārtha conquered even the Nivātakavacas, who were difficult to defeat even for Vāsava; that is sufficient proof. This must certainly be done by the wise son of Pṛṣata, who desires our welfare.

For who indeed is able to defeat the impetuous Pāṇḍava in battle— he whose protector is Vāsudeva, the guardian of the world, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace, possessed of infinite power, and the cause of creation and destruction?
"O King Suyodhana, you have been told many times by great sages such as Nārada that you are the Lord of All, the God of Gods, the Supreme Self, and the Eternal One;
yet out of delusion, you do not understand what should and should not be said."
"For a man on the verge of death sees all trees as made of gold;
even so, O son of Gandhārī, you perceive things perversely,
having yourself created this great enmity with the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas."
Fight them today in battle; let us see it! Be a man!
The Pāṇḍavas cannot be conquered even by the gods led by Indra himself. As for me, I shall [conquer] all the Somakas assembled together with the Pañcālas.
"O tiger among men, I shall slay them all, with the sole exception of Śikhaṇḍin.
Either, being slain by them in battle, I shall go to the abode of Yama;
or, having slain them in combat, I shall surely grant you joy."
"For previously, Śikhaṇḍin was born as a woman in the royal palace; through the granting of a boon, he became a man. Yet she is truly that same woman, Śikhaṇḍinī.
Therefore, O Bhārata, I will not kill her, even at the cost of my own life."
"She who was previously created by the Creator as a woman is indeed this Śikhaṇḍinī.
Sleep well, O son of Gāndhārī; tomorrow I shall engage in a great battle about which people will speak as long as the earth endures."
Thus addressed, O lord of men, your son went forth;
having saluted his guru with his head, he departed for his own residence.
Then the king, having returned from there, dismissed the great multitude.
Then he, the destroyer of his enemies, quickly entered his palace;
having entered, that king passed that night there.
Sañjaya said:
When the night had turned to dawn, the king rose in the morning and indeed commanded the monarchs: "Marshal the army!
Today Bhīṣma, enraged in battle, shall slay the Somakas."
O King, having heard that extensive lamentation of Duryodhana at night,
and considering it as if it were a personal reproach directed at himself, he fell into a state of supreme despondency and censured his own dependence on others.
The son of Śantanu meditated for a long time, desiring to fight Arjuna in battle.
Having understood through his gestures what the son of Gaṅgā was contemplating,
Duryodhana, O great king, urged Duḥśāsana on.
"O Duḥśāsana, let the chariots for Bhīṣma’s protection be yoked quickly;
you yourself must urge forward all thirty-two divisions of the army.
For that which has been contemplated for many years has now arrived."

"The slaughter of the Pāṇḍavas along with their armies, and the acquisition of the kingdom—among these, I consider the protection of Bhīṣma himself to be our primary task. Protected by us, he will lead to our happiness; otherwise, he will slay the sons of Pṛthā in battle."

And the pure-souled one said: "I shall not slay Śikhaṇḍin, for he was previously born as a woman; therefore, he must be avoided by me in battle. The world knows that I have acted thus out of a desire to do what was pleasing to my father."
O mighty-armed one, in the past you renounced a prosperous kingdom and women; yet,
O best of men, I would never, under any circumstances, slay a woman in battle, nor anyone who was previously a woman— I tell you this as the truth.
"O King, if you have heard that this Śikhaṇḍin was formerly a woman—
just as it was told during the *Udyoga* [parvan] regarding how Śikhaṇḍinī was born—
then having been born as a girl, he has become a man, and he will fight, O Bhārata."
I would never, under any circumstances, release my arrows at him; however,
O dear one, in battle I shall slay all other Kṣatriyas of the Pāṇḍavas who seek victory, as soon as they come within the range of my shafts.

"Thus did Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā and best of the Bharatas, who is learned in the scriptures, speak to me. In this matter, I consider the protection of Bhīṣma himself to be of the utmost importance; for if he were left unprotected, even a wolf might slay a lion in the great forest."
"O tiger among men,
let us not see Bhīṣma slain by Śikhaṇḍin, as a tiger is killed by a wolf, or as a lion is killed by a crow; let such a policy be ordained."
"Let Mātula Śakuni, Śalya, Kṛpa, Droṇa, and Vivimśati stand ready and protect the son of Gaṅgā; for when he is guarded, victory is certain.
Having heard these words of Duryodhana, the kings then [acted accordingly].
From all sides, they surrounded the son of Gaṅgā with a multitude of chariots;
and your sons, surrounding the son of Gaṅgā, advanced with joy,
making the earth tremble and agitating the heavens and the Pāṇḍavas.
Those great car-warriors, clad in armor, surrounded Bhīṣma in battle with those well-yoked chariots and elephants,
just as the thirty gods stood around the wielder of the thunderbolt in the war between the gods and the asuras.
They all took their positions, guarding that great car-warrior.
Then King Duryodhana spoke again to his brother:
"Yudhāmanyu protects the left wheel, and Uttamaujas protects the right."
"These two are the protectors of Arjuna, and Arjuna himself is the protector of Śikhaṇḍin.
O Duḥśāsana, act in such a way that he, being protected by Pārtha and yet abandoned by us,
does not slay Bhīṣma."
Having heard those words of his brother, your son Duḥśāsana,
placing Bhīṣma at the head, set out with the army. Seeing Bhīṣma surrounded by that multitude of chariots, [the enemy]...
Arjuna, the best of chariot-warriors, spoke to Dhṛṣṭadyumna:
"O sinless tiger among men, O Pāñcālya, station Śikhaṇḍin today at the front of Bhīṣma; I myself shall be his protector."
