Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, set forth with his army and formed a great battle array called Sarvatobhadra for the combat. Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and the great car-warrior Śaibya [stood at its head].
Śakuni, the ruler of the Sindhus, and Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja,
O Bhārata, together with Bhīṣma and all your sons,
stood at the front of the entire army, at the head of the formation.
O Sire, Droṇa, Bhūriśravas, Śalya, and Bhagadatta,
clad in armor, took their positions on the right wing of the formation;
as did Aśvatthāman, Somadatta, and the two great car-warriors from Avanti.
Accompanied by a great army, they protected the left wing.
O great king, Duryodhana, surrounded on all sides by the Trigartas,
stood in the center of the formation facing the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata.
Alambusa, the best of chariot-warriors, and Śrutāyus, the great car-warrior,
stood armored at the rear of all the troops at the head of the formation. Having thus arranged the battle array, O Bhārata, your men then took their positions.
Fully armored, they appeared like blazing fires.
Likewise did King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena,
and both Nakula and Sahadeva, the two sons of Mādrī.
Clad in armor, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki stood at the front of the entire army, positioned at the head of the formation;
these destroyers of enemy forces were stationed with a vast host.
And many other heroes by the hundreds and thousands—
brave warriors adorned with various weapons and equipped with diverse arms—
such as Śikhaṇḍin, Vijaya, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca.
The mighty-armed Cekitāna and the heroic Kuntibhoja,
O great king, stood in battle surrounded by a vast army;
as did the great archer Abhimanyu and the great car-warrior Drupada.
Yuyudhāna, the great archer, and the heroic Yudhāmanyu,
as well as the five Kekaya brothers, stood armored and ready for battle.
Having thus formed a counter-array against that most difficult-to-vanquish great formation, they took their positions.
O noble one, the heroic Pāṇḍavas stood ready for battle in the fray;
but your kings, O monarch, together with their armies and striving in the fight,
advanced against the sons of Pṛthā, placing Bhīṣma at their head.
In the same way, O King, the Pāṇḍavas, led by Bhīmasena and desiring victory in battle, [attacked] Bhīṣma as he sought to engage them in combat,
[making] lion-roars, shouts of joy, and the sounds of krakacas and cow-horns.
Sounding kettledrums, clay drums, small drums, and *puṣkara* drums,
the Pāṇḍavas rushed forward, uttering terrible roars;
with the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, and war-drums, they advanced.
With loud lion-roars and various kinds of leaps,
we rushed toward them, shouting back in response;
suddenly provoked to great anger, there arose a massive tumult.
Then, rushing at one another, they engaged in combat;
by that great noise, the earth trembled,
and birds flew about uttering most terrible cries.
The radiant sun, though impelled, became lusterless;
tumultuous winds blew, portending a very great danger;
and terrible jackals, emitting horrific cries, howled there.
O Great King, announcing that a great slaughter had arrived,
the quarters of the sky blazed forth, O King, and a rain of dust fell,
mixed with blood and likewise a rain of bones.

O lord of the people, as they wept, water fell from the eyes of the mounts; and lost in deep thought, they discharged excrement and urine. O bull of the Bharatas, great sounds were heard even though they had vanished from sight.
Jackals, cranes, and crows were seen swooping down toward the man-eating *rākṣasas* as they uttered terrifying cries;
and dogs stood there, barking with various kinds of howls.
Blazing great meteors, having struck the sun,
suddenly fell to the earth, portending a great danger; the vast armies stood in a great assembly.
At the encounter of the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras,
the sounds of conchs and drums resounded,
making the forests tremble as if shaken by the wind.
As the armies, crowded with men, elephants,
and horses, advanced during that inauspicious moment,
a tumultuous roar arose from the hosts.
Like oceans tossed by the wind,
Sañjaya said:
"The noble car-warrior Abhimanyu, with his excellent tawny horses..."
The radiant hero rushed against the great army of Duryodhana,
scattering showers of arrows like a cloud pouring down torrents of rain;
they were unable to withstand the enraged son of Subhadrā, that slayer of foes, in battle.
O King, even your own kuru-foremost warriors were unable to check him in battle as he plunged into that inexhaustible ocean of an army with its flood of weapons;
for by him, O monarch, were arrows released in the fray that destroyed the enemy.

Enraged in battle, the son of Subhadrā dispatched his arrows toward the heroic Kṣatriyas, sending them to the abode of the King of the Dead— arrows as terrible as the staff of Yama and like blazing venomous serpents.

The son of Phalguna swiftly felled chariot-warriors from their chariots, horsemen from the backs of their horses, and elephant-riders along with their elephants. As he performed that great and wonderful feat in battle, the kings—
Delighted, they paid him honor and praised Phālguni;
scattering those armies in all directions like the wind blowing away a heap of cotton, the son of Subhadrā shone most brightly.
O Bhārata, as your armies were being put to flight by him,
they found no protector, like elephants sunk in the mud.
Having routed all your troops, that best of men—
O King, Abhimanyu stood blazing like a smokeless fire; none of your men could withstand that slayer of enemies,
just as moths driven by fate cannot endure a blazing fire.
Striking at all his enemies, that great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas,
that mighty archer, appeared like the wielder of the thunderbolt with the vajra itself;
and as he moved through the directions, his gold-backed bow was seen.
O King, just as lightning flashes gleaming from the clouds,
so did sharp, polished arrows issue forth in the battle,
O King, like swarms of bees from a forest of blossoming trees.
As that high-souled son of Subhadrā thus moved about on his chariot, which rumbled like a thundercloud, the people could see no opening in his defense.
Having confounded Kṛpa, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Bṛhadbala, he [proceeded].
O noble one, we beheld the bow of that great archer Saindhava drawn into a complete circle as he moved with both swiftness and precision,
scorching your army like the orb of the sun.
Seeing him scorching [the enemy] with the rays of his arrows, the heroic Kṣatriyas,
by his deeds, considered this world to have two Phalgunas.
O Great King, that great army of the Bhāratas was thus afflicted by him.
She wandered here and there like a woman under the influence of intoxication;
having routed that army and made the great chariot-warriors tremble,
she gladdened her friends, just as Vāsava does after conquering Maya.
Being put to flight by him in the encounter,
your troops let out a terrible cry of distress, resembling the roar of rain-clouds.
O noble one, having heard that dreadful clamor of your army, [the enemy]...
Like the ocean at the time of the full moon, its force stirred up by the wind,
King Duryodhana then addressed the son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga:
"This great archer, the son of Kṛṣṇa, is like a second Phalguna."
In his rage, he puts the army to flight like Vṛtra against the host of the gods.
I see no other great remedy for him in battle,
O best of Rākṣasas, than you, who have reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge.
"Go quickly and slay the hero, the son of Subhadrā, in battle!
We, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, shall slay the Pārthas.
Thus addressed, that powerful and majestic lord of the Rākṣasas—
At the command of your son, he quickly advanced into the battle,
roaring with a great sound like a cloud in the rainy season;
by that great noise of his, the vast army of the Pāṇḍavas was [shaken].
O King, it surged in every direction like a swelling ocean.
And many men, O King, terrified by that roar,
abandoned their dear lives and fell to the surface of the earth.
And the son of Kṛṣṇa (Abhimanyu), filled with joy and grasping his bow,
rushed toward that Rākṣasa as if dancing upon the seat of his chariot.
Then that Rākṣasa, enraged, having encountered the son of Arjuna in battle—
Standing not far from him, he indeed put that army to flight. That great host of the Pāṇḍavas, being slaughtered in battle and oppressed by that evil-minded one, found no protection whatsoever.

The Rākṣasa advanced against him in battle, just as Bali was met by the army of the gods. O noble one, there was a truly great crushing conflict for that army as it was being slaughtered in the encounter by the Rākṣasa of terrible form.
Then, displaying his prowess in battle, the Rākṣasa put that great army of the Pāṇḍavas to flight with thousands of arrows. And thus was that host of the Pāṇḍavas being slaughtered.
He fled in battle out of fear of the Rakshasa of terrible form;
having crushed that army like an elephant crushing a lotus pond,
he then rushed in battle toward the mighty sons of Draupadi.

Then all those sons of Draupadī, great archers and strikers, filled with rage, rushed toward the Rākṣasa just as the five planets rush toward the sun. Oppressed by those heroic warriors, that foremost of Rākṣasas was tormented.
Just as at the terrible end of an eon the moon is surrounded by five planets,
so then the mighty Prativindhya quickly pierced the Rakshasa with sharp arrows made entirely of iron, their points unblunted.
With his armor pierced by them, that best of Rākṣasas shone like a great cloud interwoven with the rays of the sun;
he was likewise covered with those arrows equipped with golden ornaments.
O King, Ārṣyaśṛṅgi shone like a mountain with blazing peaks.
Then those five brothers pierced the lord of the Rākṣasas in that great battle with sharp arrows adorned with gold.
Pierced by those terrible arrows as if by enraged serpents,
O King, Alambusa was violently provoked like a lordly elephant;
pierced by those dreadful shafts, he blazed up on all sides.
Alambusa shone intensely, like an elephant with firebrands,
O Great King;
yet, having been deeply pierced by those great car-warriors, he was then afflicted and entered into a long darkness for a moment, O Sire.
Having regained consciousness, his fury redoubled;
with his arrows he severed their banners and bows,
striking each one as if smiling with three shafts.
Alambusa, that great car-warrior, as if dancing upon the seat of his chariot,
being both swift and enraged, the mighty Rākṣasa struck down the horses and the charioteers of those high-souled warriors.
Highly delighted, he pierced them again with well-sharpened arrows of various forms by the hundreds and thousands;
then that Rākṣasa deprived those great archers of their chariots.
The night-stalker, desiring to kill them, rushed forward with speed.
Seeing those [monkeys] afflicted in battle by that evil-minded Rākṣasa,
the son of Arjuna charged at the Rākṣasa in the fray.
A battle took place between those two, like that between Vṛtra and Vāsava;
all your men and the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas watched it.
Those two, blazing with mutual rage, encountered one another in that great conflict.
Rolling their eyes in rage, O King, with their lower lips quivering,
those two of great strength, O Great King, with eyes bloodshot with anger,
glared at one another in battle like the fires of cosmic destruction.
Like two enraged venomous serpents, they glared at one another with their eyes;
their encounter was terrible and fraught with bitter consequences,
like the battle between Śakra and Śambara in the war of the gods and asuras.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: O Sañjaya, how did Alambuṣa fight back in battle against the heroic son of Arjuna, that great car-warrior who was slaughtering him in the fray?
And how did the son of Subhadrā, the slayer of enemy heroes, fare against the son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga?
Tell me that in truth, exactly as it happened in the battle.
And what did Dhanañjaya do among my troops, O Sañjaya?
"Is it Bhīma, the best among the strong, or the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca;
or Nakula, Sahadeva, or the great car-warrior Sātyaki? Tell me all of this, for you are skilled, O Saṃjaya."
Saṃjaya said:
"Alas, O noble one, I shall describe to you that hair-raising battle as it occurred between the lord of the Rākṣasas and the son of Subhadrā."
And just as Arjuna, Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava,
Nakula, and Sahadeva displayed their prowess in the battle,
so too did all your men, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa.
They performed wonderful and diverse deeds fearlessly. But Alambusa, having let out a great roar in the battle and repeatedly challenging the great car-warrior Abhimanyu, [attacked him].
He rushed forward with speed and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
O King, the son of Subhadrā also, roaring repeatedly like a lion in battle, [attacked] the great archer Ārśyaśṛṅgi, the mortal enemy of his father.
Then, in that battle, those two— the best of chariot-warriors— rushed forward swiftly on their chariots like a god and a dānava;
the foremost of rākṣasas, a master of illusion, and the son of Phālguna, a knower of divine weapons.
Then, O great king, the son of Kṛṣṇa (the son of Subhadrā), having pierced the son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga in battle with three sharpened arrows,
struck him again with five. Alambusa,
also filled with rage, pierced the son of Kṛṣṇa with nine swift-flying shafts.
He pierced him in the heart with force, like a great elephant being struck by goads. Then, O Bhārata, that swift-acting night-stalker afflicted the son of Arjuna in battle with a thousand arrows.
Then Abhimanyu, filled with rage, loosed ninety sharp,
straight-knotted arrows into the great chest of the Rākṣasa.
They swiftly entered his body, piercing through his vital organs.
With all his limbs pierced by them, O King, that best of Rākṣasas shone like a mountain covered with blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees;
even while bearing those gold-feathered arrows, he remained possessed of great strength.
The best of the Rākṣasas shone like a mountain ablaze with fire.
Then, O great king, the mighty son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, filled with rage,
covered the son of Kṛṣṇa— who was like Mahendra himself— with feathered arrows.
Those sharp arrows, resembling the staff of Yama, released by him,
pierced Abhimanyu and entered the surface of the earth.
Likewise, the gold-adorned arrows released by the son of Arjuna [penetrated his opponent].

Having pierced through Alambusa, they entered the depths of the earth. But Saubhadra, having encountered the Rakshasa Maya in battle, turned him back with straight-jointed arrows, just as Shakra did to Maya in the fray.
Then, as the Rākṣasa turned his back and was being struck down by the enemy in battle,
that scorcher of foes manifested a great illusion of darkness.
Thereupon, they were all indeed enveloped by that darkness upon the surface of the earth.
In that battle, they could see neither Abhimanyu, nor their own men, nor the enemy.
And seeing that great darkness of terrible form, Abhimanyu,
the joy of the Kurus, manifested the exceedingly fierce Bhāskara weapon.
Then, O lord of the earth, the entire world became visible again,
and he destroyed that illusion of the evil-minded Rākṣasa.
Enraged, that best of men, possessed of great heroism, [attacked] the lord of the Rākṣasas.
In that battle, he covered [the enemy] with straight-knotted arrows; likewise,
the son of Phalguna, of immeasurable soul and skilled in all weapons, warded off the many other illusions employed by that Rākṣasa.
Then that Rākṣasa, whose illusions were destroyed and who was being struck by arrows,
abandoned his chariot right there and fled out of great fear. When that Rākṣasa, who fought with deceit, had been swiftly defeated, [the battle continued].
And the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, who had conquered fatigue in battle,
was valorous and possessed of great splendor; equal to his father in prowess,
the son of Arjuna crushed your army in the encounter.
Like a wild lord of elephants blinded by rut [overpowering] a lotus-pond with its full-blown flowers,
Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, seeing his army thus put to flight,
then surrounded the son of Subhadrā with a vast array of chariots.

Having hemmed in that hero, the many great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s side fiercely struck the solitary one with their arrows in battle. That hero, equal to his father in prowess, [faced] those chariot-fighters.
Equal to Vāsudeva in prowess and strength,
that best among all wielders of weapons performed various deeds in battle worthy of both his father and his maternal uncle.
Then, O King, Dhananjaya, slaughtering your soldiers in battle,
impetuous and desiring to find his son, encountered Bhīṣma.
Likewise, O King, your father Devavrata [encountered him] in that same battle.
Like Rahu assailing the sun, he attacked Pārtha in battle.
Then, O lord of the people, your sons, along with their chariots, elephants, and horses,
surrounded Bhīṣma in the fray and protected him on all sides.
Likewise, O King, the Pāṇḍavas, having surrounded Dhanañjaya and being armored for the great battle, stood ready, O bull of the Bharatas; then,
O King, the son of Śaradvat [stood] in front of Bhīṣma.
He covered Arjuna with twenty-five arrows;
then Satyaki,
rushing forward out of a desire to do what was pleasing to the Pāṇḍava, pierced him with sharp shafts like a tiger attacking an elephant.
Gautama also, filled with haste and provoked to anger, pierced Mādhava in the heart with nine arrows fletched with heron feathers.
Then the great car-warrior, the descendant of Śini, being deeply pierced, became enraged.
He took up a terrible, stone-tipped arrow capable of ending the Gautamas.
As it flew toward him with great speed, possessing a brilliance equal to Indra’s thunderbolt,
the son of Droṇa— highly enraged and exceedingly wrathful— cut it in two.

Then, having bypassed Gautama, the best of chariot-warriors, the descendant of Śini rushed at the son of Droṇa in battle, like Rāhu toward the moon in the sky. O Bhārata, the son of Droṇa then cut his bow in two.

Then, after his bow was severed, he struck him with arrows. Taking up another bow capable of bearing a great burden, O Great King, the son of Droṇa struck Śatrughna in the arms and chest with sixty shafts.
Pierced and pained, overcome by faintness for a moment,
he sat down on the floor of his chariot, leaning against the flagpole. Then, having regained consciousness, the powerful son of Droṇa—
Enraged in battle, he struck the descendant of Vṛṣṇi with a steel shaft;
having pierced the grandson of Śini, it entered the surface of the earth like a powerful young serpent entering its hole at the onset of spring.
Then, with another broad-headed arrow, the son of Droṇa cut down Mādhava’s excellent banner in battle and let out a lion’s roar; furthermore,
O Bhārata, he covered him once more with terrible shafts.
O Great King, just as a cloud at the end of the summer heat assails the sun,
so did Sātyaki, O Great King, having struck down that net of arrows,
swiftly rush toward the son of Droṇa with manifold showers of shafts.
And the descendant of Śini, the slayer of enemy heroes, scorched the son of Droṇa,
just as the sun shines when it is freed from a mass of clouds;
and with a thousand arrows, he again assailed him as he stood prepared for battle.
The mighty Sātyaki covered him with arrows and let out a roar.
Seeing his son thus swallowed, as the moon is by Rāhu,
the powerful son of Bharadvāja rushed toward the descendant of Śini.
And in that great battle, O King, desiring to protect his own son who was being tormented by the Vārṣṇeya, he pierced him with a very sharp arrow.
But Sātyaki, having conquered the great car-warrior, the preceptor’s son, in battle—
He pierced Droṇa with twenty arrows made entirely of iron.
At that moment, the son of Kuntī, the great car-warrior Śvetavāhana of immeasurable soul,
rushed furiously toward Droṇa in the battle.
Then, O great king, Droṇa and Pārtha encountered one another in that great battle,
like Budha and Śukra meeting in the firmament.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How did Droṇa, the great archer, and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya, both heroes, encounter one another in battle? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya;
for the son of Pāṇḍu was always dear to the wise son of Bharadvāja."
And the preceptor, O Sañjaya, was always dear to Pārtha in battle.
How did those two chariot-warriors, both proud and fierce as lions in combat,
encounter one another in the fray— the son of Bharadvāja and Dhanañjaya?
Saṃjaya said:
"O Pārtha, Droṇa does not recognize you as dear to himself in battle;
nor does Pārtha, placing the duty of a Kṣatriya foremost, recognize his teacher in the fray."
In the same way, the Pāṇḍava knows Droṇa to be dear to himself;
ever devoted to the duty of a warrior (*kṣatradharma*), he fights according to the duty of a warrior.
O King, Kṣatriyas do not avoid one another in battle.
Indeed, they fought without restraint against their own fathers and brothers;
O Bhārata, Droṇa, having been pierced by three arrows from Pārtha in battle,
paid no heed to those shafts released from Pārtha’s bow in the fray.
Once more, Pārtha covered him in battle with a shower of arrows;
and he blazed with rage like a fire that has arisen in a dense forest.
Then, in that combat, Droṇa struck Arjuna with straight-jointed shafts.
O Indra among kings, O Bhārata, he checked him before long. Then,
O King, King Duryodhana urged Suśarman to seize the rear of Droṇa in battle.
The King of Trigarta, also enraged,
drew his bow back fully and covered Pārtha in battle with iron-tipped arrows.
O King, the arrows released by those two shone resplendent in the sky.
O Great King, like swans in the sky during the autumn season,
those arrows, O Lord, having reached the son of Kuntī, all entered him together,
just as birds enter a tree laden with sweet fruit that bends under its weight.
Then Arjuna, the best of chariot-warriors, having let out a roar in battle,
pierced the King of Trigarta along with his sons in the encounter with arrows.
Being slaughtered by Pārtha like Time itself at the end of a Yuga, they [fell].
Having resolved upon death,
they rushed toward Pārtha alone and released a rain of arrows toward the chariot of the Pāṇḍava.
Then, with a shower of arrows, the Pāṇḍava [warded off] that rain of arrows.
O Indra among kings, he received [the shower] like a mountain receiving a rain of water.
There we beheld the wonderful lightness of hand of Bībhatsu,
as he warded off that unassailable rain of weapons released by many heroes.
Because he alone held them back like the wind holds back masses of clouds,
the gods and dānavas were gratified by that deed of Pārtha.
Then, O Bhārata, Pārtha became enraged in battle against the Trigartas.
O great king, he released the Vāyavya weapon at the front of the army.
Thereupon, a wind appeared, agitating the vault of the sky,
felling multitudes of trees and striking down the soldiers.

Then, O great king, having beheld that most dreadful Vāyavya weapon, Droṇa released another terrible weapon, the Śaila. When that weapon had been discharged by Droṇa in the great battle of the fray, [the earth shook].
Then the wind subsided and the quarters of the sky became clear.
Thereupon, the heroic son of Pāṇḍu rendered the multitudes of Trigarta chariots dispirited in battle, turning them away and stripping them of their prowess.
Then King Duryodhana, Kṛpa— the best of chariot-warriors— Aśvatthāman, Śalya, Sudakṣiṇa the Kamboja,
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and Bāhlika along with the Bāhlikas [all followed].
With a vast multitude of chariots, they blocked all directions against the son of Pṛthā;
likewise, Bhagadatta and the mighty Śrutāyus blocked the directions against Bhīma with a division of elephants.
O lord of the people, Bhūriśravas, Śala,
and the son of Subala quickly checked the two sons of Mādrī with various showers of arrows;
while Bhīṣma, united with all the soldiers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s army, [did the same].

Having approached Yudhiṣṭhira, he surrounded him on all sides. Seeing the elephant division charging toward him, the heroic Vṛkodara, the son of Pṛthā, licked the corners of his mouth like a lion in the forest.
Then that best of chariot-warriors, seizing his mace in that great battle,
quickly leaped down from his chariot and terrified your army,
like a lion from a mountain peak.
Standing with his mace, Bhīma was like a mountain with its peaks;
he was like a lion that has spotted a deer. Then, seeing him with mace in hand, those elephant-riders—
Exerting themselves in battle, they surrounded Bhīmasena on all sides;
yet the Pāṇḍava, having entered the midst of the elephants,
shone resplendent like the sun situated in the center of a vast mass of clouds.

That bull among the Pāṇḍavas, with his mace, scattered the elephant division like the wind dispersing a vast and incomparable mass of clouds. Those tuskers were being slaughtered by the mighty Bhīmasena.
Roaring like clouds, they raised cries of distress in the battle;
and there, torn in many places by the tusks of elephants,
Pārtha shone at the forefront of the fray like a blossoming *aśoka* tree.
Then, with his mace, he scattered the shower of weapons from the horsemen;
endowed with the force of the wind, the Pāṇḍava moved about in battle,
his limbs scratched by horns and severely struck by tusks.
Seizing the elephant by its tusks, he rendered it tuskless; then,
striking the elephant on the temple with those very tusks,
he felled it in battle like Death himself with staff in hand.
Bearing a mace smeared with blood, his appearance marred by fat and marrow,
and his armlets drenched in gore, he appeared like Rudra himself.
Thus were those great elephants, the survivors of the slaughter, being struck down.
O King, they fled in all directions, crushing their own forces.
O bull of the Bharatas, because of those great elephants fleeing on all sides,
the entire army of Duryodhana once again turned its back in retreat.
Saṃjaya said:
At midday, O great king, a battle took place—
fierce and destructive to the world— between Bhīṣma and the Somakas.
Gāṅgeya, the best of chariot-warriors, scattered the army of the Pāṇḍavas with sharpened arrows by the hundreds and thousands;
and your father Devavrata crushed that host.
Like herds of cattle upon a heap of harvested grain,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, Virāṭa,
and Drupada likewise approached Bhīṣma in battle and struck that great car-warrior with their arrows.

Then, O Bhārata, having pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa with three arrows each, he dispatched a steel shaft at Drupada. Pierced by that arrow by Bhīṣma, the crusher of enemies and great archer, those mighty bowmen were struck down.
O King, they were enraged in battle like serpents trodden upon by a foot. Śikhaṇḍin pierced that grandfather of the Bharatas,
but Acyuta, mentally reflecting on his being a woman, did not strike him.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, blazing with anger like fire in battle,
struck the grandfather in the arms and chest with three arrows;
Drupada struck him with twenty-five, and Virāṭa with ten shafts.
Śikhaṇḍin pierced Bhīṣma with twenty-five arrows. Deeply pierced in that battle by those high-souled warriors, O great king,
Bhīṣma shone like a red aśoka tree variegated with blossoms in the springtime.
The son of Gaṅgā pierced each of them with three straight-flying arrows,
O noble one, and with a broad-headed shaft he cut through Drupada’s bow. Taking up another bow, Drupada struck Bhīṣma with five arrows.
And with three well-sharpened arrows at the head of the battle, he struck the charioteer.
Then, O great king, Bhīma, the five sons of Draupadī,
the five Kekaya brothers, and Sātyaki of the Sātvata clan [assailed him].
Desiring the welfare of Yudhiṣṭhira, they rushed toward the son of Gaṅgā,
wishing to protect Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the Pāñcālya leaders in battle;
likewise, all your warriors were prepared for the sake of protecting Bhīṣma.
O lord of men, accompanied by their armies, they advanced against the Pāṇḍava host;
there occurred a great and tumultuous battle between your men and theirs,
involving infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants, which increased the population of Yama’s realm.
The chariot-warrior, having encountered another chariot-warrior, dispatched him to the abode of Yama; likewise, having encountered other men, elephants, horses, and their riders,
he sent them to the next world with his straight-jointed arrows.
O lord of the people, here and there with various terrible weapons,
chariots were deprived of their riders and likewise had their charioteers slain;
with their horses fleeing in panic, they scattered in all directions across the battlefield.
O King, crushing men and very many horses in battle,
they were seen moving like the wind, resembling cities of the Gandharvas;
and there were chariot-warriors deprived of their chariots, though clad in armor and endowed with splendor.
All of them wore earrings and turbans, and were adorned with golden neck-ornaments and armlets; they were equal to the sons of gods in beauty, and like Śakra in valor in battle;
they surpassed Vaiśravaṇa in supernatural power and Bṛhaspati in statesmanship.
O lord of people, the heroic lords of all the worlds were seen fleeing here and there like common men;
and the elephants, O best of men, were deprived of their excellent riders.
Crushing their own ranks, they rushed together, making all manner of sounds,
O noble one— amidst armor, yak-tail fans, umbrellas,
and banners; as well as with girth-straps, goads, bells, and iron lances.
With their [bodies] shattered, they were seen fleeing in the ten directions;
O lord of the people, likewise, elephant-riders were deprived of their elephants by those [beasts] resembling mountains and clouds, with roars like the rising of thunderclouds.
In that tumultuous clash between you and them,
we beheld horses adorned with gold, originating from various lands, galloping like the wind by the hundreds and thousands.
We beheld horsemen whose horses had been slain, seized on all sides with swords, fleeing and being pursued in the conflict; then,
O great king, in that interval, the powerful Bhīmasena appeared.
He waged a truly great battle, most terrible and fearsome.
In that great conflict, an elephant, having encountered another elephant fleeing in flight,
rushed forward with speed, crushing both foot soldiers and horses alike.
O King, having crushed horses with horses and chariot-warriors with chariots,
the elephant likewise crushed chariots in battle;
and the chariot, upon encountering a foot-soldier or a horse, did the same.
O King, in that battle he crushed horses and men;
thus, O mighty-armed one, those of great strength were seen here and there, crushing one another in many ways.
While that fierce and terrifying battle was thus proceeding,
a dreadful river began to flow, with blood and entrails for its waves,
heaps of bones for its rafts, and hair for its moss and grass.
With chariots for its lakes and arrows for its whirlpools, it was difficult to approach; with heads for its scattered stones and elephants for its crocodiles,
it was rich with armor and turbans for its foam, and possessed bows for its islands and swords for its turtles.
Filled with a flood of conchs and discs, with parasols for its turtles and chariots for its rafts,
rich with banners and standards for its trees, it carries away the shores of mortals;
crowded with throngs of flesh-eaters, it causes the kingdom of Yama to swell.

O King, many brave Kṣatriyas, casting aside fear in that great battle, crossed that river by means of horses, elephants, chariots, and rafts. In that conflict, it swept away the cowards who were overwhelmed by dejection.
Just as those in the city of the King of the Dead cry out toward the Vaitaraṇī river,
so too did the Kṣatriyas there cry out upon seeing that great carnage;
through the transgression of Duryodhana, the Kauravas are going to their destruction.

"How could the lord of men, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, that evil-souled one deluded by greed, harbor hatred toward the sons of Pāṇḍu who are possessed of such virtues? O Bhārata, many such words were heard there.
Those most cruel words regarding your sons, joined with praise for the Pāṇḍavas,
which were then uttered by all the warriors— having heard them, your son Duryodhana, the wrongdoer toward all the world, [remained silent].
O Bhārata, he spoke to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Śalya, saying:
"Fight without pride; why do you delay? Thus urged by Duryodhana, all the kings engaged in battle.
Then, O King, there commenced a most terrible slaughter between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, born of that gambling match with dice,
which you did not restrain in the past even though you were being entreated by the high-souled ones.
O son of Vicitravīrya, behold such a fruit as this! For the sons of Pāṇḍu, O King, along with their armies and followers, did not fight on that great stage when the sun had reached its meridian.

Having pierced Kṛtavarman with five iron arrows, Sātyaki, the grandson of Śini, who is truthful and skilled in truth, could not shake him. O lord of the people, the Kauravas protect their lives in battle.
"For this reason, O tiger among men, O King, this terrible destruction of people has occurred— whether by fate or through your own misconduct. Saṃjaya said:
But Arjuna, that tiger among men, dispatched the kings led by Suśarman to the abode of the King of the Dead with his sharp arrows. Then,
in that battle, Suśarman also pierced Pārtha with shafts.
He struck Vāsudeva with seventy arrows and Pārtha again with nine;
having warded those off with a flood of shafts, the great car-warrior, the son of Śakra,
dispatched Suśarman’s warriors in battle to the abode of Yama.
Being slaughtered by Pārtha like Time itself at the end of a Yuga,
O King, those great car-warriors fled in battle when fear arose;
some abandoning their horses, and others their chariots, O noble one.
Some, abandoning their elephants, fled in the ten directions;
others, O lord of the people, being struck by horses, elephants, and chariots, fled from the battle with the utmost haste.
The horse-riders repeatedly struck them with whips and with their heels,
urging on those excellent horses as they galloped; likewise, they did so with the falling of the reins and the brandishing of the goads.
Elephant-riders, urging their elephants forward with haste, fled swiftly;
and chariot-warriors, O King, driving their horses on by means of whips and repeated verbal goads, fled in the ten directions.
And even the foot soldiers, having cast aside their weapons in that great battle,
fled here and there without regard for anything else, O Bhārata,
though they were repeatedly restrained by Suśarman of Trigarta.
Likewise, they did not stand their ground in battle against other preeminent kings;
trampling upon their own sons fallen on the earth, as well as their maternal uncles, fathers,
and brothers, they fled here and there.
Seeing that army in flight, your son Duryodhana,
placing Bhīṣma— who was honored by the entire host— at his head,
rushed toward Dhanañjaya with a great and total exertion.
O lord of the people, for the sake of the king of Trigarta and his own life,
he alone stood firm in battle, scattering various kinds of arrows;
all the other men, together with his brothers, fled away.
In the same way, O King, the Pāṇḍavas, armored and exerting every effort,
advanced for the sake of Phalguna to where Bhīṣma was stationed,
even though they were aware of the terrible prowess of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow in battle.
Raising cries of "Alas! Alas!", they rushed toward Bhīṣma from all sides.
Then the heroic Tāladhvaja covered the army of the Pāṇḍavas in battle with straight-jointed arrows.
Then, O great king, when the sun had reached the meridian, all the Kurus united with the Pāṇḍavas and fought.
Sātyaki, having pierced Kṛtavarman with five iron arrows—
The hero stood firm in battle, scattering arrows by the thousands;
likewise, King Drupada, having pierced Droṇa with sharp shafts,
struck him again with seventy and his charioteer with seven.
Bhimasena, having pierced King Bahlika, his great-grandfather,
uttered a mighty roar like a tiger in the forest. The son of Arjuna, meanwhile, was pierced by Citrasena with many swift-flying arrows.
With three arrows, he pierced Citrasena deeply in the heart.
When those two great warriors encountered one another in battle,
O King, they shone like the most formidable Budha and Śanaiścara in the sky.

Having slain his four horses and his charioteer with nine arrows, Saubhadra, the slayer of enemy heroes, uttered a powerful roar. Then that great car-warrior, quickly leaping down from his chariot whose horses had been killed, [fled].
O lord of the people, he quickly ascended the chariot of Durmukha. And Drona, having pierced Drupada with straight-knotted arrows, swiftly struck his charioteer as well, displaying his prowess.
Then King Drupada, being hard-pressed at the head of the army,
fled on swift horses, remembering his former enmity.
Bhīmasena, however, [pursued] King Bāhlika as if in a mere moment.
While the entire army looked on, he deprived Vyaśva of his horses, charioteer, and chariot;
O great king, filled with agitation, Bāhlīka fell into a state of extreme peril. Then that best of men, Bāhlīka, leaped down from his mount.
The great car-warrior Sātyaki, having held back the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman with various kinds of arrows, O King, quickly ascended the chariot of Lakṣmaṇa and approached the grandfather.

Having pierced the descendant of Bharata with sixty sharp, feathered arrows, he seemed to dance upon the seat of his chariot while brandishing his great bow. Then the Grandfather hurled at him a massive iron spear.

The highly illustrious Vārṣṇeya, with great agility, shattered that beautiful, swift, and well-sharpened spear— which was adorned with gold, resembled a Naga maiden, and was like Death itself as it came rushing suddenly toward him.
But failing to reach the descendant of Vṛṣṇi,
that most terrible spear fell upon the surface of the earth like a great meteor shorn of its luster.
Then, O King, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi [hurled] his own spear of fearsome appearance.
Seizing it with great force, he hurled it toward the chariot of the Grandfather.
Driven by the strength of Vārṣṇeya’s arms in that great battle,
it rushed forward with speed like the Night of Doom toward a man.

O Bhārata, as it was falling suddenly upon him, he cut it in two with two extremely sharp razor-headed arrows; it fell scattered upon the earth. Having thus severed the spear, the son of Gaṅgā struck Sātyaki with nine arrows.
Laughing, that crusher of enemies struck him on the chest in his wrath.
Then, O elder brother of Pāṇḍu, the Pāṇḍavas, along with their chariots, elephants, and horses,
surrounded Bhīṣma in battle for the sake of protecting Mādhava.
Then there commenced a tumultuous battle, making the hair stand on end,
between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, both sides desiring victory in the encounter.
Saṃjaya said:
O great king, seeing Bhīṣma enraged in battle and surrounded by the Pāṇḍavas—
like the sun in the sky at the end of the summer heat shrouded by clouds—
Duryodhana, O great king, spoke to Duḥśāsana.
This hero, the great archer Bhīṣma, the destroyer of enemies, has been covered on all sides by the heroic Pāṇḍavas, O bull of the Bharatas. O hero,
it is your duty to protect that high-souled one.
For if our grandfather Bhīṣma were protected in battle,
he would surely slay the striving Pāñcālas along with the Pāṇḍavas in combat;
therefore, I believe our task there must be the protection of Bhīṣma himself.
For this great archer Bhīṣma, our grandfather, is indeed our protector.
Therefore, you, surrounding the grandfather with your entire army,
must protect him as he performs difficult deeds in battle.
Thus addressed in battle, your son Duḥśāsana stood surrounding Bhīṣma, encompassed by a vast army;
then the son of Subala [Śakuni] arrived with a hundred thousand horses.
[He was accompanied] by those holding stainless spears, bearing double-edged swords and javelins—
men who were arrogant, swift, strong, and adorned with banners,
and who were endowed with the best of men, well-trained and skilled in combat.
Surrounded by various weapons and fully armored for battle,
they hemmed in Nakula, Sahadeva, and the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja from all sides, surrounding that best of men.
Then King Duryodhana dispatched ten thousand heroic horsemen to hold back the Pāṇḍavas;
as they entered the fray with great speed, they resembled Garuḍas in battle.
O King, the earth, struck by their hooves, trembled and resounded;
and then the immense sound of the horses' hooves was heard,
like that of a great forest of bamboos burning upon a mountain.

And by those [horses] leaping up there, a great cloud of dust was raised; reaching the path of the sun, it shrouded the maker of light. By those swift horses, the Pāṇḍava army was thrown into agitation.
Like a great lake filled with swans descending with great speed,
nothing could be discerned by the sound of their neighing;
the great noise was lost within that clamor, as everyone was bewildered by it.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī forcefully checked the momentum of those horse-riders in battle,
O Great King, as they surged forward like a swollen river overflowing during the rainy season.
Just as the shore resists the surge of the great ocean on the day of the full moon,
O King, those chariot-warriors then severed the heads of the horse-riders from their bodies with straight-knotted arrows.
O great king, struck down by those firm bowmen, they fell like great elephants slain by other elephants in a mountain cave;
they too [fell] by means of well-sharpened spears and straight-jointed arrows.
Moving through the ten directions, they severed heads;
O bull of the Bharatas, horsemen who were too close were cut down by double-edged spears (ṛṣṭi),
their heads falling like fruits from a great tree.
O King, horses with their riders were slaughtered here and there;
they fell and were being felled by the hundreds and thousands. Being thus struck down, those horses fled, afflicted by fear.
Just as deer, intent on saving their lives, flee upon encountering lions,
so too did the army of Saubala break and scatter in every direction.
But the Pāṇḍavas, O great king, having conquered their enemies in that great battle, [remained firm].
They blew their conchs and struck their kettledrums in the battle.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, Duryodhana, seeing his army standing there dejected, spoke these words to the King of Madra:
Then King Duryodhana said to the lord of the Madras:
"O uncle, this eldest son of Pāṇḍu, having defeated my men,
O mighty-armed one, is putting our army to flight while we look on."
"O mighty-armed one, restrain him as the shore restrains the ocean;
for you are renowned as one of truly unbearable strength and prowess.
Having heard those words of his son, the powerful Śalya—

He proceeded with a multitude of chariots to where King Yudhiṣṭhira was. That immense force of Śalya, which was suddenly rushing forward like the current of a great flood, the Pāṇḍava held back in battle.
And in that battle, the great car-warrior Dharmarāja quickly struck the King of Madra between the breasts with ten shafts;
Nakula and Sahadeva each struck him with three straight-flying arrows.
The King of Madra also struck all of them with three arrows each;
he then pierced Yudhiṣṭhira again with sixty sharpened shafts and struck the two enraged sons of Mādrī with two arrows each.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, the conqueror of enemies, seeing the king in battle fallen under the power of the King of Madra as if he had entered the jaws of Death,
rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira in the fray.
Even as he was approaching, Bhīma struck the King of Madra with sharp iron arrows made entirely of steel, which pierce the vital organs. Then Bhīṣma and Droṇa, surrounded by a vast army, [advanced].
The two of them, raining down showers of arrows, rushed straight toward the king.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having pierced the king with three shafts, advanced against him.
Then a most terrible and exceedingly fierce battle commenced.
When the sun was shining, having reached the western quarter,
Sañjaya said:
"Then your father, filled with rage, [struck him] with sharpened, excellent arrows."
In that battle, he struck the sons of Pṛthā along with their armies from all sides;
having pierced Bhīma with twelve arrows, Sātyaki with nine,
Nakula with three shafts, and Sahadeva with seven.

He struck Yudhiṣṭhira with twelve arrows in the arms and chest; then, having pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna, that one of great strength let out a roar. Nakula struck him with six arrows, and Mādhava with three.
Sahadeva pierced the grandfather with seventy arrows, Pārtha with nine,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna with seventy, Bhīmasena with five,
and Yudhiṣṭhira with twelve.
Droṇa, having pierced Sātyaki, struck Bhīmasena with nine sharpened arrows,
and having pierced Nakula with three.
Each of them pierced him with five sharp arrows resembling the staff of Yama;
and they, in turn, pierced Drona, that bull among Brahmins, with three straight-flying shafts each, like goads used for a great elephant.
The Sauviras, Kitavas, Easterners, Westerners, Northern Mālavas, Abhīṣāhas, Śūrasenas, Śibis,
and Vasātis did not abandon Bhīṣma in battle, even while being struck by sharp arrows.
In the same way, others, being struck by the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
turned back toward the Pāṇḍavas with various weapons in their hands;
likewise, O King, the Pāṇḍavas surrounded the grandfather.

Surrounded on all sides by a multitude of chariots, that unconquered one blazed forth like a fire set loose in a thicket, consuming his enemies. His chariot was the fire-chamber, his bow the flame, and his swords, spears, and maces the fuel.
The terrible fire of Bhīṣma, with its sparks of arrows, consumed the bulls among the Kṣatriyas;
for just as a great fire accompanied by the wind moves through dry grass,
so did Bhīṣma, O Great King, discharge his divine weapon.
With gold-feathered arrows, vulture-winged and well-sharpened, and with barbed, calf-toothed, and iron-headed shafts, he covered that army;
and with his keen arrows, he brought down both standards and chariot-warriors.

He made the multitudes of chariots resemble groves of shorn palm trees; O King, in that battle, that mighty-armed one, the best among all wielders of weapons, rendered the chariots, elephants, and horses devoid of men.
O Bhārata, hearing the sound of his bowstring, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt, all living beings trembled;
for the arrows of your father, O bull of the Bharatas, never missed their mark.
The arrows released from Bhīṣma’s bow did not stick in the armor.
O Great King, we beheld on the field of battle chariots whose heroes had been slain, still yoked to swift horses, being carried away.
In that battle, he struck down the Matsyas, Pañcālas, and Kaikeyas;
fourteen thousand renowned great car-warriors (*mahāratha*) from among the Cedis, Kāśis, and Karūṣas— noble sons who were ready to sacrifice their lives.
All those who did not retreat, their banners adorned with gold,
having encountered Bhīṣma in battle— who was like Death himself with his mouth wide open—
were submerged for the sake of the next world, along with their horses, chariots, and elephants.
O King, we saw hundreds and thousands of chariots with their axles and equipment shattered, and their wheels completely broken;
there were broken chariots with their protective fenders destroyed, and fallen chariot-warriors.
O lord of the people, with arrows shattered along with fine armor, with *paṭṭiśas*,
O honorable one, with maces, pestles, swords, and stone-tipped shafts, with chariot undercarriages, quivers, and broken wheels;
The earth was strewn with arms, bows, swords, and heads adorned with earrings; with hand-guards, finger-protectors, and fallen banners; and with bows shattered in many pieces.

O King, elephants whose riders had been slain and horses whose riders had been killed fell down there swiftly by the hundreds and thousands. And those heroes, though striving [to stop them], [could not restrain] the great car-warriors who were fleeing.
Afflicted by the arrows of Bhīṣma, they were unable to resist;
O great king, that vast army, being slaughtered by him whose prowess was equal to that of Mahendra, broke apart,
and no two men fled together.
With chariots, elephants, and horses overturned, and with standards and poles fallen, the army of the sons of Pāṇḍu cried out "Alas! Alas! and became senseless;
there, father slew son, and likewise, son slew father.
Driven by the power of fate, a friend cried out for his dear comrade; O Bhārata, other soldiers of the son of Pāṇḍu were seen running away, having cast off their armor and disheveled their hair.
Then the army of the son of Pāṇḍu was seen crying out in distress, like a bewildered herd of cows, with its chariots and elephants scattered;
and seeing the army being broken, the joy of the Yādavas [acted].
Having restrained that excellent chariot, he spoke to Pārtha Bībhatsu:
"O Pārtha, that time has now arrived which you have long desired. Strike him, O tiger among men, unless you are bewildered by delusion."
O hero, O Pārtha, that which was previously spoken by you in the assembly of kings in the city of Virāṭa, in the presence of Sañjaya—
concerning all the soldiers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa— [that shall now come to pass].
"I shall slay, along with their followers, those who fight against me in battle"—
O Kaunteya, subduer of foes, make those words true;
remembering the duty of a Kshatriya, fight, O bull of the Bharatas!

Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, Bībhatsu— with his gaze cast askance and his head bowed down— spoke these words as if devoid of desire: "Having committed the slaughter of those who should not be slain, the kingdom will lead only to hell."
"Whether there be hardships in dwelling in the forest, what indeed would be well-done for me?
Drive the horses to where Bhīṣma is; I shall carry out your word. I will strike down the invincible elder, the grandfather of the Kurus."
Then Mādhava urged on his silver-colored horses toward where Bhīṣma was, O King, like the sun difficult to behold. Thereupon that great army of Yudhiṣṭhira turned back once more.
Seeing the mighty-armed Pārtha rising against Bhīṣma in battle,
Bhīṣma, the best of the Kurus, then roared repeatedly like a lion and swiftly covered Dhananjaya’s chariot with showers of arrows.
In an instant, that chariot of his, along with its horses and charioteer,
could no longer be discerned at all due to the great shower of arrows.
Vāsudeva, however, the Sātvata, remained unperturbed and maintained his composure.
He urged on those horses that had been pierced by Bhīṣma’s arrows.
Then Pārtha, seizing his divine bow which sounded like a rain-cloud,
struck down Bhīṣma’s bow, cutting it asunder with sharp shafts.
His bow having been severed, O Kauravya, your father once more took up another great bow and, in the mere twinkling of an eye, made it ready with a string;
he then drew that bow, which resounded like a rain-cloud, with both his arms.
Then Arjuna, enraged, cut that bow of his as well. The son of Śantanu praised that lightness of hand, saying, "Excellent, O Pārtha of mighty arms! Excellent, O son of Kuntī!"
Having addressed him and grasped another beautiful bow,
Bhīṣma released arrows in battle toward the chariot of Pārtha. Vāsudeva displayed supreme skill in the management of the horses.
Rendering his arrows futile and displaying various circular maneuvers, those two tigers among men, Bhīṣma and Pārtha, shone resplendent despite being wounded by arrows,
like two enraged bulls marked by the gashes of their horns.
Then there commenced a fierce battle, hair-raising,
between the chief of the Pāṇḍavas and the foremost of the Kurus;
both of them, harsh in combat, drew their bows back as far as a palm tree’s height.
Both of them, the grandson and the grandfather, held firm grips upon their bows;
that meeting of the dark youth with the gray-haired elder shone like the confluence of the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Arrows marked with the name of Pārtha fell upon Bhīṣma’s chest,
just as the hearts of those devoid of virtue and ungrateful fall toward the righteous;
then, Bhīṣma’s arrows likewise fell upon Arjuna’s chest.
Desiring to conquer the science of archery attained by Mahādeva,
Vāsudeva, however, observed Pārtha’s mildness in combat and Bhīṣma discharging showers of arrows incessantly in battle.
Having reached the center between the two armies, Bhīṣma was scorching like the sun at midday;
slaughtering the very best of the soldiers of Pāṇḍu’s son,
he brought the Yudhiṣṭhira host to what seemed like the end of an eon.
The mighty-armed Mādhava, the slayer of enemy heroes, could not endure this;
Vāsudeva, filled with rage, blazed with fury in the battle,
O noble one, as he released Pārtha’s silver-colored horses.
The great yogi named Kruddha leaped down from his great chariot;
that powerful one, using his arms as weapons, rushed toward Bhīṣma,
the radiant hero with the goad in hand, roaring repeatedly like a lion.
As if tearing the earth with his feet, that lord of the world,
Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor, his eyes copper-red with rage,
desired to slay them in the great battle, as if swallowing the very spirits of your men.
Seeing Mādhava advancing in the fray against Bhīṣma in battle, all the soldiers there cried out, "Bhīṣma is slain! Bhīṣma is slain!
and all those men fled, driven by fear of Vāsudeva.

Clad in yellow silk and dark as a sapphire, Janārdana shone as he rushed toward Bhīṣma, like a cloud wreathed in lightning. He was like a lion attacking an elephant, or a bull of the herd attacking a bull.
Roaring, the radiant bull of the Yadavas rushed forward;
with the whip in his hand, the Blessed One, the bull of the Yadavas,
shone like the sun assailing the moon on the day of the new moon.
Beholding the lotus-eyed one rushing toward him in battle,
Bhīṣma, remaining unperturbed in the fray, drew his great bow and addressed Govinda with an untroubled mind.
"Come, come, O lotus-eyed one, God of gods, homage be unto you!
O best of the Sātvatas, protect me today in this great battle! For even if I am slain by you in combat, O sinless God,"
"O Kṛṣṇa, this alone is the supreme good, both in this world and in the next:
that I have been honored today in battle by the three worlds, O Govinda.
Strike me as you wish; I am indeed your servant, O sinless one."
"O Vāsudeva, even with a goad that possesses no [supernatural] qualities, you have done this for me;
he who is difficult even for yogis to attain has come here for the purpose of slaying [me].
Thereupon, Pārtha immediately pursued Keśava from behind.
The mighty-armed one seized him, indeed grasping him with both his arms; while being restrained by Pārtha, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa,
that Supreme Person, carried him away with great speed.
But Pārtha, the slayer of enemy heroes, having forcibly planted his feet,
managed with great difficulty to seize Hṛṣīkeśa by the tenth step.
Then, afflicted and with eyes agitated by rage, he spoke to him:
Like a hissing serpent, Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, said:
"Turn back, O mighty-armed one! You ought not to act falsely, O Keśava, regarding what was previously declared by you: 'I will not fight.'"
"O Mādhava, the world will call you a liar;
indeed, this entire burden is mine, for I shall slay him who is firm in his vows. O Mādhava, I swear by our friendship, by truth, and by my own good deeds."
"O crusher of enemies, so that I may reach the end of my foes,
behold this very day, O invincible one, the one of great vows being struck down—
like the full lord of the stars [the moon] at the time of destruction by the power of fate."
Having heard the words of the high-souled Phalguna, Mādhava was exceedingly pleased, recognizing Pārtha’s prowess;
saying nothing, he ascended the chariot again in a state of wrath.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, once more showered those two tigers among men standing upon their chariot with a rain of arrows, just as a cloud drenches two mountains with its downpour;
your father Devavrata took the lives of the warriors.
Just as the sun with its rays disperses the mists at the end of winter,
so did the son of Pāṇḍu break through the armies of the Kurus in battle;
even so did your father break through the armies of the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
With their armies slain and scattered, despondent and bewildered,
they were unable even to look upon Bhīṣma,
who was peerless in battle and performing deeds of superhuman prowess in the conflict.

O great king, as they were being slaughtered by Bhīṣma like Time itself at the end of an eon, the Pāṇḍavas, oppressed by fear, looked about at him who was scorching with his own splendor like the sun reached its zenith.
O Bhārata, as the Pāṇḍava armies were being routed and slaughtered in battle by Bhīṣma, the scorcher of enemies,
they found no protector, like cows stuck in the mud.
Like weak ants crushed by a powerful one in battle,
O Indra among kings, even so were all the Pāṇḍavas along with the Sṛñjayas trampled in combat by Bhīṣma, the slayer of enemies.
O Bhārata, they were unable even to look upon Bhīṣma— that great car-warrior, difficult to assail, who scorched the lords of men with his showers of arrows.
As he crushed the Pandava army, the thousand-rayed sun, like a fire-arrow, went to its setting while scorching like the sun itself.
Then Bhīṣma, together with his forces, warded off the sons of Pāṇḍu along with their armies with showers of arrows;
and that one of great strength struck them most severely.
The high-souled Mahāvrata [encountered] the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle, who were surrounded by the forces of the lord of Karūṣa and the Cedis,
while the wielder of the discus looked on.
Then, the minds of the troops, exhausted by fatigue, turned toward the thought of withdrawal,
just as the sun, standing on the slope of the eastern mountain, turns away after awakening the lotus grove.
Having himself enjoyed those [lotuses] with the tips of his exceedingly soft rays, the sun,
filled with anger because of the contact with the soiled bees,
set while still possessing his beautiful luster.
Saṃjaya said:
While they were still fighting, when the sun had set, a terrible twilight set in; we could no longer see the battle.
Then, O Bhārata, King Yudhiṣṭhira, beholding the twilight and seeing his army being slaughtered by Bhīṣma, the slayer of enemies—
its weapons cast aside, its ranks turned back, and intent solely on flight— [reflected].
Having seen Bhīṣma following the great car-warriors with fury in battle, and having seen the Somakas defeated and the great car-warriors deprived of their enthusiasm,
and observing that the onset of night was of a terrible and fearsome form;
Having reflected for a long time and meditated deeply, he approved of the withdrawal.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira ordered the withdrawal of his troops;
likewise, there was indeed a withdrawal of your troops at that time.
Then, having ordered the withdrawal of their troops there, those great car-warriors,
O best of the Kurus, went to their quarters in the camp, wounded and mangled by battle.
The Pāṇḍavas, however, remained reflecting upon Bhīṣma’s deeds in the encounter.
Then, severely oppressed by Bhīṣma, they found no peace;
yet Bhīṣma, O Bhārata, having conquered the Pāṇḍavas along with the Sṛñjayas in battle,
was honored and praised by your sons.
He settled down on all sides together with the Kurus, who appeared joyful;
then night arrived, which bewilders all living beings.
At that terrible onset of night, the Pāṇḍavas were together with the Vṛṣṇis.
The invincible Sṛñjayas,

all of great strength, sat down together for counsel; skilled in determining the conclusions of policy, they deliberated with focused minds on what was most beneficial for themselves at that critical time.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, O monarch, having deliberated for a long time,
looked toward Vāsudeva and spoke these words:
"Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, the high-souled Bhīṣma of terrible prowess."
He is crushing my army like an elephant trampling a forest of reeds;
we do not even dare to look upon this great-souled one,
who licks up our troops like a blazing fire.
Just as the terrible and great serpent Takṣaka is indeed full of virulent poison,
so too, O Kṛṣṇa, is Bhīṣma in battle— powerful, wielding sharp weapons,
holding his bow in the fray and discharging whetted arrows.
Yama, when enraged, could be conquered, as could the king of the gods wielding the thunderbolt,
or Varuṇa bearing his noose, or even the Lord of Wealth with his mace;
but Bhīṣma, when thoroughly incensed, cannot be defeated in a great battle.

O Kṛṣṇa, such being the case, I am submerged in an ocean of grief due to the weakness of my own intellect, having encountered Bhīṣma in battle. O invincible one, I shall go to the forest; indeed, that would be better for me.
"O Kṛṣṇa, I do not favor war, for Bhīṣma always slays us.
Just as a moth rushing toward a blazing fire meets its death head-on, so too have I approached Bhīṣma."
"O Vārṣṇeya, for the sake of the kingdom, I—who am full of prowess—have been brought to ruin;
and my heroic brothers too have been severely afflicted by arrows.
Out of brotherly affection toward me, they have suffered this fall from their sovereignty."
O Madhusūdana, Kṛṣṇā has been so greatly tormented on my account;
indeed, I hold life in high esteem, for life is truly difficult to obtain today. With what remains of this life, I shall practice the highest dharma.

"O Keśava, if I am worthy of your favor along with my brothers, then speak, O Keśava, in a manner that does not conflict with our own dharma. Having heard these words of his, [Kṛṣṇa spoke] at great length out of compassion.
Then Kṛṣṇa, consoling Yudhiṣṭhira, replied:
"O son of Dharma, you who are true to your promise, do not give way to despondency,
for your brothers are heroes, invincible slayers of enemies."
Arjuna and Bhīmasena possess a splendor equal to that of Vāyu and Agni;
and the two sons of Mādrī are valiant like the lords of the thirty gods.
Out of friendship, O Pāṇḍava, either appoint me, and I shall fight with Bhīṣma.
"O King, impelled by you, what indeed would I not do in the great battle?
I shall slay Bhīṣma, that bull among men, in combat after challenging him,
even if Phalguna does not wish it, while the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra look on."
"O King, O Pāṇḍava, if you see victory upon Bhīṣma’s death,
then today I shall slay the aged grandfather of the Kurus from a single chariot.
Behold my prowess in battle, O King, like that of Mahendra himself."
I shall strike that man from his chariot as he discharges great weapons;
for he who is an enemy of the sons of Pāṇḍu is my enemy, without a doubt. Those who are for my sake are for yours, and those who are mine are yours alone.
"O lord of the earth, he is your brother, my friend, my kinsman, and indeed my disciple;
I would even cut out my own flesh and give it for the sake of Arjuna.
Moreover, this tiger among men would likewise sacrifice his life for my sake."
"This is our agreement, dear father: let us rescue one another.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, employ me so that I may become an island for you. This is the vow that was previously made by Pārtha at Upaplavya."
"I shall cause the son of Gaṅgā to be slain"—this was said by me in the presence of Ulūka;
yet that word of the wise Pārtha must be protected by me. Once authorized by Pārtha, I must carry out this task without a doubt.
Alternatively, this burden in battle is limited for Phalguna;
he shall slay Bhīṣma, the conqueror of enemy cities, in the conflict.
For Pārtha, when fully exerted, can indeed accomplish even the impossible in battle.

Arjuna could slay even the thirty gods when they are united and exerted together with the Daityas and Dānavas in battle, O lord of men; how much more so Bhīṣma? For Bhīṣma is now the opposite—he has lost his great prowess, his strength is gone, and his life is short.
"Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, surely does not understand what ought to be done.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O mighty-armed Mādhava, it is exactly as you say."
"For all these together are not sufficient to restrain your momentum.
I shall certainly obtain everything exactly as I desire,
O tiger among men, since you, who possess great strength, are my protector."

"O best among victors, with you as my protector, O Govinda, I could defeat even the gods led by Indra in battle; how much more so Bhīṣma in the great fray? Yet, out of regard for my own interest, I cannot bring myself to make you a liar."
"O Mādhava, without fighting yourself, provide me assistance as previously described.
However, O Mādhava, a certain agreement was made with Bhīṣma by me:
'I shall counsel for your sake, but I will not fight in any way whatsoever.'"
"O Lord, I shall fight for the sake of Duryodhana; this is the truth.

For he is the one who bestowed upon me the kingdom and the very counsel [of the *Gāndharva* weapon], O Mādhava. Therefore, I must once again [consult] Devavrata regarding the means for my own destruction."
"Accompanied by you, O Madhusūdana,
we shall all together go quickly to Bhīṣma, that best of men, and at your pleasure,
O Vārṣṇeya, ask that Kuru elder for counsel."

"O Janārdana, he will speak words that are beneficial and indeed true; O Kṛṣṇa, whatever he tells us in the conflict, that I shall do. He, firm in his vows, is the giver of victory and of counsel for us."
"We were children, deprived of our father, and by him we were raised.
O Mādhava, how can I wish to kill that aged grandfather,
upon whose body we used to play constantly and by whom we were nurtured in our childhood?"

O Janārdana, we have been duly trained in weapons; O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of the kingdom, we were prepared to slay him in battle. But he was the beloved father of our father—fie on the livelihood of a warrior!
"O Janārdana, listen to that which was truly spoken by Bṛhaspati in the presence of the gods, as previously declared by the Preceptor:
'O giver of honor, when a son approaches his father, or a father his son...'"
"For the sake of the kingdom, one must indeed cause [an enemy] to be slain; such is the eternal dharma of the Kṣatriya.
Sañjaya said:
"Then, O Great King, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi spoke to the joy of the Kurus."
"O mighty-armed one, your words always please me.
The accomplished Bhīṣma, Devavrata, could consume us even with a glance.
Let us go to ask that son of the River Ganges for the means of his slaughter."
"He ought to speak the truth when questioned by you, especially so; therefore,
O Mādhava, let us go there to ask the grandfather of the Kurus, and having bowed our heads to him, let us inquire about this counsel."
"He will grant us that mantra by which we shall fight the enemies. Having thus deliberated, O elder brother of Pāṇḍu, those heroic Pāṇḍavas and the valiant Vāsudeva all went together.
Having cast aside their weapons and armor,
O great king, the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls of the Bharata race, entered Bhīṣma’s abode and then paid homage to Bhīṣma with their heads bowed.
Having bowed their heads to him, they sought refuge with Bhīṣma. Taking the Pāṇḍavas by the feet as they approached, and embracing them,
he then smelled their heads and took them onto his lap.
With his face clouded by tears, the mighty-armed Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, remembering Pāṇḍu again and again, said to them:
"Welcome to you, O Vārṣṇeya; welcome to you, O Dhanañjaya."
"Welcome to the Son of Dharma, to Bhīma, and likewise to the twins!
What task may I perform for you today that will increase your joy? O children, let yourselves be pleased except through battle; do not hesitate."
"I shall do it with my whole soul, even if it should be extremely difficult. To the son of Gaṅgā who was speaking thus repeatedly with joy,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, spoke these words with a dejected heart.
O Lord, as you ask me today, so shall I tell you:
O Knower of Dharma, how may we conquer? How may we obtain the kingdom? And how, O Sovereign, may there be no destruction of the subjects? Tell me that.
"Indeed, may you yourself tell us the means for your own destruction;
O King, how might we withstand you in battle? For there is not even the slightest vulnerability in you, O grandfather of the Kurus."

In battle, you are always seen with your bow drawn into a complete circle; O mighty-armed one, we do not perceive you taking up the bow, nor fixing an arrow, nor drawing it, as you stand upon your chariot like the sun.
O bull of the Bharatas, what man would dare to slay you— the destroyer of men, horses, chariots, and elephants, the slayer of enemy heroes— while you,
O Supreme Person, rain down great showers of arrows?
"Indeed, this great army of mine has been brought to exhaustion by you. O Grandfather, tell me how I may defeat you in battle, how the kingdom may become mine,
or how there might be peace for my troops."
Then the son of Śantanu said to the Pāṇḍavas, O elder brother of Pāṇḍu: "O Kaunteya, as long as I am alive in battle, no prosperity shall be seen among you by any means; I tell you this truly."
"Once I have been defeated in battle, you will surely conquer the Kauravas. Strike me quickly if you desire victory in this fight. I give you my permission, O sons of Pṛthā; strike as you please."
"I consider this indeed well done, for I am known to you. When I am slain, all are slain; therefore, let it be so arranged.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Therefore, tell us the means by which we might conquer you in battle—
you who are enraged in combat like Antaka himself with staff in hand.
Even the wielder of the thunderbolt, Varuṇa, or likewise Yama, could be defeated.
"You cannot be overcome in battle even by the gods and asuras led by Indra.
Bhīṣma said:
"O mighty-armed Pāṇḍava, what you say is true."

I cannot be conquered in battle even by the gods and asuras led by Indra, provided I am prepared in combat, armed with weapons, and holding my excellent bow. But if I have laid down my weapons, O King, the great car-warriors might slay me in war.

O son of Dharma, when the weapons have been laid down, when one has fallen, when armor and banners have been cast off, when one is fleeing in fear, when one cries out "I am yours," when one is conquered by women, dominated by women, or subservient to women— [in these cases, there is no fault].
Against a woman, one who bears the name of a woman, one who is physically impaired, one who has only one son,
one who has not borne children, or one who is difficult to look upon— battle does not please me.
And hear this, O Pārtha, my resolve which I have long contemplated.
"Upon seeing an inauspicious banner, I shall not fight under any circumstances.
O King, this great car-warrior in your army who is the son of Drupada— O Lord of the People, his son was previously [known as] Apumān."
Śikhaṇḍin, who longs for battle, is a hero and a victor in assembly;
you know exactly how he was previously a woman and later attained manhood. You all likewise know all this according to the truth.
Let the heroic Arjuna, clad in armor and placing Śikhaṇḍin in front of him,
swiftly charge at me alone with his arrows in battle—
especially against that man whose banner bears an inauspicious sign and who was previously a woman.
"I do not wish to strike at all while my bow is grasped; therefore,
O bull of the Bharatas, having found that opportunity, let Dhananjaya the Pāṇḍava quickly strike me down from every side with his arrows."
"I do not see anyone in the worlds who could slay me while I am prepared for battle,
except for the highly blessed Kṛṣṇa or the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya.
Therefore, let him place someone else before me."
"Let Bībhatsu strike me down; in this way, victory shall be yours.
O Kaunteya, do exactly as I have said;
then you will conquer the assembled sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle."
Saṃjaya said:
Having been granted leave, those sons of Pṛthā then departed toward their own camp,
after having paid homage to the high-souled Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus.
When the son of Gaṅgā had spoken thus, having consecrated himself for the next world,
Arjuna, consumed by grief, spoke these words with shame:
"By my preceptor, the elder of the lineage, who is wise and possessed of perfected insight— "
"O Mādhava, how shall I fight in battle with my grandfather? For in my childhood, O Vāsudeva, while playing, that high-minded one was made rough by me,
his limbs covered in dust."
O elder brother of Gada, when I was but a child, I used to climb onto your lap and call you "Father," regarding you as the father of my own high-souled father Pāṇḍu.
But I am not your father; O Bhārata, I am merely the father of your father.
"How can he, who told me in my childhood, 'He who says this shall be slain by me,' be put to death by me? Let my army be slain at will; I will not fight with that high-souled one.
Whether victory or death be mine, what do you think, O Kṛṣṇa?"
"O Kṛṣ�ṇa, how could one such as I, knowing the eternal dharma, strike at his grandfather— the aged man who has laid down his weapons? Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Jiṣṇu, having previously vowed his slaughter in battle,
how is it that you, O Pārtha, remaining steadfast in the duty of a Kṣatriya, will not slay him? Strike him down from his chariot, O Pārtha, like a tree struck by a thunderbolt!
"O son of Gaṅgā, there will be no victory for you without slaying him in battle.
This was ordained long ago by the gods; it shall happen to you against your will. That Bhīṣma’s slayer is Pūrvendra—that shall not be otherwise."

For no one other than you— not even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself— could slay Bhīṣma, who is unassailable and like Death with his mouth wide open. O mighty-armed one, slay Bhīṣma and listen to these words of mine.
Just as the highly intelligent Bṛhaspati spoke to Śakra in the past: "O Śakra,
even if he is superior and endowed with virtues,
one should slay an assassin who has come as a killer after having challenged one."
"O Dhanañjaya, this is the eternal law established for Kṣatriyas:
they must fight, protect, and perform sacrifices without malice.
Arjuna said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Śikhaṇḍin will certainly be the cause of Bhīṣma's death;
for as soon as Bhīṣma sees the prince of the Pañcālas, he always turns away from battle. Therefore, we shall place Śikhaṇḍin directly in front of him."
"It is my conviction that we shall bring down the son of Gaṅgā by some stratagem.
I myself will hold back the other great archers with my arrows,
while Śikhaṇḍin, the best among warriors, shall advance against Bhīṣma himself."
"I have heard from you, O chief of the Kurus, that I shall not slay Śikhaṇḍin;
for he was previously born as a girl and later became a man.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard Arjuna’s words concerning the slaying of Bhīṣma,
the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, then rejoiced, their hair standing on end.
Sañjaya said:
Having thus made this resolution, the Pāṇḍavas,
together with Mādhava, took leave of the high-souled one and departed with joyful hearts;
those bulls among men retired to their respective beds.
Having returned to their respective homes, they dwelt happily for that night.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How did Śikhaṇḍin advance against the son of Gaṅgā in battle?"
"And likewise, what did the Pāṇḍavas do toward Bhīṣma? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
"Then, at the clear dawn, as the sun was rising,"
While the kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas, and ānakas were being sounded,
and conch shells white as curd were blown on all sides,
the Pāṇḍavas went forth into battle, placing Śikhaṇḍin at their head.

Having formed a battle array, O Great King, which was destructive of all enemies, Śikhaṇḍin stood at the head of all the troops, O Lord of the People. Then Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya were his wheel-protectors.
Behind them were the sons of Draupadī and the heroic son of Subhadrā;
then came Sātyaki and Cekitāna, the great car-warrior who was their protector;
and after them followed Dhṛṣṭadyumna, guarded by the Pāñcālas.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord, accompanied by the twins,
set forth, O bull of the Bharatas, making the earth resound with lion-like roars. Virāṭa, however, followed behind, surrounded by his own army.
And Drupada, O great king, followed behind him;
then the five Kekaya brothers and the valiant Dhṛṣṭaketu protected the rear of the Pāṇḍava army, O Bhārata.

Having thus arrayed their great army, the Pāṇḍavas rushed against your host in battle, having renounced their own lives. In the same way, O King, the Kurus, placing the mighty Bhīṣma at their head, advanced.
At the head of all the troops, they advanced toward the Pāṇḍavas,
protected by your invincible sons of great strength. Then followed the great archer Droṇa and his son, the great car-warrior.
Then Bhagadatta followed, surrounded by a division of elephants;
Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman followed behind Bhagadatta. After them came the powerful Sudakṣiṇa, the king of the Kambojas.
O Bhārata, Jayatsena the Māgadha, Bṛhadbala the son of Subala, and other great archers led by King Suśarman protected the rear of your army.
Day after day arrived, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu,
formed in battle arrays belonging to the Asuras, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas.
Then, O Bhārata, a battle commenced between your men and theirs.
O King, as they slaughtered one another, increasing the population of Yama’s realm,
the sons of Pṛthā, led by Arjuna and placing Śikhaṇḍin at their head,
advanced against Bhīṣma in battle, scattering various kinds of arrows.
There, O Bhārata, your men, tormented by Bhīma’s arrows and drenched in streams of blood, then departed for the other world. Nakula, Sahadeva, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki—
Having encountered your army, they oppressed it with their might.
O bull of the Bharatas, being slaughtered in battle,
your men were unable to check the great force of the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, O King, your army, being slaughtered on all sides and driven away by the great car-warriors, fled in every direction;
your men, O bull of the Bharatas, found no protector.
Being struck by sharp arrows from the Pāṇḍavas together with the Sṛñjayas,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Seeing his army being oppressed by the sons of Pṛthā, the valiant Bhīṣma— "
Tell me, Sañjaya, what he did in battle when enraged; tell me, Sañjaya, how that scorcher of foes advanced against the Pāṇḍavas in the fight,
slaughtering the heroic Somakas.
Saṃjaya said:
"O great king, I shall tell you what the grandfather did when your son’s army was being oppressed by the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas."
O elder brother of Pāṇḍu, with joyful hearts, the heroic Pāṇḍavas advanced,
slaughtering the army of your son.
O lord of men, that was the destruction of men, elephants, and horses.
Then Bhīṣma could not tolerate that slaughter of his army by the enemies in battle;
that great archer, difficult to overcome, disregarding his own life, rushed against the Pāṇḍavas, the Pañcālas, and the Sṛñjayas.
O King, Bhīṣma, exceedingly enraged, checked those five preeminent Pāṇḍava great-chariot warriors— who were prepared for battle and had taken up their weapons— with his straight-knotted arrows.
With iron shafts, calf-toothed arrows, and sharp *añjalika* darts,
as well as showers of various weapons and missiles hurled forth by his prowess and indignation,
he, enraged in battle, struck down immeasurable numbers of elephants and horses.
O King, that bull among men struck down chariot-warriors from their chariots,
horsemen from the backs of their horses, gathered foot-soldiers,
and elephant-riders from their elephants, instilling fear in his enemies.
