The Pāṇḍavas rushed against that lone great car-warrior Bhīṣma as he hastened in battle, just as the Asuras once assailed the wielder of the thunderbolt;
he discharged sharpened arrows whose touch was like Indra’s lightning bolt.
In all directions, he was seen maintaining a terrible form;
as he fought in battle, his great bow, resembling the bow of Śakra, was constantly seen drawn into a circle.
O lord of the people, having witnessed that feat in battle, your sons were filled with supreme wonder and honored the Grandfather;
the sons of Pṛthā, however, became despondent as they gazed upon your father.
As he fought heroically in battle like Vipracitti against the immortals,
they could not restrain him, who was like Death with his mouth wide open;
this occurred when the tenth day arrived for Śikhaṇḍin’s division of chariots.
Scorching him with sharpened arrows like fire consuming a forest,
Śikhaṇḍin pierced him in the center of the chest with three shafts—
him who was like an enraged venomous serpent or Death itself unleashed by Time.
Deeply pierced by him, Bhīṣma looked at Śikhaṇḍin and,
though unwilling and filled with rage, spoke these words while laughing:
"Whether you strike me as you wish or not, I will not fight with you under any circumstances."
"For you are indeed that very same Śikhaṇḍinī whom the Creator fashioned.
Hearing those words of his, Śikhaṇḍin, overwhelmed with rage,
spoke to Bhīṣma in the battle, licking the corners of his mouth.
O mighty-armed one, I know you to be the destroyer of the kṣatriyas, having heard of every great battle you have fought in the great war; indeed,
I have also heard of your combat with the son of Jamadagni.
This divine power of yours has been heard of by me many times;
yet, O best of men, even though I know your power, I shall fight with you today,
doing what is pleasing both to the Pāṇḍavas and to myself.
"O best of men, today I shall fight you in battle;
I swear by my own truth before you that I will certainly slay you.
Having heard these words of mine, do what is appropriate."
"Whether you practice [this] or not, you shall not escape from me alive.
O Bhīṣma, victor in assembly, let this world be seen by you clearly.
Having spoken thus, he then struck Bhīṣma with five straight-jointed arrows.
O King, he pierced him in battle, driven on by the arrows of his words.
Hearing those words of his, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes,
thinking "this is the time," urged Śikhaṇḍin forward.
"I shall follow after you, putting the enemies to flight with my arrows;
charge forward with great fury against Bhīṣma of terrible prowess,
for that one of great strength is not able to cause you pain in combat."
Therefore, O mighty-armed hero, charge against Bhīṣma today! O noble one, if you depart from the battle without having slain Bhīṣma,
you will become an object of ridicule for this world, along with me.
"O hero, act with such effort in battle that we do not become objects of ridicule in the great conflict; thus accomplish the defeat of the grandfather.
O scorcher of foes, I shall provide you protection in the fight."
Holding back all the chariot-warriors, bring success to the Grandfather,
as well as Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Suyodhana;
and Citrasena, Vikarṇa, and Jayadratha, the ruler of the Sindhus.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, the heroic Bhagadatta, the great car-warrior of Magadha,
the brave son of Somadatta, and the Rākṣasa Aśvaśṛṅgin in battle.
And I shall hold back the King of Trigarta in battle, along with all his great chariot-warriors, as the shore holds back the ocean;
and likewise all the Kurus together and those soldiers who stand with them.
"I shall hold him back in battle; proceed against the grandfather.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How did Śikhaṇḍin charge at the son of Gaṅgā, the grandfather?"
In that battle, who among the Pāṇḍava forces protected the virtuous Śikhaṇḍin, firm in his vows, as he stood with weapon raised against the enraged King of Pañcāla?
At that time of urgency, which great car-warriors, hastening and desiring victory, stood by him?
How did Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, that man of great heroism, fight on that tenth day against the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas?
I cannot endure the thought of Bhīṣma being assailed in battle by Śikhaṇḍin.
"I hope that his chariot did not break, or that his bow was not shattered as he was shooting?
Sañjaya said:
"His bow was not shattered, nor did his chariot break."
O bull of the Bharatas, as Bhīṣma fought in battle,
slaughtering his enemies in the fray with straight-jointed arrows,
many hundreds of thousands of great car-warriors on your side [perished].
O King, hosts of chariots and elephants, as well as well-equipped horses,
advanced for battle, placing the Grandfather at their head;
and he too, O Kauravya, was victorious in assembly, according to his vow.
Bhīṣma constantly brought about the destruction of the Pārthas in battle;
yet all the Pañcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, opposed that great archer as he fought and struck down his enemies with arrows.
When the tenth day arrived, he scorched the enemy host,
which was being scattered by hundreds and thousands of sharp arrows;
for the Pāṇḍavas could not withstand Bhīṣma, that great archer, O elder brother of Pāṇḍu.
Unable to defeat him in battle— who was like Death himself with noose in hand—
then, O great king, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes,
the unconquered Bībhatsu, approached, terrifying all the chariot-warriors.
Roaring loudly like a lion, repeatedly twanging his bowstring and discharging showers of arrows, Pārtha moved about the battlefield like Time itself.
O bull of the Bharatas, your troops were terrified by that sound.
O King, like deer before a lion, they fled in great terror upon seeing the Pāṇḍava victorious and your army being hard-pressed. Then Duryodhana, severely afflicted, spoke to Bhīṣma.
"O dear one, this son of Pāṇḍu, with white horses and Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer,
consumes all my men like a fire consumes a forest.
Behold, O son of Gaṅgā, the troops fleeing in every direction!"
O best among warriors,
O scorcher of enemies, my army is being driven back in battle by the Pāṇḍava, just as a herdsman drives a herd of cattle through the forest.
"Broken by the arrows of Dhanañjaya and fleeing hither and thither,
this invincible Bhīma is indeed putting my army to flight;
so too are Sātyaki, Cekitāna, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī."
The valiant Abhimanyu consumes my army,
as do the heroic Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca;
these two of great strength would suddenly put my forces to flight.
O Bhārata, as this army is being slaughtered by all these mighty warriors, I see no other course for me in this situation or in battle,
O tiger among men, except for you, whose prowess is equal to that of the gods.
"You are capable; quickly become the refuge for those who are oppressed.
Thus addressed, O Great King, your father Devavrata reflected for a moment and made his own resolution.
"I shall strike down the other enemies while guarding the Pāṇḍavas;
for victory over the high-souled Pāṇḍavas has been promised today. Thus spoke the son of Śaṃtanu, upholding your son.
"O Duryodhana, understand this; be firm, O lord of the people! O you of great strength, long ago I made a vow to you:
that after slaying ten thousand high-souled Kṣatriyas,"

"One must retreat from battle; this is my daily duty"—thinking thus, O bull of the Bharatas, I performed that task exactly as prescribed. And today, too, I shall perform a great deed in this great conflict.
Either I shall lie slain, or I shall slay the Pāṇḍavas today.
The Pāṇḍavas cannot be conquered even by the gods led by Vāsava;
how much less, O one of great strength, by a mortal Kṣatriya?
"O tiger among men, today I shall discharge my great debt incurred by the food provided by my master, O King, now that I am slain at the head of the army.
Having spoken thus, the best of the Bharatas scorched the kṣatriyas with his arrows.
The invincible one approached the army of the Pāṇḍavas. O bull of the Bharatas, the Pāṇḍavas surrounded Gāṅgeya as he stood in the midst of the host, like an enraged venomous serpent.
On that tenth day, O King, displaying his own prowess,
he slew hundreds of thousands, O joy of the Kurus—
those who were the foremost and most powerful princes among the Pāñcālas.

He took away their vital energies, just as the sun draws up water with its rays. O great king, having slain ten thousand swift elephants along with their riders, he further killed ten thousand horses.
When two full hundred-thousand foot soldiers had been slain, Bhīṣma, the best of men, blazed forth in battle like a smokeless fire;
and none among the sons of Pāṇḍu were able even to look upon him.
Taking up their superior positions, like the scorching sun,
those sons of Pāṇḍu, enraged and oppressed by that great archer,
along with the Sṛñjaya mahārathas, rushed toward Bhīṣma for his slaughter.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, fighting against many,
was surrounded by those mighty-armed warriors like a mountain enveloped by dark clouds;
meanwhile, your sons hemmed in the son of Gaṅgā on all sides.
Then, together with a great army, the battle commenced.
Sañjaya said:
"But Arjuna, O King, having witnessed Bhīṣma’s prowess in battle..."
Then he said to Śikhaṇḍin, "Approach the Grandfather;
you must not feel any fear of Bhīṣma today by any means.
I shall strike him down from his excellent chariot with my sharp arrows."
Thus addressed by Pārtha, O bull of the Bharatas,
Śikhaṇḍin rushed toward the son of Gaṅgā upon hearing Pārtha’s speech;
likewise, O King, did Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the great car-warrior Saubhadra.
Delighted upon hearing the words spoken by Pārtha,
the aged Virāṭa and Drupada, along with Kuntibhoja clad in armor,
rushed toward Bhīṣma while your son looked on.
O lord of the people, Nakula, Sahadeva, the heroic Dharmarāja,
and all the other troops likewise rushed toward the son of Gaṅgā upon hearing the words spoken by Pārtha.
Your warriors, having assembled together, advanced against those great car-warriors according to their strength and according to their zeal; hear from me as I describe them.
O great king, Citrasena rushed against Cekitāna.
O great king, as Dhṛṣṭadyumna advanced toward Bhīṣma in battle like a tiger cub attacking a bull,
Kṛtavarman, exerting himself in the fray, swiftly checked him.

O great king, the son of Somadatta, acting with haste, checked the highly enraged Bhīmasena— who was exerting himself in battle and seeking the death of Gāṅgeya. Acting with haste, the son of Somadatta held him back.
In the same way, Vikarṇa, desiring to preserve Bhīṣma’s life, held back the heroic Nakula as he scattered many arrows. Likewise,
[he opposed] Sahadeva as he proceeded with diligence toward Bhīṣma’s chariot.
Enraged in battle, Kṛpa Śāradvata checked the mighty Rākṣasa of cruel deeds, the son of Bhīmasena,
who was seeking the death of Bhīṣma; then the powerful Durmukha rushed against him.
O great king, the son of Ārśyaśṛṅga checked the enraged Sātyaki in battle as he advanced toward Bhīṣma’s chariot,
desiring the slaughter of Bhīṣma out of affection for the Pāṇḍavas.
Abhimanyu likewise proceeded toward Bhīṣma’s chariot.
O great king, Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja held him back; then,
O Bhārata, the enraged Aśvatthāman checked the two aged crushers of enemies, Virāṭa and Drupada, who had come together.
Likewise, the son of Bharadvāja, exerting himself in battle, held back the son of Dharma— the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas— who was desirous of slaying Bhīṣma,
having placed the impetuous Arjuna in front with Śikhaṇḍin.

O great king, Duḥśāsana, the mighty archer, held back in battle that seeker of Bhīṣma who was scorching the ten directions; and other warriors on your side [held back] the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas.
They warded off those who were advancing toward Bhīṣma in battle;
but Dhṛṣṭadyumna, repeatedly shouting to his troops, said:
"Attack with fury that one of great strength, Bhīṣma!"
"Here comes Arjuna, the joy of the Kurus, advancing against Bhīṣma in battle! Charge forward; do not fear, for Bhīṣma will not reach you.
Even Vāsava himself would not dare to fight Arjuna in combat."
"How much less Bhīṣma, O heroes, who in battle has lost his strength and has but little life remaining?
Hearing this from the commander-in-chief, the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas,
filled with joy, rushed toward the chariot of the son of Gaṅgā.
O great king, your warriors, those bulls among men, filled with joy, resisted those powerful torrents of troops as they advanced in battle like mighty floods,
while the great car-warrior Duḥśāsana cast off all fear.
Desirous of Bhīṣma’s life, he rushed toward Dhanañjaya;
likewise, the heroic Pāṇḍavas rushed in battle toward the chariot of the son of Gaṅgā, against your sons, the great car-warriors.
And in that battle, your son, the great car-warrior, fought him;
there, O lord of the people, we beheld a wonderful and marvelous sight:
that when Pārtha reached Duḥśāsana’s chariot, he could not prevail over it.
Just as the shore restrains the turbulent great ocean,
even so did your son restrain the enraged Pāṇḍava.
For both were the best among chariot-warriors, and both, O Bhārata, were difficult to defeat.
O Bhārata, both were like the moon and the sun in beauty and brilliance;
thus enraged and each desiring to slay the other,
they encountered one another in that great battle, just as Maya and Śakra did in ancient times.
O Great King, Duḥśāsana struck the Pāṇḍava with three arrows and Vāsudeva with twenty in that battle. Then Arjuna, his wrath aroused upon seeing the descendant of Vṛṣṇi afflicted, [attacked].
In the battle, he struck Duḥśāsana with a hundred iron arrows;
having pierced his armor, they drank his blood in the fray,
O King, just as thirsty serpents drink from a pond.

Then Duḥśāsana, filled with rage, pierced Pārtha in the forehead with five straight-knotted arrows, O best of the Bharatas. With those arrows fixed in his forehead, that foremost of the Pāṇḍavas shone resplendent.
O great king, just as Mount Meru stands exceedingly high with its peaks,
so did that great archer Pārtha, deeply pierced by your son, the bowman,
shine resplendent in battle like a *kiṃśuka* tree in full bloom.
Then the enraged Pāṇḍava tormented Duḥśāsana,
just as the fierce Rāhu, highly incensed, afflicts the moon during the full moon.
O lord of the people, your son was thus oppressed by that powerful warrior.
In that battle, he pierced Pārtha with stone-sharpened arrows feathered with heron plumes.
Then the valiant Pārtha, acting with haste, cut his bow asunder and subsequently struck your son with nine arrows.
Taking up another bow, he stood before Bhīṣma and struck Arjuna in the arms and chest with twenty-five arrows. O great king, the son of Pāṇḍu, the crusher of enemies, became enraged at him.
He discharged many terrible arrows, resembling the staff of Yama;
yet your son cut those shafts down before they had even reached him.
As Pārtha exerted himself in this way, it was like a marvel.
And your son pierced Pārtha with sharpened arrows;
then, enraged in battle, Pārtha fixed arrows upon his bow and dispatched those gold-feathered shafts, whetted on stone, into the fray.
O great king, they plunged into the body of that high-souled one,
just as swans, O Bhārata, enter a lake upon reaching it;
and thus was your son tormented by the high-souled Pāṇḍava.

Quickly abandoning Pārtha in battle, he took refuge at Bhīṣma’s chariot; for him who was sinking in the bottomless depths, Bhīṣma then became an island. Then, O lord of people, your son regained consciousness.
Then that hero, possessing even greater prowess,
warded off Pārtha with exceedingly sharp arrows, just as Vṛtra did against Purandara; though possessed of great valor, he pierced him and was not at all distressed by Arjuna.
Saṃjaya said:
Then the great archer, the son of Ārśyaśṛṅga, checked Satyaki in battle as he was clad in armor and advancing against Bhīṣma.
But Mādhava, O King, being greatly enraged, struck the Rākṣasa in battle with nine arrows, as if laughing, O Bhārata;
and likewise, O King, the Rākṣasa struck Mādhava with sharpened shafts.

O king of kings, being highly incensed, he tormented the bull of the Śinis; then Mādhava, the slayer of enemy heroes, being likewise enraged, dispatched a multitude of arrows at the Rākṣasa in that battle, O descendant of Śini.
Then the Rākṣasa pierced the mighty-armed Sātyaki, whose valor is truth,
with sharp arrows and let out a lion’s roar.
But Mādhava, having been deeply pierced by the Rākṣasa in that battle at that time, [remained steadfast].
Resorting to fortitude, the spirited hero laughed and roared.
Then Bhagadatta, enraged, struck Mādhava in battle with sharpened arrows,
as one strikes a great elephant with goads.
Leaving the Rākṣasa in battle, Śaineya, the best of chariot-warriors,
hurled straight-knotted arrows at the King of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Then the King of Prāgjyotiṣa [cut] the great bow of that Mādhava.
With a sharp-edged crescent-headed arrow, he severed it with the skill of a practiced hand. Then, taking up another bow, that slayer of enemy heroes,
filled with rage in battle, pierced Bhagadatta with swift, sharpened shafts.
Deeply pierced, that great archer repeatedly licked the corners of his mouth and hurled at Sātyaki a formidable iron spear, adorned with gold and lapis lazuli,
as firm as the staff of Yama.

O King, as that spear hurled by the strength of his arm came rushing suddenly toward him, Sātyaki cut it into three pieces in battle with his arrows; that gold-adorned spear was shattered by the shafts released from Mādhava’s arms.
Then it fell to the earth like a great meteor whose radiance had been extinguished.
O lord of the people, seeing his spear destroyed, your son obstructed Mādhava with a vast array of chariots.
Seeing the great car-warrior of the Vārṣṇeyas thus surrounded,
Duryodhana was greatly delighted and said to all his brothers:
"O Kauravas, act in such a way that Satyaki does not escape you in battle."
"He will not escape alive from this great multitude of chariots;
once he is slain, I consider the great army of the Pāṇḍavas already destroyed.
Accepting his words with the reply, "So be it," those great car-warriors [advanced].
Then they fought against the descendant of Śini in the presence of Bhīṣma; meanwhile,
the powerful king of the Kambojas held back Abhimanyu in the encounter as he was advancing toward Bhīṣma, intent on battle.
Having pierced the king with straight-jointed arrows, the son of Arjuna,
O King, struck that monarch once again with sixty-four shafts.
Sudakṣiṇa, however, pierced the son of Kṛṣṇa in the battle with five arrows.
Desiring to deprive Bhīṣma of his life, he struck the charioteer with nine arrows;
then there occurred a truly great battle between those two as they displayed their prowess,
when Śikhaṇḍin, the scorcher of enemies, rushed against the son of Gaṅgā.
Then the aged Virāṭa and Drupada,
those two great car-warriors, enraged in battle, rushed against Bhīṣma while holding back the vast army;
thereupon Aśvatthāman, the best of chariot-fighters, advanced in a fury.
Then, O Bhārata, the battle between your men and theirs commenced.
Virāṭa, the scorcher of foes, struck [the enemy] with ten broad-headed arrows.
Then, in that great battle, he [drove back] the son of Droṇa and the warriors as they were fleeing.
Seeing the son of Droṇa, that great archer who graces the battlefield, striving and discharging his arrows,
Drupada likewise pierced him with three sharpened shafts.
Having encountered the preceptor’s son standing before Bhīṣma,
Aśvatthāman then pierced both Virāṭa and Drupada— the two elders who were exerting themselves against Bhīṣma— with ten arrows.
There we beheld a wonderful and great feat performed by the two elders,
in that they warded off the terrible arrows of the son of Droṇa in battle. Likewise, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, advanced against Sahadeva as he was proceeding.
O King, just as an elephant in rut might charge an elephant in rut in the forest,
so did Kṛpa in battle swiftly strike the great car-warrior, the son of Mādrī, with seventy gold-adorned arrows.
The son of Mādrī cut his bow in two with arrows;
then he pierced him, whose bow was broken, with nine shafts.
He took up another bow in that battle, one capable of bearing a great burden.
Highly delighted and filled with rage, desiring to preserve Bhīṣma’s life, he struck the son of Mādrī in the chest with ten sharpened arrows;
and in the same way, O King, the Pāṇḍava struck the impatient son of Śaradvat.
Enraged and desiring the slaughter of Bhīṣma, he struck him on the chest.
A battle of terrible form and fearsome nature ensued between the two.
Then Vikarṇa, the scorcher of enemies, [assailed] Nakula who was enraged in the fray.
Protecting the life of Bhīṣma, he pierced him with sixty arrows;
Nakula, too, was deeply pierced by your son, the archer.
A tumultuous battle, making the hair stand on end, then took place between the two of them.
With seventy-seven stone-tipped arrows, he pierced Vikarṇa.
There, those two tigers among men, the subduers of foes, struck one another for the sake of Bhīṣma, like two bulls in a cow-pen.
As Ghaṭotkaca, exerting himself in battle, was slaughtering your army,
the valiant Durmukha advanced toward him in the encounter for the sake of Bhīṣma.
Then, O King, the son of Hiḍimbā [attacked] Durmukha, the scorner of enemies.
Enraged, he struck him in the chest with ninety sharpened arrows;
and the heroic Durmukha, shouting joyfully at the head of the battle, pierced the son of Bhīmasena with sixty well-pointed shafts.
As Dhṛṣṭadyumna advanced in battle, desiring the slaughter of Bhīṣma,
the son of Hṛdika (Kṛtavarman) checked him, protecting Bhīṣma’s life. The Vārṣṇeya pierced the heroic son of Pṛṣata with five iron arrows.
Again, with fifty [arrows], he quickly struck him in the middle of the chest; "Stay! Stay! he cried out. Then the mighty-armed one struck that great car-warrior, the son of Pṛṣata.
In that very same way, O King, the son of Pṛṣata pierced the son of Hṛdika with nine sharp, whetted arrows, fletched with the feathers of herons.
A battle took place between those two in the great conflict for the sake of Bhīṣma.
Just as there was a mutual contest of superiority between Vṛtra and Mahendra,
so too Bhūriśravas quickly advanced against the mighty Bhīmasena as he approached Bhīṣma, crying out, "Stay! Stay!"
Then the son of Somadatta struck Bhīma in the middle of the chest with an exceedingly sharp iron shaft,
gold-feathered, in that encounter. With that arrow fixed in his breast, the powerful Bhīmasena shone resplendent.
O best of kings, just as in ancient times Krauñca was struck by the spear of Skanda,
so those two, enraged in battle, repeatedly hurled at one another arrows that shone like the sun and had been polished by smiths.
Bhīma, desiring the slaughter of Bhīṣma, fought the great car-warrior Saumadatti; likewise, Saumadatti, eager for victory over Bhīṣma, fought the Pāṇḍava.
Those two best of men, equal in speed, contended with one another in battle.
Vigilant in their efforts to strike and counter-strike, they fought in battle, O great king; the son of Bharadvāja checked Yudhiṣṭhira, who was surrounded by a vast army as he advanced toward Bhīṣma.

There, a terrible battle took place between those two lions among men. O King, O noble one, hearing the roar of Droṇa’s chariot, which resembled the thundering of a rain-cloud, the Prabhadrakas trembled.
O King, that vast army of the son of Pāṇḍu in battle was checked by Droṇa; though striving with effort, it did not move even a single step from its position.
Cekitāna, enraged in battle against Bhīṣma, O lord of men—
Citrasena, your son, checked the one of wrathful aspect;
for the sake of Bhīṣma, the valiant great chariot-warrior Citrasena fought Cekitāna to the best of his power, O Bhārata.
In the same manner, Cekitāna also fought against Citrasena;
that battle between those two was truly great in its display of prowess. Arjuna, however, was repeatedly held back by your son.
Having turned your son away, he crushed your army;
Duḥśāsana also resisted Pārtha with his utmost power,
O Bhārata, having resolved that no enemy should slay Bhīṣma.
"O Bhārata, as your son’s army was being slaughtered in battle, it was agitated here and there by the foremost of chariot-warriors. Saṃjaya said:
Then the hero, the great archer, possessing the prowess of an elephant in rut,
took up his great bow— the restrainer of elephants in rut—
and brandishing that preeminent bow, he put the great chariot-warriors to flight.
That great car-warrior,
felling the host of the Pāṇḍavas and filled with affection for them, plunged into the great army; and that valiant one, skilled in omens, observed signs on every side.
As he scorched the ranks, Droṇa addressed his son:
"This is that day, my dear, when the great car-warrior Pārtha,
desiring to slay Bhīṣma in battle, will exert the utmost effort."
My arrows leap forth, my bow seems to quiver;
my weapons enter into a state of readiness, and my mind dwells upon cruelty.
Though the quarters of the sky are tranquil, beasts and birds utter terrible cries.
Vultures are swooping low toward the army of the Bharatas;
the sun has lost its radiance, and all the quarters of the sky are red. The earth groans and trembles, and the mounts are neighing and stamping.
Kankas, vultures, and cranes cried out again and again,
while jackals with inauspicious howls portended a great danger; moreover,
a massive meteor fell from the center of the solar disc.
A headless torso and a club-like meteor stood obstructing the sun, and likewise a terrible halo appeared around both the moon and the sun,
foreboding a horrific danger and the dismemberment of kings.
And the deities stationed in the sanctuary of the lord of the Kauravas trembled,
laughed, danced, and wept;
the planets moved counter-clockwise around the ill-omened moon.
The blessed moon rose with its head turned downward,
and I perceive that the bodies of the lords of men have, as it were, lost their luster;
even those clad in armor within the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son do not shine.
On all sides of both armies, a great sound is heard—
the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva bow;
likewise, the tumultuous shouting of the monkey is also heard.
At the sound of whose tail the very vault of heaven seems to burst asunder—
Bībhatsu, taking his stand on Dhruva and employing supreme weapons in battle,
bypasses all other warriors in the fray and strikes at the Grandfather.
The hairs on my body stand on end and my mind seems to sink,
O mighty-armed one, upon reflecting on the encounter between Bhīṣma and Arjuna,
and especially that Pāñcāla prince of wicked heart who is skilled in deceit.
Placing him at the forefront in battle, Pārtha went to the field of combat against Bhīṣma.
And Bhīṣma had previously said, "I shall not slay Śikhaṇḍin;
for he was created as a woman by the Creator, and only by destiny did he later become a man."
Moreover, that great car-warrior Yājñaseni bears an inauspicious banner;
the son of the River (Bhīṣma) would not strike one who possesses such an inauspicious emblem.
As I reflect upon this, my wisdom fails me utterly.
Seeing the terrifying weapon raised in battle by the son of Pāṇḍu,
Pārtha himself then rushed against the elder of the Kurus in that very moment. Such was the wrath of Yudhiṣṭhira at the encounter between Bhīṣma and Arjuna.
And my fury with weapons will surely bring misfortune to the subjects.
The son of Pāṇḍu is high-minded, powerful, heroic, skilled in weapons, firm in his prowess, a long-distance shooter, possessed of steady arrows, and an expert in omens.
Invincible in battle even by the gods led by Indra,
powerful and wise, having conquered his afflictions, the best among warriors;
the son of Pāṇḍu is ever victorious in combat and possesses terrible weapons.
Avoiding his path, proceed quickly toward him who is firm in his vows.
Behold this slaughter that has arrived, O mighty-armed one—
the great and beautiful golden ornaments of the heroes.
Armors were shattered by straight-knotted arrows;
the tops of standards, javelins, and bows were cut to pieces;
and bright, sharp spears as well as gold-glittering pikes were broken.
And by the enraged Kirīṭin, the Vaijayantī banners of the nāgas were destroyed.
"This is not the time for those who depend on their sons to protect their lives;
go to heaven, setting glory and victory before you."
With his chariot, he crosses this most terrible and difficult-to-traverse river of battle, which swirls with horses,
elephants, and chariots; for he who bears the monkey-banner previously heard [the truth] from me through my formidable ascetic power.

Phālguna practices great asceticism through the life of celibacy; that penance has borne fruit here for Savyasācin during his stay at Kairāta. He has practiced devotion to the Brahmins, self-restraint, charity, and great austerity.
Right here is seen the king whose brothers are Dhanañjaya,
the mighty Bhīmasena, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
and for whom Vāsudeva of the Vṛṣṇi clan stands as his protector.
This wrath arising from that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
whose body has been consumed by ascetic heat— is now burning the Bhāratas.
There is Pārtha seen there, taking refuge in Vāsudeva.
Tearing apart all the armies of the Dhartarāṣṭras on every side,
this host is seen being agitated by Kirīṭin,
like the mouth of a great river filled with massive waves being churned by a leviathan.
"Oaths of 'Hāhā' and cries of 'Kilakila' are heard at the front of the army!
Go toward the heir of the Pañcālas; I shall go against Yudhiṣṭhira, for it is difficult to find an opening in the formation of that king of immeasurable splendor."
Resembling the belly of the ocean, it was surrounded on all sides by great car-warriors;
Sātyaki, Abhimanyu, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Vṛkodara,
and the twins protected the king, the lord of men.
Dark-complexioned like Upendra, tall as a great *śāla* tree,
he advances against the armies like a second Phalguna;
take up your supreme weapons and grasp another great bow.
Go to the side of the king and fight Vṛkodara!
For who would not wish for his beloved son to live for eternal years? Yet, placing the duty of a Kṣatriya before us, we therefore command you.
And this Bhīṣma also consumes the great army in battle;
O dear Sañjaya, in combat he is truly equal to Yama and Varuṇa.
Having thus instructed his son, the powerful Bhāradvāja fought the great king Dharmarāja in that great battle. Having heard these words of that high-souled Droṇa, [he acted accordingly].
Saṃjaya said:
Bhagadatta, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata; Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and Jayadratha the ruler of the Sindhus.
Citrasena, Vikarṇa, and the youthful Durmarṣaṇa—
these ten warriors of yours, joined by a vast army raised from various lands, fought against Bhīmasena.
O King, seeking great glory in battle for Bhīṣma,
Śalya struck Bhīmasena with nine arrows,
Kṛtavarman with three arrows, and Kṛpa with nine shafts.
O noble one, Citrasena, Vikarṇa, and Bhagadatta each struck Bhīmasena with ten broad-headed arrows;
and the ruler of the Sindhus struck him in the region of the collarbone with three shafts.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti each struck the Pāṇḍava with five arrows,
and Durmarṣaṇa struck him with twenty sharpened shafts.
O great king, he [the Pāṇḍava] [assailed] all of them individually as they shone forth.
The mighty Bhīmasena pierced with many arrows the heroic great-chariot warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s side, the preeminent heroes of all the world;
having struck Śalya with fifty shafts, he pierced Kṛtavarman with eight.
O Bhārata, he cut Kṛpa’s bow, with arrow fixed, in the middle;
then he pierced him, whose bow was broken, again with five arrows. He likewise struck both Vinda and Anuvinda with three arrows each.
Having pierced Durmarṣaṇa with twenty arrows, Citrasena with five,
Vikarṇa with ten shafts, and Jayadratha with five,
Bhīma roared joyfully, and then struck the ruler of the Sindhus again with three more.
Bhīma cut Droṇa’s bow with three arrows.
Then, taking up another bow, Gautama, the best of chariot-warriors,
being enraged, pierced Bhīma with ten sharpened shafts.
Pierced by many arrows like a great elephant by goads,
the mighty-armed and powerful Bhīmasena then became enraged and struck Gautama with numerous shafts in the battle.
Then he, whose splendor was like that of Kāla the Destroyer at the end of time, dispatched Saindhava’s horses and his charioteer to the world of death with three arrows.
Thereupon, that great car-warrior quickly leaped down from his chariot whose horses had been slain.
In that battle, O Bhārata, he discharged sharpened arrows at Bhīmasena;
Bhīma, however, O best of the Bharatas, cut the bow of that high-souled Saindhava in the middle with two broad-headed shafts.
With his bow severed, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
O King, he swiftly ascended the chariot of Citrasena. There, the Pāṇḍava performed a most wonderful feat in battle.
Having pierced the great car-warriors with his arrows and checked them, that great car-warrior deprived the ruler of the Sindhus of his chariot while all the world looked on;
Śalya could not at all endure Bhīmasena’s prowess.
Having aimed sharp arrows polished by smiths, he pierced Bhīma with seventy shafts and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
And Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and Bhagadatta, O Sire—
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, Citrasena,
Durmarṣaṇa, Vikarṇa, and the heroic King of the Sindhus—
those subduers of enemies quickly pierced Bhīma in the encounter for the sake of Śalya.
He, however, pierced them back with five arrows each;
he pierced Śalya with seventy, and again with ten arrows.
Having pierced him with nine, Śalya pierced him once more with five.

And with a broad-headed arrow, he deeply pierced his charioteer in a vital organ. Seeing Viśoka thus transfixed, the powerful Bhīmasena struck the King of Madra in the arms and chest with three arrows.

Likewise, he struck the other great archers with three straight-flying arrows each in that battle and roared like a lion. For those great archers, though striving with effort against the son of Pāṇḍu who was fierce in combat, [could not prevail].
With three arrows each, having sharp points, they struck him violently in his vital parts. Though deeply pierced, the great archer Bhīmasena did not waver,
like a mountain under torrents of water from raining clouds.
But the immensely powerful and highly illustrious Bhīmasena, overcome with rage,
pierced the lord of Madra deeply with three arrows;
and the highly illustrious one, having pierced Śalya deeply with nine arrows, [struck him again].
O King, he pierced Prāgjyotiṣa firmly with a hundred arrows in battle;
then, with a very sharp razor-headed shaft, he— acting with great manual skill— cut through the bow and arrow of the high-souled Sātvata.
Then, taking up another bow, Kṛtavarman struck Vṛkodara between the eyebrows with a steel shaft, O scorcher of foes;
the mighty-armed one shone with that feathered arrow fixed in his forehead.
O Great King, like the one-horned Ekaśṛṅga, the best of mountains;
then the mighty-armed Bhīma, filled with rage, having turned back all the great chariot-warriors with floods of arrows, stood firm and immovable like a mountain.
But Bhīma, having pierced Śalya with nine iron arrows in the battle,
struck Bhagadatta with three, Kṛtavarman with eight,
and each of the car-warriors beginning with Gautama with two arrows.
But they, O King, pierced him in that battle with sharpened arrows. Though thus afflicted on all sides by those great car-warriors,
he moved about free from pain, regarding them as equal to blades of grass.

And those best of chariot-warriors, remaining unperturbed, dispatched sharpened arrows at Bhīma by the hundreds and thousands. Then the great car-warrior Bhagadatta hurled a spear of great velocity at him.
In that battle, the heroic king of the Sindhus, the mighty-armed one, hurled a gold-staffed,
highly precious *tomara* and a *paṭṭiśa*;
and Kṛpa, O King, hurled a *śataghnī*, while Śalya discharged an arrow in the encounter.
Then those other great archers, with great force, dispatched five feathered arrows each toward Bhīmasena. Thereupon,
the mighty-armed Bhīma of terrible prowess became enraged.

In that battle, the hero pierced him with three straight-flying arrows each. And the son of the Wind-god, as if smiling, O Bhārata, split the lance hurled by Gautama into two pieces with a razor-edged arrow.

And that hero, with his chariot remaining unperturbed, cut down in battle with his arrows the silken banner sent by Hārdikya, which resembled a cluster of *tilaka* flowers; he also violently severed the *śataghnī* weapon hurled by the ruler of the Sindhus.
Bhīmasena, who delights in battle, [struck] with nine heron-feathered arrows;
that son of the Wind-god split the *tomara* in two with a razor-headed shaft,
and with three arrows he cut the *paṭṭiśa* weapon as if it were a sesame stalk.
That one of great strength shattered the *śataghnī* with nine heron-feathered arrows; having cut down the shaft discharged by the King of Madra,
he suddenly severed the spear hurled by Bhagadatta in the battle.
Then Bhīmasena, who delights in battle, severed each of those other terrible arrows with his own straight-knotted shafts— cutting each one into three—
and struck all those great bowmen with three arrows each.
Then, while that great battle was raging, Dhanañjaya,
seeing the great car-warrior Bhīma slaying his enemies in the conflict and fighting them with his arrows, proceeded there on his chariot.
But seeing those two high-souled Pāṇḍavas joined together there,
O bull among men, your warriors had no hope of victory.
Then Arjuna, indeed, engaged the great car-warrior Bhīṣma in battle.
Desiring the death of Bhīṣma and placing Śikhaṇḍin at his forefront,
O Bhārata, he assailed ten of your warriors in battle,
O King, who stood firm in the fray, fighting against Bhīma.
Then Bībhatsu (Arjuna) pierced them, desiring to do what was pleasing to Bhīma. Thereupon King Duryodhana urged Suśarman forward for the sake of slaying both Arjuna and Bhīmasena.
"O Suśarman, go quickly, surrounded by a flood of troops;
slay these two sons of Pāṇḍu, Dhanañjaya and Vṛkodara.
Having heard that command of his, the Trigarta king, the lord of Prasthala, [set out].
Having rushed in battle toward the two archers Bhīma and Arjuna,
[the enemy] surrounded them on all sides with many thousands of chariots;
then a battle commenced between Arjuna and his foes.
Saṃjaya said:
But Arjuna, in the battle, covered the great car-warrior Śalya— who was striving in the encounter— with straight-jointed arrows.
He pierced Suśarman and Kṛpa each with three arrows;
likewise in that battle, he struck the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa, Jayadratha the king of the Sindhus,
Citrasena, Vikarṇa, and Kṛtavarman.
O Indra among kings,
that great car-warrior, afflicting your army in battle, struck Durmarṣaṇa and the two Āvantyas— each one of them— with three arrows feathered with the plumes of herons and peacocks.

O Bhārata, Jayadratha, having pierced Pārtha in battle with his arrows, stood upon Citrasena’s chariot and swiftly struck Bhīma. And Śalya and Kṛpa, the best of chariot-warriors, [assailed] Jiṣṇu in the encounter.
They pierced the mighty-armed one in many places with arrows that strike the vital organs;
and Citrasena and your other sons, O lord of the people,
swiftly struck him in the encounter with five sharp arrows each.
O sire, they struck Arjuna and Bhīmasena in the battle.
There, those two sons of Kuntī, the best of chariot-warriors and bulls among the Bharatas,
oppressed the great army of the Trigartas in that encounter.
Suśarman also, having pierced Pārtha in battle with many iron shafts,
let out a powerful roar that made the vault of heaven resound.
And other heroic chariot-warriors [attacked] Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya.
They pierced him with sharp, straight-flying arrows, gold-feathered and keen.
But in the midst of those chariot-warriors, the two sons of Kuntī, the best of car-borne heroes,
shone with wonderful splendor as they sported upon their magnificent chariots.
Desiring flesh, like two lions of superior strength in the midst of cattle,
those two heroes cut the bows and arrows of the warriors in many ways in battle and struck off the heads of hundreds of men.
Many chariots were shattered and horses slain by the hundreds;
elephants together with their riders fell upon the earth in that great battle. Chariot-warriors and horsemen alike were slaughtered here and there.
O King, they were seen in many places writhing on all sides;
the earth was strewn with slain hosts of elephants and foot-soldiers, with slaughtered horses, and with chariots broken in many ways.
The earth was strewn with parasols shattered in many ways, with fallen banners, and with yak-tail fans having golden handles; it was covered,
O Bhārata, with discarded hooks and elephant housings.
The earth was strewn with bells and whips;
likewise, it was covered with crushed armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and blankets from the *rāṅkava* deer,
as well as with earrings variegated with jewels.
The earth was strewn here and there with discarded turbans and yak-tail fans, and with the sandalwood-smeared arms and thighs of those lords of men.
There we beheld the wonderful prowess of Pārtha in battle;
having warded off those heroes with his arrows, he struck down your army.
But your son, seeing that encounter between Bhīma and Arjuna, [was filled with anxiety].
In that great danger,
Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, Jayadratha the Saindhava,
and Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti approached the vicinity of Gāṅgeya’s chariot and arrived at the battle.
Then Bhīma, the great archer, and Phalguna, the great chariot-warrior,
violently assailed the terrible army of the Kauravas in battle.
Then, tens of thousands and hundreds of millions of peacock-feathered arrows [fell].
In that battle, they swiftly brought down [arrows] upon Dhanañjaya’s chariot;
then, having warded off those great car-warriors with a net of arrows,
Pārtha dispatched them from all sides in the encounter to their death.
But the great car-warrior Śalya, as if playing in the battle,
angrily struck Jṛṣṇu on the chest with straight-knotted broad-headed arrows.
Pārtha, having severed his bow and his hand-guard with five [arrows], [struck him further].
Then he pierced him violently in his vital organs with sharp arrows;
then, taking up another bow capable of bearing a great burden in battle,
the enraged lord of the Madras struck Jiṣṇu in the fray.

O great king, with three arrows he struck Vāsudeva, with five he struck Bhīmasena, and with nine he pierced him in the arms and chest. Then, O great king, Droṇa and the great car-warrior of Magadha [assailed him].
Commanded by Duryodhana, those two great car-warriors approached that place,
O great king, where Pārtha and Bhīmasena, the son of Pāṇḍu,
were slaughtering the vast army of the Kuru king.
But the youth Jayatsena, O bull of the Bharatas, pierced Bhīma of the terrible weapons with eight sharp arrows in that battle;
Bhīma, having pierced him with ten, struck him again with seven.
And with a broad-headed arrow, he struck down the king's charioteer from the seat of the chariot.
Then, with his horses wandering and galloping in every direction,
the King of Magadha was carried away while the entire army looked on.
But Droṇa, having found an opening, pierced Bhīmasena with sixty-five well-sharpened iron arrows. To him,
who was his teacher and like a father, Bhīma— priding himself on his prowess in battle— [responded] in the fray.
O Bhārata, he pierced him with nine broad-headed arrows and then with sixty more;
Arjuna, having pierced Suśarman with many iron shafts,
scattered that army of his as the wind disperses great clouds.
Then Bhīṣma, the king, the son of Subala, and Bṛhadbala,
filled with rage, rushed against Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya;
likewise did the heroic Pāṇḍavas and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata.
They rushed at Bhīṣma in battle, who was like Death with his mouth wide open. But Śikhaṇḍin, having encountered the grandfather of the Bharatas,
cast aside all fear and, filled with joy, charged at him who was firm in his vows.
The Pārthas, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, placing Śikhaṇḍin at their front,
fought Bhīṣma in battle, united with the Sṛñjayas. Likewise, all your men, placing the one of firm vows (Bhīṣma) at their front, [fought].
They fought in battle against the Pārthas, headed by Śikhaṇḍin;
then there commenced a battle between the Kauravas and the sons of Pāṇḍu, which brought great fear and was directed toward Bhīṣma’s victory.
O lord of the people, Bhīṣma was the stake for your men in that battle;
for there the game of dice proceeded, leading either to victory or its opposite.
Then, O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna urged on all the troops.
"Rush toward the son of Gaṅgā; do not fear, O best of men!
Hearing these words of the commander-in-chief, the army of the Pāṇḍavas quickly advanced against Bhīṣma alone in that great battle, casting away their very lives.
Bhīṣma too, the best of chariot-warriors, received that onrushing army,
O great king, as the vast ocean receives the shore.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Saṃjaya, how did Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, fight on the tenth day against the Pāṇḍavas of great heroism along with the Sṛñjayas?
And how did the Kurus resist the Pāṇḍavas in battle?
"Tell me of the great battle of Bhīṣma, who shines in combat.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Bhārata, hear how the Kurus fought together with the Pāṇḍavas."
I shall describe to you, as you listen, how that battle took place:
day after day, the multitudes of chariots belonging to your side were dispatched to the other world by Kiritin with his supreme weapons.

And Bhīṣma, the descendant of Kuru and victor in assemblies, acting according to his vow, constantly brought about the destruction of the Pārthas in battle. [The Pārthas beheld] that great car-warrior Bhīṣma fighting together with the Kurus.
Seeing Arjuna together with the Pāñcālya prince, the people were filled with doubt;
on that tenth day, during the encounter between Bhīṣma and Arjuna,
there occurred a most terrible and continuous destruction of the assembly.
In that battle, O King, Bhīṣma the son of Śāntanu— that scorcher of foes and master of supreme weapons— slew warriors by the tens of thousands and even more;
their names and lineages, O Ruler of the Earth, were almost unknown.

All those heroes, who never retreated, were slain there by Bhīṣma. Then, having scorched the Pāṇḍava army for ten days, the righteous-souled Bhīṣma, the scorcher of foes, became indifferent to his own life.
Seeking his own swift death in battle while facing his enemies, your father Devavrata, the mighty-armed one, reflected: "I must not slay these best of men who stand facing me in combat."
Standing nearby, O Great King, he spoke these words to the Pāṇḍava:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, of great wisdom and learned in all the scriptures,
listen, my son, to my words as I speak them— words that are righteous and lead to heaven."
"I am deeply weary, O dear one, of this body, O Bhārata.
Much time has passed for me while slaying very many living beings in battle.
Therefore, placing Pārtha at our head, as well as the Pañcālas and the Sṛñjayas—"
"If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, let an effort be made for my slaughter.
Having understood his intention, the Pāṇḍava, who perceives the truth,
prepared himself and advanced against Bhīṣma in battle along with the Sṛñjayas.
Then, O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Yudhiṣṭhira the Pāṇḍava, having heard those words of Bhīṣma, urged on their army:
"Rush forward! Fight! Conquer Bhīṣma in battle!"
Protected by Jishnu, who is true to his promise and the conqueror of enemies,
and also by this great archer, the son of Prishata, the commander of the army,
as well as Bhimasena, you will certainly be guarded in battle.
"O Sṛñjayas, you need have no fear at all of Bhīṣma in battle;
we shall certainly defeat Bhīṣma by placing Śikhaṇḍin at our head. Having promised "So be it," they placed Śikhaṇḍin at their front.
Having thus made that agreement, on the tenth day, the Pāṇḍavas—
intent upon the world of Brahmā and frantic with rage— set forth,
placing Śikhaṇḍin and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya at their head.
They exerted their utmost effort toward the felling of Bhīṣma. Then, commanded by your son, the lords of various realms,
possessed of great strength, set out with Droṇa and his son at the head of their armies.
And the powerful Duḥśāsana, together with all his brothers,
then protected Bhīṣma as he stood in the midst of the battle.
Then your heroic warriors, placing the one of firm vows at their head, [advanced].
They fought in battle against the Pārthas, headed by Śikhaṇḍin; and the one whose banner bears the monkey, accompanied by the Cedis and the Pañcālas,
advanced toward Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, placing Śikhaṇḍin at the forefront.
The grandson of Śini fought with the son of Droṇa; Dhṛṣṭaketu fought with the Paurava;
and Yudhāmanyu fought with Duryodhana and his ministers.
Virāṭa, however, together with his army, fought against Jayadratha and his host.
The scorcher of foes, Citrasena, assailed the heir of Vrddhakshatra— your son, who possessed wonderful arrows and a bow—
while Yudhishthira confronted the great archer, the King of Madra, together with his army.
Protected by Bhīmasena, he rushed against the elephant division—
the invincible, irresistible force, the best among all wielders of weapons—
and the Pāñcālya king, along with the Somakas, advanced resolutely toward Droṇa.

And the prince Bṛhadbala, the subduer of enemies whose banner bore a lion and whose standard was the Karṇikāra flower, went forth to meet the son of Subhadrā. And your sons advanced against Śikhaṇḍin and Dhananjaya, the son of Pāṇḍu.
Desirous of slaying him, they rushed together with the kings in battle.
During that most terrifying display of prowess by the two armies,
as the ranks charged forward, the earth trembled.
O Bhārata,
those divisions of your men and those of the enemy clashed against one another upon seeing the son of Śantanu in battle;
then, as they exerted themselves and rushed at each other, [the fray began].
A great sound arose in all directions, O Bhārata,
produced by the blare of conchs and kettledrums, the trumpeting of elephants,
and the lion-like roars of the troops; it became truly terrible.
And that splendor of all the lords of men, resembling the moon and the sun,
became lusterless upon the armlets and crowns of the heroes. And clouds of dust arose, enveloped by the lightnings of weapons.
A terrible roar of bows arose,
along with the sounds of arrows and conchs and the great clamor of kettledrums;
the din of chariots also joined together from both armies.
Crowded with multitudes of spears, javelins, and double-edged swords, and with floods of arrows,
the sky became as if devoid of light;
in that great battle, chariot-warriors and horses fell upon one another.
Elephants slew elephants, and foot-soldiers slew foot-soldiers;
that battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas was truly great,
O tiger among men, fought for the sake of Bhīṣma like two hawks over a piece of meat.
O Bhārata, a terrible encounter took place between those two in battle on the field of combat,
as they sought to conquer one another for the sake of slaying each other.
Sañjaya said:
O great king, the valiant Abhimanyu, joined by a vast army, fought against your son for the sake of Bhīṣma; meanwhile,
Duryodhana struck the son of Kṛṣṇa in battle with nine straight-knotted arrows.
Enraged in battle, he struck him again with three arrows;
then the son of Kṛṣṇa, filled with wrath, hurled at Duryodhana’s chariot a spear that was like the terrible sister of Death herself.
O lord of the people, as that spear of terrible form was suddenly descending,
your son, a great car-warrior, cut it in two with a razor-headed arrow.
Seeing that spear fallen, the son of Kṛṣṇa became exceedingly enraged.
He struck Duryodhana with three arrows in the arms and the chest; then again, O best of the Bharatas, he struck the impatient Duryodhana between the breasts with ten terrible shafts.
That battle, O Bhārata, became terrible and wonderful to behold; it produced delight in the spectators and was honored by all the kings,
for the sake of Bhīṣma’s death and Pārtha’s victory.
The two heroes, the son of Subhadrā and the bull among the Kurus, fought in battle.
Then the son of Droṇa, that bull among brahmins and scorcher of foes, being enraged, struck the impetuous Sātyaki in the chest with an iron shaft in the midst of the fray.

O Bhārata, the son of Śini, whose soul is immeasurable, also struck the preceptor’s son in all his vital parts with nine heron-feathered arrows. Aśvatthāman, however, struck Sātyaki in the battle with nine shafts.

Then, with thirty more arrows, he quickly struck him in the arms and chest. Deeply pierced by the son of Droṇa, that great archer, the highly illustrious Sātvata, struck the son of Droṇa in return with three arrows.

In that battle, Paurava, having assailed Dhṛṣṭaketu with arrows, pierced that great archer and mighty car-warrior in many places. Likewise, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭaketu [assailed] Paurava in the fight.
The exceedingly powerful [Paurava] pierced him with thirty sharpened arrows. But the great car-warrior Paurava, having cut through Dhṛṣṭaketu’s bow,
let out a mighty roar and pierced him with ten shafts.
Taking up another bow, O great king, he struck Paurava with seventy-three sharp, stone-tipped arrows. There,
those two great archers, both high-ranking mahārathas, stood firm.
They rained upon each other with a great shower of arrows;
having cut each other’s bows and slain each other’s horses, O Bhārata,
those two great car-warriors, deprived of their chariots, encountered one another for a sword-fight.
O King, grasping two variegated bull-hide shields adorned with a hundred moons, and two stainless swords of great luster marked with a hundred stars, the two of them rushed at one another.
Like two lions in a great forest intent on mating with a female,
they moved in various circles and in forward and backward motions,
both displaying their prowess and seeking one another.
Enraged, Paurava struck Dhṛṣṭaketu on the temple of his forehead with a great sword and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
The King of Cedi also [struck] Paurava, that bull among men, in the battle.
He struck him in the region of the collarbone with a great sword whose tip was sharp.
O Great King, having encountered one another in that great battle,
those two subduers of enemies fell down, struck by each other's force.

Then, O King, your son Jayatsena, having placed the Paurava upon his own chariot, carried him away from the field of battle. And in that encounter, the son of Mādrī, the scorcher of foes, [encountered] Dhṛṣṭaketu.
O King, the powerful Sahadeva carried him away from the battle.
Citrasena, having pierced Suśarman with nine swift arrows,
struck him again with sixty, and once more with nine shafts.
But Suśarman, enraged in battle, O lord of the people, pierced your son with ten sharp arrows each;
and Citrasena, O king, struck him with thirty straight-knotted shafts.
Enraged in battle, he struck him, and he in turn pierced him back,
O King, increasing Bhīṣma’s fame and honor in the encounter; meanwhile,
the son of Subhadrā fought against Prince Bṛhadbala.
Exerting his prowess for the sake of the son of Pṛthā against Bhīṣma in the field of battle,
the Lord of Kosala pierced the son of Arjuna with five iron arrows and struck him again with twenty straight-knotted shafts.
Having pierced Bṛhadbala with nine iron arrows, the son of Subhadrā could not make him waver in battle, though he struck him again and again; furthermore,
the son of Phalguna cut asunder the bow of the King of Kosala.
He struck him with thirty arrows feathered with heron plumes.
Taking up another bow, the prince Bṛhadbala,
enraged in battle, pierced the son of Phalguna with many arrows.
O scorcher of foes, O great king, a battle then took place between those two furious warriors, both skilled in diverse modes of combat for the sake of Bhīṣma,
just as it occurred between Maya and Vāsava in the war between the gods and the asuras.
Bhimasena, fighting against the elephant division, shone greatly,
like Śakra with the thunderbolt in hand as he splits the highest mountains.
Those mountain-like elephants were being slaughtered by Bhima.
They fell together upon the earth, making the ground resound;
for those serpents, as large as mountains and resembling heaps of crushed collyrium,
shone like scattered peaks once they had reached the earth.
The great archer Yudhiṣṭhira, having joined the battle, assailed the King of Madra,
who was protected by a vast army;
and the Lord of Madra, in turn, confronted the great car-warrior, the son of Dharma, in the encounter.
Enraged for the sake of Bhīṣma,
the powerful King of the Sindhus afflicted Virāṭa,
having pierced him with nine sharp, straight-knotted arrows, and then struck him again with thirty.

And Virāṭa, O great king, struck the ruler of the Sindhus in the center of his chest with thirty sharpened arrows at the head of the army; both were equipped with variegated bows and swords, and possessed wonderful armor, weapons, and banners.
Those two of variegated form, the Matsya and the Saindhava, trembled in that battle.
Droṇa, having encountered the son of the Pañcālas in the great fray,
created a vast multitude [of arrows] with his straight-jointed shafts.

Then, O great king, Droṇa, having severed the great bow of the son of Pṛṣata, pierced that son of Pṛṣata with fifty arrows. Taking up another bow, the son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of enemy heroes, [prepared for battle].
While Droṇa looked on in battle, he dispatched his arrows;
but having warded off those shafts with a multitude of his own arrows, that great car-warrior Droṇa loosed five arrows at the son of Drupada.
Enraged at him, O great king, the son of Pṛṣata, slayer of enemy heroes,
hurled in battle a mace resembling the staff of Yama at Droṇa.
As it came rushing suddenly, adorned with bands of gold—
In that battle, Droṇa warded it off with fifty arrows;
O King, severed in many pieces by the shafts released from Droṇa’s bow,
it fell shattered and pulverized upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing his mace destroyed, the son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of enemies,
hurled a beautiful spear made entirely of iron at Droṇa.
O Bhārata, Droṇa cut that spear apart in battle with nine arrows.
And he afflicted the great archer, the son of Pṛṣata, in the encounter.
Thus, O Great King, this great battle between Droṇa and the son of Pṛṣata took place;
it was terrible in form and fearsome, centered upon Bhīṣma.
Arjuna, having reached the son of Gaṅgā and afflicting him with sharpened arrows,
rushed at him as he stood prepared, like a rutting elephant in the forest.
And the powerful Bhagadatta advanced against that son of Pṛthā.
With his elephant, which was divided into three parts and blinded by rut, the one of great strength [attacked];
as that beast, resembling the elephant of great Indra, suddenly charged toward him,
Bībhatsu exerted the utmost effort and countered it.
Then the powerful King Bhagadatta, mounted upon his elephant,
checked Arjuna in battle with a shower of arrows;
but Arjuna [encountered] the silver-white elephant approaching in the fray.
In that great battle, he pierced Śikhaṇḍin with stainless, sharp iron arrows.
And the son of Kuntī urged him on, saying, "Go! Go!
O Great King, he said to him, "Attack Bhīṣma; slay him!"

Then, O King, descendant of Pāṇḍu and elder brother of the Pāṇḍavas, having left Prāgjyotiṣa, quickly proceeded toward the chariot of Drupada. Thereupon, O great king, Arjuna swiftly charged at Bhīṣma.
Placing Śikhaṇḍin at their head, the battle then commenced.
Then all those heroes of yours rushed impetuously against the Pāṇḍava in the fray, shouting aloud; it was like a marvel.
O lord of men, Arjuna scattered the various divisions of your sons like the wind disperses clouds in the sky at the proper time; meanwhile,
Śikhaṇḍin encountered the grandfather of the Bharatas.
With many arrows, he quickly and calmly covered them; Bhīṣma slew the Somakas and the followers of Pārtha in battle,
while that great car-warrior held back the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
With chariots for its fire-chamber, bows for its flames, swords, spears, and maces for its fuel,
and the great blaze of volleys of arrows, he consumed the kṣatriyas in battle,
just as a vast fire accompanied by the wind moves through dry undergrowth.
In that same manner, Bhīṣma also blazed forth, discharging divine weapons;
with sharp, gold-feathered arrows of straight joints,
the highly illustrious Bhīṣma made the quarters and intermediate directions resound.

O King, felling chariot-warriors and elephants along with their riders, he made the multitudes of chariots resemble groves of palm trees stripped of their crowns; O King, in that battle, he left the chariots, elephants, and horses devoid of men.
Then Bhīṣma, the best among all wielders of weapons,
drew his bow; O King, hearing the sound of his bowstring and palms, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt, the soldiers trembled on all sides.
O lord of men, for the arrows discharged from your father’s bow were indeed unfailing;
those shafts released from Bhīṣma’s bow did not merely stick in bodies. O King, he rendered chariots devoid of men, even those well-yoked with swift horses.
O Lord of the People, we see fourteen thousand of the Cedis, Kāśis, and Karūṣas being carried away like the wind—
renowned great car-warriors, sons of noble families, who have cast off their bodies.
Irreversible heroes with banners adorned in gold,
together with their horses, chariots, and elephants, having encountered Bhīṣma in battle,
went to the other world as if into Death himself with his mouth wide open.
O great king, there was not a single great car-warrior among the Somakas who,
having encountered Bhīṣma in battle, still set his heart on living;
for all those warriors in that fray were sent toward the city of the King of the Dead.
Seeing Bhīṣma’s prowess, the people thought they had been led away;
no great car-warrior advanced against him in battle,
except for the heroic son of Pāṇḍu, who has white horses and Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer.
And Śikhaṇḍin, the Pāñcālya of immeasurable energy, [attacked] in battle;
but Śikhaṇḍin, O bull of the Bharatas, having encountered Bhīṣma in the fray,
struck him with ten arrows each in that great conflict.
But the son of Gaṅgā, O Bhārata, with eyes blazing with anger, looked askance at Śikhaṇḍin as if consuming him,
while remembering his womanhood, O King, in the sight of all the world.
Bhīṣma did not strike him in battle, nor did he perceive him;
but Arjuna, O great king, addressed Śikhaṇḍin:
"Hasten, and quickly slay this grandfather."
"O hero, what is the use of your further speech? Slay the great car-warrior Bhīṣma!
For I do not see anyone else in Yudhiṣṭhira’s army who is capable of fighting the grandfather Bhīṣma in battle."
"Except for you, O tiger among men— I tell you this as the truth.
Thus addressed by Pārtha, O bull of the Bharatas,
Śikhaṇḍin quickly rushed toward the grandfather with various kinds of arrows.
Disregarding those arrows, your father Devavrata,
enraged in battle, checked the furious Arjuna with his shafts;
and in the same manner, that great car-warrior held back the entire army of the Pāṇḍavas.
O noble one, he dispatched them with sharp weapons in battle toward the other world.
Likewise, O King, the Pāṇḍavas, surrounded by a great army,
covered Bhīṣma as clouds shroud the sun.
Surrounded on all sides, O bull of the Bharatas, that descendant of Bharata consumed the heroes in battle like a blazing fire consuming a forest. There we beheld the wonderful prowess of your son.
Because he fought against Pārtha and protected the one of firm vows,
all the worlds were gratified by that deed of your high-souled son, the archer Duḥśāsana, in battle.
That he alone fought the Pārthas along with their followers in battle,
and that the Pāṇḍavas could not overcome that fierce warrior in combat;
that car-warriors were deprived of their chariots in battle by Duḥśāsana.
O Great King, riders and mighty elephants,
pierced by sharp arrows, fell to the surface of the earth;
likewise, other elephants, afflicted by arrows, fled in all directions.

Just as a fire, having reached its fuel, blazes with fierce and radiant flames, so did your son blaze forth, utterly consuming the Pāṇḍavas. Against that great minister of the Bharatas, the great car-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas—
No one at all dares to conquer him, nor even to advance against him in any way,
except for the son of Mahendra, the one with white horses who has Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer;
for that Vijaya Arjuna, O King, having defeated him in battle—
While the entire army looked on, he rushed toward Bhīṣma himself;
though defeated, your son, relying on the strength of Bhīṣma’s arms,
took heart again and again and fought with fierce valor in the battle.
And fighting Arjuna in battle, O King, he shone resplendent;
but Śikhaṇḍin, O King, pierced the Grandfather in battle with arrows whose touch was like thunderbolts and which were like the venom of serpents.
And they did not cause any pain to your father, O lord of men;
for the son of Gaṅgā (Bhīṣma) likewise struck down the arrows discharged by Śikhaṇḍin,
smiling as he then caught those shafts.
Just as a man afflicted by heat welcomes showers of water,
even so did the son of Gaṅgā receive the showers of arrows from Śikhaṇḍin.
O great king, the kṣatriyas beheld him in that terrible combat.
As Bhīṣma was consuming the armies of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
O Sire, your son then said to all the troops:
"Attack Phalguna from all sides with your chariots in this battle!"

"Bhīṣma, the knower of dharma, will protect you all in battle. Casting aside this great fear, fight against the Pāṇḍavas! Here stands Bhīṣma, protecting [the army] with his blazing palm-tree standard."
He is the refuge and the armor for all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle;
even the thirty gods, though fully exerted, are not able to withstand Bhīṣma—
how much less the sons of Pṛthā, who are but mortals of such limited strength?
"Therefore, O warriors, charge at Phalguna in battle! Today, O lords of the earth, I shall fight Phalguna with diligence in this conflict, supported on all sides by you who are prepared."
O King, having heard those words of your archer son,
the powerful great car-warriors prepared themselves against Arjuna—
those Videhas and Kalingas, together with the hosts of Dāśerakas.
In that great battle, the Niṣādas and Sauvīras rushed forward,
as did the Bāhlikas, the Daradas, the Mālavas of the east and north,
the Abhīṣāhas, the Śūrasenas, the Śibis, and the Vasātis.
The Śālvas, the Trigartas, and the Ambaṣṭhas, together with the Kekayas,
rushed at Pārtha in battle like moths into a fire; O Indra among kings, they were like locusts against the peerless Pārtha in combat.

O great king, Dhananjaya, having meditated upon and aimed all those divine weapons, that mighty warrior of great strength quickly consumed all those great car-warriors along with their armies by means of those high-velocity missiles.
Like a fire consuming moths with the heat of its arrows, Bībhatsu [Arjuna]—
that firm bowman discharging thousands of shafts—
made the Gāṇḍīva appear as if blazing in the sky.
Afflicted by those arrows, O great king, with their chariots and banners scattered,
the kings could not turn back against him whose banner bears the monkey; together with their standards,
the chariot-warriors fell, as did the horsemen along with their horses.
Elephants, along with their riders, were struck by the arrows of Kirīṭin;
then the earth was covered by the many fleeing forces of the kings from every side, released by the arms of Arjuna.
Then the mighty-armed Pārtha, having put the army to flight, dispatched arrows at Duḥśāsana in the encounter. Those iron-tipped shafts, having pierced your son Duḥśāsana, [entered the earth].
They all entered the earth like snakes entering an anthill.
Then he slew his horses and struck down his charioteer. And, O Lord, he deprived Vivimshati of his chariot with twenty arrows.
He struck him violently with five straight-knotted arrows;
having pierced Kṛpa, Śalya, and Vikarṇa with many iron shafts,
the son of Kuntī, borne by white steeds, deprived them all of their chariots.
Thus, O noble one, those five— Kṛpa, Śalya, Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, and likewise Vivimśati— were deprived of their chariots;
defeated in battle by Savyasācin, they fled away.
O King, having thus defeated the great car-warriors in the forenoon,
Pārtha blazed forth in battle like a smokeless fire;
likewise, with his shower of arrows, he was like the sun endowed with its rays.
O Great King, he also struck down other monarchs;
having turned those great car-warriors away with showers of arrows,
he set flowing in that battle a great river whose waters were blood.
In the midst of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies, O Bhārata,
elephants and throngs of chariots were slain in many ways by car-warriors; chariots were struck down by elephants, and elephants by horses and foot-soldiers.

In the midst of it, the bodies and heads of elephant-riders, horsemen, chariot-warriors, and foot-soldiers were being severed and fell in all directions. The battlefield, strewn with those wearing earrings and armlets, shone brilliantly.
With princes and great car-warriors fallen and being felled, and with foot-soldiers—
along with their horses and horsemen— seen cut down by chariot rims and trampled by elephants, [the field was strewn].
Multitudes of elephants, horses, and chariots fell on all sides;
and chariots lay shattered upon the ground, their wheels, yokes, and banners broken.
That field was drenched with the blood of the floods of elephants, horses, and chariots.
The battlefield, covered [with blood], shone like an autumn sky filled with crimson clouds.
Dogs, crows, vultures, and wolves, together with jackals and various deformed beasts and birds, let out cries upon finding their prey.
And winds of many kinds blew from all directions while the rākṣasas and bhūtas were visible and roaring;
and there were golden chains and costly banners.
Driven suddenly by the wind, they were seen smoking;
thousands of white umbrellas and great chariots with their banners were seen scattered by the hundreds and thousands.
And elephants, accompanied by banners and afflicted by arrows, fled in all directions;
and O lord of men, Kṣatriyas bearing maces, spears,
and bows were seen fallen everywhere upon the surface of the earth.
They were seen running everywhere in the battle.
Then, O great king, Bhīṣma, invoking a divine weapon,
rushed toward the son of Kuntī while all the archers looked on.
Śikhaṇḍin, clad in armor, rushed toward him as he exerted himself in battle;
then Bhīṣma withdrew that weapon which resembled fire.
At that very moment, however, the son of Kuntī, whose horses are white, [arrived].
Having deluded the Grandfather (Bhīṣma), he struck down your army.
Sañjaya said:
"When the armies had been thus arrayed, and the majority were following [the plan]..."
O Bhārata, all became intent upon reaching the world of Brahmā; for in that tumultuous fray, army did not clash with army,
chariots did not engage with chariot-warriors, nor did foot-soldiers fight with foot-soldiers.
Horses did not fight with horses, nor elephants with elephant-warriors;
O Great King, O Bhārata, they fought there like madmen. A great and terrible confusion arose between the two armies.
Thus, as men, elephants, and chariots were scattered on all sides in that most terrible slaughter,
no distinction remained.
Then, O Bhārata, Śalya, Kṛpa, and Citrasena—
Duḥśāsana and Vikarṇa, swiftly mounting their chariots,
those heroes in battle caused the bannered army of the Pāṇḍavas to tremble.
That army of the Pāṇḍavas was being slaughtered in the encounter by those high-souled warriors.
He found no protector at all, like a ship sinking in the water;
for just as the winter season cuts through the vital organs of cattle,
so did Bhīṣma cut through the vital organs of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
The Somakas together with the Sṛñjayas— all of them intoxicated by battle—
were utterly overwhelmed by the high-souled Pārtha; and many elephants, resembling mountains or clouds, were struck down in various ways from your army.
And those leaders of men were seen being crushed by Pārtha;
struck by thousands of arrows and iron shafts,
the great elephants fell here and there, uttering cries of distress.
The battlefield shone, covered with the bodies of the high-souled slain, adorned with their ornaments, and with heads still wearing earrings;
O King, in that most terrifying slaughter of the best of heroes.
While Bhīṣma was displaying his prowess in battle and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya was likewise valorous,
O King, seeing the grandfather exerting such power in the fray,
the Kauravas did not retreat, even though they held the world of Brahmā before them as their goal.
Desiring death in battle and making heaven their ultimate goal,
they advanced against the Pāṇḍavas in that slaughter of the best of heroes;
eager for victory, they marched upon the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
O great king, O lord of men, the heroic Pāṇḍavas, remembering the many various sufferings previously inflicted upon them by you and your sons,
have cast off all fear in battle and set their hearts on the world of Brahmā.
Your men and your sons fought joyfully against them.
Then the great car-warrior commander-in-chief spoke to his army in the midst of battle:
"O Somakas, together with the Sṛñjayas, charge at the son of Gaṅgā!"
Having heard the words of the commander-in-chief, the Somakas together with the Sṛñjayas rushed from all sides against the son of Gaṅgā with a shower of weapons.
Then, O King, your father, the son of Śantanu, being thus struck—

Overcome by indignation, he fought against the Sṛñjayas. O dear one, in former times, the wise Rāma had indeed bestowed upon that illustrious king the instruction in weapons which destroys the enemy's ranks.
Having mastered that training and having brought about the destruction of the enemy's forces,
the aged grandfather of the Kurus, Bhīṣma— the slayer of hostile heroes— slew ten thousand [enemies] day after day among the sons of Pṛthā.
When that tenth day arrived, O bull of the Bharatas,
Bhīṣma alone, in battle against the Matsyas and the Pañcālas,
having slain immeasurable elephants and horses, killed seven great car-warriors.
Having slain five thousand chariot-warriors and fourteen thousand men in that great battle, the Great-Grandfather likewise destroyed a thousand elephants and ten thousand horses.
O lord of the people, Śikhaṇḍin was struck down by your father through the power of his training.
Then, having thrown the army of all the kings into turmoil,
Virāṭa’s beloved brother, Śatānīka, was felled.
And having slain Śatānīka in battle, the powerful Bhīṣma,
O great king, struck down thousands of kings with broad-headed arrows.
Distressed in the fray, the warriors cried out for Dhanañjaya.

And whatever kings among the Pārthas advanced against Dhanañjaya, having encountered Bhīṣma, they went to the abode of Yama. Thus did Bhīṣma [envelop] the ten directions on all sides with nets of arrows.
Having passed beyond the army of the Pārthas, he stood at the head of the host.
Having performed that most great deed on that tenth day,
under the conjunction of Śuci and Śukra, during the *yāva-yava* [lunar] period.
Like clusters of arrows stretched and heated on a bowstring,
the army of Pārtha was brought to exhaustion by the multitudes of shafts released from Bhīṣma’s bow.
Standing between the two armies with his bow grasped,
O King, no monarchs at all were able even to look upon him;
he was like the sun scorching in the sky when it has reached the meridian in summer.
Just as Śakra scorched the army of the Daityas in battle, so did Bhīṣma scorch the sons of Pāṇḍu, O Bhārata. And beholding him thus exerting his prowess, Madhusūdana—
The son of Devakī, being well-pleased, said to Dhanañjaya:
"Here stands Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, positioned between the two armies.
Without slaying him by force, victory will not be yours."
"Be vigilant and steady him where this army is being shattered;
for no one else, O Lord, dares to withstand the arrows of Bhīṣma.
Then, at that moment, O King, the one whose banner bears the monkey was urged forward.
With his arrows, he shrouded Bhīṣma along with his standard, chariot,
and horses; and that bull among the leaders of the Kurus, in turn, scattered those multitudes of arrows discharged by the Pāṇḍava in many ways with his own volleys of shafts.
By him [were protected] the King of Pañcāla, the heroic Dhṛṣṭaketu,
Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
the twins, Cekitāna, and the five Kekayas.
O great king, Sātyaki, the son of Subhadrā, Ghaṭotkaca, the sons of Draupadī, Śikhaṇḍin, the heroic Kuntibhoja,
Suśarman, Virāṭa, and the mighty Pāṇḍaveyas [all advanced].
These and many others, tormented by Bhīṣma’s arrows and submerged in an ocean of grief, were rescued by Phalguna. Then Śikhaṇḍin, seizing his supreme weapon with speed, [rushed forward].
Protected by the Diademed One (Kiritin), he rushed toward Bhīṣma himself. Then, having slain all of his followers, the unvanquished Bībhatsu, who was skilled in the divisions of battle,
rushed toward Bhīṣma alone.
Sātyaki, Cekitāna, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, Virāṭa, Drupada, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
rushed toward Bhīṣma alone in battle, who was protected by that firm bowman.
Abhimanyu and the five sons of Draupadī,
with their great weapons raised, rushed toward Bhīṣma in battle;
all of them were firm bowmen who never fled from combat.
Those who had perfected their aim struck Bhīṣma in many ways with their shafts;
but having shaken off those multitudes of arrows released by the best of kings,
the undaunted-souled one plunged into the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having struck back at the arrows as if playing, the Grandfather Bhīṣma,
repeatedly smiling and recollecting Śikhaṇḍin’s femininity, did not aim his shafts at the Pāñcālya prince.
That great car-warrior slew seven chariots in Drupada’s army; then,
in an instant, a tumultuous roar arose from the Matsyas,
Pañcālas, and Cedis as they rushed toward him alone.
With multitudes of excellent horses and chariots, elephants,
and foot-soldiers, they shrouded that solitary Bhīṣma, the son of Bhāgīrathī, who was scorching his enemies in battle, just as clouds shroud the sun.
Then, in that battle between him and them, which was like the war between the gods and the asuras,
Kiritin (Arjuna) struck Bhishma, placing Shikhandin in front.
Sanjaya said:
Thus all those Pāṇḍavas, placing Śikhaṇḍin at their head,
surrounded Bhīṣma on all sides in battle and pierced him with most terrible *śataghnīs*, *paṭṭiśas*, and battle-axes.
O Bhārata, [they fought] on all sides with mallets, clubs, spears,
and slings, with gold-feathered arrows, javelins, iron pikes, and kampanas,
with iron shafts (nārācas), calf-toothed arrows (vatsadantas), and bhuśuṇḍīs.
All the Sṛñjayas together struck Bhīṣma in battle;
though his armor was shattered and he was then afflicted by many,
the son of Gaṅgā did not waver even as his vital organs were being pierced.
