With the blazing rays of his bow as its flames and the discharge of his weapons as its wind, with the rattling of his chariot-rims as its roar, he was a fire of the great rising of weapons; with his variegated bow as its great crest of fire, he had the destruction of heroes as his massive fuel.
Bhīṣma became like the fire at the end of an eon to his enemies;
having descended and emerged from amidst the throngs of chariots,
he was seen moving once again in the midst of the lords of men.
Then, having bypassed both the King of the Pañcālas and Dhṛṣṭaketu,
he rushed with speed into the midst of the Pāṇḍava army. Thereupon, [he encountered] Sātyaki, Bhīma, and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya.

With six arrows resembling the sun— possessing a terrible roar, great velocity, and capable of piercing the elephants of his enemies— he struck these six: Drupada, Virāṭa, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata.
Having warded off his sharp arrows, those great car-warriors afflicted Bhīṣma with ten shafts each by their might.
But Śikhaṇḍin, in that battle, released arrows at the one of great vows.
Those gold-feathered arrows, sharpened on stone, swiftly entered Bhīṣma.
Then the diadem-wearing Arjuna, filled with fury, advanced against Bhīṣma himself,
placing Śikhaṇḍin in front and cutting his bow asunder.
The great car-warriors—
Droṇa, Kṛtavarman, Jayadratha the ruler of the Sindhus,
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, and likewise Bhagadatta— could not endure the severing of Bhīṣma’s bow.
These seven great car-warriors, exceedingly enraged, rushed toward Kirīṭin; displaying supreme divine weapons,
they fell upon him in a fury, shrouding the Pāṇḍavas.
The sound of those rushing toward Phalguna was heard like the roar of the oceans overflowing at the end of a Yuga: "Kill! Bring him!
Seize him! Fight! And cut him down!"
Thus arose a tumultuous clamor toward Phalguna’s chariot.
Hearing that tumultuous noise, O bull of the Bharatas, the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas rushed forward, desiring to protect Phalguna.
Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, both Virāṭa and Drupada, the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca,
and Abhimanyu— these seven were enraged and overcome with fury.
Bearing variegated bows, they rushed forward in haste.
A tumultuous battle, hair-raising and fierce, broke out between them in that conflict,
O best of the Bharatas, like the battle between the gods and the Dānavas.
But Śikhaṇḍin, that best of chariot-warriors, being protected by Kirīṭin,
pierced Bhīṣma— who had his bow broken— with ten arrows in the combat;
he also struck his charioteer with ten and cut down his standard with one.
Then, in that battle, he severed [Bhīṣma’s] bow with a single arrow. Gāṅgeya took up another bow of greater speed,
but Phalguna cut that one down as well with three sharp broad-headed arrows.
Thus the enraged Pāṇḍava, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, repeatedly cut down every bow that Bhīṣma took up. With his bow shattered, he became furious and licked the corners of his mouth.
Enraged, he seized a spear capable of splitting even mountains;
filled with wrath, he hurled it toward Phalguna’s chariot and launched that firm dart,
which resembled the fangs of Yama.
Beholding it falling like a blazing thunderbolt,
the joy of the Pāṇḍavas took up five sharp bhalla-arrows;
with those five shafts, he cut that spear into five pieces.
O best of the Bharatas, that [mace], hurled by the strength of Bhīṣma’s arms, fell severed by the enraged Kirīṭin,
like a flash of lightning broken and fallen from a mass of clouds.
Seeing that spear shattered, the heroic Bhīṣma, filled with wrath and conqueror of enemy cities, reflected in battle with his intellect:
"I am capable of slaying all the Pāṇḍavas with a single bow."
"If Viṣvaksena, the one of great strength, were not their protector—
and it is my conviction that he is indeed unconquerable by all the worlds—
I would not fight with the Pāṇḍavas, relying upon two reasons."
Because the Pāṇḍavas were unslayable, and because Śikhaṇḍin was a woman,
[I did not strike him]. Previously, when my father married Kālī, being well-pleased,
he granted me the power to die at my own will as well as invincibility in battle.
"Therefore, I consider death to have arrived for myself at its appointed time. Having thus understood the resolve of Bhīṣma of immeasurable splendor,
the Ṛṣis and the Vasus, stationed in the sky, spoke to Bhīṣma.
"O hero, O great archer, that which you have resolved is very dear to us; therefore, carry it out, but turn your mind away from battle. At the conclusion of those words, an auspicious breeze arose.
It was fragrant, blowing in a favorable direction, and filled with speckled raindrops; divine drums resounded with great noise,
and a shower of flowers fell upon Bhīṣma, O King.
O King, no one heard those words as they were being spoken by them,
except for the mighty-armed Bhīṣma and myself, owing to the ascetic power of the sage;
and a great agitation arose among the gods, O lord of the people.
"He will fall from his chariot before Bhīṣma, who is beloved by all the worlds"— having heard these words of the hosts of gods, the high-minded Bhīṣma,
son of Śāntanu, did not advance against Bībhatsu.
O great king, being pierced by sharp arrows capable of penetrating all armor,
Śikhaṇḍin, filled with rage, struck the grandfather of the Bharatas in the chest with nine sharpened shafts.
Struck by him in that battle, Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus,
did not tremble, O great king, like a mountain during an earthquake.
Then Bībhatsu, laughing, drew his bow Gāṇḍīva.
He struck the son of Gaṅgā with twenty-five small arrows;
then Dhananjaya, acting with haste and filled with rage, struck him again with a hundred shafts in all his limbs and vital organs.
Thus, even while being struck violently by others in that great battle,
the great car-warrior Bhīṣma swiftly pierced them back with his arrows;
and Bhīṣma, whose prowess is truth, [cut down] the arrows released by them in the fray.
He warded them off with straight-knotted arrows;
yet those gold-feathered shafts, sharpened on stone, which the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin released in battle, caused him no pain.
Then the diadem-wearing Arjuna, filled with fury, advanced against Bhīṣma himself; placing Śikhaṇḍin in front, he cut off Bhīṣma’s bow.
Then, having pierced him with ten arrows, he severed his standard with one.
And with ten arrows, he made his charioteer tremble. Gāṅgeya took up another, more powerful bow;
but Bhīma struck that one down as well, splitting it into three pieces with three sharp broad-headed shafts.
In that great battle, in the mere twinkling of an eye, he cut down bow after bow;
thus did he sever very many of his bows in the fray. Thereupon, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, could no longer withstand Bībhatsu.
Then, while all the Kuru heroes were looking on, O Bhārata, he struck him with twenty-five small arrows. Having been deeply pierced, that great archer addressed Duḥśāsana.
"This Pārtha, the great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) of the Pāṇḍavas, enraged in battle,
is assailing me alone with many thousands of arrows in this conflict.
And he cannot be defeated in combat even by the wielder of the thunderbolt himself."

Even the heroes—the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas—united together would not be able to defeat me; how much less so extremely weak mortals? Nor am I capable of being defeated by all the great chariot-warriors combined.
"Except for Arjuna, [no one can stand] against those who are well-enraged; I tell you this truly.
While the two were thus conversing, Phalguna, placing Śikhaṇḍin in front, pierced Bhīṣma in the battle with sharpened arrows.
Then, smiling, he spoke again to Duḥśāsana,
who had been deeply pierced by the sharp arrows of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow—
arrows with sharpened tips whose touch was like the thunderbolt and lightning.
Released in an unbroken stream, these are not the arrows of Śikhaṇḍin;
piercing through firm armor and cutting into my vital organs,
they strike me like clubs— these are not the arrows of Śikhaṇḍin.
With a touch like the staff of Brahmā, possessing the speed of a thunderbolt and difficult to withstand, these arrows are rending my very life-breaths; they are not the arrows of Śikhaṇḍin,
but rather like enraged serpents, licking with their tongues and overflowing with virulent poison.
These arrows of Śikhaṇḍin pierce my vital organs; they are not the arrows of Śikhaṇḍin. Like messengers of Yama dispatched against me, they seem to destroy my very life-breaths.
They possess the touch of clubs and iron bars; these are not the arrows of Śikhaṇḍin.
"My limbs are being cut asunder like those of cattle in the month of Māgha;
these arrows belong to Arjuna, not to Śikhaṇḍin.
Indeed, even all other lords of men together could not cause me such pain."
"Except for the hero Jishnu, the wielder of the Gandiva bow who bears the ape upon his standard," so saying,
O Bharata, the son of Shantanu, as if wishing to consume the Pandava, hurled a flaming spear with blazing tips and flying sparks.
Having severed that [shield] of his into three pieces with three arrows,
he caused it to fall while all the Kuru heroes were looking on there, O Bhārata.
Then the son of Gaṅgā took up a shield adorned with gold.
Seeking either the sword or another [missile] for victory over Death himself,
he [Kṛṣṇa] shattered that shield of the armored warrior into a hundred pieces while he was still standing on his chariot; it was like a marvel.
Roaring loudly like a lion, he urged on his own troops:
"Rush toward the son of Gaṅgā! Let there not be even the slightest fear in you!
Then they [assailed him] from all sides with iron clubs, spears, and floods of arrows.
With spears, swords, and various other weapons, as well as calf-tooth-headed arrows and broad-headed shafts, they all rushed together against that single warrior;
then a terrible lion-roar arose from the Pāṇḍavas.
In the same way, O King, your sons, seeking victory for Bhīṣma,
rushed against that single warrior and let out lion-like roars;
there, a tumultuous battle took place between your men and the enemy.
On the tenth day, O Indra among kings, at the encounter of Bhīṣma and Arjuna,
there arose for a moment a whirlpool like that of the Gaṅgā in the ocean among the troops as they fought and struck one another.
At that time, the earth became impassable, drenched in blood; neither the level nor the uneven ground could be discerned at all. Having slain ten thousand warriors on that tenth day, he—
Bhīṣma stood firm in the battle even as his vital organs were being pierced;
then Pārtha Dhanañjaya, stationed at the head of that army,
drove back the host through the midst of the Kuru forces.
There we beheld the marvelous prowess of the Pāṇḍavas;
with their arrows, they put to flight all the followers of Bhīṣma. We were terrified of Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, who possesses white horses.
Afflicted by sharp weapons, let us flee from this great battle—
the Sauviras, Kitavas, Easterners, Westerners, Northerners, and Mālavas—
along with the five Pāṇḍavas and the archer Sātyaki.
Being pierced on all sides by sharp arrows from Dhṛṣṭadyumna and all the Pāñcālas led by the son of Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna), Droṇa, the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), Kṛpa,
Śalya, Kṛpa, and all the others were overwhelmed.
O King, in that great battle,
your warriors— the Abhīṣāhas, Śūrasenas, Śibis, Vasātis,
Śālvas, Trigartas, and Ambaṣṭhas, together with the Kekayas— abandoned Bhīṣma in the midst of the fray.
These twelve peoples, afflicted by arrows and tormented by wounds,
did not abandon Bhīṣma as he fought with the Diademed One (Arjuna) in battle;
then, many surrounded that single warrior on all sides.
Having driven back all the Kurus, he overwhelmed them with showers of arrows;
"Strike them down! Seize them! Pierce them!
And drag them away!"—such was the tumultuous roar, O King, directed toward Bhīṣma’s chariot.
Having struck him with showers of arrows by the hundreds and thousands,
there was not even a space the size of a finger on his limbs that remained unpierced;
thus, O Lord, was your father torn to pieces by those shafts.

With sharp-pointed arrows by Phalguna in battle, he fell from his chariot with his head facing east while but a small portion of the sun remained, as all your sons looked on. "Alas! Alas! cried the gods in heaven and the kings on every side.
As Bhīṣma was falling from his chariot, a truly great roar arose. Beholding that high-souled grandfather falling,
the hearts of all of us sank along with Bhīṣma.
That mighty-armed one fell, making the earth resound,
like the banner of Indra cast down— the emblem of all archers— yet,
though covered by a multitude of arrows, he did not even touch the ground.
As that great archer, a bull among men, lay upon a bed of arrows after falling from his chariot, a divine state entered him;
Parjanya poured down rain and the earth trembled.
As he was falling, O Bhārata, that hero beheld the sun shorn of its brilliance; regaining his consciousness after reflecting upon the time,
he heard a divine voice resounding from all sides in the sky.

"How will the high-souled son of Gaṅgā, the best among all wielders of weapons and a tiger among men, meet his end when the southern solstice has arrived? Having heard these words, the son of Gaṅgā replied, "I am standing ready."
And Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, though fallen upon the earth, maintained his life-breaths while awaiting the northern solstice;
and Gaṅgā, the daughter of Himavat, having understood his intention, [acted accordingly].
He indeed dispatched great ṛṣis there in the form of swans. Then those swift-swimming swans, inhabitants of Lake Mānasa,
arrived together to see Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus.
Where the grandfather, the best of men, lay upon his bed of arrows—
there those sages in the form of swans approached Bhīṣma and beheld the grandfather of the Kurus lying upon that bed of arrows.
Having seen that high-souled one, the son of Gaṅgā, the best of the Bharatas, and having circumambulated him from the right as they did the sun,
those wise men addressed one another and spoke there.
"Only the high-souled Bhīṣma shall pass away during the southern course of the sun.
Having spoken thus to the swans departing toward the southern direction,
O Bhārata, the one of great intelligence gazed after them and reflected.
The son of Śantanu said to them: "I shall not go under any circumstances while the sun has turned south; this is the resolve fixed in my mind. I shall go to my own place, which was mine from of old."
When the sun has turned northward, I tell you truly, O swans:
out of a longing for the northern solstice, I shall sustain my life-breaths;
for I am one who has attained mastery over the relinquishing of these breaths.
Therefore, desiring death during the northern course of the sun, I shall maintain my vital breaths;
and as for the boon granted to me by my high-souled father— that death should be at his own will— let that boon of his likewise be fulfilled.
"Then, when the time for my departure has arrived, I shall maintain my life-breaths.
Having spoken thus to those swans, he lay down upon his bed of arrows.
Thus fell Bhīṣma, of great prowess, like a peak of the Kurus.
The Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas let out lion-like roars when that great being,
the peerless among the Bharatas, had been slain;
yet your sons, O bull of the Bharatas, could not find any recourse.
Then a tumultuous confusion arose among the Kurus;
King Duryodhana and the others sighed and wept,
and for a long time they stood there in despair, their senses overwhelmed.
O great king, they were filled with anxiety and set their minds not on battle; seized as if by a paralysis of the thighs, the Pāṇḍavas did not charge forward,
now that the mighty Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu who was incapable of being slain, had been killed.
O King, those lords of the Kurus were then afflicted by suffering; O King, a most great destruction came upon the Kurus without ceasing. We, whose heroes have been slain, are mangled by sharp arrows.
"We do not know what must be done now that we have been utterly defeated by Savyasācin.
But the Pāṇḍavas, having secured victory and the supreme state in the hereafter,
all those heroes with arms like iron bars blew their great conch shells.
The Somakas and the Pañcālas rejoiced, O lord of men. Then, while thousands of trumpets were sounding, the exceedingly powerful Bhīmasena slapped his arms loudly and danced.
When the son of Gaṅgā had been struck down, the heroes of both armies laid aside their weapons and fell into deep reflection on all sides;
some cried out, others collapsed, and still others were overcome by a swoon.
Some censured the Kṣatriya order, while others honored Bhīṣma;
the Ṛṣis and the Pitṛs praised him of the great vows,
as did those who were the ancestors of the Bharatas.
Having resorted to yoga and the Great Upaniṣad,
the valiant and wise son of Śantanu remained there muttering prayers, awaiting his time.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How did the warriors fare then, Sañjaya, when they were deprived of Bhīṣma—
the mighty one who was like a god, who observed the vow of celibacy for the sake of his guru?
At that very moment, I considered the Kurus and the other kings already slain."
When Bhīṣma did not strike the son of Drupada out of compassion,
I consider that to be more painful than anything else could possibly be—
that today I have heard that my father has been slain by that evil-minded one.
"O Sañjaya, my heart must surely be made of stone,
since it does not shatter into a hundred pieces upon hearing that Bhīṣma has been slain;
again and again, I cannot bear that Devavrata has been killed in battle."
He who was formerly unslain by the son of Jamadagni even with celestial weapons—
he has now been slain by Śikhaṇḍin, the Pāñcāla son of Draupadī.
This occurred today in battle when Bhīṣma, though desiring victory, was struck down.
"Tell me, Sañjaya, what was done by that lion among men.
Sañjaya said:
"In the evening, he fell upon the earth, bringing despair to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
The aged grandfather of the Kurus, who had inspired the Pāñcālas with courage,
now lies upon a bed of arrows;
having fallen from his chariot, Bhīṣma has descended to the surface of the earth, no longer touching it.
"Alas! Alas!"—such was the tumultuous cry that arose from all beings when the boundary tree fell at the site of the Kurus' assembly. O King, fear entered the hearts of the kṣatriyas of both armies.
O lord of the people, seeing Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, with his armor and standard shattered,
the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas rallied around him;
the sky became shrouded in darkness, and the light of the sun vanished.

When Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, was slain—the umbrella and the support of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, and the refuge of archers—the earth itself resounded with a great roar. "He is the best among the knowers of Brahman; he is the ultimate goal of those who know Brahman."
Thus did all beings speak as the bull of the Bharatas lay there.
"In former times, having learned that his father Śantanu was afflicted by desire,
this bull among men made himself one whose vital seed was drawn up."
Thus, when Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu and the grandfather of the Bharatas, lay upon his bed of arrows, the Ṛṣis, together with the Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
gathered around that foremost of the Bharatas.
O Bhārata, your sons did not offer any response;
their faces were pale, they were shorn of their splendor, O Bhārata,
and they stood there ashamed, overcome with modesty, with their heads cast down.
And the Pāṇḍavas, having obtained victory and standing at the head of the battle,
all blew their great conchs adorned with nets of gold,
O sinless one, while the sounds of trumpets were being played most intensely.
O King, we beheld the mighty Bhīmasena,
the son of Kuntī, sporting in battle with great joy after having slain his enemies who were endowed with great strength.
A tumultuous confusion then seized the Kurus;
both Karṇa and Duryodhana sighed again and again when Bhīṣma, the bearer of the burden of the Kauravas, had thus fallen.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and everything broke out of all bounds. Seeing Bhīṣma fallen, your son Duḥśāsana, exerting the utmost speed, rushed toward Droṇa’s army.
Arriving in haste, surrounded by a great force, that tiger among men, a mighty chariot-warrior,
met with Duḥśāsana and urged him even more swiftly to inform Droṇa.
Dispatched by his brother, the hero, clad in armor with his own division,
set forth, that tiger among men, urging on his own army. Seeing him approaching, the Kurus surrounded him.
"O Great King, what indeed will he say to Duḥśāsana?
Then the Kaurava informed Droṇa that Bhīṣma had been slain.
Upon hearing that unpleasant news, Droṇa suddenly fell from his chariot.
Then, O noble one, having regained consciousness, the powerful Bhāradvāja restrained his own troops;
and seeing the Kurus turned back, the Pāṇḍavas likewise withdrew their own soldiers.
By means of messengers mounted on swift horses, they ordered a withdrawal.
When the armies had retreated in every direction through that succession of movements,
all the lords of men, having cast off their armor, approached Bhīṣma.
Then, having ceased from the battle, warriors by the hundreds of thousands approached that high-souled one, as the immortals approach Prajāpati.
Having reached Bhīṣma, that bull of the Bharatas, as he lay there, they...
Having offered their salutations, the Pāṇḍavas stood together with the Kurus. Then,
to the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus who were standing before him after having prostrated,
the righteous-souled Bhīṣma, son of Śāntanu, addressed them at that time.
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones; welcome to you, O great chariot-warriors! I am delighted by the sight of you, who are like the immortals.
Having thus greeted them, he spoke with his head bowed low.
"O Bhārata, seeing your sons standing at your side, my head hangs down excessively; let a pillow be provided. Having heard these words from Bhīṣma, the son of Bhagīrathī, [Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke].
Then the kings brought forward many excellent pillows, both thin and soft;
yet the Grandfather did not desire them.
And that tiger among men spoke to those kings as if laughing:
"O kings, these are not fitting for the beds of heroes. Then,
having looked upon that best of men, the Pāṇḍava Dhananjaya— the long-armed great chariot-warrior of all the worlds— he addressed him.
"O Dhananjaya, O mighty-armed one, let a pillow be given for this head of mine that hangs down—
whatever you deem appropriate here.
Having set aside his great bow and having saluted his grandfather, [he spoke].
With eyes filled with tears, he spoke these words:
"Command me, O best of the Kurus, O foremost of all wielders of weapons!
I am your servant, O invincible one; what shall I do for you, O Grandfather?"
The son of Śantanu said to him, "My head, dear one, hangs down;
O best of the Kurus, O Phalguna, provide a pillow for me.
O hero, quickly give me something suitable for this bed."
"For you, O Pārtha, O mighty-armed one, are the best among all archers;
you are a knower of the duty of the Kṣatriya and are endowed with the qualities of intelligence and goodness.
Phalguna, however, having said "So be it," was driven forward by his resolve.
Having taken up the Gāṇḍīva bow and his straight-knotted arrows,
and having paid homage to that high-souled one who is not the middlemost of the Bharatas,
he severed the head with three sharp, high-velocity shafts.
When his intention was understood by Savyasācin,
Bhīṣma— the best of the Bharatas, whose soul is dharma, and who knows the true essence of dharma and purpose— was satisfied.
Thus, when the pillow had been provided for Bhīṣma by Savyasācin, he rejoiced.
Bhīṣma, the best of the Bharatas and knower of the true essence of all duties and goals,
welcomed Dhanañjaya with the gift of that pillow.
Looking toward all the Bharatas, he spoke regarding the descendant of Bharata.
"O son of Kuntī, best among warriors, who increases the joy of your friends—
this gift provided for you by the Pāṇḍava while you were lying down is worthy of you.
Had you acted otherwise, I would have cursed you in my wrath."
"O mighty-armed one, it is even so; this is firmly established in the codes of dharma:
a Kṣatriya must indeed sleep upon a bed of arrows on the battlefield.
Having spoken thus to Bībhatsu, he addressed these words to them all.
"O kings and princes gathered here with the Pāṇḍava,
behold this pillow of mine prepared by the Pāṇḍava!
I shall lie upon this bed until the turning of the sun."

Those kings who shall cross over at that time will indeed behold me. When the sun, blazing with rays and possessing supreme splendor, goes by chariot to heat the worlds in the direction presided over by Vaiśravaṇa, [they shall see me].
"Then I shall give up my life, even though my friends are so dear to me.
O kings, let a trench be dug here around my dwelling;
covered thus by hundreds of arrows, I shall wait upon the Sun."
"Cease from battle, O kings, and cast aside your enmities! Then physicians skilled in extracting arrows approached,
equipped with all necessary instruments, proficient and well-trained.
Seeing them, the son of Jahnavī then spoke these words:
"Let the physicians be honored and dismissed, for they have received what was to be given;
since things stand thus, I have no further need for doctors here."
"Sirs, you are skilled physicians who constantly remove pain;
yet the son of Gaṅgā said, 'I have no need for physicians,
for I have attained the supreme state praised by the dharma of the Kṣatriyas.'"
"O protectors of the earth, this is not the dharma for me as I lie upon my bed of arrows.
O Indra among kings, honor these [sages] with garments, ornaments, and other gifts;
O lords of men, I am to be cremated at the end by these very arrows."
"Medical sciences remain ever effective in treating diseases.
Having heard those words of his, your son Duryodhana honored the physicians as was fitting and dismissed them.
Then those lords of various realms were filled with wonder,
beholding the supreme steadfastness in dharma of Bhīṣma of immeasurable splendor. Having then provided a pillow for your father, O lord of men, [he spoke].
All the Pāṇḍavas together with the Kuru great-chariot warriors approached the high-souled one as he lay upon his auspicious bed;
having saluted Bhīṣma, they then performed a circumambulation of him.
Having provided protection for Bhīṣma on all sides,
all those heroes, extremely distressed and drenched in blood, returned to their own camps at twilight, dwelling upon his thoughts as they prepared for rest.
Approaching the great car-warriors, the Pāṇḍavas, who were settled there, rejoicing,
and emboldened by the fall of Bhīṣma,
the Yādava spoke at that time to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
"By good fortune you are victorious, O Kauravya; by good fortune Bhīṣma has been struck down.
This great car-warrior was true to his promise and was incapable of being slain by humans, O Pārtha, nor even by the gods, for he had reached the further shore of all weapons and missiles."
"But having encountered you, who can destroy with a glance, he was consumed by your terrible eye.
Thus addressed, Dharmarāja replied to Janārdana:
"Through your grace there is victory; through your wrath there is defeat."

For you, O Kṛṣṇa, are our refuge and the granter of fearlessness to your devotees. Victory is no wonder for those who have you as their protector, O Keśava, for you are ever their savior in battle and always devoted to their welfare.
"In every way, it is my opinion that there is nothing surprising about having encountered you.
Thus addressed, Janārdana replied with a smile:
"O best of kings, these words are most appropriate for you alone."
Saṃjaya said:
"O great king, when the night had turned to dawn, all the kings—
the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras— approached the grandfather."
Having saluted that hero, the best of the Kurus, as he lay upon the hero’s bed, the kṣatriyas stood around that bull among kṣatriyas;
and the maidens [honored him] from all sides with sandalwood powder, parched grain, and garlands.
Having gone there by the thousands, women, children, the elderly, and common folk as spectators showered the son of Śāntanu;
they flocked toward the son of Śāntanu like living beings toward the dispeller of darkness.

Musical instruments were played, and courtesans, as well as actors and dancers, danced and sang before the aged grandfather of the Kurus. Having ceased from their battles and cast off their armor, they stood there.
Having laid aside their weapons, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas together sat beside the invincible Devavrata, the subduer of enemies,
affectionate toward one another as they had been of old, according to their seniority.
That assembly, crowded with hundreds of kings and graced by Bhīṣma,
shone like the radiant solar orb in the sky;
all the soldiers of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas sat waiting upon it.
And that assembly of kings, as they sat waiting upon the Grandfather,
shone like the gods waiting upon the Lord of Gods, the Grandfather.
But Bhīṣma, O bull of the Bharatas, restrained his agony through fortitude.
Pierced by various weapons and lying upon a bed of arrows,
scorched by those shafts and with a mind not at all joyful, he spoke:
"My body is tormented by arrows, and I am fainting from the heat of the darts."
"I desire water," he replied to those kings.
Then, O King, those kṣatriyas brought from all sides various kinds of food there, as well as jars of cool water.
Seeing that which had been brought forward, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, said:
"O dear one, today I am no longer able to enjoy any human pleasures whatsoever.
This water is not fit for me to drink, for indeed, I am no longer capable."
"Indeed, lying upon my bed of arrows among men, I remain waiting for the cessation of the moon and the sun, so that I may be consumed [by fire] for the sake of humans.
Having spoken thus, Bhīṣma, covered with hundreds of arrows, then said:
"O cowherds, I shall drink milk; I do not wish for cow dung.
With cow dung as hot as fire, I do not wish for cow dung.
Having spoken thus to all the kings with a dejected voice, the son of Śāntanu—
O Bhārata, he addressed the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya;
then the mighty-armed one, having approached and saluted his grandfather,
stood with palms joined in reverence and said, "What shall I do?"
O King, seeing that Pāṇḍava standing before him after he had offered his salutations, the righteous-souled Bhīṣma spoke joyfully to Dhanañjaya:
"This body of mine is burning; I am pierced through by these great arrows."
My vital organs are tormented and my mouth is parching;
O Arjuna, give me water to refresh this body.
O Lord of Cows, my cattle have perished while I was being oppressed by the bull-faced demons.
"I wish to drink the milk of cows that has not been defiled by other cattle;
for you, O great archer, are capable of giving me water according to the prescribed rite.
Having said, "So be it," the heroic Arjuna mounted his chariot.
Having firmly strung the Gāṇḍīva bow, he drew it back;
hearing the sound of his bowstring and palms, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt,
all living beings and all the kings were struck with terror.
Then, having circumambulated him by chariot, that best of chariot-warriors,
the highly illustrious one, fixed a blazing arrow and consecrated it with mantras over the best of the Bharatas, the foremost of all wielders of weapons, as he lay there.
Having joined it with the Parjanya weapon while all the world looked on,
Pārtha pierced the earth on the right side of Bhīṣma;
thereupon, a pure and auspicious stream of water welled up.
Then Pārtha, whose deeds and prowess were divine, gratified Bhīṣma— the bull among the Kurus— with a cool stream of water that was like nectar and possessed celestial fragrance and flavor.
By that deed of Pārtha, who was performing transformations like Śakra,
those lords of the earth were filled with the utmost amazement;
for they beheld that superhuman and wonderful feat of Bībhatsu.
The Kurus trembled like cows afflicted by the cold;
out of wonder, the kings on all sides waved their upper garments,
and a tumultuous roar arose everywhere from the sounds of conchs and drums.
O King, Śāṃtanava, being satisfied, spoke to Bībhatsu in the presence of all the heroic kings, as if honoring him:
"O mighty-armed joy of the Kauravas, this is not surprising in you."
"You were described by Nārada as an ancient seer of immeasurable luster;
as an associate of Vāsudeva, you will perform a great deed that even the Lord of the Gods,
together with the deities, certainly cannot accomplish."
Those who know the truth, O Pārtha, know you to be the destruction of all the kṣatriyas;
for among men on earth, you alone are the preeminent and foremost of bowmen. Just as humans are the best in the world and Garuḍa is the most excellent of birds, so are you.
The ocean is the best of bodies of water; the cow is the most excellent of quadrupeds; the sun is the foremost of luminous bodies; the Himavat is the best of mountains;
the Brāhmaṇa is the preeminent among all classes; and you, O wielder of the bow, are the greatest of archers.
Indeed, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not heed the words spoken to him as he was being exhorted by Vidura,
by Droṇa, by Rāma, and by Janārdana.
Again and again Sañjaya also said:
"For Duryodhana, his intellect overwhelmed and nearly unconscious, did not welcome my words."
"Slain, he shall indeed lie there for a long time,
having transgressed the scriptures and being overcome by one of terrible strength.
Having heard those words, the lord of the Kauravas—
Duryodhana became dejected in spirit.
Seeing him, the son of Śaṃtanu said to him:
"Understand this, O King; be free from anger."
"O Duryodhana, you have seen this which was produced by the wise Pārtha:
a stream of cool water, fragrant as nectar. There is no one else in this world who could be its creator."
The divine weapons of Agni, Varuṇa, Soma, Vāyu, and Viṣṇu;
those of Indra, Paśupati, Brahmā, Parameṣṭhin, and Prajāpati; and all the celestial weapons of Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Savitṛ.

In the entire world of men, Dhananjaya alone knows [this], or Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī; indeed, no one else knows it at all. O dear one, the Pāṇḍavas cannot be defeated in battle by any means whatsoever.
O King, since these deeds of that great-souled one are superhuman, let peace be made with that virtuous hero who shines in battle, O dear one, for he is skilled in combat.
"As long as the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa remains under his own control in the assembly of the Kurus,
so long, my dear son, let peace be made with the heroic Pārtha.
As long as your remaining army has not been destroyed by his straight-jointed arrows."
"Arjuna will destroy them all; therefore, my dear son, let peace be made while your brothers remain in the battle as survivors,
and while many kings still stand there, O King— let peace be concluded."

As long as Yudhiṣṭhira does not consume your army with his eyes blazing with anger, my dear son, you should indeed form an alliance. Nakula, Sahadeva, and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava [are still under his command].
As long as they do not destroy the warrior class, let peace be established; as long as they do not utterly annihilate the army, O Great King,
let brotherly affection with the Pāṇḍavas be pleasing to you, my dear.
"O dear one, let the war end right now; make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
O sinless one, may these words that I have spoken to you be pleasing to you;
I consider this to be for the welfare of both yourself and your lineage."
Abandoning your wrath, make peace with the sons of Pṛthā;
what has been accomplished by Phalguna is sufficient.
Let there be friendship among you until the end of Bhīṣma's life.
"O King, let there be a reconciliation; be gracious.
Let half of the kingdom be given to the Pāṇḍavas, and let the Dharmarāja rule Indraprastha."
O Indra among the Kauravas, do not be a betrayer of friends, for you are the lowest of kings; you shall attain an evil reputation.
From my passing away, let there be peace for all creatures.
Let the kings meet with joy,
O King: let the father go to his son, the nephew to his maternal uncle, and the brother to his brother.
If you do not accept these words of mine, which are appropriate for the occasion,
because you are possessed by delusion and lack understanding,
then you alone shall suffer in the end due to your state of greed.
And all you other rulers of the earth who have assembled here—
you shall all end with the end of Bhīṣma;
I utter these words of truth.
"Destined to depart, having abandoned dharma, artha, and kāma,
and deprived of sons, brothers, kinsmen, and relatives—
let this be known to you, O descendants of Kuru."
Having caused this speech to be heard by the descendant of Bharata in the midst of the kings out of friendship, the son of the River (Bhīṣma),
his vital organs tormented by the shafts, became silent.
Having restrained himself and his feelings,
and having heard words consistent with the Dharma and its purpose— beneficial and wholesome—
your son did not accept them, like one on the verge of death refusing medicine.
Saṃjaya said:
Then all those kings returned once more to their own abodes,
O great king, when Bhīṣma, the delighter of Śantanu, had become silent.
Having heard that Bhīṣma had been slain, Rādheya, that bull among men,
feeling a slight tremor of fear, approached him with haste.
He then beheld the high-souled one lying upon his bed of arrows.
Then Vṛṣa, his throat choked with tears, spoke to that hero who lay upon his bed of birth like the lord Kārttikeya with eyes closed:
"Bhīṣma! Bhīṣma! O mighty-armed one!"—so said he of great splendor.
Approaching him, the immensely radiant one fell at his feet and said to him:
"O best of the Kurus, I am Rādheya, who has always been devoted to you;
yet, though I am entirely innocent, I have been exceedingly hated by you."
Having heard that, the elder of the Kurus, his eyes suddenly clouded with tears,
slowly looked up and spoke these words with affection:
"Beholding the empty dwelling and having dismissed the guards..."
Like a father embracing his son, the son of Gaṅgā embraced him with one arm and said:
"Come, come to me, O you who act contrary! You are vying with me;
had you not approached me, it is certain that no good would have befallen you."
"You are the son of Kuntī, not the son of Rādhā; this was known to me through Nārada. Your father is not Adhiratha; you are born of the Sun, O mighty-armed one."
"There is no doubt that [this knowledge] came from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and Keśava;
nor do I harbor any hatred toward you, my dear, for I tell you the truth. However, I spoke harsh words because of the injury to my vital energy."
"It is my conviction that you hate the Pāṇḍavas without cause,
O son of the Sun, since you have been repeatedly addressed with harsh words by them;
it is because you were born through a violation of dharma that your intellect has become such as this."
Out of envy, she took refuge with the base and became hostile even toward those possessed of virtue;
for that reason, you were repeatedly addressed with harsh words by her in the assembly of the Kurus.
I know your prowess in battle, which is difficult for enemies to withstand.
Devotion to sacred knowledge, heroism, and the highest perfection in generosity—
there is no one among men equal to you, O god-like one. Yet,
perceiving the potential for a rift in our family, I have always spoken harshly to you.
In the science of archery, in the drawing of heavy loads, in swiftness, and likewise in the power of weapons,
you are the equal of Phalguna and the high-souled Krishna.
O Karna, having gone to Rājapura, by you alone as an archer—
For the sake of that Kuru king, kings were crushed in battle;
likewise, the powerful King Jarāsaṃdha, difficult to approach and boasting in combat,
was not your equal in war.
Devoted to the Brahmins and truthful in speech, he is like another sun in his splendor;
a divine child, unconquered in battle, and superior to all men on earth. Today, my anger toward you, which was previously harbored, has been removed.
Fate cannot be overcome by human effort.
O slayer of enemies, those heroic Pāṇḍavas are your uterine brothers;
O mighty-armed one, unite with them if you wish to do what is pleasing to me.
"O son of the Sun, let my enmity be brought to an end;
let all kings on earth be free from affliction today.
Karṇa said:

"O one of great wisdom, I know all this without a doubt, just as you say, O invincible one: I am the son of Kuntī, not born of a charioteer. However, I was cast aside by Kuntī and reared by a charioteer."
Having enjoyed the sovereignty of Duryodhana, I cannot bring myself to act falsely,
just as the son of Vasudeva, firm in his vows, acted toward the Pāṇḍava;
for both my wealth and my body, as well as my noble fame, [depend upon it].
O giver of abundant sacrificial fees, everything has been sacrificed by me for the sake of Duryodhana;
relying upon Suyodhana, I have constantly provoked the Pāṇḍavas. Thus, for the sake of Duryodhana, I have followed the path of heroes.

"O Kaurava, let it not be that this disease and death shall befall the Kṣatriyas; yet that which is destined to happen cannot be turned back. Who would dare to turn back destiny by means of human effort?"
"O Grandfather, you have perceived and described in this assembly the omens foretelling the destruction of the earth;
and the Pāṇḍavas and Vāsudeva are known to me in every respect."

"Since they cannot be conquered by other men, we shall exert ourselves against them; it is my firm conviction that I shall defeat the Pāṇḍavas in battle. For this most terrible enmity cannot be cast aside."

"With my mind delighted by my own duty (*svadharma*), I shall fight against Dhanañjaya. O Grandfather, death from disease is unrighteous for a Kṣatriya; therefore, O Father, always grant me your permission with a joyful heart for battle."
"O hero, it is my thought that I may fight only with your permission. Whatever harsh words or contrary speech I have uttered out of agitation or impulsiveness,
and whatever offense I have committed, you ought to forgive all of that."
Bhīṣma said:
"If it is not possible to abandon this most terrible enmity, then I give you my permission, Karṇa; fight with the desire for heaven."
Free from resentment and devoid of agitation, perform the king’s duty according to your strength and according to your energy, conducting yourself in accordance with the conduct of the virtuous.
I grant you my permission; obtain whatever you desire.
"You will attain the worlds won by the dharma of the kṣatriya; of this there is no doubt.
Fight without egoism, relying upon your strength and heroism. For indeed, nothing other than battle exists for a kṣatriya that is more conducive to dharma."
"For a very long time, indeed, I have made every effort for peace;
yet it was not possible to achieve it. Where there is righteousness, there is victory. Sañjaya said:
Having thus addressed the son of Gaṅgā, and having saluted and propitiated him,
the son of Rādhā mounted his chariot and set out toward your son.
Whoever listens with devotion to this most wonderful Bhīṣma-parvan—
One is liberated from sins accumulated since birth; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this Bhīṣmaparvan, one should provide a hundred meals [to the Brahmins].
One shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrtha) as well as the fruit of all sacrifices.

Having given this gift on a festival day (parva) along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) such as gold and so forth, the attainment of concentrated fruits arises; there is no doubt in this matter. [It is equal to] a thousand horse-sacrifices (aśvamedha) and a hundred royal consecrations (rājasūya).
On the Bhīṣmaparvan, there shall be the fruit of giving away ten million cows for one who,
having heard this Bhīṣmaparvan, honors the reciter;
by him Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and likewise the Vasus [are honored].

All the sages and the ancestors, together with the sacred fires, are honored; when the reciting Brahmin is pleased, all the deities are pleased. That man shall obtain the fruit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Five thousand eight hundred and eighty-four verses were thus spoken by the wise Vyāsa. Whoever listens to the Bhīṣma Parvan, endowed with supreme faith, [attains great merit].
One is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin and certainly attains victory;
a householder should properly feed the Brahmins with garments, ornaments, cattle, and wealth,
and should indeed honor the reciter during the Bhīṣmaparvan.
